title: ‘Future generations will curse us for its loss’: can nothing save Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh’s masterpiece? | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Stratospheric costs could prevent the fire-damaged landmark from returning to its former glory. Now, unless a wealthy patron is found, the building seems destined for ‘soulless’ facade retention or ‘curated decay’
Author: Catherine Slessor
Headline: Stratospheric costs could prevent the fire-damaged landmark from returning to its former glory. Now, unless a wealthy patron is found, the building seems destined for ‘soulless’ facade retention or ‘curated decay’
Content: ‘A building of such national importance requires a national response’ … the Mackintosh building of the Glasgow School of Art in 2002, before the fires.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘A building of such national importance requires a national response’ … the Mackintosh building of the Glasgow School of Art in 2002, before the fires.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/the GuardianArchitecture‘Future generations will curse us for its loss’: can nothing save Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh’s masterpiece?Stratospheric costs could prevent the fire-damaged landmark from returning to its former glory. Now, unless a wealthy patron is found, the building seems destined for ‘soulless’ facade retention or ‘curated decay’Catherine SlessorFri 24 Jul 2026 11.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoubly destroyed by two fires, Scotland’s finest piece of architecture, the Mackintosh building at theGlasgow School of Art(GSA), cuts a lamentable sight.A 12-year saga ofdestruction, rebuilding andyet more destruction, all underscored by an unedifying seam of political and institutional wrangling, reached an apologetic conclusion of sorts, with therecent announcementthat Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s exquisite art nouveau creation is unlikely to be rebuilt in its original form because of stratospheric cost.The GSA said a full rebuild or “faithful reinstatement” of the burnt-out 1909 landmark, which, while still remaining a long-term ambition, would cost £265m, four times previous estimates and five times the GSA’s annual turnover.The school admitted that it could not afford this comprehensive reconstruction on its own, and outlined how it was moving forward by stabilising the building’s remaining shell and removing external scaffolding. The plastic shroud will also be removed, revealing the surviving stone walls. How things progress from there is still the subject of debate. The cost of the stabilisation work, though unconfirmed, is understood to have been covered by a recent settlement with insurers following arbitration.View image in fullscreenLike a vacuum-packed Christo sculpture … the Mackintosh building in 2024.Photograph: Wattie Cheung/the GuardianThe fate of a building considered Scotland’s equivalent of Gaudí’s epic Sagrada Familia in Barcelona or Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris still hangs precariously in the balance. But while Notre Dame,damaged by fire in 2019, was the subject of a concerted national rebuilding that allowed it toreopen five years later, Mackintosh’s masterpiece still languishes more than a decade on, and seems no closer to being restored as a working art school.Charles Rennie Mackintosh: architect of choice for Doctor Who and MadonnaRead moreProfessional bodies including the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland and the Royal Institute of British Architects have given a cautious welcome to the current interim strategy but said that “faithful reinstatement should remain everyone’s preferred outcome”.In a joint statement, they added: “We need leadership from the Scottish and UK governments to find the resources needed to ensure the faithful reinstatement of the Mackintosh building and to secure its future as a revitalised creative hub servingGlasgow, Scotland and the world. A building of such national importance requires a national response if future generations are not to curse us for its loss or mutilation.”Writing in the Architects’ Journal, Labour MSP for Glasgow Paul Sweeney echoed this call. Sweeney, who has long campaigned for full restoration of the building, argued that a joint venture partnership approach to rebuilding the Mac should now be considered. “It’s about the Scottish and UK governments putting their arms around the art school and trying to support the restoration as a national project,” he said.View image in fullscreenCatastrophic … the south facade of the Mackintosh building in July 2018, after a second fire caused extensive damage in June.Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/the GuardianBut in a cost of living crisis, riven with attendant political and cultural jeopardy, it’s highly doubtful whether such resources can or will be found. Time for a wealthy patron to sponsor the project of a lifetime?Others have been more critical. “The loss of the Mackintosh building would be catastrophic,” says architect and former GSA lecturer Gordon Gibb. “Even a partial rebuild, or a soulless facade retention with highlights, would result in the loss of our heritage and in the further diminution of Glasgow. If you do not rebuild it as it was imagined, you lose all of its integrity – and you do nothing more than celebrate the incompetence of its temporary custodians that led to its demise.”The entire sorry debacle began with a small fire breaking out at an end-of-year student show in 2014, when an aerosol canister of expanding foam placed near a hot projector caused flammable gases to ignite. It could and should have been contained, but Mackintosh’s arrangement of timber-lined voids and ducts contrived to spread the flames. Nonetheless, almost all of the building was saved, and a £35m restoration commenced. Weeks before its completion in 2018, the building was gutted by a second fire.View image in fullscreenDouble destruction … the 2018 fire.Photograph: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service/PACosily familiar to patrons of museum gift shops, it’s perhaps hard to envisage just how radical and unsettling Mackintosh’s art and architecture were in his day. A temperamental dandy who took his cue from movements in fin de siècle Europe – art nouveau, Japonism, symbolism – his oeuvre was a zinging riposte to the conventions of Victorian neoclassicism. “How absurd it is to see modern buildings made in imitation of Greek temples!” he fulminated in 1893. “We must clothe modern ideas in modern dress.”Mackintosh experienced extreme reversals of fortune. In 1900, his fame was such that during a trip to Vienna, “Toshie” and his wife, artist Margaret Macdonald, were feted as Caledonian heroes by the secessionist movement and cheered through the streets in a flower-decked cart. But the first world war sundered connections with Europe and a slow decline into poverty and obscurity ensued. By 1928, Mackintosh was dead of mouth cancer at 60, induced by his penchant for drinking and smoking, a grimly bohemian end to a fitfully stellar life.View image in fullscreen‘If you do not rebuild it as it was imagined, you lose all of its integrity’ … the interior basement level of the Mackintosh building in 2023.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAIf the Mac is not to be rebuilt as it was, there are precedents for a strategy of what might be described as “curated decay”, mixing new and old parts to relate the wider story of the building. Gutted by wartime bombing, Berlin’s neoclassicalNeues Museumlay in ruins for more than 40 years until an evocative scheme by David Chipperfield, abetted by conservative specialist Julian Harrap, transformed its fortunes. The city’s Reichstag building, remodelled by Norman Foster, retained graffiti scrawled by victorious Russian soldiers.Yet the glory of the Mac is the fact that it is all of a piece, from door handles to furniture, stained glass to light fittings, all minutely considered by Mackintosh as an exemplary Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art. Its double destruction has been a disaster, but, at present, its rebirth as a hugely costly phoenix from the flames feels as far away as it ever was.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureGlasgowGlasgow School of ArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone review – the self-serving narcissist ruins this documentary | Television | The Guardian
description: Just by his being there, the ex-prime minister undermines the honour of every brave fighter he meets in this tour of the war’s frontline. It should never have made it to TV
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Just by his being there, the ex-prime minister undermines the honour of every brave fighter he meets in this tour of the war’s frontline. It should never have made it to TV
Content: ‘Presented by a known liar’ … the host of Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill ZonePhotograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/Two Rivers Media/Soho Studios EntertainmentView image in fullscreen‘Presented by a known liar’ … the host of Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill ZonePhotograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/Two Rivers Media/Soho Studios EntertainmentTV reviewTelevisionReviewBoris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone review – the self-serving narcissist ruins this documentaryJust by his being there, the ex-prime minister undermines the honour of every brave fighter he meets in this tour of the war’s frontline. It should never have made it to TVLucy ManganFri 24 Jul 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is the caption viewers are presented with at the start of Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone, an hour-long documentary following the former prime minister on his journey to the frontline of the ongoing hostilities between Russia and its coveted neighbour:“This film presents Boris Johnson’s perspective on the conflict in Ukraine. The views expressed are subjective and reflect his own interpretations of events.”What is this? A disclaimer? Arse-covering by a company that saw the rushes and took fright? A reminder of the inherent bias in all accounts of history, in all stories? Or is it as blatant a warning as possible that what you are about to see is presented by a known liar, a shapeshifting, self-serving narcissist whose mask long ago ate the face? Did the first draft of the caption read “Yes, we know, he’s full of it” or “Regrets? We have a few”? Or perhaps just “Sorry”?From the moment it begins, you are beset by such questions instead of the ones Boris wants you to be thinking about (“Does Putin’s cruelty have any chance of success?”), as he interrupts the soldiers trying to explain their individual and national situation with his painful attempts at blokey camaraderie. He refers endlessly to their guns as “50 cal [calibre], right?”. He crows, “You shot the arse off that one!” He assures an army chaplain “I’ll pray for Ukraine’s victory all right!”Your own questions nag throughout. One which I suspect many people will be asking is: does putting a man who long ago ceded any kind of moral authority, a man whose reputation for untruth taints everything he touches, in charge of a documentary not instantly hole the entire endeavour below the waterline?View image in fullscreenA lot of questions … Boris Johnson journeys to the frontline of the Ukrainian / Russian war, deep into the area known as the kill zone.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/Two Rivers Media/Soho Studios EntertainmentI would say yes, and that the thing lists further and further with just about every contribution made by its ever-blustering presenter. Over the course of the hour, he turns it from serious undertaking to a new edition of the Boris Show, which most of us hoped had been cancelled for good after its increasingly shabby three-year run, 2019-22.Much dwelt on is the fact that he needs to remain incognito to keep himself and his companions safe. So he clumsily – such a natural clown! – puts on a balaclava. Then he gets his flak jacket on backwards, and even once it is fitted properly on him it rides up at the back so that he looks ridiculous. This could be sorted. This is not real, nags that background voice again. This is showmanship in a war zone.The dazzling rhetoric for which he was always so unjustly famed is on full, matte display here. When he and the crew spend their first night in an apartment at the edge of the kill zone, he is woken by the sound of bombs exploding nearby. “The truth is,” he says the next day, “if it had come through our window, we wouldn’t have known a thing about it, and there you go.” It really makes the endless suffering of the civilians and soldiers who have been under bombardment for the last four years live, you know? Sometimes it is combined with a faux modest heroism that grates even more than the blokey camaraderie. When they have to leave a street whose bomb damage they are inspecting with local troops because a drone is incoming, he assures us it is because “I don’t want to query the authority of a battalion commander. If he says we’ve gotta pull out, we’ve gotta pull out.” The careful elision to connote real emotion is really nicely done.Maybe he will make up for the fly-on-the-wall stuff with the film of Reflective Boris back in the studio? Surely then we will get some political analysis of the situation, how it came to be, how it might be solved, what options are open to national and international powers? “I just don’t think I’ve ever seen such a clear case of right and wrong … This thing has gotta stop and the west has just gotta snap out of its complacency … It’s wrong.” And there you go.At best, you might think it’s Alan Partridge Does Geopolitics. But then it ends with this caption: “It is widely acknowledged, including by Ukrainian officials, that Mr Johnson played a direct part in persuading Kyiv to abandon the Istanbul talks of spring 2022 – that were close to a settlement – in favour of continued fighting. He therefore has a share of responsibility for the resulting loss of life, Ukrainian, Russian and British alike.”And you realise that your worst take was right. This is not merely a shambolic programme shambolically presented. It is a programme on which the plug should have been pulled early, instead of gifted to a man who undermines the honour and dignity of every fierce, brave, homesick fighter he meets just by being there.Boris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone aired on Channel 5Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewBoris JohnsonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Scoff at cheaper bus fares and No 10 North if you like, but Andy Burnham knows what he’s doing | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Retail politics while taking power out of London: if this works, Burnham’s premiership could be seriously transformational, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Retail politics while taking power out of London: if this works, Burnham’s premiership could be seriously transformational, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Andy Burnham and Helen Godwin, Mayor for the West of England, pose with locals at a bus station in Bath, 22 July 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Helen Godwin, Mayor for the West of England, pose with locals at a bus station in Bath, 22 July 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/PAOpinionAndy BurnhamScoff at cheaper bus fares and No 10 North if you like, but Andy Burnham knows what he’s doingJonathan FreedlandRetail politics while taking power out of London: if this works, Burnham’s premiership could be seriously transformationalFri 24 Jul 2026 12.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.57 EDTShareOne of Andy Burnham’s first policy moves brought back a sharp memory. On Wednesday, heannouncedthat single bus fares across England would be capped at £2, starting from January. It was part of a series of small, practical measures designed, said the new prime minister, to offer a little “breathing space” to a hard-pressed public, but this was the one that registered with me most. That’s because it echoed the first time I ever experienced a specific public policy that I realised affected me directly.It was in the autumn of 1981 when the newly elected Greater London Council, led by Labour’s Ken Livingstone,slashed bus faresin the city. The headline-grabber was a new, short-hop fare of only 10p. I was 14 years old at the time, so for me it was even better: all child tickets were reduced to 5p. Theycalledthe scheme Fares Fair.It became a legal and political battle – Margaret Thatcher’s government objected to the extra local tax levied on Londoners to pay for it – and eventually Fares Fair was declared illegal and shut down. But I never forgot it and nor, I suspect, did many of the residents of the capital who would make Livingstone London’s first elected mayor nearly 20 years later.Fares Fair had what no one at the time called cut-through. It was a simple, clear offer to voters that had a direct, positive impact on their lives, one they would remember long after bigger, grander strategies had been lost to oblivion. It worked because politics is, in part, a retail business.Burnham’s first week as PM, and his tenure as mayor of Greater Manchester, suggest he understands that very well. Yes, there can be grand talk of ending a 40-year model of political centralisation and economic privatisation, but you also need to do something for voters that is immediate, tangible and uncomplicated. Everyone understands a lower energy bill or, indeed, a cheaper bus fare.Kemi Badenoch’sresponseto these first moves of Burnham’s was unintentionally revealing. They were too unambitious, the Conservative leader said, amounting to “small answers to big problems”. As she put it: “He is not the mayor of Manchester. These are mayor of Manchester ideas. Where is our prime minister?”0:59Andy Burnham opens No 10 North in Manchester – videoObviously, it’s daft to deliver a verdict on an administration a few days old, not least when Burnham has said that bigger decisions are coming, including a 10-year plan for the country to be unveiled in the autumn. But the language of her dismissal was telling, and not only because it confirms that she does not grasp the retail dimension of politics or its value.She associates such things with the municipal realm and therefore sees them as insufficient and unserious: they are mere “mayor of Manchester ideas”. It’s true that municipal leaders often do retail well. Several of them made their name that way – think Rudy Giuliani, before his disgrace, and his“broken windows”policing strategy that cracked down on relatively minor offences, whether a stolen bike or a snatched handbag. That’s in the nature of a local politician’s job. They’re closer to the ground than national governments, able to improve voters’ immediate circumstances directly. But Badenoch is wrong to see that as a weakness: for a politician, it’s a strength.For national leaders, envious of that municipal impact, there are two possible responses. One option is to think retail, even when operating on the largest scale. Harold Wilson named as hisgreatest achievementthe Open University, a simple idea that made higher education available to those who’d been denied it. Thatcher defined an era by allowing council house tenants the right to buy their homes. Or consider the ultimate retail offer – the guarantee of free medical care – in the form of what went on to become Britain’s most cherished institution, the National Health Service.The other option is for a government not to emulate the municipal so much as to empower it. This seems to be the animating project of Burnham government, embodied by his No 10 North plan to decentralise the running of the country. Opening the new site in Manchester on Friday, the PMdescribedit as “the best day of my life”.Burnham’s view is that the key to Britain’s future is allowing more and more places to repeat Manchester’s experience. As hewrotein the Guardian: “We built a city-region with twice the economic growth of anywhere else in the UK. What we did in Greater Manchester, we can do across the nation.” What Badenoch meant as an insult, Burnham regards as a badge of honour: these are indeed “mayor of Manchester ideas”.The core belief is that devolution, giving more powers to cities and regions, is Britain’s best shot at grabbing the prize that has proved so elusive for so long: economic growth. Anew paperfrom the Harvard Kennedy School and King’s College London, authored by Ed Balls and others, argues that Britain’s national productivity problem is a function of its “persistent regional productivity problem”, with the divide between the south-east and the rest leading to “productivity gaps wider than between east and west Germany”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt argues that Keir Starmer’s government talked a good game on devolution but didn’t match words with deeds – and says this has been the story of British governance for decades. The Harvard-Kings team did 95 hour-long interviews, including with 10 former prime ministers or chancellors, and found not only a Whitehall machine reluctant to let go, but politicians failing to act boldly enough, early enough. John Major, Tony Blair and George Osborne all spoke of their regret that they did not push regional growth from the start, when they had the political capital to do so.Regional mayors to take key roles in UK policy decisions as part of No 10 North plansRead moreThis time, it could be different. At long last there is, simultaneously, a devolution true believer in No 10 and allies in both No 11 and the key Whitehall department. As Balls puts it, the combination of Burnham, John Healey and Angela Rayner makes this “the best moment we have ever had on this agenda”.Badenoch is not the only one grumbling that Burnham’s opening days have offered small beer. Even some Labour voices have wondered when they will see the equivalent of Gordon Brown’s 1997 granting of independence to the Bank of England or windfall tax on the privatised utilities, both of which came in week one. That fails to take account of the obstacles that stand in Burnham’s path: he has to find many billions to fund increased spending on defence, social care and much else, and yet is hemmed in by a 2024 manifesto that blocks off the most obvious routes to raising the cash.But those grumbling may also be missing what is right in front of them. A rebalancing of British power is shaping up to be the big-ticket item of the Burnham government. If it works, it will unleash myriad policy moves as yet unimagined across the country, bringing the growth that is the prerequisite for all else. And, who knows, it might even improve the life of a teenager somehow and somewhere – one who will never forget it.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionKemi BadenochBus faresTransport policycommentShareReuse this content

title: Prince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Sacha Baron Cohen’s doofus voice of yoof has been making fresh mischief with new film Who Iz I? But who will he catch out this time? And what does his fictional hometown make of his return?
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Sacha Baron Cohen’s doofus voice of yoof has been making fresh mischief with new film Who Iz I? But who will he catch out this time? And what does his fictional hometown make of his return?
Content: ‘If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed, I iz here wif de hookup’ … Sacha Baron Cohen dressed as Ali G departs the Wimbledon tennis tournament where he attended the men’s singles final earlier this month.Photograph: Eleventh Hour Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed, I iz here wif de hookup’ … Sacha Baron Cohen dressed as Ali G departs the Wimbledon tennis tournament where he attended the men’s singles final earlier this month.Photograph: Eleventh Hour Photography/AlamyMoviesPrince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G filmSacha Baron Cohen’s doofus voice-of-yoof has been making fresh mischief with new film Who Iz I? But who will he catch out this time? And what does his fictional hometown make of his return?Catherine ShoardFri 24 Jul 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Wimbledon lawn tennis championships are not generally a hotbed of crime. Yet this year, unprecedented infringements ocurred. Eleven players were fined a total of £34,000 for “audible obscenities” and “racquet abuse”. Meanwhile, a spectator at the men’s singles final called a heckler a “bumbaclat” before inviting them to fight,badgeredPrince William to repay a drugs debt of £1,400 allegedly owed to him by Prince Harry from his days at Eton, and attempted to sell illegal substances to those seated near him – and beyond. “If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed,” he posted on Instagram, touting for business, “I iz here wif de hookup.”The culprit was Ali G, real name Alistair Leslie Graham, AKA the malapropism-dropping home counties wide boy played by Sacha Baron Cohen, kitted out for the occasion in trademark skullcap and gold chain, plus custom Wimbledon jacket, traditional crossed rackets replaced with cannabis leaves. Security released him without penalty, but thereprimandwas captured on scores of smartphones – including one held by Cohen himself.View image in fullscreenAli G at the tournament.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImageSuch footage is likely to find its way into a movie that will be released worldwide on 23 October and whoseexistence was only revealed four days before the Wimbledon incident. This week, a title was announced – Ali G: Who Iz I? – as well as the fact the film is to be the directorial debut of its star: a new development in the career of one of the UK’s most audacious, ambitious – and powerful – comedy actors, apparently taking greater agency over his projects as hisown political engagement intensifies. (The appalled reaction to his recent Netflix comedy Ladies First, which he neither wrote nor directed, suggests this is a sage move.)It also makes sense logistically: Ali G is a character who would energetically embrace selfie-mode shooting, which presumably streamlines a film crew considerably. Meanwhile the absence of a US theatrical release for the first Ali G film, 2002’s Indahouse, means targets in America would be easier to hoodwink.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueCohen first rose to fame as the tracksuit-wearing naïf and committed cultural appropriator in 1998, when Ali G was introduced as the “voice of the yoof” on Channel 4’s The 11 O’Clock Show. His own show followed in the early 2000s, constructed around interviews with unsuspecting subjects including Buzz Aldrin (whom he called Buzz Lightyear and asked if he was “ever jealous of Louis Armstrong”), Naomi Wolf (whom he complimented by telling her she’s attractive enough to be a sex worker) and Tony Benn. The late MP was outraged by the character’s dismissal of striking workers in 1984 as lazy skivers; Cohen later told Benn he was the only interviewee who had “dealt seriously with his loud, sexist, materialist image of youth”. (Benn’s letter of reply ended with the words: “You’re my main man.”)Although Cohen declared both Ali G andBorat– his Kazakh TV presenter and the star of a 2006 film that was a commercial and critical hit – retired in 2007, both have since returned. Borat was resurrected in 2020, forBorat Subsequent Moviefilm, intended by Baron Cohen as an intervention in the impending US presidential election. As with his 2018 seriesWho is America?, it secured a number of high-profile and highly-embarrassing scalps – most notably Rudy Giuliani, who was caught with his hand down his trousers in a hotel room with an actor pretending to be Borat’s 15-year-old daughter.Before his recent reappearance, Ali G was last seen presenting an award at the 2016 Oscars: a surprise even to the show’s producers, who understood Cohen would appear as himself. The ruse involved the star feigning food poisoning then locking himself and then-wife Isla Fisher in a disabled loo for 40 minutes to change into his costume.View image in fullscreenCritical approval … Borat Subsequent Moviefilm (2020).Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon StudiosWhile Ali G Indahouse was a scripted comedy concerning the character’s inadvertent role in the downfall of the government, indications are that its sequel will be closer to the more politically intentionalBoratfollowup, returning Ali G to his origins as an interviewer whose dubious views prompt his subjects to reveal their own.The film was shot in secret – as was 2009’s Brüno, in which Baron Cohen skewered the fashion industry – but some of the leaked locations in the UK and US give early clues as to whom Cohen may have had in his crosshairs.Last summer, there were sightings of the character in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire - home to the likes of David Cameron, Rebekah Brooks, Ellen DeGeneres and Jeremy Clarkson. The town was also, during the dates Ali G was spotted, playing host to US vice president JD Vance and his family, there to enjoy a Cotswolds holiday.Vance travelled with a considerable security detail, so it remains uncertain how close Cohen would have been able to get, had he been in pursuit.The Sun ran a photograph of the charactersporting a Rastafarian beret while filming at a nearby wildlife park in Burford. A source told the paper: “He was with a whole film crew and was in full character. He seemed very comfortable in the role. I was amazed, I thought to myself, ‘that’s Ali G’.”A crew member on the film to whom the Guardian spoke said an NDA prevented them from comment, but added: “I CAN tell you that it’s gonna be big. And packed full of laughs.”Ali G at the Oscars in 2016.Representatives for Kellie Bright, Charles Dance and Martin Freeman, all of who had roles in the original film, did not respond to enquiries, but the actor Adam Deacon confirmed he was not returning, “even though I would have loved to be a part of it”. He added that he could also do a “perfect” Borat accent so would be happy to be kept in mind for further films featuring that character too. “I’m a massive fan of what Sacha creates and I hope the new movie is a success.”In the first film, Deacon played a member of the East Staines Massiv, the rivals of Ali G’s less-than-intimidating gang from the other end of town. The Surrey commuter town wasscepticalabout the fame bestowed on it by the Ali G connection, and in 2010, a group spearheaded by the Spelthorne business forum lobbied the borough council to change the town’s name to Staines-upon-Thames inan attempt to add distance. The area, said Alex Tribick, chair of the forum at the time, “is really rather nice and it has some fantastic natural beauty around it”.He added: “Staines has had some adverse press further to that with it being portrayed as an urban wasteland off the end of the M25. The purpose of the exercise is to improve the image of Staines, rebrand it, and denote its greatest natural resource.”The then MP for Spelthorne, Kwasi Kwarteng, supported the move – which was duly voted through by the local council in 2011 – saying “if anyone knows anything about Staines, then one would know that Ali G is a million miles from it. It’s a very charming place actually.”Yet in his Thursdayvideoannouncing the title and release date, Ali G announces himself as “representing the westside of Staines-upon-Thames” – suggesting the area is unlikely to shake off the association any time soon.View image in fullscreenRepresenting for the West Staines Massiv in Ali G Indahouse (2002).Photograph: Film Four/AllstarHappily, the sitting Spelthorne MP, Lincoln Jopp, said he welcomed news of the return of the town’s prodigal son. “I can’t believe Ali G is coming back!” he said. “I loved Ali G Indahouse; it’s hilarious.Sacha Baron Cohenis a genius.”Jopp, who specified to the Guardian that his constituency includes the “West Staines Massiv”, added that the town was “a great place. We can take a bit of mickey-taking, trust me. Booyakasha!”Posts on local Facebook forums suggest resurgent grassroots support for the character putting the town on the map. “Oh happy days, loved the film,” wroteBlossom Welch, while longtime Staines resident Joanna Barlow added: “Loved Ali G not ashamed saw the show being filmed thought it was hilarious.”However one user,Bettafisheye, demurred, venturing that Ali Gis “like a bad smell that never leaves. I just say I’m from Laleham now. If u say Staines it’s like being around a constipated dog talking through there arse.”Explore more on these topicsFilmSacha Baron CohenPrince WilliamBoratBorat Subsequent MoviefilmfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Feeling lost without the World Cup? Six ways to survive the weekend | World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: What to watch on TV plus other ways to occupy your time now that the party is over
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: What to watch on TV plus other ways to occupy your time now that the party is over
Content: Lionel Messi shedding tears after Argentina lost to Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APView image in fullscreenLionel Messi shedding tears after Argentina lost to Spain in the 2026 World Cup final.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APWorld Cup 2026Feeling lost without the World Cup? Six ways to survive the weekendWhat to watch on TV plus other ways to occupy your time now that the party is overStuart HeritageFri 24 Jul 2026 10.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 2026World Cupis over, and the millions of people who enjoyed it now find themselves presented with a yawning chasm this weekend. In the UK alone, ITV and the BBC broadcast approximately 275 hours of live coverage over the duration of the tournament, and something that colossal will be hard to replace.But fear not. Just because the football is over, we are still brimming with things similarly designed to take our minds off the screaming hellpit that is the world around us. Here’s a guide, hope it helps.If you miss sportThe good news is that, while the World Cup is over, the Commonwealth Games have just begun in Glasgow with a wealth of sports to watch, including swimming, netball, boxing, gymnastics and bowls. The bad news, however, is that all of this will be crammed into a single hour of joyless highlights on Channel 5 at 10.30pm, because TNT bought the rights and you need a subscription to watch it.The same goes for the Tour de France, now that ITV’s 24 years of coverage has ended.If it’s normal, old-fashioned, free-to-air televised sport you’re after, you’ll have a harder time getting your fill. There’s a rugby league match on BBC Two this afternoon, and some cricket tomorrow, but other than that your best hope is to put ITV4 on today and just let its trickle of low-level sport wash over you. Highlights of Man Utd v Nottingham Forest from December 1979 at 6.20am. World rally highlights at 7.20am. Racing at Ascot at 9.30am. Then Formula E. To top it off, Sean Bean in Sharpe this afternoon and Tom Cruise, who gave the opening speech at the World Cup final, is back again in Top Gun at 10.05pm.That’s basically the same as the World Cup, isn’t it? Isn’t it?View image in fullscreenAfter declaring that ‘football is unity’ before a World Cup final that ended with the losing teamphysically attacking the winners, Tom Cruise is back on your screens on Saturday night in Top Gun.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIf you miss feeling part of something bigYou should really go and watch The Odyssey. Christopher Nolan’s epic film is breaking box office records left and right, with tickets in his preferred format (70mm Imax) genuinely hard to come by.And, quite honestly, it isn’t so different from the World Cup. It is loud and long and exciting. It offers no end of topics to get mock-angry about (where were the Phaeacians? What happened to all the sex? What was Nolan thinking, infusing Judeo-Christian themes of guilt into an ancient poem whose climactic solution is an orgy of violent vengeance?).Also, it is essentially the story of a man who, in the cold light of day, looks back at a period of intense tribalism with a sense of newfound regret, and if that isn’t the post-World Cup mood writ large, I don’t know what is.View image in fullscreenA strong attacking front three in the shape of Jimmy Gonzales (Cepheus, left), Matt Damon (Odysseus, centre) and Himesh Patel (Eurylochus) in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APIf you miss staying up latePerhaps you have simply grown accustomed in the UK to staying on American time, and that habit is proving hard to shift. If that’s the case, then you have some options to prolong your new nocturnal hours. If you’re a Netflix subscriber, then WWE SummerSlam starts at 11pm BST on 1 August and will run for several hours. Also, the San Diego Comic-Con starts tonight, and runs on California time, providing you with the chance to stay up all night refreshing social media in the hope that you get to see a cool new trailer in real time.Alternatively, the Delta Aquariid meteor shower is likely to peak on the night of 30 July. It isn’t guaranteed that you’ll see it from the UK, but it’s that or going to bed like a loser.If you miss hydration breaksGo and drink something. Urinary tract infections are no fun, especially at this time of year. And watch an advert while you’re at it, just for the full FIFA effect.If you miss all the speculationMost of the fun of the World Cup is all the second-guessing and conjecture that goes with it. Luckily, British political life is especially ripe for this exact thing at the moment. We have (another) new prime minister, providing us with endless potential for amateur punditry. Is Angela Rayner being played out of position? Has Ed Miliband still got the legs for international diplomacy? How many disappointing performances will it take before the country begins demanding yet another change of manager?View image in fullscreenAngela Rayner is back in the squad, but is the manager playing her in the right position?Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianEven better, the Clacton byelection is coming up, which is a great opportunity to get an office sweepstake going. Which of the 34 candidates will you draw? Binface? Farage? Baron Von Thunderclap? Abi Hookway from Channel 5’s Rich House Poor House? Woke Trump Carrzee? Laurence Fox? What excitement.If you specifically miss watching male football World Cups that are (mostly) hosted by the USThis is the best news of all. It was reported this week that Donald Trump wants America to host the 2038 World Cup. He would be in his fifth term as president by then, too. Joy upon joy.Explore more on these topicsWorld Cup 2026World CupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 13 surprising reasons you’re always dog tired – and what to do about it | Sleep | The Guardian
description: Feel lethargic even after a full night’s sleep? From not enough fibre to too much sitting, experts explain why your get up and go has got up and gone
Author: Laura Potter
Headline: Feel lethargic even after a full night’s sleep? From not enough fibre to too much sitting, experts explain why your get up and go has got up and gone
Content: Composite: Martin Gallagher/AlamyView image in fullscreenComposite: Martin Gallagher/AlamySleep13 surprising reasons you’re always dog tired – and what to do about itFeel lethargic even after a full night’s sleep? From not enough fibre to too much sitting, experts explain why your get up and go has got up and goneLaura PotterFri 24 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou need to open the windowThe very air you breathe could be an issue. “Close the door, shut the window, add a partner and a heater, and by 3am a typical bedroom sits at 1,500 to 2,500 parts per million of carbon dioxide,” says Dr Jemma King, author of Sleep First: Sleep Smarter, Think Sharper, Feel Better. “Research showsthat above 1,000 ppm sleep efficiency drops, deep sleep reduces and salivary cortisol rises on waking. You’re sleeping, but your nervous system is mildly activated all night.” Luckily, it’s an easy fix: open a window – even 2cm will do the job, according to King.Your creatine stores are lowThis supplement isn’t just for bodybuilders. What we think of as “energy” is a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP), produced by mitochondria. It stores and then delivers energy to cells. As you age, you have fewer mitochondria, so your body struggles to produce enough ATP.Creatine can help. “When creatine is combined with phosphagen (a compound linked to energy), you get phosphocreatine, which regenerates ATP,” says Justin Roberts,professor of nutritional physiology at Anglia Ruskin University.As well as older adults, research consistently shows benefits for regular exercisers, women, vegans and vegetarians (as creatine largely comes from meat and fish), says Roberts. Research shows supplementing can improvemental fatigueandreduce fatigue during exercise.In terms of sleep, in three separate studies people taking 5g daily showedimproved mood and cognitive functionafter a poor night’s sleep,slept for longerand experiencedimproved sleep quality. Look for micronised creatine monohydrate and take 3-5g daily to increase muscle stores of ATP over two to four weeks. You cycle creatine, so try taking it for six weeks, then come off it for two to four weeks, and repeat.You’re not getting outdoors enough“Emerging evidence suggests thatexposure to daylight improves our sleepandblood sugar control,” says Dr Brendan Gabriel, whose research at the University of Aberdeen focuses on metabolic biochemistry. It’s all down to our circadian rhythms. “We have a body clock in nearly every cell in our body,” says Gabriel. “One of the most important is the brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus, which is most responsive to daylight. Getting exposure to outdoor daylight helps our body distinguish between day and night, which can improve sleep quality.”You need to eat more fibreA massive96% of peoplein the UK don’t meet daily fibre recommendations of at least 30g. But a fibre-rich meal can help to slow the release of sugar into your bloodstream, giving you longer lasting, steadier energy, says Dr Emily Leeming, research fellow at King’s College London and author ofFibre Power: Transform Your Energy and Feel Amazing. She thinks we’re confused and discouraged by “a rather unfortunate PR run that fibre hasn’t been able to shake off. We think fibre is brown stodge.”Time for a fibre rebrand, then. She suggests we all add “the BGBGs to our diets – beans, greens, berries, grains and seeds – and nuts. Make those the foundation of your meal, then add other things.”View image in fullscreen‘Small shifts, like reading, sitting in nature or cuddling a pet, can help you rest properly’.Photograph: Getty Images/iStockphotoYou sleep but you don’t restGetting eight hours sleep but still exhausted? “We live in a world that equates our worth with productivity,” says Zahabiyah Yamasaki, author of Protect Your Energy. She believes we need to stop rushing when we don’t have to and start to “move at a slower pace, be intentional about commitments, and choose presence over productivity. That might mean closing your eyes rather than reaching for your phone, or sitting quietly looking out the window. Over time, these small shifts help make rest more accessible.” So nap, listen to a podcast, stretch, read, sit in nature, turn down a plan, cuddle your pet.You’ve sworn off smoothies and fruit juiceFoggy head? A lack of polyphenols could be to blame. “These antioxidants give pigment to fruits and vegetables – the deep purple of an aubergine, the redness of a strawberry,” says Leeming. We get most of ours from tea and coffee, but dark chocolate, black beans and herbs and spices are particularly concentrated sources, alongside berries.Leeming points to research showing polyphenol supplements help with oxygen and nutrient delivery to the brain, improvingreaction time and mental fatigue. But you don’t need to supplement, just eat the rainbow – or blitz it. “Asmall studygave people a 400ml smoothie containing blueberry, strawberry, raspberry and blackberry, or a placebo, and tracked them across a work day. The berry smoothie people maintained accuracy and response times throughout the day.”Sworn off smoothies or juice over sugar concerns? “Your blood sugar going up is a very normal response,” says Leeming. “It’s when it stays elevated out of range for a long time that it’s problematic – 150ml of fruit juice is a good source of polyphenols and is one of your five a day.” And include berries. “Blending fruit with seeds givesless of a blood sugar responsethan something like a banana.”You need a brain dumpWhile you sleep, your brain is putting in a shift. Dr Jemma King provides an analogy: “Imagine all the events that happen during the day get documented and put into a manila folder that’s stacked on the desk of your personal librarian, who works through the night, deciding what to keep and what to discard. Usually this happens smoothly, but sometimes folders need the boss to decide, and you’ll be woken at 3am with a burning thought that makes you feel stressed. The stress hormone cortisol has a half-life of at least 30 minutes, so if you engage with that thought, you have at least until 3.30am before your stress levels go back to a ‘sleep-permissive’ level.”Help your midnight librarian by spending a few minutes in the early evening creating a list of what you’ll address tomorrow. “Be sure to add times,” says King. “For example: call Sammy’s teachers at 10.30am; call my tax accountant at 11.15am.”You’re eating too lateIdeally you need to clear your plate by 7.30pm, especially on steak night. “Protein – particularly big chunks of meat – takes four to six hours to leave the stomach,” says King. “Fat slows it further, while digestion raises core body temperature and draws blood toward the gut, pushing against the nocturnal cooling trend needed for deep sleep.” This is why eating within three hours of bedtime decreases the quality of your sleep. “Your body doesn’t like digesting and repairing at the same time, and will opt to get rid of meat over replenishing maintenance.” Eat heavier protein and fat at lunchtime, and build evening meals around veggies, lighter protein such as fish, chicken or tofu, and plant-based carbohydrates.Your sluggish bowel is making you, well, sluggish“There is two-way communication between your gut and your brain via the vagus nerve, and 80-90% of that communication goes in the direction of gut to brain,” says Leeming. “If things are sluggish, that can make you feel lethargic because your gut is communicating back to your brain that things are not optimal.” According to one study, there’s an incredibly simple fix: eattwo kiwis a day(skins optional – the research was done without). “There are different types of fibre, and the particular type found in kiwis helps to draw water in to soften the stool and move it through.”You’re too focused on proteinProtein is definitely having a moment – the UK market for it is expected to be worth £643m by 2031. But sacrificing carbs to make way for more protein could be detrimental. As sports dietitian and personal trainer Kerri Major says: “If this puts carb intake too low for someone’s activity levels, it can impact energy.” As a general rule, for a steady energy releasing meal, half your plate should be made up of colourful veggies, a quarter carbs and a quarter protein, alongside some healthy fats.Your bed needs airingThere’s a reason you sleep soundly in those fresh hotel bedsheets. “Mite droppings, fragranced laundry powder and synthetic fibres can all trigger low-grade inflammatory responses, producing nocturnal congestion, itching and microarousals you don’t consciously remember,” says King. “People with house dust mite allergies are farlikelier to report insomnia.” Wash your bedding weekly using fragrance-free detergent, put dust mite covers on your mattress and pillows, and air your bed for 10 minutes in the morning.You’re sitting too muchOur ancestors spent their days hunting and gathering, rarely sitting, so from an evolutionary perspective, “long hours of being sedentary sends a message that something is wrong,” says King. “One theory suggests that in order to conserve energy to fight potential sickness and to promote sleeping to heal, our brains will make us feel sleepy, despite not actually being ill. It will also make us withdraw and isolate so we don’t infect the other tribe members.” Every 30 minutes, stand and move for two minutes. “A 10-minute walk after lunch lowers postprandial glucose and supports afternoon energy.”You need a blood testHas your GP ruled out iron or B12 deficiency, or thyroid problems, asks Dr Linia Patel, dietitian and author of Food for Menopause? Iron deficiency, she says, produces “a heavy, physical exhaustion and breathlessness on exertion, heart palpitations, pale skin and that frustrating inability to get through the day despite adequate sleep. It can also trigger restless legs, disrupting sleep further.”B12 deficiency fatigue “feels more neurological, so brain fog, poor concentration, low mood, tingling in the hands or feet, and a deep, bone-level weariness.” Thyroid problems, whether under or overactive, cause tiredness. “An underactive thyroid brings sluggishness, weight gain and feeling cold; an overactive one can cause anxious, wired exhaustion.” Request a blood test from your GP.Explore more on these topicsSleepHealth & wellbeingHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More than 200,000 people flee or lock down as wildfires sweep France and Spain | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: ‘Highly unpredictable’ blaze forces evacuation of Cap Ferret on French coast and Spain declares national emergency
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: ‘Highly unpredictable’ blaze forces evacuation of Cap Ferret on French coast and Spain declares national emergency
Content: 1:12Thousands evacuated in south of France as wildfire rages across pine forest – videoWildfiresMore than 200,000 people flee or lock down as wildfires sweep France and Spain‘Highly unpredictable’ blaze forces evacuation of Cap Ferret on French coast and Spain declares national emergencyJon Henleyin Paris andSam Jonesin MadridFri 24 Jul 2026 18.18 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 200,000 people have fled or been ordered to lock down as huge wildfires swept Spain andFranceon Friday, prompting Madrid to declare a national emergency and the French authorities to order the total evacuation, by land and sea, of one of the country’s best-known holiday spots.Authorities in south-west France ordered the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast to be evacuated “village by village” in the face of an “intense, highly unpredictable” wildfire that has burned through more than 19,000 hectares (47,000 acres) of forest.Spain’s government declared its first national emergency for a wildfire as two large blazes merged into one outside Madrid and a third was on the verge of joining them, amid searing heat and tinder-dry conditions across much of southernEurope.Both countries sought EU help. “This is the worst wildfire in our region’s history,” said Madrid’s regional leader, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, describing “an unprecedented situation: a perfect storm of extremely high temperatures and relentless winds”.View image in fullscreenA volunteer guides holidaymakers evacuated from Cap Ferret after they arrive by boat in Arcachon.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/GettyMore than 110,000 people had been evacuated in two days to escape the Cap Ferret fire, the Gironde prefecture said, including thousands of holidaymakers in campsites and rental homes.Boats ferried hundreds off piers on the peninsula on Friday as the blaze threatened to cut off the only access road.Scientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events,evaporating soilsand waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading tothousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate.About 800 firefighters and four water-bombing planes were battling the Gironde blaze north of Arcachon Bay, butthe fire, which began on Wednesdaynear the village of Saumos 25 miles (40km) west of Bordeaux, was not yet stabilised.Map of all the burnt areas near Arcachon Bay in the last 72 hoursNumerous roads in the area, including those leading to Cap Ferret, which contains many villas owned by celebrities and millionaires, were closed to all but essential traffic. Eighty houses had burned.“I’ve seen plenty of fires before, but never one of this intensity,” Jean Mazodier, 86, who owns 150 hectares of forest and was evacuated from his home at 6am, told Le Monde. “Everything’s burned. It’s like losing a child.”A second fire raging in the region, farther south near the popular holiday resort of Biscarrosse, had also burned through more than 2,500 hectares, the Landes prefect, Gilles Clavreul, said on Friday, and led to the evacuation of about 31,000 people.View image in fullscreenWildfire smoke shrouds the sky over Biscarrosse in an ash-grey haze.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA firefighter battles a wildfire spreading in Lège-Cap-Ferret in the Gironde.Photograph: SDIS33/Damien Rembert/EPAView image in fullscreenA firefighter battles flames in Cap Ferret.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersMore than 600 firefighters were struggling to contain that blaze, Clavreul said.“There are a great many new fire starts ahead of the main blaze. The situation is highly dynamic and unfavourable,” he added.In 2022, a wildfireburned more than 30,000 hectaresin France’s south-west, forcing 50,000 evacuations. In parched conditions and fanned by strong winds, the two latest blazes have torn through coastal pine forests with flames up to 10 metres (30ft) high.France’s president, ​Emmanuel Macron, said he had activated the EU’s civil protection mechanism as the country, which has endured three almost back-to-back heatwaves since May, battled numerous wildfires.“We will soon be able to count ‌on reinforcements from two Croatian aircraft, two Portuguese planes, as well as two heavy helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia,” Macron said.View image in fullscreenA helicopter drops water over a burning area as a wildfire flares up again in Pontevès, south-east France.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/GettyFrance’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Friday that 32 wildfires were burning, with 50,000 hectares scorched already so far this year – nearly four times the total by the same date last year.About 800 firefighters were battling a blaze in the south-eastern Var area, where weather conditions were improving, Nuñez said, allowing some firefighting resources to be redeployed to the south-west.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe severity of fires in the EU has broken records for the time of year, data from the European Forest Fire Information System shows.Spain’s government declared a national emergency on Thursday evening after wildfires ⁠threatened areas near the capital and in the neighbouring province of Ávila, leading to the evacuation or confinement of more than 63,000 people.A national emergency, which allows central government to assume overall control of powers and responsibilities that are usually the domain of Spain’s self-governing regions, has only been declared once before, during the countrywide blackout of April 2025.View image in fullscreenPeople spend the night at a sports centre after being evacuated from their homes in Cebreros, Ávila province.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APThe regional government of Madrid requested assistance, describing the situation as one of “extreme gravity”. It said at least four active fires could advance “beyond current extinguishing capacity”. The fires remained uncontained on Friday.Spanish authorities said on Friday afternoon there was “very little time left” before the blaze in Madrid, already made up of two merged fires, combined with the Ávila fire.On Friday night, Madrid’s regional environment minister, Carlos Novillo, said the fire had reached “a critical moment” and was “beyond our extinguishing capability”. He added: “The priority at the moment is protecting people, helping those who have been evacuated, and making the most of windows of opportunity.”José Cobos, who fled his home about 30 miles south-west of Madrid on Friday morning with his wife and three dogs, told Antena 3 television: “The smoke was incredibly thick. You couldn’t breathe.”Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, chaired an emergency response meeting at the Moncloa palace on Friday morning as the state meteorological office warned that the danger of more fires remained very high.View image in fullscreenSmoke plumes rise from wildfires near Madrid.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockHe said the government had deployed “all available resources”, adding: “It will be by your side during the emergency and the recovery.”The prime minister also thanked “all the emergency services that are fighting day and night”. Sánchez is due to visit the affected area on Saturday morning.On Friday morning, Spain’s environment ministry said 29 big forest fires had been recorded so far in 2026, compared with an annual average of nine between January and the end of July per year over the past decade. Forest fires had burned about 114,796 hectares, compared with 25,133 by the same time last year.Spain’s interior ministry has also requested fire-fighting aircraft through the EU’s civil protection mechanism, which aims to strengthen civil protection cooperation between EU countries and 10 additional participating states.Spain’s Guardia Civil force, which polices rural areas, said late on Friday that one man had been arrested and another was under investigation in connection with the forest fire in the Burgohondo municipality of Ávila. It said the two suspects had apparently ignored a ban on the use of heavy machinery, thereby creating “sparks … that may have caused the fire”.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresClimate crisisFranceSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Water bosses’ pay rises despite bonus ban and public fury over bills and pollution | Water industry | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Eight companies expect to be covered by the ban for 2025-26, the Guardian can reveal
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Exclusive: Eight companies expect to be covered by the ban for 2025-26, the Guardian can reveal
Content: South West Water’s Countess Wear sewage treatment works in Devon. Its sewer storm overflow has spilled in the past.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyView image in fullscreenSouth West Water’s Countess Wear sewage treatment works in Devon. Its sewer storm overflow has spilled in the past.Photograph: Graham Hunt/AlamyWater industryWater bosses’ pay rises despite bonus ban and public fury over bills and pollutionExclusive: Eight companies expect to be covered by the ban for 2025-26, the Guardian can revealJasper JollyFri 24 Jul 2026 13.09 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWater company bosses’ total pay rose over the past year despite a government bonus ban and public outrage over pollution and bills, the Guardian can reveal.One chief executive, Mark Thurston of Anglian Water, received £1.9m – including a £500,000 “retention payment”, despite the bonus ban.The biggest package went to Louise Beardmore, chief executive of United Utilities, who received £2.5m – £1.1m more than the previous year.Overall reported pay packets rose by 1.5% to £25.3m for chief executives and chief financial officers in the year, thanks to salary rises and the use of pay loopholes, according to analysis of the 14 companies that serve most ofEnglandand Wales.Withwater bills soaringand with Britain’s biggest water company, Thames, on thebrink of insolvencyand about 23 million people covered byhosepipe bansas drought status looms, the revelation sparked criticism of companies for allegedly finding ways to pay their bosses more, despite the bonus ban being introduced in 2025.The news will add to pressure on Andy Burnham to clamp down on the industry. Burnham has said hewants to exert “more public control” over the water industry, and has suggested he could move Thames into temporary government ownership after years of financial struggles and mismanagement.View image in fullscreenMark Thurston, chief executive of Anglian Water, received £1.9m, including a £500,000 ‘retention payment’.Photograph: Geoff Moore/Rex/ShutterstockAdrian Ramsay, a Green party MP, said: “The astronomical sums paid to water company executives are a perfect illustration of everything that is wrong with treating this essential public resource as a private commodity.“Andy Burnham must surely now reach the obvious conclusion that water should be brought back into public ownership, as the Green party would do, so that any money raised goes back into the system, not into shareholders’ pockets and excessive executive pay.”Water company pay has come under intense scrutiny in recent years because of persistent dumping of sewage into Britain’s rivers and seas. The utilities have been allowed to raise bills sharply to make belated investments in their leaking pipes, ageing treatment works and new reservoirs. Recent hot weather has added to the frustrations of customers.Eight companies said they expect to be covered by the bonus ban for 2025-26, with bans applied retrospectively to companies responsible for the most serious pollution incidents or financial failings.Yet despite the ban and heavy criticism, total pay for chief executives and chief financial officers reported by water companies was £25.3m for the year to the end of March, up from £24.9m the year before, according to analysis of company accounts. It is thesecond year in a row that executive pay has risendespite the bonus ban.In some cases the companies have given their bosses extra awards that they claim are not “performance-related payments”, or bonuses, which they argue means the cash is not covered by the ban.Anglian Water said it will be caught by the bonus ban, but still gave more to Thurston. The chief executive, who was Britain’s best-paid public servant when he ran thelate and hugely over-budget HS2rail project, received the bulk of his pay through Anglian’s parent company, including a £500,000 “retention payment”.Anglian, which provides water and sewerage services to nearly 7 million customers in the East of England, claimed the payment did not count as a bonus because it was not linked to the regulated water company’s performance. The company said the payout was funded by shareholders for work outside the regulated company, and it needed “targeted, time-limited retention arrangements to maintain leadership continuity”.Yorkshire Water said it was likely to be banned from paying bonuses, but its parent company, Kelda Holdings, paid another £600,000 to its chief executive, Nicola Shaw, on top of her fixed pay of £732,000. The regular payment – which Yorkshire has said is not related to the water company’s performance – was firstrevealed last year by the Guardian.View image in fullscreenNicola Shaw received remuneration from Kelda Holdings as well as Yorkshire Water.Composite: Graham Turner; Yui MokGary Carter, a national officer for the GMB union, which represents many water workers, said: “Finding ways round the bonus ban further tarnishes the reputations of private water companies. It makes them look like money-grabbing asset strippers who care more about lining their own pockets than providing fresh, clean water for the UK public.“Senior executive pay is out of control and the government needs to fundamentally overhaul the water companies – with more public control – to fix it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExecutive pay dropped at some of the companies covered by the ban, including Severn Trent, Southern Water and Northumbrian Water – although Northumbrian also made a £300,000 “retention payment” to its chief executive, Heidi Mottram. However, theHigh Pay Centre, which scrutinises executive pay, said the analysis raises questions over whether the government’s bonus ban has been effective in cutting pay for those companies who are responsible for serious pollution, or which have failed financially.Andrew Speke, the High Pay Centre’s interim director, said: “These figures show the government’s current measures have not gone far enough. Restricting bonuses makes little difference if executives continue to receive broadly the same overall level of pay through other forms of remuneration. The government could go further by introducing measures such as maximum pay ratios, but more fundamentally it needs to address the corporate governance model that has allowed these levels of executive pay to persist despite years of poor performance.“If Thames Water does come under public ownership or control, ministers should seize the opportunity to demonstrate a different approach to executive pay and corporate governance. Setting clear expectations that pay should reflect performance and the public interest would establish a benchmark for the rest of the sector and increase pressure on other water companies to follow suit.”The water company reports showed other ways used by water companies and their owners to reward executives. United Utilities does not expect to be banned from paying bonuses this year, but it still gave Beardmore a £435,000 “annual allowance” with no performance conditions, on top of a 16% increase in fixed pay to £971,000. The FTSE 100 company, which has 7.3million customers, said the money came from shareholders, and was required to retain its leaders.View image in fullscreenUnited Utilities gave Louise Beardmore a £435,000 ‘annual allowance’ with no performance conditions on top of a 16% rise in fixed pay to £971,000Wessex Water was also banned from paying bonuses. However, it granted its chief executive, Ruth Jefferson, a14% salary increase. Wessex said the higher salary better reflected the job’s responsibilities.The other companies that indicated they would be covered by the ban were Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water and Thames. Thames stillpaid £4.1m in bonuses to senior staffnot covered by the ban.The water regulator for England andWales, Ofwat, is not expected to confirm formally which companies are subject to the bonus ban until the autumn. However, the ban applies retrospectively to any company responsible for the most serious pollution incidents during that year, as well as those such as Thames Water which are failing financially.A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “We have banned undeserved bonuses for water company bosses. Any attempt to circumvent the rules is completely unacceptable.“We will leave no stone unturned in ensuring bonuses can only be paid where companies deliver environmental and customer outcomes and Ofwat’s review of the bonus rule will carefully consider if any requirements need to be tightened.”Water UK, which represents companies across country, declined to comment.The Guardian’s analysis included pay awarded to all people who held chief executive or chief financial officer roles during the respective years, including from parent companies where reported. Two companies did not disclose pay for chief financial officers.Explore more on these topicsWater industryExecutive pay and bonusesWaterEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Karim Khan ousted as prosecutor of international criminal court | International criminal court | The Guardian
description: Member states vote to remove British barrister after allegations of sexual abuse
Author: Harry Davies
Headline: Member states vote to remove British barrister after allegations of sexual abuse
Content: Karim Khan has repeatedly denied the allegations.Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersView image in fullscreenKarim Khan has repeatedly denied the allegations.Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersInternational criminal courtKarim Khan ousted as prosecutor of international criminal courtMember states vote to remove British barrister after allegations of sexual abuseHarry DaviesFri 24 Jul 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prosecutor of the international criminal court, Karim Khan, has been removed from office after the court’s governing body concluded in June that he had committed serious misconduct in connection to allegations of sexual abuse.The ICC’s member states voted on Friday to oust the British prosecutor in an unprecedented move that concludes a damaging episode for the court two years after the allegations were first raised.According to sources familiar with the result, 82 of the court’s 125 member states voted in favour of removing Khan at a special meeting at the UN’s headquarters in New York.ICC chief prosecutor Karim Khan suspended amid sexual misconduct inquiryRead moreThe vote follows a drawn-outdisciplinary processthat examined the abuse allegations, which were made by a woman who worked for Khan at the ICC.Khan has repeatedly denied all the allegations against him, which include claims that he engaged in coercive and non-consensual sexual behaviour over an extended period.His lawyers have criticised the disciplinary process as procedurally unfair. Responding to the vote, they said Khan would “challenge the lawfulness and fairness of the decision through all available legal mechanisms”.The prominent British barrister was elected in 2021 to serve a nine-year mandate running the court’s prosecution division, which is tasked with investigating and bringing to trial individuals accused of atrocities.During his tenure, Khan’s decisions to obtain arrest warrants for the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, raised the ICC’s profile and thrust it into the crosshairs of major powers.The warrants, issued by judges, are unaffected by his removal. However, the court’s prosecution division, which has about 400 staff, has been left bruised by a protracted scandal and convoluted process to resolve the matter.Last month, the executive committee of the ICC’s governing bodysuspended Khan after concludinghe had committed serious misconduct in connection to the sexual abuse claims, referring the outcome to member states for a decision on whether to permanently remove him.In a closed-door session on Friday, diplomats voted after reviewing the findings of the executive committee, alongside a fact-finding report by a UN watchdog and a legal analysis of its investigation by a panel of judges.Thirteen member states voted against removing Khan in the secret ballot, while 11 countries abstained.After the allegationsfirst emerged in 2024, Khan’s representatives have sought to suggest the claims may be part of a plot to discredit him in response to his 2024 decision to seek arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his then defence minister.In a report detailing the outcome of the disciplinary process against Khan, the ICC’s governing body found there was no evidence to support claims the woman was “being used by third parties, including intelligence agencies”.Last week, the staffer spoke out against claims she was some sort of “state agent”in an interviewwith CNN’s Christiane Amanpour. She said: “My complaint was because of what happened to me, not for any other reason.”Danya Chaikel, the International Federation for Human Rights’ representative to the ICC, said the vote was a testament to the complainant’s “extraordinary courage in coming forward, despite everything she risked in doing so”.Khan also faced sexual misconduct allegations from a second woman. Shecame forward to the Guardian last yearand accused Khan of mistreating her while she was working for him as an intern earlier in his career.Khan lawyers have previously said he categorically denies having “harassed or mistreated any individual”.In a statement, his lawyer Tayab Ali said: “Khan’s removal was determined by a process in which he was never given a fair opportunity to be heard.” He said the decision was “unsupported by any lawful or properly reasoned finding”.Khan’s dismissal comes as the court faces an array of pressures, includingrenewed threatsfrom the US. The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on several ICC judges and prosecutors andlast week vowedto “systematically disable the ICC’s ability to operate”.Senior officials at the court’s headquarters in The Hague do not expect the US government’s hostility towards the court to diminish with a change in prosecutor.Against this backdrop, the court must now appoint a new prosecutor. After Khan stepped aside last year pending an outcome to the disciplinary process, his two deputies took over the running of the court’s prosecution office.Prosecutors are elected by the ICC’s member states. Some in the prosecution division believe one of the deputies should take over, while others feel it needs a fresh start after two years of turmoil.Explore more on these topicsInternational criminal courtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Existing care workers could be exempt from UK’s tough new immigration rules  | Social care | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sector
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sector
Content: Ghanaian nurse Evans Sarbeng with resident Phyllis Padham at St Cecilia’s nursing home in Scarborough.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenGhanaian nurse Evans Sarbeng with resident Phyllis Padham at St Cecilia’s nursing home in Scarborough.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverSocial careExisting care workers could be exempt from UK’s tough new immigration rulesExclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sectorKiran StaceyandPatrick ButlerFri 24 Jul 2026 14.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands of care workers could be exempted from the home secretary’s plans to toughen up the immigration system under proposals being considered by Andy Burnham as he looks for ways to relieve pressure on the social care sector.The prime minister will give a speech next week spelling out his determination to start creating a National Care Service before the next general election as he looks to accelerate the process set up by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.In a highly personal speech, Burnham will talk about his experience of the care system through his father, Roy, who has Alzheimer’s, and announce that he is bringing forwardLouise Casey’s review into the sector, which was due to conclude in 2028.He is now also considering granting widespread exemptions from Shabana Mahmood’s plans to make it harder for people to achieve settled status in the UK.The measure is not likely to be included in next week’s speech but could come later in the year once theHome Officehas considered responses to a public consultation on the issue.One person briefed on the plans said: “Andy is determined to do something about the social care system, and quickly. This is highly personal for him, and he will talk about why he wants to push some of it through before the election, even if that comes at a political price.”Burnham has put reform of the social care system near the top of his list of priorities, having tried and failed to do so as health secretary more than 15 years ago.Hetold broadcastersthis week: “I think it’s about being prepared to grasp the nettle. I’ve got personal experience of the system. My dad has Alzheimer’s, and you see what the staff have to put up with. It’s not their fault. The system’s broken.”He added: “You can’t leave social care like this. And this is part of my criticism of Westminster. It has flinched over the years from these big decisions.”The prime minister has previously argued for replacing inheritance tax with a 10% levy on all estates once a person dies to pay directly for a universal care system, but those proposals were scrapped after the Conservatives labelled them a “death tax”.People inEnglandget state-funded care if they have less than £23,250 in assets, but those with more must pay the entire cost themselves.Meanwhile, social care providers say they are financially stretched and increasingly unable to provide the services for which they have been contracted given the low value of their contracts with local authorities.Many have complained bitterly about the likely impact of Mahmood’s plans to double the length of time it takes migrant workers to qualify for settled status, known as indefinite leave to remain, which could disproportionately affect the care sector.Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, the country’s biggest union, said: “Vulnerable people and those with complex needs won’t get the help they deserve unless ministers focus on recruitment and retention. That means dropping plans to push migrant care workers out of the UK.”Mahmood has said she will consider exemptions to the new ILR (indefinite leave to remain) rules, though carving out those on social care visas would make a significant dent in the numbers affected.The Home Officehas grantedabout 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more coming as their dependants.Burnham is understood to be considering exempting those already in the country from the changes but allowing them to be applied to new entrants.While the changes are not likely to be included in his speech next week, he is set to lay out some short-term fixes to alleviate the burden on the sector.They could include putting more money into the £9bn Better Care Fund, a ringfenced pot of money designed to be used to boost social care where doing so would relieve pressure on the NHS.One option he is understood to be looking at is increasing the fund to offer patients free short-term care once they leave hospital in an attempt to prevent them having to go back into acute care.The prime minister will also leave the door open to levying extra taxes to pay for a new system in the longer term, saying that funding options should be considered as part of Lady Casey’s review.My generation shouldn’t be scared of a care tax – we’re paying one already | Gaby HinsliffRead
