moreCasey was commissioned by the former health secretary Wes Streeting to publish an interim report this year and a final one in 2028 but those close to the process say she could now simply accelerate her final report instead.Burnhamtold the Guardianlast month he would like to see the review published by the end of the year, though sector experts said this is likely to prove overambitious.Casey has said the UK faces a “moment of reckoning” over its longstanding failure to match sufficient resources and action to the demands of growing numbers of frail elderly people and disabled adults.She has been scathing of the way patients with dementia or Alzheimer’s are undermined by institutional fights over whether a person qualifies for free NHS care or is means-tested and charged for social care, and smoothing the fault lines between the services is expected to be a key focus of the review.Casey will launch a public consultation in the next two weeks calling for a “challenging conversation” with the public this summer.Sources said she wants to answer a series of questions including who should qualify for social care, how far families should provide care for loved ones, and how far individuals should pay for care.Explore more on these topicsSocial careImmigration and asylumEnglandHome OfficeShabana MahmoodPublic services policyAlzheimer'snewsShareReuse title: US expands Iran attacks as Trump warns Tehran and Houthis over Red Sea strikes | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: No end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: No end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
Content: Smoke and flames rise after an explosion in Bandar Abbas in Iran’s Hormozgan province before dawn on Friday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke and flames rise after an explosion in Bandar Abbas in Iran’s Hormozgan province before dawn on Friday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranUS expands Iran attacks as Trump warns Tehran and Houthis over Red Sea strikesNo end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and KuwaitPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentFri 24 Jul 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has struck targets across Iran, reaching as far as the Caspian Sea, as Donald Trump threatened “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies inYemenfor extending the war to a second shipping ⁠chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea.As Iran retaliated on Friday with missile and drone fire against US bases and allies across the region, the New York Times reportedthat Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire proposaldelivered by the Iraq prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi. This despite the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claiming a day earlier that Iran was begging for a ceasefire. Iraq later disputed the report.Iran’s much improved missile systems pose a real threat to the USRead moreTrump warned China and Russia on Friday against selling weapons toIran, saying he believed assurances from Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin that they were not yet doing so. Iran said it was in consultations with both countries.On his Truth Social network, the US president wrote: “Therefore, two major Countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them – Certainly not in their best interests.”Iran’s military said it had launched drone strikes on Friday morning againstUS militarytargets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait as it appeared there was no end in sight to the fighting. It told civilians across the region to stay 500 metres away from locations where US troops were present.TheHouthis, who control northern and western Yemen, continued to claim a naval blockade on Saudi Arabian ports and ships using the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea.View image in fullscreenHouthi fighters take part in a pro-Iran rally in Sana’a, Yemen, in April.Photograph: Khaled Abdullah/ReutersThe Houthis insisted on Friday that only Saudi-linked trade was under blockade as ships in the Red Sea broadcast messages to the group identifying ownership, flag and crew in the hope of securing a safe passage.The Houthis struck two Saudi tankers on Thursday in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, pushing oil prices up 7% to more than $100 per ​barrel for the first time since May. The attacks forced several other tankers to turn around and head north through the Suez canal, a much longer and more expensive route to reach Asia by sailing around ‌Africa.Shipping insurance costs through the southern Red Sea doubled for some companies on Thursday, sources said. Still, half of the 18 ships exiting Bab el-Mandeb on Thursday were carrying crude oil, including two Chinese supertankers.The number of tankers crossing through the strait of Hormuz fell to just one on Thursday, the lowest figure since 7 May.Trump wrote on social media that he would hold Iran accountable for any further Red Sea attacks, saying “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis themselves”.He told Axios he was considering relaunching major combat against Iran. “They haven’t received enough pain yet,” the US news outlet quoted Truump as saying.Washington and Tehran appear to remain fundamentally at odds over future control of the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, insisted the problem with advancing peace talks was “the American approach”.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi (left), meets his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, in Kyrgyzstan on Friday.Photograph: Russian Foreign Ministry Press Service/APAraghchi said: “Preserving Iran’s interests in the strait of Hormuz is among our principles and we are committed to them. We are neither intimidated by threats nor will we yield to pressure.“As long as the legitimate goals and demands of the Iranian people are not met, it is natural that we continue our efforts.”Iranian officials had earlier suggested that the most recent US proposal involved a temporary arrangement that did not address control of the strait of Hormuz.Pakistan, which has acted as a mediator in the conflict, has also been pushing for fresh talks between the two sides after an initiative by ⁠China.Exploratory discussions took place during ​a visit by Iran’s interior minister, Eskandar Momeni, to Islamabad this week – his second within the last 10 days, sources said.Iranian state media said US missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz. Tehran said it had attacked US military equipment depots at Al-Adiri, officially named Camp Buehring, in northern ​Kuwait, and US troop positions at Camp Arifjan and Camp Doha near Kuwait City. It also said it had significantly damaged a surveillance tower used by the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain.In an example of how shipping disruption caused by the war affects other countries, ‌Coca-Cola has raised the prices of Diet Coke in India – where it is mainly sold in aluminium cans – by more than 10% as the conflict chokes its supply chain.Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranUS militaryUS foreign policyTrump administrationYemenHouthisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Law student charged after military-grade bomb intercepted near Irish border | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Isobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, remanded in custody after intelligence-led operation against dissident republicans
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Isobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, remanded in custody after intelligence-led operation against dissident republicans
Content: Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Clane, County Kildare, was charged with possession of explosives.Photograph: Damien Eagers/PAView image in fullscreenIsobella Perrie Sullivan, from Clane, County Kildare, was charged with possession of explosives.Photograph: Damien Eagers/PAIrelandLaw student charged after military-grade bomb intercepted near Irish borderIsobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, remanded in custody after intelligence-led operation against dissident republicansLisa O’Carrollin Donegal and agenciesFri 24 Jul 2026 18.18 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 25-year-old law student has been charged in relation to an “extremely significant” bomb intercepted near the UK-Irish border.Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Clane, County Kildare, was charged with possession of explosives at a special sitting of Trim district court on Friday evening.Garda Síochána said in a statement that a second person, a man in his 40s arrested in connection with the investigation, remained detained in relation to offences against the state.Both were arrested after police in Ireland targeting dissident republicans intercepted a vehicle that was allegedly transporting the device, after receiving intelligence information, police said.Members of the Garda Síochána’s special detective unit stopped the vehicle travelling on the N2 south of Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday afternoonRevealing details of the interception on Friday, Garda sources said the bomb was “highly sophisticated”, had been completed and was ready for use. It contained a power unit, a detonator and military-grade explosives they believed to be semtex.Security sources said the probable intended use was as an under-car explosive for an attack in Northern Ireland.Gardaí requested the assistance of the Irish Defence Forces explosive ordnance disposal team, which completed an examination of the vehicle south of Carrickmacross.The Garda commissioner, Justin Kelly, confirmed details of the operation as he spoke to media at a Garda graduation event in County Tipperary on Friday.“To be clear, what we found was an extremely significant seizure,” he said. “So this was an explosive device.“Any seizure of this nature is really concerning. However, we certainly know that there are a small minority of dissident republicans who did not agree with the Good Friday agreement, they did not put weapons and explosives [out of use], they didn’t, you know, go through with the proper process in relation to decommissioning. So that is something that we continue to deal with.”Kelly added: “There’s a small minority of these individuals, I would describe them as radicalised republicans, and this is a threat that we’re going to continue to face for some time in An Garda Síochána.“But what I will say, certainly, it was a significant explosive device. So certainly not just the seizure of components or pieces. This was an explosive device and it would have or could have potentially caused significant damage.”The commissioner confirmed the operation relied on intelligence. “Obviously, this was not a random stop,” Kelly said. “This is an intelligence-led operation, so we certainly do have information in relation to the individuals involved.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA security source said the fact a bomb of that nature had been built and transported to the border was worrying because of the level of skill involved. It required mechanical and electrical knowledge and the sourcing of explosives.They said that “radicalisation of individuals captured by the internet” meant individuals, rather than organised networks, could be at the centre of the incident.Pipe bombs that have been used in the recent past to target members of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) can be “relatively crude” but this bomb appeared to be different and would have needed an initiating device and a timer.The fact that the Garda intercepted the bomb showed its intelligence gathering was working. However, the incident will fuel concerns about the level of counter-terrorism resourcing since the 1998 peace deal.Kelly said: “We work very closely with our colleagues in PSNI and the intelligence services in the UK to deal with this threat. But I want to commend the members of An Garda Síochána who are involved in this operation.”Perrie Sullivan was remanded in custody until a bail hearing on Monday. Bail would only be granted under a series of strict conditions.Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropeNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Singer D4vd had impregnated teenager he is accused of fatally stabbing | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Celeste Rivas Hernandez, who was 13 at the time, later received an abortion, text messages indicate
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Celeste Rivas Hernandez, who was 13 at the time, later received an abortion, text messages indicate
Content: A picture of Celeste Rivas Hernandez at a press conference following the arrest of David Anthony Burke in Los Angeles, California, on 20 April 2026.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersView image in fullscreenA picture of Celeste Rivas Hernandez at a press conference following the arrest of David Anthony Burke in Los Angeles, California, on 20 April 2026.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersLos AngelesSinger D4vd had impregnated teenager he is accused of fatally stabbingCeleste Rivas Hernandez, who was 13 at the time, later received an abortion, text messages indicateUwa Ede-OsifoFri 24 Jul 2026 19.25 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 16.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSinger D4vd had impregnated the teenager he is accused of fatally stabbing, according to evidence presented in aLos Angelescourtroom on Friday. Celeste Rivas Hernandez later received an abortion, text messages between the two indicate.The musician, who was born David Anthony Burke, apologized to Rivas Hernandez in January 2024 for “putting her through this”, in a text message obtained from his phone.“Neither of us are capable of watching and taking care of the baby. it’s for the best no?” Rivas Hernandez replied. She was 13 years old at the time.The revelation came on the fourth day of a hearing to determine whether the musician will stand trial for murder and child sexual abuse charges linked to Rivas Hernandez’s death. He has pleaded not guilty.Speculation swirled online over whether Rivas Hernandez had been pregnant after prosecutors previewed their plan to present text correspondence with references to pregnancy, abortion and a Plan B emergency contraceptive in an April court filing.Prosecutors say Burke fatally stabbed Rivas Hernandez, who was 14, in April 2025 to silence her from divulging the sexual nature of their relationship as his career soared. He was 18 and she was 13 when the sexual abuse began, according to prosecutors.The abortion appeared to have weighed heavily on Rivas Hernandez.“I care abt u i killed my kid [for] you,” she wrote in an August 2024 text to Burke, theLos Angeles Times reported. “i don’t like talking about it cause it gets [me really] upset but id do anything to have it back.”Rivas Hernandez’s parents left the room as Corey Farell, a Los Angeles police detective, discussed explicit photographs the pair took of each other naked, Courthouse Newsreported.Beth Silverman, the deputy district attorney, apologized to Rivas Hernandez’s mother, Mercedes Martinez. “It’s too much,” she said.In February 2024, Burke suggested to police officers he believed that Rivas Hernandez was 18, according to a video presented to court earlier in the week. Law enforcement had been investigating a missing person’s report.In text messages, shown on Friday, Burke seemed to reference past encounters with authorities.“I can’t wait to move in tg without the cops bitching baby,” he wrote to Rivas Hernandez in June 2024, according to Courthouse News.He also floated the prospect of the two eloping in Italy.The autopsy of Rivas Hernandez’s body was also discussed on Friday.Last September, Los Angeles police discovered Rivas Hernandez’s remains in the front trunk of a Tesla, registered to Burke, five months after prosecutors allege Burke killed her.The court has seen graphic photographs of Rivas Hernandez’s dismembered and decomposing body this week.The degraded conditions of her remains posed challenges to the autopsy, Grant Ho, the doctor who performed the postmortem examination, testified on Friday.Rivas Hernandez had been dead for weeks when her body was found, but Ho noted it was “extremely difficult to tell” when exactly she died.In April, Rivas Hernandez’s autopsy report was unsealed amid mounting scrutiny and speculation over the circumstances of her death. According to the Los Angeles county medical examiner’s office, she died from multiple penetrating injuries.On Friday, Ho said he had identified two stab wounds – one on her abdomen that struck her liver and another on her left chest that damaged her ribs.Defense attorney Marilyn Bednarski appeared to call into question the extent to which the autopsy report could reveal what preceded Rivas Hernandez’s death.“You can’t rule out that she was holding an instrument that caused either of those wounds?” she asked Ho.The doctor said he could not, but noted that self-inflicted injuries typically are paired with “hesitation marks” on the skin, which the teenager’s remains did not have.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsLos AngelesUS crimeCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Parts of England under heat alert with 30C temperatures possible | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Warning in place until Sunday morning in southern and central regions after drought declared in parts of Wales
Author: Hayden Vernon
Headline: Warning in place until Sunday morning in southern and central regions after drought declared in parts of Wales
Content: The depleted Swithland reservoir in Leicestershire. This summer’s dry conditions follow last year’s summer drought.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenThe depleted Swithland reservoir in Leicestershire. This summer’s dry conditions follow last year’s summer drought.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAUK weatherParts of England under heat alert with 30C temperatures possibleWarning in place until Sunday morning in southern and central regions after drought declared in parts of WalesHayden Vernonand agencyFri 24 Jul 2026 12.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeat alerts are in place across parts ofEngland, with possible highs of 30C (86F) and officials saying temperatures are likely to have an impact on health and wellbeing.The yellow heat health alerts issued for the East Midlands, east of England, London, south-east, south-west and West Midlands are in place until 9am on Sunday.Temperatures in the affected areas are forecast to reach the mid- to high 20s, with a high of 30C a possibility, as a prolonged period of dry, warm weather continues in much of the country.The heat health warning from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) comes after drought was declared in north Wales and the upper Severn region, following record dry conditions, heatwaves, wildfires and dwindling rivers.View image in fullscreenThe grass on Wimbledon Common has turned yellow-brown as London experiences severe dry conditions after record-breaking heatwaves.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockIt was the first part of the UK to declare drought status amid a summer of record-breaking heatwaves.Many parts of England have had prolonged dry weather as the country has received just 3% of its average July rainfall. Hosepipe bans are in place for 23 million customers and suppliers are warning they may last all summer.Wildfires have been raging in England, while Scotland has also been hit by a major fire in the Cairngorms. In Ireland, a nationwide hosepipe ban is in place.This summer’s dry conditions follow last year’s summer drought, as the UK increasingly faces more extreme weather fuelled by human-caused climate change, mostly from burning fossil fuels.The Met Office said temperatures could reach 30C in parts of south-east England on Friday, while parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland will see patches of cloud.The forecaster Craig Snell said outbreaks of rain would move southwards on Saturday, spreading from Scotland and Northern Ireland into northern England and parts of Wales.View image in fullscreenA grassfire in Swansea, in south Wales.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/GettyBy Sunday, temperatures were expected to become “fresher” across much of the UK, with rain possible in “areas that haven’t seen much” over the past few weeks, he added.The Met Office said that while some areas would experience rain and showers, the wettest conditions were likely to remain confined to northern and north-western parts of the UK.The Met Office chief meteorologist, Dan Suri, said: “For much of southern England, dry conditions are expected to remain the dominant feature, with temperatures recovering quickly next week and the potential for very warm or locally hot weather to return.”The UK’s climatic extremes are becoming increasingly normal, the Met Office’s annualState of the UK Climatereport found, with last year the hottest on record and further “unprecedented changes” likely to break the record again soon.Data stretching back to 1884 shows the UK has never experienced a year as hot as 2025, according to the report, with temperatures pushed to dizzying heights by carbon pollution clogging the atmosphere.While the UK’s climate is becoming wetter overall, punishing droughts amid hot and dry summers are expected to worsen as average temperatures increase further, the report found.Earlier this month, the Met Office said the UK had already recorded as many 30C days in 2026 as in theextraordinarily hot year of 1976.View image in fullscreenA closed road in Greenfield near Manchester due to a moorland fire.Photograph: Jon Super/AP“What we used to think of as extreme, we increasingly consider as normal,” said Mike Kendon, a scientist at the National Climate Information Centre and lead author of the report. “We are seeing unprecedented changes continuing … and every year adds to this body of evidence.”The heat alerts are in place at the beginning of a period in which millions of motorists are expected to take to the roads for summer getaways. The AA said about 6.3 million drivers were planning a road trip of more than 100 miles between Friday and next Thursday.The port of Dover is expecting another busy weekend but has worked to smooth any delays caused by new EU border checks.The ferry company DFDS said its waiting times at Dover were up to 60 minutes at border controls but “free-flowing” at check-in.The weather health alerting system is provided by the UKHSA in partnership with the Met Office and is intended to provide early warning to the health and social care sector, emergency services, the voluntary and community sector and government departments when temperatures are likely to affect people’s health and wellbeing.With PA MediaExplore more on these topicsUK weatherEnglandDroughtWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on power | India | The Guardian
description: Prime minister’s propaganda machine falters as fiercely secular youth protests reclaim nationalism
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Prime minister’s propaganda machine falters as fiercely secular youth protests reclaim nationalism
Content: Cockroach supporters form a human chain to control the crowd during the continuing protests at the Jantar Mantar in DelhiPhotograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersView image in fullscreenCockroach supporters form a human chain to control the crowd during the continuing protests at the Jantar Mantar in DelhiPhotograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersIndia‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on powerPrime minister’s propaganda machine falters as fiercely secular youth protests reclaim nationalismbyHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiFri 24 Jul 2026 19.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 22.23 EDTShareAs the poster bearing the face of the prime minister,Narendra Modi, was thrown to the floor, a cheer went up. Then came the feet, trampling the image into the muddy ground with gleeful abandon. “Thief, thief,” chanted the crowd.Just a week earlier, such scenes in the heart of India’s capital would have been almost unthinkable. For the 12 years Modi and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) have been in power it was widely acknowledged that you criticised the government at your peril. Dissent was swiftly, routinely and expertly crushed.View image in fullscreenCockroach supporters wave their phone lights in Delhi.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersView image in fullscreenProtesters try to march to  parliament, demanding the resignation of the education minister.Photograph: Vipin/APView image in fullscreenOpposition leader Rahul Gandhi is detained as he stages a protest outside Modi’s residence calling for his resignation.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesThat was, until the cockroaches came along.A movement that began as an online memehas swiftly escalated into one of the most unexpected and significant challenges to Modi’s political power in years, instigated by a young generation who are fed up and startlingly unafraid of their government. Humour has become their greatest weapon and insults to Modi now abound online in the form of memes and Instagram reels as gen Z Indians vilify the government.Education, and the scandal over a leaked examination for medical colleges, remain at the heart of the protest, and the resignation of Modi’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, is the core demand. But after a peaceful protest held on Monday in Delhiwas met with police batons, teargas, pellet guns and the alleged manhandling of female protesters, it has escalated into something far bigger: a fight for the country’s flailing democracy.The ‘cockroaches’ marching on India’s government – podcastRead moreView image in fullscreenCockroach spokesperson Saurav Das leaves after meeting government ministers in New Delhi.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAView image in fullscreenMinister Jitendra Singh leaves the government’s meeting with Cockroach leaders.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAAmong those who braved the police response to take part in the Delhi demonstrations this week was Aniruddh Gautam, a 21-year-old law student from the capital. “I had a place to study at a UK university and I chose to stay in India because I believe in my country,” he said. “But this government has taken away the hopes and dreams of young people. Young people have died because of their failures. I will die for this cause if I need to.”While protests have erupted in India under the Modi government before – first in 2019 against a divisive citizenship law and then in 2020 with a huge farmers’ strike – analysts say the “cockroach” movement presents a more complex problem for the government.View image in fullscreenProtesters climb a police barricade in Delhi.Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOfficers stand guard at the protest site at the Jantar Mantar in Delhi.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAView image in fullscreenPolice detain Cockroach supporters as they gather for a march in Mumbai.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAEducation failures and exam leaks are uniquely bipartisan issues that concern even Modi’s most vital vote bank: upper-class Hindu families. The visuals of children and young students being beaten by police caused discomfort even among the BJP’s own ranks.“Modi has always been very good at overcoming a crisis,” said Tavleen Singh, a political columnist. “But I talk to people who are quite close to him and they’re all really puzzled and not sure what to do next. They say that he’s been listening to the wrong people and misread the mood completely.”View image in fullscreenA CJP supporter rests during the continuing protest at the Jantar Mantar.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVolunteers distribute food at the protest site in Delhi.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesWhile previous protests have been smeared by the government as the actions of Muslim or Pakistani terrorists, or sinister forces abroad, the fiercely secular nature of these demonstrations has made that impossible. Those taking part are from across religions and social classes and many of them are children of BJP supporters. At the Delhi protest site, Hindus and Muslims have prayed and eaten together. A Muslim cook has become a celebrity for feeding protesters every day and Sikh gurdwaras have set up community kitchens on site.“They are clever because they’ve made these protests deeply patriotic and taken back the nationalism card from the BJP,” said Singh. “They’ve also taken back secularism. These guys are using religion to unite.”View image in fullscreenA solidarity protest in Kolkata for the march towards parliament in Delhi.Photograph: Avijit Ghosh/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA march in Mumbai in support of the Delhi protest.Photograph: Punit Paranjpe/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe All India Students’ Association stages a protest in Patna demanding accountability for police action against students.Photograph: Sonu Kishan/ReutersCrucially, the BJP has come up against the limits of its own propaganda machine. While in the past decade mainstream media outlets have been co-opted to follow a strict government line, gen Z protesters have taken to social media to create their own information ecosystem, exposing the stark dissonance between what is being broadcast on mainstream news channels – referred to asgodi,or lapdog, media – and what they are experiencing on the ground.“Our media is disgusting. Night after night they have broadcast lies to try and bring down our movement, calling us terrorists, Pakistanis and anti-nationals,” said Sanna, 26. “But unfortunately for them, we are here getting the message out.”Anish Gawande, a young politician who has been a champion of the cockroach movement, said the protests were erupting en masse because “increasingly, young people do not see a bright future for themselves in this country”.View image in fullscreenPolitician Anish Gawande says the protests are taking place because ‘increasingly, young people do not see a bright future for themselves’.Photograph: Hindustan Times/Getty Images“An entire generation of aspirational young Indians grew up on the idea – and this includes me – that the country had flaws and needed to improve, but was on the whole heading towards progress,” he said.Now, he added, “we are confronted with the bitter reality that the whole story we were sold by the BJP in 2014 never materialised. The promises that have been made over the last 12 years have been repeatedly broken – and the crushing of that illusion is unleashing a pent-up rage unlike any other.”Gawande was insistent they posed an unassailable challenge to the BJP’s grip on power: “This is a rude awakening for the government that the people of India cannot be silenced forever.”When it first emerged in early May, it was easy for the government to dismiss theCockroach Janata party(CJP), whose name was a deliberate poke at Modi’s ruling party. Its founder, Abhijit Dipke, 30, who had recently completed a masters at Boston University, initially created the CJP as a parody website in response to remarks by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, referring to the swathes of unemployed young people and activists as “parasites” and “cockroaches” during a court hearing (though he later denied saying it). The CJP’s original tagline was: “A voice for the lazy, unemployed and chronically online”.But when young Indians pounced upon it with delight, following in their tens of millions online, it became clear to Dipke that satire was proving more representative of their frustrations than mainstream politics.Two days before Kant’s alleged “cockroach” comment, the lives of more than 2 million students were upended when it emerged that a highly competitive exam for admission to medical college had been leaked and sold for millions of rupees. About 2.2 million students would have to take the gruelling test for a second time, competing for just 130,000 places. For some, it was too much to bear. More than a dozen took their own lives.View image in fullscreenCJP founder Abhijeet Dipke at a protest in Delhi in June over alleged irregularities in national examinations for medical college.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDipke launches a nationwide protest campaign at a rally in Pune on 11 June.Photograph: Mahendra Kohle/APView image in fullscreenA police officer patrols as students queue to retake their exams in Srinagar.Photograph: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIt was not the first time this had happened: dozens of leaks had blighted these exams and others in recent years. The government had set up the private agency responsible, yet has never been held accountable. As he flew back into Delhi in early June, Dipke formalised the CJP’s core objectives: accountability for the exam leak, the resignation of Pradhan and the reform of a higher education system seen as chronically underfunded, corrupt and systematically failing millions of young Indians.The turnout at the CJP’s first Delhi protest was just a few hundred. But by the end of June, they returned, vowing they would not move from their Delhi protest site until Modi sacked his education minister.View image in fullscreenActivist Sonam Wangchuk went on hunger strike in support of the protesters.This time, the CJP had a new powerful figurehead. Sonam Wangchuk, a renowned Indian engineer and activist, announced that he would go on hunger strike in solidarity with the “cockroaches” – resonant of the hunger strikes made by Mahatma Gandhi in the fight for Indian independence. He too had come up against the Modi government’s crackdown on dissent, when he was jailed under terror laws for a protest last year.View image in fullscreenThe Congress party leader, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, at a protest in Delhi calling for Modi’s resignation.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Modi government initially met the protests with silence. But after the Delhi police aggressively removed Wangchuk on the 20th day of his hunger strike and dragged him to hospital against his will, popular outrage galvanised the movement.Delhi police, who are directly under the control of the home minister, Amit Shah, Modi’s closest political ally, had refused permission for protesters to march on parliament the following Monday. But that did not stop young people coming in unprecedented numbers. Delhi police prepared for 10,000 – an estimated 100,000 turned up, many chanting Wangchuk’s name.View image in fullscreenSonam Wangchuk on 7 July during his hunger strike in Delhi.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemonstrators hold a portrait of Wangchuk during his  hunger strike.Photograph: Vijay Pandey/EPAView image in fullscreenYouth organisations, Cockroach supporters and social activists rally against Modi’s government in Bangalore.Photograph: Jagadeesh Nv/EPAThe demonstration was a critical turning point, an expression of dissent unlike anything seen in Delhi in years. For many of the young people, it was their first ever protest, marking something of a political awakening. They sobbed at the solidarity and fanned each other in the heat. But as the numbers swelled, the police were far outnumbered and began to resort to brutal tactics to prevent people marching on parliament.The use of teargas, batons and alleged pellet guns against young people made for horrifying footage, and hardened the position of many protesters. Among those targeted was 17-year-old Deeksha Mishra. She was there for her sister, whose dream was to be a doctor, but who had fallen into depression since the exam leaks. “I watched her losing her dream and passion and I knew I had to come,” she said.“We came peacefully but they treated us as terrorists,” she added. “The police beat us so badly. Some had blood flowing down their skulls and their noses were broken.” Hundreds ended up in hospital, some in intensive care.At the protest site days later, Mishra said she was now standing for more than just exam leaks. “This is about corruption, it’s about our dying democracy,” she said. “The government want to keep ignoring us until the protest dies but it’s not going to happen. We are not afraid any more.”On the ground at India’s ‘Cockroach’ protestWhile Modi has promised fast action against those responsible for the exam leaks, he has still refused to sack his minister. Analysts say he has been backed into a tricky corner: Pradhan is one of his most loyal and politically important ministers – to fire him could undermine cabinet loyalty and be seen as a sign of weakness for the strongman leader. Yet protesters say they won’t move until he’s gone.It remains to be seen just how much the movement has rattled the electoral grip of Modi, who still has three years left in office and recently won a string of crucial state elections. But as the political analyst and columnist Pratap Bhanu Mehta said: “Most importantly, this movement has lifted the pall of fear.”“This government is used to governing with impunity,” he said. “Re-establishing unchallenged authority is going to be difficult for them.”

title: Was Keir Starmer’s leaving party the boozy birth of a new Labour force? | Labour | The Guardian
description: A £10,000 bar tab was drunk, there was a ‘lot of anger’, and now ex-ministers are thinking how to cooperate in future
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: A £10,000 bar tab was drunk, there was a ‘lot of anger’, and now ex-ministers are thinking how to cooperate in future
Content: Keir Starmer was photographed, drink in hand, outside the Grafton pub in Kentish Town on Monday night.View image in fullscreenKeir Starmer was photographed, drink in hand, outside the Grafton pub in Kentish Town on Monday night.LabourWas Keir Starmer’s leaving party the boozy birth of a new Labour force?A £10,000 bar tab was drunk, there was a ‘lot of anger’, and now ex-ministers are thinking how to cooperate in futureKiran StaceyPolicy editorFri 24 Jul 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeir Starmer’s leaving party had been planned for some time. But in years to come it might be seen as the birth of a new Labour movement.Dozens of ministers, aides and Starmer himself headed to the Grafton pub in Kentish Town on Monday night to drown their sorrows, hours after the former prime minister left Downing Street for the last time.By 7pm, revellers had exhausted a £10,000 bar tab. But as a boozy late-night karaoke session started, several were learning they had lost their ministerial jobs, victims of whatsome believewas a purge of Starmer allies being punished for their loyalty to the former prime minister.Now the group – at the centre of which are 11 former cabinet ministers – are considering how to cooperate in the future, whether in supporting the government ofAndy Burnhamor, occasionally, pointing out where it is going wrong.Starmer allies see ‘hint of retribution’ in Burnham reshuffleRead more“There was a lot of anger at the party,” said one person who was there. “There were some decent, competent people who seemed to be losing their jobs simply because they did not call for Keir Starmer to quit.”One of Starmer’s biggest problems in government was that he did not have an identifiable faction of people who were willing to defend him at all costs – a symptom of both his late entry into politics and of his relative lack of ideology.But many of those whom Burnham sacked or demoted after entering office did have one thing in common: they were close to the former prime minister and had not called for him to resign.They included the chancellor, Rachel Reeves, who turned down the chance to be education secretary; the prime minister’s chief secretary, Darren Jones; the attorney general and longtime Starmer friend, Richard Hermer, and the housing secretary, Steve Reed.Many had been expected to lose their jobs as Burnham made space for his own allies. But others were more of a surprise. Nick Thomas-Symonds was ousted from his position as chief negotiator with the EU, Hilary Benn lost his job as Northern Ireland secretary, and at a more junior level, Alison Levitt, who worked with Starmer at the Crown Prosecution Service, was sacked from the Ministry of Justice.Two people who previously worked at the heart of Starmer’s office in opposition, Jenny Chapman and Chris Ward, both lost their positions.“Obviously Andy was always going to bring his own people in,” one Starmer ally said, “but the fact that he kept in everyone who called for Keir to go and ousted everyone who didn’t feels very deliberate.”View image in fullscreenSome close to Starmer believe Darren Jones (pictured) was wrong to question Burnham in such a public way.Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockBurnham has said his cabinet “reflects the party, the country, all backgrounds”, and has promised to take a “one-team approach” within theLabourparty.Guardiananalysis showshis first cabinet has a better gender balance than any other in history, although it is more privately educated than Starmer’s and less ethnically diverse than Rishi Sunak’s.Now Starmer’s former ministers and advisers are thinking about how they can best contribute to the Labour party from outside the government. Jones showed one possible route on Tuesday morning when he publicly pointed out the flaws in Burnham’s plan to scrap the government’s digital ID scheme to pay for a cut in VAT on electricity bills.“Good news that VAT will be cut on electricity bills. It’s a simple way for families to save a few quid, and to mechanically help to keep inflation that little bit lower,” he posted onX.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But the DigitalID program was unfunded. The government will have to set out how it will pay for its new policies at the budget.”That post had an immediate impact, as Downing Street found itself having to defend how the policy was costed. Burnham told cabinet ministers to take a “hard look” at their budgets in a sign that they could soon be asked to make spending cuts to pay for some of his commitments.Despite that, some close to Starmer believe Jones was wrong to question the new prime minister in such a public way. “I’m not sure that helped,” said one. “There is a risk it just makes us look bitter.”But those who served at the top of Starmer’s government want to keep posing difficult questions to the prime minister, whether in public or private. There is talk of a new WhatsApp group, to be set up when MPs return in September, to help coordinate their efforts.Race, school, gender: the makeup of Andy Burnham’s cabinet – in chartsRead moreSome MPs are likely to take up committee roles, while others, including Starmer, will sit on the backbenches and only intervene on a limited number of issues. Several have careers in other fields that they can now return to, such as Hermer, who was a practising KC before Starmer appointed him to the government.But given that many know the government’s accounts and priorities in detail, they are in a unique position to scrutinise Burnham’s decisions or point the way for others who wish to do so.“Yes, we know where the bodies are buried,” said one Starmer ally. “But it’s not so much that, it’s more a case of explaining why we made the decisions we did, and what the downsides are of the ones Burnham might make instead.”Others believe they will need to keep quiet at least in the short term, given the weight of support Burnham has in the party and, increasingly, the country.But they say the example he has set in appointing his first government could come back to haunt him. “He has chosen not to reward loyalty to the leader,” said one Starmer ally. “That is sending out a message he may come to regret.”Explore more on these topicsLabourKeir StarmerDarren JonesAndy BurnhamLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rebel Wilson had a legal win but didn’t come out of The Deb defamation trial unscathed | Rebel Wilson | The Guardian
description: Judgment dismissing Charlotte MacInnes’s case expressed doubts about credibility of three key witnesses, and is likely to be appealed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Judgment dismissing Charlotte MacInnes’s case expressed doubts about credibility of three key witnesses, and is likely to be appealed
Content: Rebel Wilson speaks to reporters as she arrives at court  during the nine-day defamation trial that was decided in her favour.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenRebel Wilson speaks to reporters as she arrives at court  during the nine-day defamation trial that was decided in her favour.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersRebel WilsonRebel Wilson had a legal win but didn’t come out of The Deb defamation trial unscathedJudgment dismissing Charlotte MacInnes’s case expressed doubts about credibility of three key witnesses, and is likely to be appealedAustralian Associated PressFri 24 Jul 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRebel Wilson’s self-styled brand as a truth teller was put to the test during a fiery defamation feud where rivals called her a bully.But the Hollywood A-lister, referred to as “very difficult to be around” and “fucking nuts” during an at-times bruising trial, emerged from the federal court battlewith the last laugh.The Pitch Perfect star came under fire while being sued by the Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut film The Deb.MacInnes claimed she was defamed by Wilson in four social media posts implying she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.Wilson wrote the young actor confided – and later recanted – she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.MacInnes denied making a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.View image in fullscreenCharlotte MacInnes during a break in the trial in April.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPBut in her ruling handed down on Wednesday, Justice Elizabeth Raper found evidence established MacInnes did make a complaint about feeling uncomfortable.The young actor then walked it back, at least partially because she was concerned about losing control of the situation and wanted to contain it, the judge determined.She ruled none of the four social media posts were defamatory in a comprehensive win for Wilson.“This has been a long process and throughout I have tried to stay grounded in my values and what I believed was right,” Wilson wrote upon her victory. “I’m thankful that process has now reached its conclusion.”Rebel Wilson wins defamation case brought by co-star after bitter disputeRead moreYet the Bridesmaids star did not escape the hotly contested trial without wounds.For all Wilson’s protestations that she was known as a truth teller, Raper found the actor’s testimony had been untruthful on occasion, self-serving at times and punctuated with exaggeration.MacInnes’s claims the first-time director would be believed because of her status in the entertainment industry were dismissed.“It was my impression from all the evidence Ms Wilson is known for being outspoken but not necessarily reliable,” Raper wrote.MacInnes faced the same scrutiny, with the judge finding she had been less than frank at times and combative when asked to accept reasonable suggestions.She determined the young actor gave multiple inconsistent accounts of what happened in the Bondi apartment after the medical episode, as had Ghost.“I have serious misgivings as to the truthfulness of the testimony of each of Ms MacInnes, Ms Ghost and Ms Wilson,” she wrote.The scathing assessments may have MacInnes questioning why she sued her famous co-star.But the defamation law expert Prof David Rolph said the case highlighted the risk of defamation litigation.“People who sue for defamation or become involved in defamation cases don’t know and can’t control what’s going to come out in court,” the University of Sydney law professor said. “Once you start, it’s difficult to control and it’s difficult to stop what may be said about you in court.”That became abundantly clear for Wilson, who waslabelled a bully and a liarduring the weeks-long hearing.The Deb director denied the claims, labelling accusations of private and public bullying as nonsense and insisting she had been a champion of women throughout her 25-year career.Raper noted she maintained her composure while being repeatedly charged with lying and fabricating evidence during her two-day cross-examination.The accusations included that Wilson lied about having no involvement in the creation of smear websites attacking Ghost as the “Indian Ghislaine Maxwell” and a sex trafficker.View image in fullscreenAmanda Ghost arrives at the federal court in Sydney during the trial.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPRaper made no determination of the contentious websites that loomed large during the trial, nor MacInnes’s allegation that Wilson was involved in a hack that resulted in a nude photo of hers being leaked.Ultimately, the judge found, even if one of the posts had been defamatory, she could not be satisfied MacInnes had shown that she suffered serious harm.The four posts had been visible to Wilson’s 11 million followers for 24 hours.“The ordinary reasonable reader would have scrolled through the post relatively quickly and his or her reaction would have been impressionistic and fleeting,” she said.The threshold of serious harm is a relatively new requirement yet to be tested in the country’s highest court, Rolph noted.“The courts haven’t yet worked out precisely how to approach this issue and what’s required of it,” he said.Rebel Wilson’s courtroom makeover shows why style matters on the standRead more“It wouldn’t surprise me if a ground of appeal is raised in relation to serious harm because of the novelty of the issues and the novelty of the law.”MacInnes indicated her intention to appeal against the decision, which has left her holding a hefty bill for the costs incurred by Wilson during the legal fight.Rolph suggested such a high-profile loss may have a chilling effect on others considering litigation.With a possible appeal looming, neither Wilson nor MacInnes can be said to have escaped without a scratch.The actors began their relationship full of mutual admiration, working together on a film that was to elevate both of their careers.But ended it on opposite sides of a stale Sydney courtroom, slinging accusations of lying and greed.As Wilson wrote in her affidavit to the court: “Unfortunately, what started as a dream has turned out to be a nightmare.”Explore more on these topicsRebel WilsonAustralian lawfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can’t paper over the cracks of history. It will haunt you’: Gugu Mbatha-Raw on her race-horror thriller  | Television | The Guardian
description: She paved the way for Bridgerton, lit up Black Mirror’s most joyful episode – and now she stars in a grisly supernatural horror about slavery. The Belle star talks about Possession, partying with Prince and why she loves to shake things up
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: She paved the way for Bridgerton, lit up Black Mirror’s most joyful episode – and now she stars in a grisly supernatural horror about slavery. The Belle star talks about Possession, partying with Prince and why she loves to shake things up
Content: ‘It’s hard to talk about slavery’, says Gugu Mbatha-Raw.Photograph: David ReissView image in fullscreen‘It’s hard to talk about slavery’, says Gugu Mbatha-Raw.Photograph: David ReissTelevisionInterview‘You can’t paper over the cracks of history. It will haunt you’: Gugu Mbatha-Raw on her race-horror thrillerEmma LoffhagenShe paved the way for Bridgerton, lit up Black Mirror’s most joyful episode – and now she stars in a grisly supernatural horror about slavery. The Belle star talks about Possession, partying with Prince and why she loves to shake things upFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGugu Mbatha-Raw seems blissfully immune to the heat. London is pushing 40C on one of those heatwave mornings when everyone is wearing the weather: damp collars, flushed faces, hair slicked to foreheads. Arriving at the cafe of the central London hotel where we meet, however, the star looks as if she’s stepped in from an altogether different climate. Dressed in a pristine white linen two-piece, makeup free, hair scraped back, she carries herself with a composure that makes everyone else’s perspiration seem faintly melodramatic.She is, in every sense of the word, cool. This impression is only reinforced as we settle in for some small talk and she mentions that she’s been to the hotel once before.“I stayed here during the premiere of Belle – gosh, almost 15 years ago now,” she says. Then, almost as an afterthought: “And Prince performed at the afterparty.” She laughs at the look on my face. “It was incredible,” she says. “Just completely surreal.” It’s the sort of global cut-through all British actors dream of, and an anecdote that perhaps feels slightly out of place in the orbit of Mbatha-Raw’s career. SinceBelle– Amma Asante’s luminous 2013 period drama about Dido Elizabeth Belle, the real-life mixed-race daughter of an enslaved African woman raised in the English aristocracy –Mbatha-Raw has become one of Britain’s most fascinating actors.View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw as Claudia with Sheldon Shepherd as Cudjoe East in Possession.Photograph: Des WillieFrom playing the lead in Charlie Brooker’s acclaimed queer Black Mirror episodeSan Juniperoand starring in Jennifer Aniston and Reese Witherspoon’s workplace #MeToo drama The Morning Show to leading Apple TV’s identity-bending psychological thrillerSurfacein which she plays a woman recovering after a suicide attempt, the 43-year-old has consistently chosen projects that are intellectually and politically ambitious – roles one might summarise as having “something to say”.“I don’t want to do the same thing all of the time,” Mbatha-Raw tells me. “It’s fun for me to go from a period drama to a romantic drama to a comedy – it keeps me stimulated.”That instinct is precisely what drew her to Possession, Sky’s new supernatural thriller. Mbatha-Raw plays Claudia, a Bristol lawyer dispatched to Jamaica after a white plantation owner’s wealthy descendant dies suddenly, leaving his fortune not to his family but to a Jamaican man nobody can seem to track down. Claudia is assigned the case partly because, as one colleague bluntly puts it, having a Black, half-Jamaican lawyer would be “better optics”. But the legal work slowly gives way to something far more unsettling: the ghosts of Britain’s colonial legacy – both literal and metaphorical – intrude upon the present.“I was fascinated by Claudia because she’s caught between her professional obligations and her own personal history,” says Mbatha-Raw. “[She goes] from this relatively detached, brittle, ambitious career woman who was quite numb to her heritage and disconnected from her Jamaican background to becoming more grounded and rooted.”The story slips between modern Jamaica and the brutal realities of plantation slavery. But the enslaved do not remain confined to history: the enigmatic Cudjoe East, the man at the centre of the inheritance dispute, claims to be an enslaved man cursed centuries earlier to wander the Earth. In the past, a plantation mistress keeps grisly relics – locks of hair, severed ears – to perform magic on the bodies of those she enslaved. Present-day characters find themselves possessed by the spirits of enslavers, while Claudia struggles to resist being claimed herself.Filmed on location, much of the show’s richness comes from the vision of its Jamaican director,Storm Saulter, whose work has long explored the country’s layered histories and identity. The island is rendered in full polyphonic Technicolor: music and traditional masquerade rituals punctuate the narrative, while Obeah – the African-Caribbean spiritual practice of contacting ancestors, long feared by colonial authorities for its association with resistance and rebellion – becomes one of the show’s recurring motifs.“We wanted everything to feel as real as possible – the beauty of the colour, music and smells of Jamaica, but also its darkness,” says Mbatha-Raw. “We filmed at a real plantation house – all the scenes in the grounds, with enslaved people working on the land – real people lived and died there. Driving up the hill towards the house, you could really feel the weight of history.”View image in fullscreenLegal action … Mbatha-Raw in Possession.Photograph: Des WillieThe show belongs to the same lineage as Jordan Peele’sGet Out– racially conscious horror, in which the supernatural is merely a conduit for the far more terrifying legacy of racism. It is a provocation about reparations, colonial wealth and Britain’s historic relationship with slavery. In one pointed exchange, Claudia and the son of the plantation owner discuss the fact that the British government compensated former slave owners after abolition – a debt underwritten bytaxpayers until 2015– while those who had been enslaved received nothing. These are conversations that feel particularly pointed with the rise of far-right nationalism and racism in the UK and beyond. Is this something she was conscious of when making the show?“It’s uncomfortable to talk about reparations, it’s hard to talk about slavery and how we make peace with that history,” she says. “I think that’s what makes [the show] so compelling,” she continues. “You can’t just paper over the cracks of history. If we don’t deal with it, it will find ways of haunting us.”More than a decade separates Possession and Belle, but the two projects feel in conversation with one another in their meditations on empire.View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw with Sarah Gadon in Belle.Photograph: Cinematic/Alamy“It’s funny because it wasn’t like a huge blockbuster film,” she says when I ask how the movie changed her life. “But it was my first lead role, and it opened up lots of opportunities for me. And it was an important story to tell. A lot of people didn’t know that mixed-race characters existed in history – certainly not of any status, because you never saw them in movies unless they were a slave or being brutalised in some way.”Before we meet, she tells me she took a walk through Hampstead Heath to Kenwood House, once the stately home where Dido lived. “I wanted to immerse myself in that history again before speaking to you,” she says. Looking back now, she believes Belle helped widen ideas about who gets to exist in Britain’s period dramas.“I do think Belle helped pave the way for a show like Bridgerton,” she adds. “Just having Black and brown people visible is a huge change in the last 10 years or so.” Belle also marked the beginning of her friendship with Oprah, who was an early champion and offered to help with its US marketing; the pair have remained in touch ever since.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolitics has never been optional in Mbatha-Raw’s life. She was born in 1983 in Witney, a town just outside Oxford. Her father was a student anti-apartheid activist and ANC campaigner who fled South Africa to avoid imprisonment on Robben Island, eventually rebuilding his life with support from the UN’s Refugee Agency.“I remember we would talk about politics at the dinner table, but when you’re South African, you don’t know any different,” she says.She grew up an only child, living with her mother, a British nurse. Her parents split when she was young, but her father remained in her life. Ballet was her first love, as well as music – she trained with the National Youth Music Theatre before going on to Rada.As a young, biracial aspiring actor – particularly one growing up outside of London – has she ever felt held back by her race? She demurs.“There were certainly some roles that would have been closed off to me, like those early Regency-era roles, but the industry is changing in a really positive direction,” she says.She does mention that early on in her career, an older – white – actor suggested she change her name to something easier to pronounce. It was advice she politely ignored.“I love my name, it’s what makes me who I am,” she says. “I don’t think it’s that hard to pronounce. Plus, it translates to ‘our pride’ in Zulu, so changing that would feel so wrong – the opposite of what it means!”View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw with Boris Kodjoe in Undercovers.Photograph: Chris Haston/Everett Collection Inc/AlamyAfter graduating from Rada in 2004, Mbatha-Raw built her career the old-fashioned way: on stage. In 2005, she appeared in Antony and Cleopatra before landing one of her first major roles opposite Andrew Garfield inRomeo and Juliet at Manchester’s Royal Exchange. Supporting screen roles in Bad Girls, Marple and Doctor Who followed, before a celebrated turn as Ophelia opposite Jude Law’sHamlet in the West Endand on Broadway. JJ Abrams saw the production and cast her in his American spy drama Undercovers, opening the door to Hollywood. For years she lived peripatetically, dividing her life between sets in the US and London. For now, she is London-based again.Her move coincided with a broader exodus of Black British actors across the Atlantic. Daniel Kaluuya has spoken about not getting roles in the UK “because of the colour of my skin”; David Oyelowo has talked of being “pushed out” because of the racial “glass ceiling”, as has David Harewood. Blockbuster names such as Cynthia Erivo and Damson Idris have found some of their biggest roles in the US, fuelling a long-running debate about whether Britain’s film and television industry truly nurtures its Black talent.“It’s definitely something I’ve heard, but it hasn’t been my personal experience,” she says when I ask about this. “I didn’t go to the US looking for opportunities; I got offered a role in Hollywood because of the work I’d already done here – and that’s not really something you turn down. I was very lucky.”Mbatha-Raw is thoughtful and politically engaged, but I get the sense she would rather speak through her characters. “I wouldn’t ever want to tell people what to think or experience,” she says. “Maybe Possession will inspire people to think about the more thought-provoking conversations around slavery, the idea of reparations and the complexity of that. But mostly, I just hope people find it entertaining.”Possession starts on 6 August on Sky Atlantic at 9pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionSlaveryDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not fair’: cafe owners frustrated over exclusion from business rates cut | UK news | The Guardian
description: Business owners in England say prioritising venues selling alcohol leaves vital community spaces behind
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Business owners in England say prioritising venues selling alcohol leaves vital community spaces behind
Content: The targeted relief package will support pubs, social clubs and live music venues, but not cafes.Photograph: Guerilla/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe targeted relief package will support pubs, social clubs and live music venues, but not cafes.Photograph: Guerilla/AlamyUK news‘It’s not fair’: cafe owners frustrated over exclusion from business rates cutBusiness owners in England say prioritising venues selling alcohol leaves vital community spaces behindAmelia HillFri 24 Jul 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFerdinand Geus is proud of the positive, global impact his small speciality coffee business is having.“Around 3,000 small, family-owned farms in Yemen rely on us – we’ve persuaded many to stop growing khat, the drug, and start growing coffee instead,” said the business manager of ShebaCoffee, which supplies Yemeni coffee beans to independent cafes across the world, including the UK.“We sell their coffee to cafes across five continents, fuelling employment for an entire chain of people that spans the seas and reaches into local high streets and neighbourhoods around the UK.”Despite Geus’s enthusiasm, Sheba has been struggling under the weight of increased energy bills and a soaring cost of living.“Coffee is a luxury and people are cutting back,” he said. “To survive at this point in our business journey, we need to expand – to employ more people – but we can’t do that.”He might have been able, however, had Andy Burnham’s 20% cut to business rates bills embraced cafes and restaurants. But to Geus’s frustration, the targeted package, worth roughly £100m a year, will only support specific high street sectors: pubs, social clubs and live music venues across England.Taking effect from next April, it will save a typical pub an estimated £1,100 next year, a figure that would have helped Geus’s business “grow and survive”, he said.“Burnham says he wants to support high streets but independent cafes are more than retail businesses; they are workplaces, meeting places and important parts of their local communities,” he added.“Supporting pubs while excluding cafes risks creating an artificial distinction between businesses facing many of the same commercial pressures.”Hakan Elbir, founder of the deaf-run Dialogue Cafe, an inclusive social enterprise based at the University of East London that supports deaf and hard of hearing baristas, is also frustrated.View image in fullscreenHakan Elbir at the Dialogue Cafe, which supports deaf and hard of hearing baristas.Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian“We’ve been trying to hold down our prices – despite the rise in the cost of coffee beans, which came on top of all the other price hikes we’ve had to absorb – because any increase will push footfall down even further,” he said.“But this incentive to our competitors is definitely going to affect us in a bad way. Our customers will now prefer to go to the pub for their hot drinks because they’ll be able to undercut our prices. It’s not fair.”Elbir said he is particularly disappointed because, listening to Burnham’s speeches since he became prime minister, he had been anticipating receiving help.“I feel that he has missed an important point,” he said. “We are helping the government employ disabled people. We’re saving them money – but instead of rewarding us, they put more barriers in our way.”Elbir also argues that Burnham’s exclusive focus on venues that sell alcohol is based on a fundamental misunderstanding of where people want their community hubs to be.“Our cafe actually does have an alcohol licence but predominantly and increasingly, people prefer to buy coffee or tea,” he said.“If Burnham wants to help communities, he needs to look at what communities really want, rather than what he thinks they want, and focus his support there.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsSmall businessCoffeeUK cost of living crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The captain told me to wear a nappy on board’ – why is air travel so humiliating for disabled passengers? | Disability | The Guardian
description: From being abused by staff and other travellers to being denied access to toilets, flying is an increasingly distressing and frustrating experience for many wheelchair users. Here, they share their stories
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: From being abused by staff and other travellers to being denied access to toilets, flying is an increasingly distressing and frustrating experience for many wheelchair users. Here, they share their stories
Content: Samanta Bullock, a former No 1 wheelchair tennis player, was told she couldn’t board a flight to the UK without a carer to help her use the toilet.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSamanta Bullock, a former No 1 wheelchair tennis player, was told she couldn’t board a flight to the UK without a carer to help her use the toilet.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianDisability‘The captain told me to wear a nappy on board’ – why is air travel so humiliating for disabled passengers?From being abused by staff and other travellers to being denied access to toilets, flying is an increasingly distressing and frustrating experience for many wheelchair users. Here, they share their storiesDiane TaylorFri 24 Jul 2026 06.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 06.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenHannah Babalolaboarded KLM flight 598 on 26 May, she was tired. A Paralympic athlete, she had been competing at an event in South Africa’s Cape Town, and was hoping there would be no hold ups on her journey back home to Chicago.Babalola, 37, is well-travelled. A former wheelchair racer, she now competes in marathons and has flown to dozens of countries over the years without big problems.The first stretch of her journey home was a flight of almost 11 hours to Amsterdam. After boarding, she was told by the captain and crew that she wouldn’t be able to access an onboard wheelchair, known as an aisle chair. These narrow wheelchairs are used by people with disabilities so they can access the toilet during a flight. Crew members told her when she boarded the plane that if she needed to use the toilet, she would have to do so without a wheelchair – if this wasn’t possible, she was told she would have to get off the flight altogether.View image in fullscreenParalympian Hannah Babalola was told by KLM that they couldn’t provide her with an onboard wheelchair for her long-haul flight.Photograph: Star Tribune/Getty ImagesAstounded by this – aisle chairs are generally available on wide-bodied aircraft – Babalola stood her ground, despite becoming increasingly distressed. The crew offered various justifications for their position, including the captain’s fears that the chair would be unsafe to use if there was turbulence. She was also wrongly told that she hadn’t booked the flight as a disabled person (disabled passengers are advised to book special assistanceat least 48 hours before taking a flight – which Babalola had done). She had bought a return ticket​ and had​ had no trouble receiv​ing assistance as a disabled passenger on her outward journey​.double quotation markThey made me feel as if I wasn’t a human. The humiliation was unbearable“It was the first time anything like this had happened to me on a plane,” says Babalola. “They made me feel as if I wasn’t a human.” The crew called the police and security. Both declined to take any action against her, as there was no evidence she had done anything wrong. Desperate to get home, she finally agreed not to use the toilet during the flight. “The humiliation was unbearable,” she says.What happened to her is not an isolated incident.When the Guardian first reported on Babalola’s case, a flurry of emails followed from others who had had similar experiences.According to datapublished by the World Health Organization in 2023 approximately 16% of the global population experiences significant disability – about 1.3 billion people. The UK’s Civil Aviation Authority outlines therights of passengersto accessible air travel, which includes assistance moving through airports, and when boarding and disembarking planes. But such assistance has limitations. It applies only to people flying from UK airports on any airline, and for returns to the UK on either UK or EU airlines.View image in fullscreenThe UK’s Civil Aviation Authority outlines passengers’ rights to accessible travel, but the rules only apply on certain routes.Photograph: AndreyPopov/Getty ImagesThe National Centre for Accessible Transport published a report in July 2025, calledInvisible Barriers: How public attitudes affect inclusive travel. It found that people with impairments or access needs that fall outside certain models have to fight to get those needs met. Those who were interviewed for the report said they had experienced negative treatment when travelling, due to assumptions and stereotypes around disability. The report looked at various types of transport, including planes; it found that disabled travellers sometimes have to endure abuse from other passengers, and that transport staff have a limited understanding of disability. One wheelchair user quoted in the report, who was travelling by plane, was denied assistance as they had limited mobility; they could stand up and walk in certain circumstances, but were unable to get down the plane steps without assistance. A crew member said: “Well you can stand, you can get off, you can go down the stairs.”Sophie Morgan, a British TV presenter, writer and disability rights campaigner, is co-founder ofRights on Flightsand an energetic campaigner for people with disabilities who fly. She was paralysed from the chest down after a car accident at 18, and began campaigning because her wheelchair was broken so many times by airport staff when she flew.double quotation markThey just don’t care. One plane captain told me I should wear a nappy on board“I honestly think that if the airlines could ban us from flying, they would,” she says. “I feel sad that the same problems that were happening three years ago are still happening now. It feels like a case of one step forward, 200 steps back. When I was campaigning in the beginning I thought: ‘They just need to be told.’ In fact, they actually know full well, but they just don’t care. Where are we? We are nowhere. One plane captain told me I should wear a nappy on board.”Sarah Richardson has a disability called arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, which causes severe problems with her joints and bones. This makes travel, including plane travel, very challenging, and led her to conduct research for her MBA with 36 disabled travellers from around the world. Half the respondents encountered problems “almost always”. None reported no problems.More than 83% of her respondents experienced stress and anxiety when travelling, and restricted food and drink in the hours before travelling to avoid the struggle of using the onboard toilet. Some resorted to wearing nappies on flights in case toilet access was impossible.“I was really shocked by what I found in the interviews,” says Richardson. “Travelling systems are just not made for people with disabilities, and things have got worse with automation.” While researching her thesis, Richardson found that, as travel infrastructures have become more automated to boost efficiency and economic return, accessibility for disabled travellers is increasingly treated as a conditional service rather than something baked into the design of systems. “Travel systems are designed for average bodies and toilets are not designed for people with disabilities. It is particularly terrifying on long-haul flights.”On a recent flight, she asked if she could move to a seat with more leg room, which was vacant, but was told she could only switch if she paid an extra $300. “When you are up in the air, you are a hostage.Disabilityis not a niche market. We are part of the community. Being disabled is seen as not important, not sexy, not interesting,” she says.View image in fullscreenHasan Adeel says he is frequently transferred from his wheelchair to the plane seat in an inappropriate manner.Photograph: Courtesy of Hasan AdeelSome disabled travellers say they have to prepare for the worst when they book a plane ticket. Hasan Adeel has muscular dystrophy and flies frequently to visit family and to speak at conferences about his disability. He says he is frequently wrongly handled when being transferred between his wheelchair and his plane seat. “I have never yet used an aeroplane bathroom, as I can’t get through the door,” he says. “I feel that for airlines, rules are ranked higher than humanity. But you can’t argue with the airlines or they won’t let you get on the plane.”On one trip, Adeel landed in Doha in Qatar and asked staff to help him transfer from his aeroplane seat to his wheelchair. He was left for 20 minutes. “They said they had never transferred a person like me before but that they would try,” says Adeel. “First they transferred me to the narrow aisle chair and from there into my wheelchair. They did not know the correct way to transfer someone with my disability and the transfer was not done in a professional way.”double quotation markHours before I travel to the airport I stop drinking water, because I know I won’t be able to use the toilet on the planePayal Shrishrimal, an artist who lives in India, is determined not to let the significant challenges of air travel get her down. She also has muscular dystrophy and, at 41, has far outlived the life expectancy of 20 that she was given as a child. “On one journey, when I was travelling home after recovering from surgery, the crew started whispering about me and my disability. They kept asking why I was using a wheelchair, and it made me feel very nervous and humiliated … Two or three hours before I leave home to travel to the airport I have to stop drinking water, because I know I won’t be able to use the toilet on the plane. Once, I was even asked to pay for the transport of my wheelchair, although there are [supposed to be] no charges for this.”View image in fullscreenPayal Shrishrimal was once asked to pay for her wheelchair’s transport, despite it being a free service.Photograph: Courtesy of Payal ShrishrimalA recurrent complaint among wheelchair users is that, when their chairs are stored in the hold – in perfectly good condition – on landing they are returned to them battered and broken. One man discovered his electric wheelchair had been badly damaged when he arrived in London on an Emirates flight on 18 May. He is completely reliant on the chair and, as a result of the damage, has been confined to his home. “I have effectively been trapped inside my home, and unable to attend medical appointments, shop independently, or carry out normal daily activities,” he says. “This situation has caused significant distress, loss of independence, emotional suffering and disruption to my life.” He received no response from the airline, and nor did others who wrote to Emirates trying to advocate for him.After the Guardian contacted Emirates, the airline agreed to take action. A spokesperson said: “We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience he experienced. We are in direct contact with him and have arranged a temporary mobility device. We are also assessing options to replace his wheelchair as a permanent solution, and will continue to support him until the issue is fully resolved.”View image in fullscreenDisabled passengers frequently say that their wheelchairs getting damaged in the hold is a big issue when travelling.Photograph: MarioGuti/Getty ImagesEven those who are powerful and high-profile report appalling experiences when they travel by plane.
