Samanta Bullock, Brazil’s former No 1 wheelchair tennis player, now lives in the UK. She founded Bullock Inclusion, which creates social projects in fashion and sport to promote inclusion for all, and aims to change attitudes to transform the lives of people living with disabilities. Last month, she flew to New York to take part in the UN’s 19th Conference of States Parties to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which aims to further the rights of people with disabilities. She and her team had organised a fashion show for the event and discussed with officials how best to advance the rights of disabled people. But when she arrived at JFK airport for her flight back to the UK, she was told by British Airways staff that she couldn’t board the flight without a carer to take her to the toilet, as the flight crew wouldn’t be able to assist her. This would have required her to buy an expensive extra ticket.“I have travelled my whole life and never had this experience before,” she says. “Eventually, they said they could transfer me to an American Airlines flight. I thought about not accepting the transfer and fighting this. But I was so tired from my trip and I just wanted to get home, so I agreed to the change.”A British Airways spokesperson said: “We want to ensure a seamless flying experience for everyone and we’re sorry that our customer had a negative experience on this occasion. We are aware our customer has expressed concerns regarding her experience and we have reached out to her to discuss further.“We serve hundreds of thousands of customers who require additional assistance every year and while we’re committed to continually improving our service, we work hard to support accessibility requirements throughout their journey.”double quotation markI fly with my rights in my pocket, but our rights continue to be violated. We need to rebrand this as a crisisMorgan says that, because cases like Bullock’s continue to happen, she will keep on fighting. “I fly with my rights in my pocket, but our rights continue to be violated. We need to rebrand this as a crisis.”As for Babalola, she continues to fight KLM. When the Guardian asked the airline to comment on her case, KLM said in a statement: “We regret that an incident occurred involving one of our passengers on the flight from Cape Town to Amsterdam on 26 May. Out of respect for the privacy of both the passenger and our crew, we find it inappropriate to discuss the details of the situation.”Babalola has now engaged a lawyer to help her. “I need to take legal action, because otherwise this abuse of power against disabled people will continue. The experience I had on that KLM flight was distressing, degrading and humiliating. I felt intimidated by the flight crew.” On 19 June, she received a further letter from KLM, saying it was important to the company that all passengers are treated with “the utmost respect and dignity”.“We are disappointed that we fell short of that expectation,” the airline added. It went on to apologise for the fact she hadn’t received the assistance she requested and included “sincere apologies” for her experience. The letter concluded: “We once again apologise for Ms Babalola’s experience on board flight KL598 and are making efforts to ensure that such a situation does not reoccur in the future.”None of the people interviewed for this piece are holding their breath.Explore more on these topicsDisabilityAirline industryFlightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: England gymnast Gabriel Langton suffers nasty fall in Commonwealth Games final | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Session was halted as medical staff attended to Gabriel Langton, who landed head-first during his high bar routine in the men’s team competition
Author: Yara El-Shaboury
Headline: Session was halted as medical staff attended to Gabriel Langton, who landed head-first during his high bar routine in the men’s team competition
Content: England’s Gabriel Langton chalks up prior to his floor routine on day one.Photograph: Naomi Baker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEngland’s Gabriel Langton chalks up prior to his floor routine on day one.Photograph: Naomi Baker/Getty ImagesCommonwealth Games 2026England gymnast Gabriel Langton suffers nasty fall in Commonwealth Games finalTeenager lands head-first during high bar routineCanada win men’s team gold, with England secondYara El-Shabouryat Glasgow International ArenaFri 24 Jul 2026 16.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s bid for a fourth successiveCommonwealth Gamesmen’s artistic gymnastics team title ended with silver after a dramatic final overshadowed by an injury to the teenager Gabriel Langton, who was taken from the arena on a stretcher after a heavy fall from the high bar.The 19-year-old fell head and neck first on to the mat during the final rotation of the team final, bringing competition to a halt as medical staff rushed to his aid. The arena fell silent while Langton received treatment, with fellow gymnasts watching on in visible concern.Commonwealth Games 2026: Canada win men’s gymnastics team final marred by fall – liveRead moreAfter initially lying motionless, Langton responded to medical staff, moving his legs and later his hands. A dozen medical personnel carefully stabilised the England gymnast before lifting him on to a stretcher about 11 minutes after the fall. He was applauded by the crowd as he was taken from the competition floor.The incident came with England locked in a battle with Canada for the team title. At the time of the stoppage, Canada led the standings, narrowly ahead of England, while Australia occupied the bronze-medal position. Scotland remained within touching distance in fourth, with Cyprus fifth and Wales sixth.After Langton’s fall and the lengthy delay, Luke Whitehouse faced the daunting task of competing on the same apparatus immediately after his teammate’s accident. Despite a composed routine under difficult circumstances, he lost his balance on the dismount and finished on the mat, visibly disappointed as he walked away.“When something like that happens, you’ve just got to forget about it and reset,” Whitehouse said on performing after his teammate’s fall. “I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time.“Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It’s one of those things you have to put out of your mind. From what we’ve heard [Langton] is doing OK.”England finished with 238.250, leaving Canada needing 36.450 points from their final three floor routines to secure gold. The Canadians held their nerve with the veteran René Cournoyer opening with 13.500 before Félix Dolci, one of the standout performers of the day, followed with 13.700 to effectively seal the title. Canada finished on 241.400 to claim their first Commonwealth men’s team gold since 2006, upgrading the silver medals they won in 2018 and 2022.England took silver on 238.250, while Australia secured bronze with 235.650 after holding off a stirring late challenge from Scotland, who finished fourth on 234.300. Cyprus placed fifth on 228.350, with Wales sixth on 227.000.Whitehouse, expected to spearhead England’s title defence, made an excellent start by posting an impressive 14.400 on floor exercise. However, halfway through the contest England found themselves fourth behind Canada, Australia and Cyprus after three rotations, with the Canadians leading on 122.200 points.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland steadily clawed their way back into contention as Australia encountered problems on the high bar. Alexander Yolshin-Cash played a key role in the resurgence, producing the best parallel bars score of the evening with a 14.100.Canada’s grip on gold briefly looked vulnerable when the experienced Cournoyer came off the high bar and scored 11.550, allowing England to close the gap. However, Dolci immediately steadied Canadian nerves with the apparatus’ highest score of the night, 14.250, to preserve their slender advantage heading into the final rotation.England responded admirably after Whitehouse’s slight stumble, with Yolshin-Cash producing another confident high bar routine. His score of 13.250 ranked fifth on the apparatus, secured qualification for the individual final and added valuable points to England’s overall total.Scotland also mounted a late push for bronze. Cameron Lynn thrilled the home crowd with a near-flawless high bar routine worth 13.500 before Hamish Carter added 12.350 after sticking his landing. Reuben Ward then scored 13.150, leaving Connor Sullivan needing something special in the final routine. Despite another excellent performance, Scotland fell just 1.350 points short as Australia’s consistency on pommel horse proved decisive.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026GymnasticsCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Duncan Scott shines for Scotland again with 200m individual medley gold  | Swimming | The Guardian
description: Duncan Scott added to his trophy cabinet with gold for Scotland in the men’s 200m individual medley at the Commonwealth Games
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Duncan Scott added to his trophy cabinet with gold for Scotland in the men’s 200m individual medley at the Commonwealth Games
Content: Duncan Scott celebrates his latest medal success for Scotland.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDuncan Scott celebrates his latest medal success for Scotland.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianSwimmingDuncan Scott shines for Scotland again with 200m individual medley goldScott holds off Clareburt and England’s Tom Dean to winAdam Ramsay-Peaty wins 100m breaststroke semi-finalSean Ingleat Tollcross International Swimming CentreFri 24 Jul 2026 17.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are generals from banana republics with fewer medals on their chests than Duncan Scott. And when the pressure was highest at a homeCommonwealth Games, the most decorated Scottish athlete of all time delivered again.On paper it looked like a stacked men’s 200m individual medley, with world and Olympic champions, including New Zealander Lewis Clareburt and England’s Tom Dean, lurking with intent. But Scott had other ideas.Lani Pallister opens Australia’s Commonwealth Games tally with 400m freestyle goldRead moreAfter a strong butterfly, the 29-year-old applied the squeeze on the backstroke and breaststroke and then delivered the coup de grace on the freestyle to take gold in 1min 56.38sec, nearly half a second clear of Clareburt, who took silver, with Dean claiming bronze.To make Scott’s victory even sweeter, he also broke the Commonwealth record. No wonder he lifted his arms up in the air and started to pound his chest like a silverback after leaving the pool. “I was a wee bit nervous before that,” he said. “Being one of the senior members of the team, the onus is kind of me. Those boys made it tough.”View image in fullscreenDuncan Scott glides through the water during the butterfly leg of the 200m individual medley final.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianScott has now won eight Olympic medals, 10 world medals and 14 at the Commonwealth Games. The way he is swimming, he is going to need a bigger medal cabinet by the end of next week.But this is just the start of a gruelling process. At the 2018 Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast, he swam 11 races in five days and won six medals. In Birmingham in 2022 it was 12 in five and he won six more. So when asked how he would celebrate this latest gold, he said he did not know. “Probably an early night,” he eventually replied.View image in fullscreenA happy looking Duncan Scott shows off his gold medal.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianMeanwhile, Dean was happy with his individual bronze, knowing that better chances of winning gold lie ahead. “I have raced Duncan my whole adult career,” he said. “To stand next to him, to walk out with him in front of his crowd, it was something I will never forget. I am fortunate to call him a training partner as well as a friend.”Another star of these Games, Adam Ramsay-Peaty had to work to win his 100m breaststroke semi-final ahead of Jersey’s teenage sensation Filip Nowacki.Ramsay-Peaty was through halfway in a lightning quick 27.40sec but the 18-year-old Nowacki came back at him in the second half. But it was not quite enough as Ramsay-Peaty held on to win by less than half a second in 59.19. Australia’s Sam Williamson finished fastest in the other semi-final in 59.27.Asked about his thoughts on Saturday’s final, Ramsay-Peaty smiled. “I’m not going to shy away from the fact that I want to win,” Ramsay-Peaty replied. “I’m still going to be a scrapper.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty powers through the water during his men’s 100m breaststroke semi-final.Photograph: The GuardianBut Nowacki, who is awaiting his A-Level results in maths, economics and physics, believes he can spring a surprise. “To race arguably the greatest breaststroker of all time is very special,” he said. “Can I beat him? I’m going to say yes. My training’s been progressing really well, so I’m going to give it my best and we’ll see who gets their hand on the wall first.”Elsewhere, it was a great night for Australia, who won four golds. It started on the first race of the night, as Lani Pallister pushed clear in the last 100m to beat New Zealander Erika Fairweather in the 400m freestyle in 3:59.56, with another Australian Hannah Fredericks taking bronze.Just 44 minutes later, Fredericks was back in the pool and had the energy to launch a late surge to win the 200m backstroke ahead of Scotland’s Katie Shanahan in a thriller.Two more golds followed as Australia then won the women’s and men’s 4x100m freestyle relays, with England taking silver in both races.Explore more on these topicsSwimmingCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shirtless heroes, bucket hats and gold: reimagined Games find their glow | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Some big stars are absent, but day one in Glasgow showed the Commonwealth Games have retained plenty of soul
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Some big stars are absent, but day one in Glasgow showed the Commonwealth Games have retained plenty of soul
Content: Australia’s Sam McDaniel drives to the basket to score during his team's 3x3 basketball victory over New Zealand.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAustralia’s Sam McDaniel drives to the basket to score during his team's 3x3 basketball victory over New Zealand.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Shirtless heroes, bucket hats and gold: reimagined Games find their glowSome big stars are absent, but day one in Glasgow showed the Commonwealth Games have retained plenty of soulSean Inglein GlasgowFri 24 Jul 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere will be many extraordinary sights at theseCommonwealth Gamesin Glasgow over the next 10 days. But few, you imagine, will top that of a volunteer ripping his T-shirt off and nosediving under the water, without goggles, to fix a broken rope while Adam Ramsay-Peaty waited on at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre.The crowd, who had watched other volunteers fail to deal with the problem using large nets, cheered. And, after a 10-minute delay, Ramsay-Peaty was back smoking his rivals in the heats of the 100m breaststroke.England’s Mark Swan powerlifts to Games’ first gold by fraction of a pointRead moreSo was the double Olympic champion tempted to jump in and retrieve the item himself? “Definitely not,” he said. “Even if it’s a first – scoreboards break, clocks break – the guys got it together pretty well. Hopefully it doesn’t happen again.”Over at the para powerlifting, meanwhile, there was more confusion as England’sMark Swan won the first gold of these Games– but couldn’t fathom why it was given when he had ended with the same score as Nigeria’s Roland Ezuruike.Only an hour or so later did officials explain that a second decimal point had separated them.But do you know what? Despite these initial teething problems, and a fair number of empty seats, it didn’t matter. These Games might be “reimagined” – which is management speak for “made smaller”. But, as the first full day of action showed, they retain plenty of soul and glow.The soul? That was provided by the Botswanan lawn bowler Diza Mphotho, who delighted the crowd at the indoor SEC arena with his bucket hat and languid style, even if he ended up being on the reverse of a 10-3, 16-1 thrashing by Guernsey’s Jason Greenslade.View image in fullscreenDiza Mphotho during his men’s bowls singles loss to Jason Greenslade.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“It’s very hot in Botswana,” said Mphotho, an IT worker who took up the sport 10 years ago when his mother’s friend told him it could be his passport to see the world. “So I always play in my bucket hat.”Bowls is not big in Botswana. Only about 200 people play it across four clubs. There was a fifth, Mphotho explained, but then a copper mine shut down and the funding dried up. But it has proven life-changing to him.There was one other message Mphotho wanted to impart: he gets 20 days of annual leave a year – and he is using pretty much all of them to play in Glasgow. “We’ve already been here two weeks,” he said. “And it’s completely worth it.”And the glow? That came from watching Swan’s celebration after he bench-pressed 222kg to win gold – a weight that, staggeringly, is more than three times his bodyweight.It has also been some journey for the 25-year-old geordie, who started his powerlifting journey at an event for the Dwarf Sports Association Games, where he lifted 70kg to earn a bronze medal.And it helped that he was roared on by a packed Armadillo Arena, partly because members of the Tartan Army were given four free tickets each to certain events to fill the blank spaces.View image in fullscreenEngland’s Mark Swan celebrates after a successful lift on his way to gold.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianHowever, it is noticeable that there are fewer fans than usual from around the globe. That is largely explained by simple economics. When Glasgow rescued the Games afterVictoria dropped out in 2023, there was no time to build an athletes’ village. And so athletes and officials are staying in hotels and other accommodation, which means a lack of supply – and crazy high prices – for everyone else.One person said they were paying nearly £300 a night for a tiny room in a three-star hotel. And the kicker? It doesn’t even have a window. However, Phil Batty, the chief executive of Glasgow 2026, insists that plenty of people are still coming to Scotland to watch – but are staying outside the city.And despite the empty seats, he insists momentum is building.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’ve got facilities like the velodrome where we’re completely sold out,” he said.“But we have taken bold and brave decisions, like taking netball centre stage in the Hydro for nine days with 21 sessions. A Commonwealth Games of the past would have just had the final and the bronze medal match there.”Insiders have told the Guardian that the 10,000-seater Hydro will look very empty for some netball matches. Batty’s response? “We have sold more tickets for netball than have ever been sold in the history of Scotland. But, yes, there’s still midweek netball tickets for £10 to buy.”There have been some other missteps. When you walk through the city centre it is not obvious that a major event is taking place.That is in striking contrast to Birmingham 2022, when Commonwealth branding was everywhere – and the bull from the opening ceremony became an overnight tourist attraction.View image in fullscreenEngland’s medal favourite Adam Ramsay-Peaty competes in the 100m breaststroke heats.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAYet the sense is that Glasgow is making a decent fist of staging a budget games where many of the big stars, including the Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson, have stayed away.In the arenas, the commentators are enthusiastic, the crowds involved and the music upbeat. Although as the Stone Roses’ Made of Stone segues to another indie classic, it was tempting to ask whether Andy Burnham had hijacked the playlist.But perhaps the abiding memory of day one was watching two young boys being utterly transfixed by Australia’s men’s 3x3 basketball team squeeze past New Zealand 21-15.Their mother, Eilidh Rooney, who paid £150 for four tickets, said it had been worth it. “It’s lower key this year compared to 2014, when the entire city felt alive,” she said. “But there is a great buzz here.”The roar that followed shortly after as Australia celebrated their victory suggested that plenty of others agreed.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pogacar conquers Alpe d’Huez in record climb to win stage 19 and extend Tour de France lead | Tour de France 2026 | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar conquered the famed hairpins of the Alpe d’Huez in a record time as he won stage 19 of the Tour de France to extend his overall lead
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tadej Pogacar conquered the famed hairpins of the Alpe d’Huez in a record time as he won stage 19 of the Tour de France to extend his overall lead
Content: Slovenia's Tadej Pogacar looks to the sky after his incredible stage win on Alpe d’Huez.Photograph: Thibault Camus/Pool AP/APView image in fullscreenSlovenia's Tadej Pogacar looks to the sky after his incredible stage win on Alpe d’Huez.Photograph: Thibault Camus/Pool AP/APTour de France 2026Pogacar conquers Alpe d’Huez in record climb to win stage 19 and extend Tour de France leadSlovenian only second man to win in yellow on mountainLeader opens up gap of more than seven minutesJeremy Whittlein Alpe d'HuezFri 24 Jul 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 19.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTadej Pogacar put further distance between himself and his last remaining rivals, winning the Alpe d’Huez stage of theTour de Franceand extending his overall lead to more than seven minutes.There was a brutal inevitability about the defending Tour champion’s win on the legendary climb of the Alpe, despite all the rumours of illness and gastric problems within his UAE Emirates XRG team.Pogacar’s climbing time, of 35 minutes and 26 seconds, shattered the longstanding record set by Marco Pantani in 1997, by more than a minute.“I don’t know what the time of Pantani was,” he said. “I don’t take too much into that, but I heard that I broke the record, so I’m happy.“I would say this means as much as any other win, but now everyone has emphasised how big this win is, maybe I will start to realise it is quite important.“I just wanted to do a good race and to win. A thirtysomething year record finally broken is good for us.”So feverish was the speculation over Pogacar switching from yellow shorts to black earlier this week, that one French TV commentator even suggested it was to conceal an excess of flatulence. But on the Alpe, it didn’t matter what colour Pogacar’s shorts were: he still won.View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar chases down the lead breakaway group on the Alpe d’Huez ascent.Photograph: Anne-Christine Poujoulat/AFP/Getty ImagesThe only wind emanating from the four-time Tour winner, now close to taking a record-equalling fifth win in Paris on Sunday, came from the metronomic climbing style that took him to a record-breaking ascent of the Alpe’s 21 hairpin bends.The Slovene looked the picture of health as he sped up the 13.8 kilometre climb, the theatre for many of the Tour’s most dramatic finishes, and with one final mountain stage still to come, now seems assured of overall victory in Paris.The old adage, that the Tour is won on the Alpe, was proven again with Pogacar’s latest demolition of his hapless rivals. With 25km left to race, the day’s breakaway led by almost four minutes, but three kilometres from the finish, Pogacar had caught and overtaken them.Pogacar’s sports director, Matxin Fernández, was reduced to tears by his rider’s performance. “I don’t know why they get so emotional,” Pogacar said of his team management. “I don’t cry often. I guess it meant a lot to the team and also the way we are riding as a team, the team spirit we have. It cannot be better, so when we win, the emotions come to the surface.”Huge and rowdy crowds, estimated to be in the region of 500,000, and at times out of control, greeted the riders at the foot of the Alpe. Some had arrived six days in advance, while others seemed too intoxicated to know why they were there in the first place.“It was a crazy atmosphere on the climb,” Pogacar said.The damage done to his rivals was extensive, with Remco Evenepoel the least wounded by the onslaught. The Belgian remains in second place overall, but any hopes of challenging for the final victory are long gone. He and Pogacar’s teammate, Isaac del Toro, are now the only riders within 10 minutes of the race leader.View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar fights through the throng on stage 19.Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Getty ImagesOn another day of desperation for the teams that have yet to taste success in this year’s Tour, a big breakaway took shape on the early climbs of the Bayard and Noyer.In that leading group of 40 were some now familiar names, including past stage winners, Richard Carapaz, Thymen Arensman, winner of two stages in 2025, and the recovering Adam Yates, teammate to Pogacar, who won in Bilbao in 2023.It was a Lazarus-like performance from Yates, who was so sick earlier this week that he was barely able to pedal through the finish line to his team bus after Wednesday’s stage to Voiron. But as soon as the main contenders began to climb the first steep ramps of the Alpe, the stage took on a new look, as Pogacar shifted up a gear.His decisive acceleration came 12km from the summit and immediately left his closest rivals in his wake. After joining forces with Yates, the pair ate into the break’s advantage, until with 10km remaining, Pogacar set off alone.The denouement was obvious. It was a cruel and relentless win, wholly in character with Pogacar’s domination of the Tour. He has taken five wins in 19 stages. Saturday’s “queen” stage, over four of the hardest climbs in the Alps, now offers him the chance to take a sixth. Another victory now seems almost inevitable.Explore more on these topicsTour de France 2026Tour de FranceCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris hits out at Formula One for putting money ahead of drivers | Lando Norris | The Guardian
description: Many drivers are unhappy with the new regulations and Lando Norris, the reigning world champion, said: ‘F1’s gone too heavily led by the fact it’s a business’
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Many drivers are unhappy with the new regulations and Lando Norris, the reigning world champion, said: ‘F1’s gone too heavily led by the fact it’s a business’
Content: Lando Norris has spoken out about his frustrations this season.Photograph: Boglárka Bodnár/EPAView image in fullscreenLando Norris has spoken out about his frustrations this season.Photograph: Boglárka Bodnár/EPALando NorrisLando Norris hits out at Formula One for putting money ahead of driversMany drivers also unhappy with new regulations‘F1’s gone too heavily led by the fact it’s a business’Giles Richardsat the HunagroringFri 24 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLando Norris has delivered a scathing critique of Formula One and its management for prioritising making money over sporting considerations when forming the sport’s new regulations. The world champion argued that the drivers should have been more involved in the process.Norris is amongmany drivers who have been clear this seasonhe is unhappy with the new regulations, their focus on energy management and how it has affected negatively their enjoyment of driving. It is a problem he believes had been created because F1 framed the rules in order to attract new engine manufacturers into the sport.‘Eyes forward now’: George Russell upbeat after Mercedes solve engine problemRead more“The thing that’s a shame is that Formula One’s gone too heavily led by the fact it’s a business nowadays and not how can you make the sport the best possible,” he said. “It’s how can you just make the most money as a business and that’s just not what it should simply be. That’s not how a sport should be run.”The use of an almost 50-50 split in electrical power and the internal combustion engine is understood to have been central in attracting manufacturers such as Audi and Honda into F1 this season. However, it has proved hugely unpopular with drivers, who now have to manage their use of energy rather than being able to race flat out and has introduced some variables into performance influenced by the algorithm that governs the deployment of electrical power.Norris believes drivers’ complaints were being listened to but they did not carry great weight against the financial imperative he felt was driving the sport.“They listen but you can’t just change your engine in the middle of the year and you can’t change it even with one or two years’ notice because it’s not about making the best performance of a car … it’s a business,” he said. “Everyone wants to make money, so in order for Audi and other teams to come in we had to change these things. It’s a shame, it should never have been like that. But that’s how businesses work.“The biggest voice should always be ours as drivers and that’s not because we’re selfish in saying that but because we have the best idea of how racing should be, how it can be, what’s possible, what’s not. We would just want the best for everything and at the minute, we don’t.“We have very, very little say and a lot more of it’s done because if you can have Audi and other teams in it, it’s a bigger win than the drivers being happy.”The shortcomings of the new regulations were shown starkly at the last two rounds at Silverstone and Spa. Both circuits are considered energy-starved, leading to a chorus of complaints over race weekends, and at Spa the lack of power left one of the great tracks an anodyne affair.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen was second in Friday’s first practice.Photograph: Marco Canoniero/ShutterstockAt the Hungaroring this weekend there will at least be some respite from the issue, with the preponderance of corners ensuring plentiful recharging and that the race to be run at full pace in what will likely be a tightly contested fight.The Mercedes engine advantage will not be so pronounced on the tightly twisting circuit, where Ferrari and Red Bull will expect strong form, with Ferrari’s pace out of the corners a major boon in the last race before the summer break.In first practice, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc topped the timesheets from the Red Bull of Max Verstappen with Lewis Hamilton in third. In the second session Hamilton was on top with Leclerc in second and McLaren’s Lando Norris third. Antonelli was in 13th place and his Mercedes teammate George Russell in fifth.Explore more on these topicsLando NorrisFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Presence of Brendon McCullum affecting England’s hunt for a new Test coach | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The hunt for the next coach of the England men’s Test team is being complicated by the need for the new appointee to work alongside the man he would be replacing, Brendon McCullum
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: The hunt for the next coach of the England men’s Test team is being complicated by the need for the new appointee to work alongside the man he would be replacing, Brendon McCullum
Content: Brendon McCullum is still the England white-ball coach and will work alongside whoever fills the Test vacancy.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrendon McCullum is still the England white-ball coach and will work alongside whoever fills the Test vacancy.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersEngland cricket teamPresence of Brendon McCullum affecting England’s hunt for a new Test coachNew appointee will have to work alongside ODI coachJoe Root emerges as frontrunner for Test captaincySimon BurntonandMatt HughesFri 24 Jul 2026 14.01 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe hunt for the next coach of the England men’s Test team is being complicated by the need for the new appointee to work alongside the man he would be replacing,Brendon McCullum, rather than taking full control of both red- and white-ball squads.Some high-profile candidates have been unwilling to work within such a setup, either because they want full oversight over the senior men’s teams or because of the unique ­challenge of working alongside ­the person who was sacked as Test coach earlier this month.England’s white-ball success risks baking in a divide with future Test setup | Ali MartinRead moreThe issue is exacerbated by next year’s schedule: though the Test side will be the focus of attention until the end of the Ashes in early August they would then take a backseat to the ODI team before the World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia in October and November. Even with the Ashes on the horizon the white-ball coach would be expected to argue that multi-format players, including the current white-ball captain, Harry Brook, should play the five-game ODI series against Pakistan that starts the international summer, while the Test coach could demand they concentrate on the one-off Test against Bangladesh that begins less than 48 hours after its conclusion.As a result the process of appointing a new coach is taking longer than first hoped. Rob Key, the ­managing director of men’s cricket at the ­England and WalesCricketBoard, who is leading the recruitment ­process, was initially optimistic that someone would be in place before the three-match Test series against ­Pakistan that starts on 19 August. But the ECB is increasingly resigned to – and relaxed about – the process dragging on beyond that date. Once that series ends on 13 September there is a gap of 87 days before the team is next in action, when their tour of South Africa starts with a three-day game against a CSA Invitational XI in ­Durban, and sources say they are determined to pursue the best appointment rather than the quickest.View image in fullscreenJoe Root stepped in as Test captain during the series against New Zealand earlier in the summer and seems likely to do so again.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe ECB has started the process of meeting leading candidates, and expect to hold multiple rounds of interviews over several weeks. ­Justin Langer, the Australian who is ­coaching Manchester Super Giants in the Hundred, is believed to have fallen from favour, with the former England batter Jonathan Trott, the Glamorgan head coach, Richard ­Dawson, and McCullum’s former New Zealand teammate Stephen Fleming among those still in contention.If there is no permanent appointment before the Pakistan series, Key will name both an interim coach and an interim captain, with ­Marcus Trescothick – who worked as ­assistant coach under ­ McCullum – the presumptive frontrunner to take the coaching role, though ­alternatives are being considered, and Joe Root the clear frontrunner to lead the team once again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter retiring from international cricket earlier this month, Ben Stokes anointed Brook as his permanent successor as captain and Brook has publicly indicated his willingness to take the job on. But the 27-year-old also leads the white-ball teams and is doing so with such success that there is no desire to distract him unnecessarily. It is unlikely that anyone will be asked to captain in all three formats given England’s congested schedule – the white-ball side could be playing a T20 against Sri Lanka at Southampton’s Utilita Bowl in ­September within 48 hours of the Pakistan series ending at Edgbaston.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamBrendon McCullumJoe RootCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rampant Wigan sweep to derby win as St Helens’ Rowley sacking fails to spark change | Rugby league | The Guardian
description: St Helens began life after head coach Paul Rowley with a heavy 38-16 Super League defeat at rivals Wigan
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: St Helens began life after head coach Paul Rowley with a heavy 38-16 Super League defeat at rivals Wigan
Content: Bevan French touches down Wigan’s first try against St Helens.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBevan French touches down Wigan’s first try against St Helens.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockRugby leagueRampant Wigan sweep to derby win as St Helens’ Rowley sacking fails to spark changeSuper League: Wigan 38-16 St HelensSaints thrashed day after sacking head coach RowleyAaron Bowerat Brick Community StadiumFri 24 Jul 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 20.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere may only be eight miles between rugby league’s two greatest rivals but in sporting terms,Wigan Warriorsand St Helens are simply worlds apart right now.The most tumultuous of weeks for the Saints ended in the way many it expected to: with a straightforward derby defeat. There was no shortage of effort, but there are bigger problems at a club that expects greatness – which is why Paul Rowley was relieved of his duties as Saints coach after nine months in charge on the eve of this game.Dismissed solicitor is still acting for footballers in brain injury court caseRead moreThe timing was perhaps a surprise; the decision, not so much. It simply didn’t work out, with the Saints regressing under Rowley to such an extent that he became their shortest-serving coach in 50 years. His successor has a huge job on his hands; not just to make the playoffs this year, but to oversee a rebuild beyond.The very fact there was some talk ofSt Helenskeeping this respectable representing a successful outcome for a club world champions just three years ago should be humiliating for all associated with their downfall. Yes, they are struggling with injuries, but their lowly league position underlines the size of the task Rowley’s successor has ahead.But that talk is for another day. Here, this was Wigan’s night – and there is perhaps no player that emphasises the gulf between these two legendary clubs quite like the man who stole the show here: the Warriors’ talismanic half-back, Bevan French.Back from a hamstring injury, French scored one try and created another four and added further weight to the argument he is Super League’s greatest-ever overseas player. It was in the balance at the break, with Saints’ players providing a response to Rowley’s sacking to trail by six at half-time.View image in fullscreenWigan’s Adam Keighran celebrates a try against St Helens.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockTries for Jacob Douglas and Jack Welsby put them ahead on two separate occasions either side of French’s try. The Australian then produced two superb assists for Zach Eckersley to put Wigan in front; they didn’t go behind again as they ran riot after the break, with the Saints’ young bench unable to keep up amid three more injuries to add to their mounting list.But tellingly, even after an ultimately comfortable win, Wigan’s coach demanded more. “There’s elements we can do better,” Matt Peet said. “It shows how far we’ve come as a group though that we could still get the win.”It was closely contested in the first half. The second was a mismatch. French teed up Oli Partington to score four minutes after the restart, before the half-back decided to let someone else make mischief for a brief moment, as Harry Smith’s kick sent Partington over for a second as the contest rapidly moved away from the Saints.Adam Keighran then claimed a kick from – who else – French before Wigan’s maestro was withdrawn to a standing ovation with 15 minutes left. Lewis Murphy scored a late consolation for the Saints but realistically, there is only one of these sides heading to Old Trafford for the Grand Final in October: and it is not the Saints.Their interim coach, Eamon O’Carroll, was right to praise the effort his side displayed post-match. England full-back Welsby’s performance offered some hope too. But the problems at this club run much deeper, and Rowley’s replacement will have watched this contest from wherever in the world he is currently based and seen a club with a transitional period ahead of them.In contrast, Wigan look equipped to go the distance again this year under Peet. They are a beacon of consistency while the winds of change will blow through the Saints at hurricane-strength force in the coming months. Two great clubs, with two very different autumns ahead.Explore more on these topicsRugby leagueWigan WarriorsSt HelensSuper LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You need to evolve’: Enzo Maresca plots life after Pep at Manchester City | Enzo Maresca | The Guardian
description: The Italian does not shy away from the task of following a legend in Pep Guardiola but his previous time at the club may help him
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The Italian does not shy away from the task of following a legend in Pep Guardiola but his previous time at the club may help him
Content: ‘I’m confident we can do a great job,’ Enzo Maresca said as he returned to Manchester City to replace Pep Guardiola.Photograph: Manchester City FCView image in fullscreen‘I’m confident we can do a great job,’ Enzo Maresca said as he returned to Manchester City to replace Pep Guardiola.Photograph: Manchester City FCEnzo Maresca‘You need to evolve’: Enzo Maresca plots life after Pep at Manchester CityItalian does not shy away from the task of following a legend but his previous time at the club may help himJamie JacksonFri 24 Jul 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRelaxed and tanned, Enzo Maresca offered a warm note with his first words to the media as the manager ofManchester City, who must somehow follow the generational Pep Guardiola. “Before we start, I would like to send a message and a big hug to Kevin Keegan’s family for this moment,” said the Italian in tribute to a football legend, following his death on Monday.Keegan, of course, was a former City manager who had at Newcastle famously locked horns with Sir Alex Ferguson when he led Manchester United, the fierce rivals of Maresca’s new team. When the 46-year-old, sat on the dais occupied for 10 mostly glittering years by Guardiola, offered an unsolicited reference to Ferguson – and Arsène Wenger – you could see he comprehended the mammoth task before him.Elliot Anderson lauds City as ‘kings of Manchester’ after £116m Forest transferRead moreHow do you follow the man who claimed 20 trophies in a decade and who ranks alongside Ferguson? Well, by mentioning, and so trying to tame, the elephant in the room. “The history of the manager with many years in the same club always struggled a little bit. After Sir Alex, after Arsène,” Maresca said. “But also, it’s a challenge to try to do the right things immediately for this organisation, for the fans, for everyone.”Speaking in front of a giant “Welcome back Enzo” billboard, a reference to his previous leading of City’s elite development squad in 2020-21 as well as his stint as Guardiola’s assistant manager in the 2022-23 treble season, Maresca would have been aware the font of goodwill will not prove deep if results go south. Certainly not from that most fickle of constituencies – fans. So Maresca cutely pointed to the patience of City’s chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, and his executive. “This club has had three managers in 17 years,” he said. “This is not normal, so this is one of the things that I’m confident we can do a great job and continue to do the job that has been done in the last years. Roberto [Mancini] was here, then Manuel [Pellegrini] and then Pep – for 10 years.”View image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca with Pep Guardiola at a June 2023 Manchester City training session.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAMancini’s tenure began in December 2009, ended with his sacking in May 2013, and was angst-ridden: anathema to al-Mubarak and his chief executive, Ferran Soriano. If Mancini could be volatile, Pellegrini proved serene, and Guardiola was, simply, a genius. Al-Mubarak’s and Soriano’s experience of Maresca during his two previous seasons at City obviously convinced them that he is the full package: an accomplished football man who is of equable character.Yet Maresca’s exit from his previous post at Chelsea on New Year’s Day ended with an apology from him, and City paying the west London club £17m in compensation. Maresca’s shutters came down for the first – and only – time when his conduct was raised. “I feel quite lucky in terms of my former clubs – Leicester, Chelsea – I think we did a great job,” he said. “In both clubs, the identity of the team was clear, the success of the team was clear, and I feel very lucky to be part of these clubs. But now we are here today. That is the most important thing, just about City. And nothing to add.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaresca says managing Manchester City ‘a privilege’ but admits challenge of following GuardiolaRead moreMaresca made Leicester Championship champions and the next season took Chelsea to fourth in the Premier League and a Conference League triumph before claiming the Fifa Club World Cup last summer, a 3-0 evisceration of Paris Saint-Germain in the final a calling card that may well have sealed the City job.He talked of “titles” for the coming season. To aid this mission, Maresca has Elliot Anderson, a £116m buy from Nottingham Forest, to patrol midfield, and potentially Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, who shone for Morocco at the World Cup, to further bolster this department. He also retains an interest in Malo Gusto, one of his right-backs when at Chelsea, and if Omar Marmoush leaves, the market will be entered for a similar, pacy forward.One player Maresca certainly does not wish to lose is the peerless Rodri, who lifted the World Cup for Spain on Sunday and received the Golden Ball, and whose control of a contest in the ever-more frantic domestic game is priceless. The 30-year-old will have surgery on a back problem on Monday. The word is it is not too serious, though he will miss out when City host Bournemouth on the opening weekend of the season. The more important date is 1 September, when the transfer window closes: will Real Madrid have made a move for a footballer who has a year left on his terms and is declining to sign the new deal offered by City?Of more immediate concern for Maresca is flying out on Tuesday for a pre‑season tour of Asia that features matches with Inter in Hong Kong and K-League All Stars and Atlético Madrid in Seoul. For the trip Maresca will have back City’s A-listers who exited the World Cup early, including Josko Gvardiol, Mateo Kovacic and Abdukodir Khusanov.View image in fullscreenElliot Anderson was a key player for England at the World Cup and was Manchester City’s first signing of the summer.Photograph: Marta Lavandier/AP“I’m working at the moment with many young players,” he said. “That is always good because they are full of energy and some of them are very good. The last group of players are going to join three or four days before the Community Shield and we will have all the squad.” After that Cardiff game with Arsenal on Sunday 16 August, the bid to successfully succeed Guardiola begins in earnest.“You need to adapt, evolve,” Maresca added in reference to his playing style. “Set pieces, man to man – it’s a little bit the direction where football is going. We managers, it’s our duty to find solutions.” We are about to discover how good he is at this.Explore more on these topicsEnzo MarescaManchester CityFootball tacticsPep GuardiolafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: When is an apology not an apology? When it comes from an AI boss with an out-of-control chatbot | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: An incident in which an autonomous OpenAI agent hacked a startup either confirms that the end is nigh – or that the product is just amazingly sophisticated, says the Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: An incident in which an autonomous OpenAI agent hacked a startup either confirms that the end is nigh – or that the product is just amazingly sophisticated, says the Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: The OpenAI Ceo, Sam Altman, in Sun Valley, Idaho in July 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe OpenAI Ceo, Sam Altman, in Sun Valley, Idaho in July 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)When is an apology not an apology? When it comes from an AI boss with an out-of-control chatbotMarina HydeAn incident in which an autonomous OpenAI agent hacked a startup either confirms that the end is nigh – or that the product is just amazingly sophisticatedFri 24 Jul 2026 08.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTShareThroughout history, many things have been seen by terrified populaces as a harbinger of doom. Acomet. Acrow on the battlefield. A solar eclipse. A mutant livestock birth. Yet times move on. In the modern era, the leading harbinger of doom is literally any picture of the OpenAI CEO,Sam Altman, attached to a news story. You know it’s not going to be good, right? You know that by the time you’ve read it, you’ll be begging to go back to the time when the worst thing that could happen to us at the hands of the techlords was just some democracy-subversion, or childhood destruction, usually followed by Mark Zuckerberg putting on a suit and claiming: “We will learn from this.”Anyway: a lot of pictures of Sam Altman in the news of late. Most recently, this week, one darkened the skies alongside the tale of how an OpenAI autonomous agentwent rogueduring a supposedly sandboxed/guardrailed test, and hacked a major startup that functions as a repository of coding information. (I’m slightly obsessed with the fact that the startup in question is called Hugging Face, adding weight to my suspicion that some vast, tweely benign emoji is the last face humanity will see before it dies.)Needless to say, an affectlessOpenAI statementbroke the news. “We are sharing preliminary findings at this stage to help defenders understand what happened and to help calibrate on what models are now capable of,” this droned calmly, trundling on toward its inevitable “learnings”. “We’re improving and adding stronger protections around future training and evaluations.” It’s such a particular tone, isn’t it, dressed in the psychopathically desiccated language of management speak. Like having to listen to a homicidal sex criminal talk about killing people by “close of play”, and then “circling back” to victims to remove a trophy.Then again, for a company that likes to present itself as the planet’s leading agent of revolutionary prosperity when things go right,OpenAIlapses tellingly into the passive when things go wrong. Bad things seem to happen to it, not because of it, at which point it takes on the role of tirelessly unflappable investigator, like one of those firemen who moonlights as a serial arsonist.Amazingly, it was possible to detect even a note of self-congratulation in OpenAI’s take on the whole situation. “We consider this incident to be an unprecedented cyber-incident,” the company’s statement remarked, “involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities.” I don’t know what you’d call this general vibe for Earthlings. Death by humblebrag? I increasingly feel we’ll find out the answer to the question “What’s the worst that can happen?” in a blog post from OpenAI entitled “OpenAI first to discover the worst that can happen”. Already, a significant section of AI watchers are convinced that the only reason OpenAI would tell the world about this incident is as a marketing tool, or even a come-and-get-me plea for regulation that will in effect protect them and burn the bridge behind them for smaller competitors.After all, these are testing times for the firm. This is a month in which Open AI was discovered to be exploiting a legal loophole to sell its advanced AI modelsto Chinese tech firms blacklisted by the Pentagon. S&P Global Ratings cited OpenAI as a “key credit risk” in the course of downgrading US tech giant Oracle to BBB-, which is one notch above junk status. And it seems to be on track to miss its five-year ad revenue projection by90 – NINETY – per cent. Which, without getting too financially technical, feels like a lot of per cent. And it’s not great news on the hardware front, either, withApple suing it, alleging that its consumer hardware plans are based on stolen intellectual property. Meanwhile China’s much cheaper provider, DeepSeek, is believed to be preparing for an IPO, maybe even filing this year.Back to the old worst-that-can-happen question again, though, with a reminder that the Pentagon dramaticallybinned off and threatened to destroyanother AI firm, Anthropic, earlier this year after itresisted loosening its ethical guidelinesthat prevented use of its technology for, among other things, autonomous lethal weapons. Needless to say, a certain more relaxed company was only too glad to step into the breach, with OpenAI initially claiming its deal had the same guardrails as Anthropic’s, before it emerged – inevitably –that it didn’t.No doubt no one too invested wishes to extrapolate too much from the Hugging Face incident. Yet the fact is that AI safety researchers have already spent literally years warning of three particularly dangerous scenarios: deception (when the model decides against solving tasks honestly in favour of achieving the goal via any means necessary); reward hacking (when the model finds a way to maximise its score without actually doing the work it was told to do); and escaping oversight (let’s just say in this case that no one at OpenAI seems to have realised what was happening for an entire weekend). All of these were part of the latest incident.In terms of what happens next, something tells you that we will not be experiencing a downturn in photos ofSam Altmanattached to news reports. The co-founder of Hugging Face said it should serve as a “wake-up call” to the industry. Maybe! As I think I’ve mentioned before, at university I had a friend who pressed snooze on his alarm clock every 10 minutes for eight-and-a-half hours, which feels a lot like the way this particular industry experiences its wake-up calls. Definitely getting up when the next one goes, seriously, I promise …skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina Hyde is a Guardian columnistMarina Hyde’s new book, What a Time to be Alive!, is out in September (Guardian Faber Publishing, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy atguardianbookshop.com.
