title: If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: Forced labor is a problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at all
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Forced labor is a problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at all
Content: Shipping containers at the port of Tacoma in Washington state on 4 March 2025. Trump said his latest round of tariffs was imposed to fight forced labor.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShipping containers at the port of Tacoma in Washington state on 4 March 2025. Trump said his latest round of tariffs was imposed to fight forced labor.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsIf Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the worldEduardo PorterForced laborisa problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at allUS politics live – latest updatesFri 24 Jul 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 14.26 EDTShareDon’t believe theTrump administration’s rationale for its new volley oftariffsagainst everybody.The new levies, ostensibly to punish countries for failing to do enough to curb forced labor, switched on at 12.01am on Friday, to coincide with the expiration of a temporary 10% blanket duty thatDonald Trumpimposed in February, ostensibly to protect the United States from a balance-of-payments crisis.That duty was imposed right afterthe supreme court struck downtariffs the president unleashed on US trading partners last year on the also spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies.The shifting justifications alone underscore how Trump’s arguments are bullshit. But the specific nature of the latest accusation truly takes the cake.Trump accused of using forced labor as ‘convenient’ justification for tariffsRead moreThe US is arguing that tariffs of 10% or 12.5% are justified against 60 trading partners because they import stuff made with forced labor, unfairly undercutting American producers. But the charge omits that forced labor is not only prevalent across the US. It is also actively enforced by the state.Americans import lots of stuff made with forced labor: $170bn worth of imported goods are at risk of being tainted at some stage along the supply chain, according to theGlobal Slavery Index(GSI), from raw materials through to finished products. In 2023, this was the most among the countries in the G20.It includes electronics imported from China and Malaysia; clothing from India, Vietnam and Bangladesh; fish from Ghana; and timber from Russia, Brazil and Peru. The mining of essential minerals used in many electronics the US buys from abroad, from cobalt and copper to lithium and nickel, is rife with allegations of human rights abuses.To be sure, until recently the US was the only country that explicitly prohibited importing goods made with forced, convict or indentured labor. Still, the GSI reports no evidence that penalties are enforced against companies that fail to comply with reporting mandates, due diligence or other procurement regulations.Then there’s the issue of forced labor at home. There were 1.1 million people living in modern slavery in the US on any given day in 2021, according to the GSI, mostly doing domestic work, or toiling in agriculture, construction, retail, hospitality and illicit activities.That amounts to 3.3 forced workers for every thousand people in the population, which is more than in many of the countries Trump wants to punish. In the Netherlands and Germany, there are 0.6 forced workers per thousand people. In Britain there are 1.8.Canada also has a law on the books prohibiting imports made with forced labor. The prevalence of slave labor in Canada is only 1.8 per thousand people. Still, it just got hit with a 10% tariff because according to the US trade representative it is not doing enough to enforce the law. (The European Unionwill ban importsthat involve forced labor starting in 2027.)But here is the real rub: a significant share of modern slavery in the US is enforced by the state.The US stands out among the world’s democracies by allowingforced labor in prisons. And there isno legal obstacleto export goods made by prisoners forced to work against their will.The 13th amendmentto the constitution bans slavery and involuntary servitude, but it exempts work “as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted”. In Alabama prisons, they call the forced labor “mandatory chores”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAbout 800,000 of the 1.2 million people in state and federal prisons work,according to a reportin 2022 by the American Civil Liberties Union and the University of Chicago – often against their will, under the threat of further punishment. Incarcerated workers, the report adds, “are under the complete control of their employers, and they have been stripped of even the most minimal protections against labor exploitation and abuse”.Most work for the prisons themselves and other government businesses. In Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and Texas, more than 10,000 prisoners are assigned to agricultural work on penal plantations or prison farms, according to the ACLU report. They are also often farmed out to the private sector. In Alabama, according to aninvestigation by the Associated Press, they were leased out to at least 500 private businesses between 2018 and mid-March 2024.Prisoners toilinpoultry processing plantsand work in the kitchens of some of the biggestfast-food chains. They cook, wash dishes, fix plumbing and clean buildings. They are paid pennies an hour. And their wages are often garnished by the state.In seven southern states – Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas – almost all work by prisoners remains unpaid.If he is so inclined, Trump could help the fight against slave labor by taking a hard line against the US’ssouthern states, which generally raise less tax revenue and thus rely more on “free” work by the incarcerated to both operate prisons and generate revenue for the public sector.The ACLU report estimated that the incarcerated produce stuff worth more than $2bn a year and provide $9bn worth of services to their prisons.Other countries could help by slapping some tariffs on American goods to retaliate against these blatantly unfair practices.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsForced labourDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS prisonsTariffsLaw (US)commentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: History shrugs off Keir and makes room for brilliant Kerr  | John Crace | The Guardian
description: A low-key PM leaves the stage briskly, while a breathtaking athlete misses out on the attention he deserves
Author: John Crace
Headline: A low-key PM leaves the stage briskly, while a breathtaking athlete misses out on the attention he deserves
Content: Another one bites the dust … the press photographs a dead mouse caught by Larry the cat.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenAnother one bites the dust … the press photographs a dead mouse caught by Larry the cat.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PADigested weekUK newsDigested week: History shrugs off Keir and makes room for brilliant KerrJohn CraceA low-key PM leaves the stage briskly, while a breathtaking athlete misses out on the attention he deservesFri 24 Jul 2026 07.54 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.21 EDTShareMondayAnd so it was over. You normally get a bit more notice when a prime minister is about to deliver their resignation speech outside No 10. The buildup. The sense of occasion.Keir Starmer did things differently.No sooner had “Hot Podium Guy” set up the lectern in Downing Street than Keir was out the front door. As if he couldn’t wait for it all to be over. His speech was done in little more than five minutes.There was no David Cameron confected nonchalance. No tears as there were with Theresa May. No unconcealed bitterness and resentment like Boris Johnson. No bewilderment at the speed of the ending like Liz Truss. And no symbolic rainstorm as with Rish Sunak.Keir said he was going with good grace and he looked as though he meant it. He may still feel angry at the way some of his cabinet turned on him, but it was no longer consuming his every waking minute. What was done was done. He would miss the attention but could see the upside of no longer being the bloke who got woken up at 4am to be told of Donald Trump’s latest efforts to start world war three.Despite the rapid turnover of prime ministers in the last 10 years, there is still something quite poignant about these moments. To see the very public end of a frontline political career. Keir did his best to cement his legacy by saying he had left the country in a better place than he had found it. Which was probably true. He just hadn’t changed the country enough. Or given us a reason to believe in him. And now it was like watching him being airbrushed out of history.From now on, anything that goes wrong for Andy will be Keir’s fault. And anything that goes right, Andy will take the credit for. It was always thus.View image in fullscreen‘I guess this is our 15 minutes of fame.’Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/GettyTuesdayWe’re going to have to reset the clock. Coming in to theWorld Cup, all the talk was of ending “60 years of hurt”. Now we’re going to have to up that to “64 years of hurt” for the next tournament in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. I feel like I really should know better, but this time round I did allow myself to believe that this might be the year when we got to the final and maybe even win it.A team that seemed to be able to play as a team and a manager with the nous to be able to find a way to win matches that we appeared to be losing. Then camethe Argentina semi-final. It was like watching Spurs again. Mind you, I knew the game was up when we took the lead. It was far too early in the second half. Far too much time to think about all the ways they could screw it up.The only way we were ever going to win that game was to keep the score at 0-0 until injury time and then go for the winner. Whose idea it was to try and defend for the last 40 minutes is still not clear.I was just screaming at the TV for England to carry on playing in the way that had got them the lead and had kept Lionel Messi relatively quiet. Desperate for someone on the pitch to realise that another way to have won the game was to score a second goal.Still, we did get to participate in the most entertaining match of the whole World Cup when we took on France inthe third-place playoff. Not that we should read too much into the 6-4 scoreline other than that it was a joy to watch what was basically a friendly between two teams that were demob happy. And we did get to miss out on Trump making a fool of himself by trying to gatecrash the celebrations. Swings and roundabouts.View image in fullscreenBukayo Saka (centre) celebrates with Jude Bellingham and Reece James during the 2026 World Cup third-place match between France and England.Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/AFP/GettyWednesdayThis time last year, Reform was setting the political agenda. While Labour and the Tories seemed to have shut up shop, having decided the public must have been as fed up with politics as they were,Nigel Farageand co were dominating the headlines with new policy announcements every week. Now it seems that the two main parties are trying not to make the same mistake again.Andy Burnham’s government is dripping us a new policy every day while Kemi Badenoch has become desperate to get television airtime at every opportunity. The latest is to tell us that she doesn’t really trust Andy. Who would have guessed?As for Reform, it appears to have stalled somewhat. From leading the polls it now finds itself neck and neck with Labour in many samples and it feels more and more as if Nige can’t stand the level of scrutiny he is coming under with regard to his own finances. Ever sincethe Guardian revealedhe had received a £5m gift from the Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, Nige has rather gone to ground. Refusing to do regular press conferences, taking no questions from the media and reduced to posting videos on social media from the middle of random fields. Moreover, his financial affairs are becoming more opaque the more he tries to explain them. First the £5m was to pay for his security, then a gift. Now it is alleged it was a downpayment on his demand for £1m a year to stand as an MP for Clacton. All this before we get to the donations both in kind and cash from the convicted fraudsterGeorge Cottrell and his mum, Fiona. It’s not very Man of the People.Also, despite protestations to the contrary, it becomes more and more clear that Reform is really a one-man band. Dicky Tice is a halfwit, Robert Jenrick a liability and Zia Yusuf so dislikable that even Reform constituency associations don’t want him to stand as their MP. All of which seems to be getting to Nige. This week he turned up at a rally – if you can call it that – in Norfolk and appeared as bored as the 200 people in the audience. Just a rehash of some of his favourite lines that we’ve all heard before. Nothing new to say. Just a need for some attention. And no questions from anyone. He’s desperate for all the talk about his finances to go away but the more he deflects, the greater the interest. The Reform bubble might just be bursting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThursdayRegular readers of this column will have realised that I was away two weeks ago while visiting my daughter in Minneapolis. At least that was the plan. But a couple of days before we were due to fly, my wife tripped on an uneven pavement and broke her shoulder. So we had to stay at home. Chemo can make the bones more brittle, so that’s another thing to blame cancer for.The charge sheet gets ever longer. It was meant as a short trip – I was going for four days, my wife for eight – but I was still gutted. This was the second trip to the US we have had to cancel in the past year and we are yet to see Anna’s new house – she moved in the middle of last year – or to meet her new dog, Pearl.I have also yet to discover whether I will actually be allowed into the US or if I will be put on the first return flight home. Fingers crossed that border security have better things to do than read satirical sketches about the president in the Guardian. We are now planning/hoping/not counting our chickens that we can get to Minnesota for Christmas. So I guess I will find out then. Maybe Trump will still be too moany about the midterm election results to bother with the odd UK journalist.Talking of dogs, we have also had a massive disappointment. We had made it down to the last two to rehome a six-year-old cockapoo called Tinka whose owner had died unexpectedly. We did get to meet Tinka once and take her for a walk. She was very different to Herbie, much more nervy and insecure. But we had fallen in love with her on the spot and had dared to look forward to making her a part of our lives. But it was not to be.So the hunt goes on. If any of you knows of a house-trained cockapoo that is in need of a home or even a cockapoo puppy that nobody wants, then please do get in touch. We are both feeling very much dog deprived. The last year has been unremittingly shit. We are due a break.FridayMaybe it was the excitement of the third place playoff and the buildup to the World Cup final. Maybe it’s just that the UK no longer cares that much about athletics. The Commonwealth Games start today and they barely register on the public consciousness.Ticket sales are sluggish and they aren’t even being broadcast on terrestrial TV. When I was young they were almost as big a deal as the Olympics. Probably because it was the one Games back then when we won a shedload of medals.But even so, I can’t help feeling that Josh Kerr hasn’t got quite the credit he deserves forbreaking the world recordfor the mile at the London Stadium last Saturday. A remarkable achievement by any standard, but all the more so because he beat the record set by Hicham El Guerrouj in 1999 by nearly half a second. A breathtaking piece of running that had been more than a year in the planning. Kerr had dedicated his whole season – he called it Project 222 because that’s the precise number of seconds he needed to run to finish in 3.42 – to this one race.From March this year, he was telling the world what he planned to do. The time and place he would achieve sporting immortality. And yet … While most papers covered the world record on the night, Kerr seems to have rather slipped out of the British public’s mind since. As if, everyone was thinking, “That’s nice”, before forgetting about it.The US media seem far more impressed, with the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both having written in-depth analysis of how Kerr did it. All very different from the late 70s and early 80s when Steve Ovett and Sebastian Coe were regularly swapping the mile record. Back then almost everyone had a favourite – mine was Ovett; I found Coe unbearably smug. Still do, in fact – and their races didn’t just lead the sports pages, they made front-page news as well.They were both personalities as well as athletics greats. Instantly recognisable. Josh Kerr could walk into a pub and there’s a fair chance no one would know who he was. So let’s hear it for Josh. I’m biased, of course. I used to run myself. Though my best 10K time was 10 minutes outside the world record. Call this the start of a campaign for Josh to win this year’s sports personality of the year. Let’s face it. No other athlete is going to come close to achieving what he has.View image in fullscreenTardis to Charles: What planet are you from?Photograph: François Nel/GettyExplore more on these topicsUK newsDigested weekKeir StarmerWorld CupWorld Cup 2026Nigel FaragecommentShareReuse this content

title: Johnny Depp is playing Scrooge? I am not here for his big Hollywood comeback | Johnny Depp | The Guardian
description: ‘It’s good to be back,’ says the actor in a new trailer for the forthcoming Ebenezer. Has everyone forgotten about the ghosts of his past?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: ‘It’s good to be back,’ says the actor in a new trailer for the forthcoming Ebenezer. Has everyone forgotten about the ghosts of his past?
Content: ‘The master of misfits returns’ … Johnny Depp dressed as Ebenezer Scrooge at Comic-Con International in San Diego on Thursday.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The master of misfits returns’ … Johnny Depp dressed as Ebenezer Scrooge at Comic-Con International in San Diego on Thursday.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Variety/Getty ImagesJohnny DeppJohnny Depp is playing Scrooge? I am not here for his big Hollywood comebackStuart Heritage‘It’s good to be back,’ says the actor in a new trailer for the forthcoming Ebenezer. Has everyone forgotten about the ghosts of his past?Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.11 EDTShareIt is fair to say that, professionally speaking, Johnny Depp has had a quiet few years. Since he andAmber Heardsued each other amid a whirlwind of genuinely ugly accusations in 2019, and went to trial in 2022, Depp has struggled to reclaim his position in Hollywood.His 2020 filmMinimatamade less than a million dollars at the box office. Jeanne du Barry fared better in 2023, althoughits Cannes premierewas marked by feminist demonstrations and an open letter signed by 100 members of the French film industry, furious that the festival appeared to be offering alleged abusers institutional protection. Aside from that, he voiced a Puffin called Johnny Puff in a cartoon series called Puffins, and that’s about it.Rather, it was. Because now Depp is back on top. Yesterday he made a surprise appearance atComic-Conin San Diego in costume as Ebenezer Scrooge, shuffling and slurring in front of a crowd of delighted onlookers. He shouted insults (“Have you people no jobs?”) and made Trump jokes (threatening to put a tariff on some railings) and interrupted a Directors on Directing panel to wander about and mutter.The reason for Depp’s appearance is simple. Paramount has made a film about Ebenezer Scrooge, and he is playing the lead. The trailer could not be more clear that this is to be Depp’s big comeback vehicle, either. As Scrooge hobbles about the screen, the trailer’s captions proclaim: “He brought us Jack Sparrow, Edward Scissorhands and the Mad Hatter. This November, the master of misfits returns.” And then Depp, his face as close to the camera as it can possibly be, whispers, “It’s good to be back.”It is hard to see how the trailer could have made the comeback any more explicit, although some people might take the trailer’s wording with a pinch of salt. It is, after all, a piece of extraordinary public relations to take a man who wasfound by a UK civil courtto have repeatedly punched his wife in her head while screaming “I fucking hate you” and rebrand him as “the master of misfits”. It does seem like booking Bill Cosby for a film and calling him “TV’s Mr Sex”.Still, the trailer has received almost universal approval from commenters on YouTube, whose feedback ranges from “I think many will go see this film even if it’s not good, just to see Johnny back on the screen” to “Good to seeJohnny Deppback!!!”. Which is great and everything, but where were you when Minimata came out, you cowards?View image in fullscreenDepp in character at Comic-Con.Photograph: Tony Forte/MediaPunch/ShutterstockAnd in fairness, the film does seem to offer precisely what people expect from a mainstream Johnny Depp performance. His Scrooge is an overblown caricature of a thing, all hunched and cackling, and filled with the sort of overblown reaction shots that have come to be his stock in trade. His eyes bulge. His tongue sticks out. He folds his mouth upside down like Silvio from The Sopranos. It’s like watching Jack Sparrow after a few too many years on the pies, or Willy Wonka after being hauled to a riverbank with a lawn rake after being found face-down.What’s more, Ebenezer is being directed by Ti West, a man who knows his way around a horror movie better than almost anyone. He madeMaXXXine, Pearl and House of the Devil, and there are elements of the Ebenezer trailer that hint at something much darker than its breezy homecoming trailer would suggest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat would be a good thing, because as things stand, it would take all manner of mental gymnastics to square the cutesy double-taking character in the trailer with a man who, let’s not forget, was accused of banging his wife’s head on a countertop and then writing messages about her sexual activity on the walls in his own blood. Perhaps a horror movie would be the best way to ease him back into the mainstream. If nothing else, it would fit the public perception of him.As comebacks go, it’s hard to fault the boldness here. The true test will come in November, when audiences will either flock to Ebenzer or stay away in droves. Still, it could be worse. At least Depp isn’t selling cheap rings on the internetlike Kevin Spaceyyet.In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsJohnny DeppFamily filmsAmber HeardComic-ConCharles DickenscommentShareReuse this content

title: So many British people have it better than they think – it’s up to Burnham to make them see that  | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: A new survey suggests voters are becoming more cynical and pessimistic. A few goodwill gestures from No 10 won’t change all that – but it’s a start, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: A new survey suggests voters are becoming more cynical and pessimistic. A few goodwill gestures from No 10 won’t change all that – but it’s a start, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andy Burnham speaking with people at the Hare Inn, Harlow, Essex, 23 July 2026.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaking with people at the Hare Inn, Harlow, Essex, 23 July 2026.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionPoliticsSo many British people have it better than they think – it’s up to Burnham to make them see thatPolly ToynbeeA new survey suggests voters are becoming more cynical and pessimistic. A few goodwill gestures from No 10 won’t change all that – but it’s a startFri 24 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 06.46 EDTShareWho are we, the peopleAndy Burnhamnow governs? He inherits a miserable lot: grudging, angry pessimists, expecting the worst of all politicians, trusting no one to lead the country well, according to a long-running study. British folk feel the social contract is broken, they feel let down. Ignorant of basic facts, they are wilfully misled by malevolents.Over half a century of taking their pulse,Ipsos has collected dataon shifting attitudes for the mightyUnderstanding Society, the largest longitudinal household study in the world, run by the Institute for Social and Economic Research. By chance, this latest national portrait will be the benchmark for Burnham’s era. Here are his people: can he make them feel better? In the end, that’s the great purpose of all politics: you can have good policies, make improvements, do your honest best, as Keir Starmer tried, but if you don’t make the people feel it, then it’s a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal, as Paul told the Corinthians. Can Burnham lift up their hearts, a bit?Reading this survey, he may sink his head in his hands. Earning any trust is a Himalayan climb: it was bad enough back in 1989 when just 33% believed politicians were good people in general, but now that’s fallen to 20%.The people’s contradictory desires are many: they want lower taxes and better services – a higher standard of living without paying for it. They admire Sweden above all other countries, yet show little sign they would accept Swedish taxes at42% of GDP, while ours are about 33%.Impossibilism is everywhere. Launching the report, Gideon Skinner, Ipsos’s director of UK politics in public affairs, said: “We are seeing a sharpening public friction between high expectations for public services like the NHS and a declining appetite for the taxation required to sustain them.” Belief in the welfare state remains high, but it has slipped. The old divide between collectivists and individualists has deepened: “a society which emphasises the social and collective provision of welfare” gets 46% support, fallen from 54% in 1989, while 47% now want “a society where the individual is encouraged to look after themselves”, compared with 40% in 1989.But people are contradictory, torn between public spirit and private greed. Asked if they would prefer “a mainly socialist society in which public interests and a more controlled economy are most important” or “a mainly capitalist society in which private interest and free enterprise are most important”, support for socialism has risen to 57%, which is 10 percentage points higher than in 1989. More people now support “a society which emphasises similar incomes and rewards for everyone” than in 1989. What does that mean and how canLabourseize on those sentiments, not the meaner impulses?People see some glaring truths – they are not hoodwinked by the Americanised myth that everyone can make it if they only try harder. “Belief in social mobility has halved since 1989”, as only one in four (26%) now believe that the best people rise to the top regardless of their start in life, down from 52% in 1989. The facts show how birth and inheritances arecementing future chances.Pessimism is at its worst in 50 years and 72% expect a world war within the next 25 years (many more than at the height of the cold war in 1983). And yet people are not unhappy: “The clear majority of Britons remain happy with their life at present, even if fewer are ‘very happy’ than in 1991.” Live-and-let-live liberal values have made the country more tolerant since the 1980s.Yet here’s the alarm sounded by Ipsos. “This moment feels different in character to the cycles of political dissatisfaction we have seen before,” Gideon Skinner warns. “What is worrying is that pessimism risks becoming more embedded in Britons’ sense of national identity.”People may be less despairing if they knew the basics of the social contract they think is broken. Wild misunderstanding of what they pay in tax and what they get from the state fuels resentment of government. The political psephologistPeter Kellner, poring over the Office for National Statistics’s treasure trove “Effects of taxes and benefits on household income”, finds that 53% of the population gets back more from the state than they pay in: that includes not just all taxes and VAT, and cash transfers in benefits and pensions, but non-cash benefits such as the NHS, social care, education and transport subsidies (omitting collective benefits, such as the police and the armed forces).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf you’ve heard that London is dystopian and dangerous – read this. It just isn’t | Sadiq KhanRead moreBut very few know it: only 12% think they get more than they pay in. Very few over-65s recognise the ONS calculation that 90% of them gain more: even those on incomes over £70,000 on average get more than they pay, mostly because of how much they use care services and the NHS. Everyone needs a well-funded state, the old most of all, yet they vote against it.That’s the ignorance and the ingratitude Burnham faces. Whenhe says, “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity,” it needs a burst of public education to counter the daily blast of bad-faith misinformation from the right and its media. Ignorance is inexcusable when it has never been easier to find out anything at the click of a mouse.Starmer and Rachel Reeves tried to square with the people, telling brutal truths about hard choices and high debts. The people hated it. That’s Burnham’s template for what not to do. But how does he revive faith in the state? He starts with small goodwill gestures to show the government is there to help – with cuts to electricity bills, bus fares, tax for state pensioners, and business rates for pubs and clubs. Saving music venues chimes with his aim to change the mood of the nation. The public’s demand for urgent change is no guide: it points chaotically in contrary directions. Good leaders seize on guiding the better parts of human nature to believe things can be better.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionAndy BurnhamLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan worries the end of politeness will destroy civilisation. I fear he’s right | Joseph Earp | The Guardian
description: Since I saw the movie, I have found it difficult not to see Trojan horses everywhere. We live now in a state of perpetual distrustfulness
Author: Joseph Earp
Headline: Since I saw the movie, I have found it difficult not to see Trojan horses everywhere. We live now in a state of perpetual distrustfulness
Content: ‘The horse only succeeds in a world where humans are used to taking each other at their word ... the Trojans weren’t comically ignorant – just decent,’ writes Joseph Earp.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreen‘The horse only succeeds in a world where humans are used to taking each other at their word ... the Trojans weren’t comically ignorant – just decent,’ writes Joseph Earp.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesOpinionThe OdysseyIn The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan worries the end of politeness will destroy civilisation. I fear he’s rightJoseph EarpSince I saw the movie, I have found it difficult not to see Trojan horses everywhere. We live now in a state of perpetual distrustfulnessFri 24 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrior to the release of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, I’m not sure many of us would have conceived of the Trojan Horse as a kind of proto-atomic bomb, the sort of norm-obliterating device from which civilisation cannot turn back. If anything, the horse has long existed in our collective imaginations as at best a credulity-stretching plot device – why did those overly trusting Trojans not think to look that particular horse in its wooden mouth? – and at worst a cutely comedic non-threat. The greatest civilisation of its age was taken down by a timberwhat?But the true masterstroke of Nolan’s film is its parallels to the last one he dropped on us, Oppenheimer. Like that film,The Odysseyis about a haunted genius who, when presented with a problem, solves it with such speed and significance that he must necessarily cast aside implication. But rather than splitting the atom, Odysseus (Matt Damon), dismembers something considerably more significant – the social fabric.The world of Nolan’s The Odyssey is one obsessed with civility and rules. Characters talk endlessly about Zeus’ law: a basic currency of interpersonal kindness, where each human being is treated as though they might contain the divine. Odysseus, upstanding man of the world that he is, will not even kill a deer without alerting it of his arrival via a twang of his bow: to sneak up on prey without warning is to turn a “fight” into a “hunt”, he tells us.The Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilersRead moreOf course, no such bow twanging accompanies the Trojan horse. Odysseus even hides its threat from his own cousin, Sinon (Elliot Page), who is impaled on its wooden side in the opening minutes of the movie. Poor hapless Sinon isn’t even aware of what he’s dying for. And when the horse breaches Troy’s walls, the resulting massacre is depicted by Nolan as exactly that: a massacre.But, Nolan frets, the cost is greater than just bloodshed. The horse only succeeds in a world where humans are used to taking each other at their word; where a gift is a gift, and a surrender is a surrender. Turns out the Trojans weren’t comically ignorant. They were just decent. And so, in Nolan’s film, what Odysseus invents is the world’s first lie – its firstimpoliteness.Such a concern might strike us oddly these days. In our world, handwringing over rudeness too often has the blush of quaint conservatism to it, and for decades now the centre-right have lectured the left on the importance of keeping the world “civil” even when the world in question is burning. Sure, polluters might be destroying all life on the planet, but there’s no need to deface a painting to protest them or block traffic for an hour or so. That’s justrude.5:25The Odyssey was filmed on Imax film. Only one southern hemisphere cinema can screen it – videoFor that reason, the cynical could be forgiven for bristling at Nolan’s suggestion that telling a grand ole fib damned us to eternal destruction. There are surely larger fish to fry; problems more significant than a lie. Nolan even seems to understand that bigger picture himself: the sorceress Circe (Samantha Morton) tells Odysseus that men’s evil has existed a lot longer than the construction of some wretched horse. As she explains it, civility has just been a thin layer on top of a deep wellspring of rot. And in this version, Circe doesn’t turn Odysseus’ men into pigs. She reveals them for what they are. Which is pigs.The Odyssey review – Nolan goes god-tier with breathtaking epic of men, monsters and moral metamorphosisRead moreBut, Nolan seems to say, at least they were once pigs who told each other the truth. And I must admit, such a framing shook me far more deeply than the bomb testing that wrenches Oppenheimer in two. Fire is fire; a nuke is a nuke. A horse that is not a horse does something perhaps less immediately destructive, but no less horrifying. It casts aside the notion that there are things we have all agreed not to do.In the days since I saw The Odyssey, I have found it difficult not to see Trojan horses everywhere. We live now in a state of perpetual distrustfulness. The paranoiacs, it turns out, are right – there is poison in every water supply. Thanks to AI, no picture is a picture. To borrow a turn of phrase from David Foster Wallace, the content we endlessly consume – whether it be on our phones, or our TV screens – is not being made by people who love us. It’s being made by people whowantsomething from us. Our politicians will lie to us, endlessly, for no other reason than they can. Cruelty now takes a friendly face, and our biggest polluters have carefully curated Instagram pages.In short, I can’t remember the last time I saw a stranger as containing the divine; a horse as just a horse. And looking back from the point of view of our post-fall of Troy world, politeness no longer seems like the vaguely pathetic instruction that we mind our p’s and q’s. Instead it’s a bond, a default approach of care that says, the other is not a demon, but possibly a God in disguise. An approach that says, this person you do not know has something for you, and you should take it. Because, after all, what are the chances that they mean you harm?Joseph Earp is a critic, painter and novelist. His latest book isPainting Portraits of Everyone I’ve Ever DatedExplore more on these topicsThe OdysseyOpinionChristopher NolanFilm criticismcommentShareReuse this content

title: Wedding gift registries are great – but divorce registries would be a lifesaver | Nick Dothée | The Guardian
description: Marriage offers an opportunity to ask for help creating a home. But what about when the marriage ends – and the household with it?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Marriage offers an opportunity to ask for help creating a home. But what about when the marriage ends – and the household with it?
Content: ‘Divorce turns one household into two, usually at the exact moment everyone is least equipped to comparison-shop bath mats.’Photograph: Giles Angel/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Divorce turns one household into two, usually at the exact moment everyone is least equipped to comparison-shop bath mats.’Photograph: Giles Angel/AlamyOpinionDivorceWedding gift registries are great – but divorce registries would be a lifesaverNick DothéeMarriage offers an opportunity to ask for help creating a home. But what about when the marriage ends – and the household with it?Fri 24 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.18 EDTShareIt’s peak wedding season, and my own divorce is waiting on a judge’s signature. People are being congratulated with Dutch ovens and serving bowls for dinner parties they may not ever host.Marriage comes with an etiquette system for asking people to help build a home. The registry says the embarrassing part for you.Divorcedeserves the same grace.Meanwhile, I was standing alone in my new-to-me condo kitchen, rereading a text I had drafted to my mother, trying to make quartz countertops sound like a normal thing to need.“Would you and Fred consider making this my birthday, Christmas, divorce and condo-warming gift?” I wrote, referring to the countertops and single-basin sink I had been fixating on. I attached a screenshot of Calacatta almond quartz, as if the visual aid might make the request seem less unhinged.The price point is why I piled on the occasions. But I am a 44-year-old man with a mortgage and two dogs, so “birthday and Christmas” was not really the headline. Divorce was.‘Loneliness influencers’ are racking up views. After a breakup, I see the appeal | Dave SchillingRead moreMy mother’s response was not yes.“Your stepdad and I are in the ER. I can’t think about this right now.”Fair. Terrible timing, but the shame had been there before she even replied.It’s hard now to imagine a wedding without a registry, but that etiquette had to start somewhere.Marshall Field’s, the Chicago department store whose State Street flagship is now a Macy’s, is often credited with introducing the modern bridal registry in 1924, when the list helped couples steer family and friends toward china, silver and crystal patterns. A century later, couples don’t even have to pretend they want china. Home funds are now common enough thatThe Knot has saidthe share of couples including them in registries has increased 55% since 2018.A few years ago, when my now ex-husband and I got married, his parents paid to finish turfing the backyard of our house so we could have the wedding there. My parents covered the tents, tables, chairs and sound system. These were not small gifts. But they turned a backyard into a wedding, so nobody had to defend the cost.For the registry itself, we mostly wanted cash. We were new homeowners in Los Angeles with nothing left for a honeymoon, so we used a platform called Hitchd to let guests click a link and donate to our new life. It helped pay for Hawaii and the house. I was a newlywed, so the ask came pre-forgiven.Then the marriage ended, and the household went with it.You can’t roll up half a backyard and bring it to a condo. The things that once meant “our future” became community property: the patio furniture, the dog bowls, the good knives, the drawer organizer that only made sense in that kitchen. Things to divide, keep, sell or leave behind.Someone should build the divorce version of Hitchd. Call it Ditchd.Actually, people already have.The Associated Press reportedthat Fresh Starts Registry, a divorce-registry service, had 50,000 to 70,000 monthly visitors, part of a broader shift toward talking more openly about divorce. So the need is not hypothetical. What still feels missing is the etiquette – a graceful way to say: we did not make it, but I’m accepting contributions toward a vacuum.A divorce registry sounds tacky because gifts are supposed to be fun, and replacing the half of a home that didn’t come with you is mostly just sad. I took the Instant Pot; the air fryer stayed. Asking for another one felt like showing everyone exactly how we split the kitchen. I did most of the cooking, and I didn’t realize how much I loved our beautiful countertops until they weren’t mine any more. So yes. Countertops made the list too.Divorce turns one household into two, usually at the exact moment everyone is least equipped to comparison-shop bath mats. First come the lawyers, movers, closing costs and a new internet account. Then come the dumber purchases: trash bags, forks, a shower curtain, a couch the puppy has not peed on yet. None of it feels giftable. All of it has to be bought anyway.I wasn’t destitute. That almost made the asking harder. I landed in the annoying middle: technically OK, but still buying my life back one receipt at a time.By the time I drafted that text to my mother, I had already spent my share of the house making the new condo feel like mine. The beige living room carpet became blonde oak flooring because the new puppy I “won” in the divorce still wasn’t potty trained. A handyperson painted the dated dark cabinets soft sage; I switched the hardware to matte black myself. I put bougainvillea and olive trees on the balcony, because maybe the dogs wouldn’t notice they had lost their backyard. At the old house, bougainvillea had covered the pergola in papery magenta blooms. Here, I had one in a pot.But in LA, the money runs out quickly.The ‘grey divorce’ phenomenon doesn’t signal a retreat from love. It’s a redefinition of it | Lisa PortolanRead moreI left the bedroom carpet and dated bathrooms alone. After the floors and cabinets, the old counters dragged the whole open-concept room back into “this was what I could afford”. Replacing them would mean I could stop balancing a cutting board over a burner. At the sink, I wouldn’t have to stretch on to my tiptoes – and I am tall – just to see my dogs asleep on and beside the couch.This was the case I made. My mother used to be horrified by how much my husband and I spent on Uber Eats. She gave us gift cards for Christmas that I joked would barely cover a dinner and a half. Now I was cooking almost every meal at home. The kitchen was where I could save money, feed myself and two expensive dogs on one income, and make the condo work as a home.The ER text made the timing comically indefensible. But the shame wasn’t really about timing. Marriage gets a table at Crate & Barrel. Divorce gets a Target cart full of things you already owned in another life.Maybe I’ll get the counters, maybe I won’t. For now, the quote sits there like one more line in a ledger that already has a mediator, a new floor and moving costs on it – one more number I keep staring at like it might solve something.I didn’t want a party for the divorce. I wanted permission to ask for help with the life I now had to build.Still, I can see the kitchen as it could be. The new sink. The cleared counter. Dinner at home. The dogs asleep in view. The bougainvillea on the balcony, doing the best it can.Nick Dothée is a Los Angeles-based writer whose work has appeared in the Atlantic; he is working on a memoir about the last-chance Hollywood recovery house where he got soberExplore more on these topicsDivorceOpinionHomesRelationshipscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s first week: polished politics allow an upbeat start | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: With a flurry of cost-of-living measures and a day in Number 10 North, the new prime minister has hit the right early notes
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: With a flurry of cost-of-living measures and a day in Number 10 North, the new prime minister has hit the right early notes
Content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrives and greets staff at No 10 North in Manchester on Friday.Photograph: James Speakman/POOL THE TIMES/APView image in fullscreenPrime Minister Andy Burnham arrives and greets staff at No 10 North in Manchester on Friday.Photograph: James Speakman/POOL THE TIMES/APOpinionAndy BurnhamThe Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s first week: polished politics allow an upbeat startEditorialWith a flurry of cost-of-living measures and a day in Number 10 North, the new prime minister has hit the right early notesFri 24 Jul 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.58 EDTShareAppropriately enough, Andy Burnham ended a week of political signalling and first impressions back in Manchester on Friday. At the offices of the new No 10 North – where the prime minister hopes to work at least one day a week – regional mayors sat alongside ministers in an example of Burnhamism at work. It was an early statement of intent, ahead of what Mr Burnham bills as “the biggestrebalancingof power our country has seen”.The same could be said of the series of cost of living measures fired out during the new government’s first few days in office. A £2capon bus fares, acutin VAT on electricity, and some business ratesrelieffor pubs, clubs and smaller music venues were all modest moves. But they were cleverly indicative ones, nodding empathetically to people’s need to have the chance to enjoy themselves as well as pay the bills.They also sent a distinctively optimistic message to the public, compared to the Starmer government’s fateful earlydecisionto cut winter fuel payments. Mr Burnham needed to sound and act differently from the off. In short order he has demonstrated the political sure-footedness so sadly lacking in his predecessor.View image in fullscreenChancellor of the Exchequer John Healey.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersGiven the relatively small scale of the spending involved, the eagerness of sections of the media to locate Liz Truss-style “unfunded commitments” has been faintly risible. There will, of course, be much more of that to come in the autumn, as Mr Burnham’s surprise choice of chancellor, John Healey, puts together his first budget. But with parliament now in recess and Nigel Faragedistractedby a political farce of his own making in Clacton, the prime minister and his team will feel they have navigated the opening act of his premiership with some aplomb.The more difficult work begins now. Recent polling, as Mr Burnham prepared to take office,pointedto an exasperated and impatient electorate which will give him only a limited window of opportunity. He intends tousethe summer to visit constituencies identified as losers from a 40-year political settlement in which “power was centralised, economic power was privatised and communities were deindustrialised”. But having arrived in No 10 after a quicker handover than he may have preferred, and without the scrutiny of a contest, the coming weeks will also be crucial in refining the strategy for reform on all three of those fronts.As economic headwindscontinueto blow from the Middle East, and fiscal caution isurgedupon the new government from the usual quarters, it will need to be bold. Mr Burnham’s analysis of the flawed political economy which has ill-served Britain in recent decades is the right one. But from radical devolution to public control of utilities and launching the biggest public housing programme since the Attlee government, his prescriptions for change will challenge entrenched orthodoxies. The viability of the 10-year plan that the prime minister intends to unveil later this year will depend on his government’s ability – and willingness – to successfully take them on.As England progressed to the semi-finals of the men’s World Cup this month, it looked at one point as if Mr Burnham might move into No 10 the day after football finally came home. Lionel Messi and Argentina denied him that “lucky general” moment. But the prime minister’s first week has been upbeat and politically polished. Trickier tests are yet to come.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on ponds: these freshwater havens need a law of their own | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Small pools don’t get the same attention as polluted rivers or seas. But they have a vital role to play in boosting nature
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Small pools don’t get the same attention as polluted rivers or seas. But they have a vital role to play in boosting nature
Content: ‘To the extent that ponds have been legally shielded, this has been largely due to great-crested newts.’Photograph: Paul Young/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘To the extent that ponds have been legally shielded, this has been largely due to great-crested newts.’Photograph: Paul Young/AlamyOpinionWaterThe Guardian view on ponds: these freshwater havens need a law of their ownEditorialSmall pools don’t get the same attention as polluted rivers or seas. But they have a vital role to play in boosting natureFri 24 Jul 2026 12.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.58 EDTShareFrogs; newts; small fish such as minnows and sticklebacks; dragonflies; water boatmen and water snails: these are just a few of the hundreds of animal species that make their homes in Britain’s ponds alongside diverse wetland plants, some of which are endangered. Yet while small bodies of water are cherished by hobbyists as well as scientists, they have startlingly few protections – even at a time when thepolluted state of rivers,lakesand coastlines is a key focus of environmentalists.With a clean water bill expected soon, this official neglect of ponds should soon be consigned to the past. Whilerewilding projectshave overseen the rediscovery of older “ghost ponds” as well as the creation of new, and householders are encouraged to create miniature ones in their gardens, charities including the specialist Freshwater Habitats Trust point to the growing body of international research that testifies to their ecological importance. In 1996 thefirst-ever national surveyestimated that there were 228,900 ponds in Britain. Thirty years on would be an apt moment to grant them enhanced status.The decline of ponds is part of a wider story of damage to the UK’s waterways by a combination of intensive agriculture, building development, pollution and thefailure to manage it. Onelocal study in Leicestershirehas found an average 1% species loss every year for 15 years. But unlike rivers, many of which disappeared underground when they were culverted by the Victorians, around two-thirds of ancient ponds in England and Wales have vanished altogether either through drainage or infilling for farmland. When horses were replaced by tractors, it was wrongly thought that these pools had served their purpose.To the extent that ponds have been legally shielded, this has been largely due to great-crested newts – a protected species since 1981 and one that cannot thrive in rivers with large fish. These rare amphibians even had the dubious honour of becoming an anti-red-tape trope, with Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, among senior politicians to have suggested that rules wereoverly tilted towards wildlife.More recently, Rachel Reeves, then chancellor, criticised the way that a development in Sussex was delayed by concerns about another freshwater creature, thelittle whirlpool ramshorn snail. While it is right for regulation to take account of individual species, the broader point about ponds is their contribution to biodiversity overall.Increasing heat anddrought, and the stress they impose on natural systems, make the presence of water in landscapes all the more urgent. Ministers should heed calls to add targets for ponds to the plans that govern England’s 10 river basin districts. They should also embrace a broader lifting of ambition, whereby the target of high ecological status would be set for a limited number of streams, rivers and lakes.Compared with the challenges around water companies, sewage and pollution from roads and farming, ponds and streams might sound unimportant. But the Climate Change Committee and other experts consistently stress the importance ofnature recovery– and one of the distinctive benefits offered by small water bodies is the speed at which they are capable of being restored under careful management. What is good for newts and snails could also be good for politicians and the public.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Our blueprint for Andy Burnham’s success  | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers advise the new prime minister and his party on how to turn Labour’s fortunes, and the country’s, around
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers advise the new prime minister and his party on how to turn Labour’s fortunes, and the country’s, around
Content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham during a visit to the Hare pub in Harlow, Essex, on Thursday.Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PAView image in fullscreenPrime Minister Andy Burnham during a visit to the Hare pub in Harlow, Essex, on Thursday.Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PAAndy BurnhamLettersOur blueprint for Andy Burnham’s successReaders advise the new prime minister and his party on how to turn Labour’s fortunes, and the country’s, aroundFri 24 Jul 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTShareRafael Behr neatly summarises Andy Burnham’s strengths as a potential leader and he rightly emphasises that he needs a united party behind him (Andy Burnham is playing the long game in an age of short attention spans, 22 July).He then accurately identifies what Burnham needs to do, but makes no reference to what the parliamentaryLabourparty needs to do. Leadership is interactional, and Labour MPs outside the government – particularly those (in Behr’s words) with hair triggers on the radical left and those aggrieved Starmer loyalists – have to realise that Labour is in the last-chance saloon here, and they have just as much a role as he does to ensure the success that leads to a second term.If Burnham is to succeed, there is no place for the kind of self-indulgent social mediaposts made by Darren Joneson funding for removing VAT on electricity bills, which provide instant fodder for the Tories, Reform UK and the rightwing media. Of course, there will be policy disagreements, but all Labour MPs must find ways to debate these while retaining a fundamental commitment to the success of this new government, given the sceptical mood of the country, and exercising appropriate judgment in the way they express their differences, however sincerely held.Dr Roger BookerClapham, LondonIf Andy Burnham is looking for ways to fund the cost of living crisis (Andy Burnham urges cabinet to examine ‘all possible ways’ to tackle cost of living crisis, 21 July), why doesn’t he just do the obvious and increase the top rate of income tax which now sits at 45%? During the second world war the top rate was 99.25%; during the Wilson government of the 1960s it was 90%; and it was 83% when Margaret Thatcher became prime minister. Back then high earners mostly lived in the UK, and it was only from the 1980s that high earners such as Rod Stewart and later Phil Collins started bleating about high taxes.The reduction of the top rate of income tax has not resulted in better compliance, as avoidance and evasion are rife, nor has it boosted enterprise. It has, however, produced a more divided and less fair society that has more millionaires and an alarming number of people struggling with the cost of living. Sadly, and I know it’s early days for Burnham, tinkering with small reductions in electricity bills and fixing bus fares won’t have the required effect.Raising income tax for wealthier people (not just the super rich) will both ensure a fairer, more cohesive society and increase the funding available for genuinely radical change. I don’t understand why no one appears to be considering this.Steve PennyAbergavenny, MonmouthshireReading Monday’s Guardian, optimistic about a fresh start with a new prime minister, I suffered abrupt heart-sink on reaching the business section when I saw the headlines (Wessex Water chief pockets above-inflation pay rise despite bonus ban over sewage spills, 18 July;Pay gap widens as UK bosses get 130 times average worker’s salary, 20 July).What can be done to stop these obscenely avaricious and selfish people from further dividing our country into a nation of haves and have-nots? It is well known that a wide disparity between the pay of rich and poor leads to discontent and unrest. Please,Andy Burnham, introduce a swingeing income tax on earned/unearned income and bonuses in excess of, for example, £1m per annum.Jane SutherlandDry Drayton, CambridgeshireLearning that Andy Burnham’s father is unable to understand that his son is the prime minister was one of those moments when the prospect of changing a muddled social care system came very much closer (The Guardian view on social care reform: Andy Burnham is right – this issue must be gripped, 21 July). When the Blair government found it easy to kick the findings of the Royal Commission on Long Term Care into the long grass, some of us involved in campaigning believed that if only someone with power and influence could relate to the issues at a personal level the situation might change.As the author of the reforms legislated by the Thatcher governmentsaid at the time, “Community care is everybody’s distant relative, but nobody’s baby”. Perhaps Burnham’s elevation will mean that this “orphan” will now receive the serious cross-party attention that has eluded it for so long. Until then, those in need of care and their families will continue to be confused, anxious and disappointed by the options open to them.Les BrightExeterTom Clark is right that transformative governments have usually been enabled by emergencies (Andy Burnham says he will go ‘faster’ than Starmer. Why is that so hard?, 20 July). Roosevelt, wartime Britain and the pandemic all show that when leaders are honest about the scale of a threat, the public are willing to support extraordinary action.Yet there is one question his piece leaves hanging: what if the emergency is already here? Extreme heat, flooding, crop losses and mounting pressures on health services, infrastructure and the economy are no longer future risks; they are today’s reality. Yet politically we continue to treat them as isolated policy problems, rather than symptoms of a climate and nature crisis with severe implications for the country.This is not simply a failure of political courage. It is also a failure of public communication. Democracies can only move at the speed that public understanding allows.If Andy Burnham wants to govern “faster and bolder”, his first task should not be announcing another initiative. It should be treating the public as adults: explaining honestly the scale and immediacy of the crisis, how it is already driving up the cost of living, and the opportunities that decisive action would bring.Britain does not lack an emergency. What it needs is political leadership to describe it honestly – and begin building a public mandate for bold national renewal.Prof Mike Berners-LeeChair, National Emergency BriefingIt has been suggested in some quarters that the Burnham premiership will take the country back to the 1970s. Here are just a few of the things that existed then. No food banks, little homelessness, little energy poverty, council houses, rent controls, British industry making things, a funded defence force, water, energy and public transport under the public’s control, and membership of the Common Market.John GarnhamAmpthill, BedfordshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Migraines are so much more than just banging headaches | Health | The Guardian
description: Letters: Until migraines are recognised as a multi-system condition, sufferers will continue to be dismissed, writes Sarah Khan. Plus a letter from Rab Hallett
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Until migraines are recognised as a multi-system condition, sufferers will continue to be dismissed, writes Sarah Khan. Plus a letter from Rab Hallett
Content: ‘The most important thing is go and talk to your GP; don’t suffer in silence trying to self-manage, avoiding triggers.’Photograph: PixelsEffect/GettyView image in fullscreen‘The most important thing is go and talk to your GP; don’t suffer in silence trying to self-manage, avoiding triggers.’Photograph: PixelsEffect/GettyHealthLettersMigraines are so much more than just banging headachesUntil migraines are recognised as a multi-system condition, sufferers will continue to be dismissed, writesSarah Khan. Plus a letter fromRab HallettFri 24 Jul 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTShareThank you for your article about migraines – a maligned, misunderstood condition (The truth about migraines: what causes them – and how to find relief, 19 July). But framing it around the headache understates what it is: a systemic neurological event in which head pain is only one component.For me, until perimenopause, the head pain was minor. The disabling symptoms were profound fatigue, body aches and cognitive fog, which dominated even the “prodrome”. This is why my migraines went undiagnosed for decades, blamed on a “poor immune system” rather than a neurological disorder.The piece also underplays how little control sufferers have. Telling patients to manage their triggers ignores those navigating puberty, or women whose reproductive years bring hormonal shifts entirely beyond their control. Many face a predictable menstrual attack plus a second at ovulation, which in severe cases can consume up to half the month. In perimenopause, hormonal triggers can be daily; the nervous system responds by lowering the threshold until attacks come ever easier. I’ve had daily migraine for over two years, prodrome and postdrome overlapping without pause.This is also why migraine cannot be left to neurologists alone. When the driver is fundamentally hormonal, gynaecological care matters – yet very few gynaecologists understand the migraine brain, and some prescribe perimenopause treatments that actively worsen it.With regard to treatment, gepants have been transformative, and GPs can now prescribe Rimegepant where triptans fall short. Yet access remains a postcode lottery.Migraine is not a banging headache. Until medicine treats it as a genetic, multi-system condition, sufferers – disproportionately women – will keep getting dismissed, even though treatment is available.Sarah KhanLondonWhile all the new research pathways are interesting, the most important thing is go and talk to your GP; don’t suffer in silence trying to self-manage, avoiding triggers. For me, it was only after years that a pain management consultant finally said: “Why has nobody ever prescribed you triptans?” Now I get on with life the best I can, with some emergency tablets in my pocket.Rab HallettEdinburghHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: When talk about the weather heats up or cools down | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers contribute words that describe how people feel in all weathers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers contribute words that describe how people feel in all weathers
Content: ‘The Historical Thesaurus of the Oxford English Dictionary has words to describe all weathers.’Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreen‘The Historical Thesaurus of the Oxford English Dictionary has words to describe all weathers.’Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAUK weatherLettersWhen talk about the weather heats up or cools downReaders contribute words that describe how people feel in all weathersFri 24 Jul 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTShareI was interested to read some of the words that your letter writers associated with the weather and our reactions to it (Puggled, scumfished or utterly shrammed, 14 July). Unsurprisingly, the English language is redolent with words to do with harsh weather, with many of the longest-established terms tending towards the cold or inclement. Perhaps as hotter weather becomes the norm rather than the exception, we’ll start to talk less about dreich days that leave us shrammed or clumsed and more about blazers that are a bit of a pech and leave us feeling mooth. The Historical Thesaurus of the Oxford English Dictionary has words to describe all weathers, including all of the above and many more.Fiona McPhersonExecutive editor, Oxford English DictionaryI can assure Jan Cooper (Letters, 21 July) that people in Yorkshire are still capable of feeling nithered, in very cold weather. On the other hand, in the recent spells of very hot weather, they are far more likely to have felt mafted, as opposed to feeling nithered.Simon GreenHullI remember a lot of snow in my 1950s Wiltshire childhood, and when it pitched, we played outside until we were shrammed and our cheeks were spreathed. My great aunts watched through the window, but in summer they sat outside on the hard wooden bench until their bottoms were dunched.Wendy NeveOver Stratton, SomersetIn Lancashire when we’re cold we say: “I’m starving”. To avoid confusion, when we’re starving, we say: “I’m clemming”.Carol HainesYealmpton, DevonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Children are the longest-lasting casualties of war | Children | The Guardian
description: Letter: Responding to a new exhibition that explores how children have experienced conflict, Arabella Dorman says they live with the consequences long after the fighting has ended
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Responding to a new exhibition that explores how children have experienced conflict, Arabella Dorman says they live with the consequences long after the fighting has ended
Content: Children in Kharkiv, Ukraine, follow their teacher in the country's first underground kindergarten, to protect against Russian air attacks.Photograph: Andrii Marienko/APView image in fullscreenChildren in Kharkiv, Ukraine, follow their teacher in the country's first underground kindergarten, to protect against Russian air attacks.Photograph: Andrii Marienko/APChildrenLettersChildren are the longest-lasting casualties of warResponding to a new exhibition that explores how children have experienced conflict,Arabella Dormansays they live with the consequences long after the fighting has endedFri 24 Jul 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTShareYour article on the Imperial War Museum’s forthcoming exhibition Childhood in War is a timely reminder that the deepest wounds of conflict are often carried by those who never chose it (‘There was absolutely no chance of being a kid’: new exhibition explores how war shapes children’s lives, 19 July). While wars are recorded through battles, borders and political decisions, children experience them very differently: through interrupted childhoods, fractured families and the loss of what should have been ordinary days.Over many years working in war zones, I came to understand that children are not simply among the victims of war; they are its longest-lasting casualties. Long after the fighting has moved on, they continue to live with its consequences – in their bodies, their memories and the futures they must somehow rebuild.My seriesChild of Wargrew out of those encounters. It was never intended to document conflict itself, but rather its enduring imprint on young lives: children whose resilience was remarkable, but whose suffering should never be mistaken for acceptance or inevitability.Art cannot change the past, but it can bear witness. If this exhibition encourages us to look beyond the headlines and recognise the human cost of conflict through the eyes of a child, it will have performed a profound service.Arabella DormanLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Maga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visit | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Rightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next week
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Rightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next week
Content: Laura Loomer, a far-right US blogger who has previously amplified Moscow’s propaganda to her millions of followers, visited a McDonald’s in Kyiv that has been hit by Russian strikes.Photograph: @LaraLoomerView image in fullscreenLaura Loomer, a far-right US blogger who has previously amplified Moscow’s propaganda to her millions of followers, visited a McDonald’s in Kyiv that has been hit by Russian strikes.Photograph: @LaraLoomerTrump administrationMaga influencer Laura Loomer reverses course on Ukraine after Kyiv visitRightwing provocateur meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who says he expects to meet Donald Trump in Washington next weekLuke Hardingin Kyiv and agenciesFri 24 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy will meet Donald Trump in Washington next week, according to the rightwing US influencer Laura Loomer, amid signs the White House’s traditional hostility towards Ukraine is beginning to crumble.In an interview with Loomer, theUkrainepresident said he will probably attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham and hold talks with Trump, which will take place as the latest version of the Russian sanctions bill makes its way through Congress.Loomer interviewed Zelenskyy in the garden of the presidential palace in Kyiv – a remarkable move for the online provocateur who has previously minimised Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and amplified Kremlin propaganda to her nearly 2 million followers on social media.This week, however, she performed a stunning about-turn. “Just experienced my first air raid in Ukraine. Sirens blaring. This is every day for every Ukrainian,” Loomer wrote on X. “I often said I don’t care. Looking back, that wasn’t very nice of me to say. We need to have moral clarity.”View image in fullscreenLaura Loomer visiting the Dormition Cathedral in Kyiv.Photograph: @LauraLoomer/XLoomer posted a photo of her one-on-one meeting with Zelenskyy as well as a clip from her interview with him in which she asks about hisinfamous confrontation last year with Trump and the US vice-president, JD Vance, in the Oval Office. No questions were off limits, she said.In the clip, Zelenskyy said his relationship with Trump had significantly improved and describes their brief conversation in the Vatican in April 2025 as a “historic moment”.“We changed the relations during 15, 20 minutes,” Zelenskyy added.Writing on Truth Social, Trump praised Loomer’s interview, calling it “Very good!!!!”. The White House later confirmed that the two leaders were scheduled to meet on Tuesday, while commentators in Kyiv said Trump’s message confirmed his administration’s once negative view of Kyiv was changing at a time when Ukrainian long-range drones are pummelling Russia.Russia has continued to strike Ukraine, with a daytime ballistic missile attack on Friday killing 10 people in the Kyiv region and injuring nearly 100 more. Another five people died when an air bomb hit the eastern city of Sloviansk.Expressing support for US sanctions on Russia, Loomer said the Kremlin was a close ally of the Iranian regime. “Russia is funding Iran and providing them with explosives to murder US soldiers as Iran has called for President Trump’s assassination,” she wrote, arguing: “The United States needs to break Russia’s economy until they submit to peace.”View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy, right, and Donald Trump met at the funeral of Pope Francis in the Vatican in April 2025, which Zelenskyy called a ‘historic moment’.Photograph: APLoomer’s comments are a reversal for a woman who has spent years criticising US support for Ukraine’s defence, declaring it “a country full ofNazi apologists” – a claim used by Russia to justify its full-scale 2022 invasion – and “led by a Jihadi apologist”.Kyiv monastery set on fire in night of Russian attacks across UkraineRead moreHer scepticism towards Kyiv has been shared by other major conservativeinfluencers, including Tucker Carlson, a former Fox News host. The issue became a big point of contention between more traditional Republicans, such as Mike Pence, a former vice-president, and Trump’s Maga base.Anton Gerashchenko, a popular blogger and former Ukrainian government adviser, described Loomer’s interview with Zelenskyy as “important and necessary”. “It records a public break with Russian narratives and propaganda by part of the Maga movement. We are seeing a shift in rhetoric regarding Russian aggression,” he said.“It is really important that @LauraLoomer is in Ukraine and sees things with her own eyes as they are,” Zelenskyy’s office added this week. “It takes courage to come to Ukraine and not be deterred by Russian propaganda or air raid sirens. Thank you, Laura.”View image in fullscreenLaura Loomer outside court in 2023 as Trump was to appear on charges including possession of national security documents after leaving office and making false statements.Photograph: Stephanie Keith/Getty ImagesLoomer also visited the Dormition Cathedral of Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, one of the country’s most significant religious landmarks, which came under Russian drone attack in June.Ukraine’s pivot to warehouse strikes brings war closer to ordinary RussiansRead moreIn a video recorded from inside the church, she accused Vladimir Putin of hypocrisy by portraying Russia as a pro-Christian nation – a perspective many US evangelicals appear to share. “I just don’t think that you should be allowed to say that you’re protecting Christianity if you’re trying to drone strike Jesus Christ,” Loomer remarked.Loomer also met Ukraine’s chief rabbi, Moshe Reuven Azman, and toured a branch of McDonald’s hit repeatedly by Russian missiles. Loomer ordered a cheeseburger and sat demonstratively on an outside table in front of a wrecked building, in Kyiv’s much-bombed Lukianivka district.On Friday, the chief rabbi wrote: “I had the honour of welcoming @LauraLoomer – whose views have a significant influence on the U.S. audience and who is well known for her close ties to PresidentDonald Trump– to the Central Synagogue of Ukraine.“The conversation was candid. I told her the truth about this terrible war – about the daily Russian shelling, the children and civilians killed, the destroyed cities and villages, and the pain that Ukrainian families endure every day.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpFar right (US)RussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Chuck Russell, director of The Mask and The Blob, dies aged 74 | Movies | The Guardian
description: The film-maker, also behind A Nightmare on Elm Street 3, died on Wednesday in his San Diego home
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The film-maker, also behind A Nightmare on Elm Street 3, died on Wednesday in his San Diego home
Content: Chuck Russell in 2023.Photograph: Chris Delmas/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChuck Russell in 2023.Photograph: Chris Delmas/AFP/Getty ImagesMoviesChuck Russell, director of The Mask and The Blob, dies aged 74The film-maker, also behind A Nightmare on Elm Street 3, died on Wednesday in his San Diego homeOwen MyersFri 24 Jul 2026 16.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDirector Chuck Russell, who helped propel actors such asJim Carrey,Cameron DiazandDwayne “The Rock” Johnsonto the Hollywood A-list, was found dead in his San Diego, California, home on Wednesday. He was 74.Russell directed several box office hits in his decades-long career including A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors, The Blob and The Mask. In 2002, his film The Scorpion King featured The Rock in his first leading role.The local fire department was called to Russell’s home on Wednesday afternoon with reports of an unconscious male, the director’s family said in a statement toTMZ. His death was confirmed by his attorney toVariety; a cause of death has not been confirmed.Born in Park Ridge, Illinois, Russell first entered the film industry as an executive producer on the cult 1981 slasher Hell Night, starring Linda Blair, before co-writing 1984’s Dreamscape, a sci-fi adventure led by Dennis Quaid.His directorial debut came with A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors in 1987, which Russell also wrote.
