The film which was hailed as a return to form for the horror franchise after mixed notices for 1985’s A Nightmare on Elm Street 2: Freddy’s Revenge.After the 1988 remake of the cult B-movie The Blob, Russell hit the Hollywood big time with The Mask, the 1994 blockbuster that made global stars of Carrey and Diaz. Collaborating withGeorge Lucas’s Industrial Light & Magic company brought the film acclaim for its practical effects, which were nominated for an Academy Award.The Mask was originally envisioned as a horror flick. “New Line wanted another shocking horror film,” Russellsaidin 2024. “There was a comic book of The Mask that was quite terrifying. I said it’s going to be too much like Freddy Krueger. It’s going to be horrible.” Russell won his argument with the studio and the film grossed more than $350m on an $18m production budget.Russell followed by working withArnold Schwarzeneggeron the 1996 action film Eraser and 2000 horror Bless the Child starring Kim Basinger and Christina Ricci. In 2002, he directed The Scorpion King, a spin-off to the popular The Mummy adventure films.The director’s final film was 2024’s Witchboard, a remake of the 1986 horror starring Tawny Kitaen.Explore more on these topicsFilmAction and adventure filmsHorror filmsComedy filmsJim CarreynewsShareReuse this content

title: Five officers injured as police boat strikes Westminster Bridge | London | The Guardian
description: Metropolitan police say officers on marine policing boat are receiving treatment after incident in central London
Author: Hayden Vernon
Headline: Metropolitan police say officers on marine policing boat are receiving treatment after incident in central London
Content: Traffic across Westminster Bridge was brought to a standstill after the incident, with a cordon in place at either end.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersView image in fullscreenTraffic across Westminster Bridge was brought to a standstill after the incident, with a cordon in place at either end.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersLondonFive officers injured as police boat strikes Westminster BridgeMetropolitan police say officers on marine policing boat are receiving treatment after incident in central LondonHayden VernonFri 24 Jul 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive officers have been injured after a police boat struck Westminster Bridge in centralLondonon Friday afternoon.TheMetropolitan policesaid the incident occurred at about 3.40pm and involved a boat from the marine policing unit.A spokesperson for the Met said: “A number of officers entered the water but were recovered. Additional officers responded alongside the London ambulance service and London fire brigade.“We understand five officers were injured and are receiving treatment. We await an update on the extent of their injuries. At this stage, we don’t believe any members of the public were involved or injured.“The circumstances of the incident will be thoroughly reviewed, but at this stage our priority is the wellbeing of the officers involved.”Responders from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution could be seen treating casualties on a boat moored at Westminster pier. A large number of police officers, fire crews and ambulances were at the scene, with a police helicopter and air ambulance circling above.Traffic across the bridge was brought to a standstill, with a cordon in place at either end.A mother and son, Cecilia Lusevic, 56, and Mateo Bilis-Lusevic, 12, said they heard a loud bang when the police boat crashed.View image in fullscreenPolice officers, fire crews and ambulances attended the scene, along with a police helicopter and air ambulance.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersThe visitors to the UK, from Chile, were on a tour boat on the north side of Westminster Bridge and saw what happened, before being evacuated from their boat.Mateo told the Press Association: “Two boats were riding extremely fast through the water. Suddenly, I heard a boom. I was looking towards the boat, and I heard a boom. Then three people went flying into the water, and one of the people was really hurt.”The police officers were in the water for an estimated 10 minutes, he said, and in that time someone threw a life ring in for one of them.In a post on X, the London fire brigade said: “We’re responding to an incident on the #RiverThames near Westminster Bridge alongside partner agencies. The brigade’s fire boat and three fire rescue units with water rescue capabilities have been mobilised to the scene. We were called at 15.58 and remain on scene.“We are supporting the response and providing assistance where needed, working closely with the Metropolitan police, HM Coastguard and partner agencies to manage the situation.”Transport for London said exits one and two at Westminster tube station were closed. Thames Clippers, which operates Uber Boat, said “some services” may be subject to disruption as a result of the incident. It said Westminster pier was closed until further notice.Explore more on these topicsLondonPoliceMetropolitan policeEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump threatens EU with ‘substantial’ tariffs over fines of US tech giants | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: After Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Brussels was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayers
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: After Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Brussels was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayers
Content: Donald Trump has lately imposed dozens of new tariffs on countries throughout the world.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump has lately imposed dozens of new tariffs on countries throughout the world.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsTrump threatens EU with ‘substantial’ tariffs over fines of US tech giantsAfter Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Brussels was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayersWhat to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countriesGaya Guptain WashingtonFri 24 Jul 2026 17.22 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas threatened the European Union with additional and “substantial” tariffs after Brussels imposed a series ofsteep fineson US tech giants.The US president accused Brussels of taking “direct aim” at several American companies including Apple, Meta Platforms, Amazon and Google,writing in a Truth Social post: “The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ forEurope, nor will we allow it to be!”Days earlier, Google was fined €890m ($1bn) by the EU after its search and app store services were found to have breached online competition laws. Last yearApple and Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, were also fined.Trump claimed in his social media post on Friday that the US would “immediately” launch an investigation into the EU’s practice of “‘ROBBING’ American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer,” and said that the EU will “pay a very big price” for its actions.It came just a day after the Trump administrationseparately imposed a sweeping round of tariffson more than 80 countries, including those in the EU.Trump accused of using forced labor as ‘convenient’ justification for tariffsRead moreThe European Commission did not immediately comment on Trump’s threat on Friday. Announcing the fine on Google on Wednesday, it said the tech company had given “preferential treatment to its own services, including shopping, hotels, transport and sports results”.Google welcomed Trump’s intervention on Friday.Jose Castaneda, a spokesperson for the company, said Google had worked hard to comply with the EU’s Digital Markets Act and expressed its concerns about the effects of recent decisions by the European Commission. “We appreciate the engagement by the administration and U.S. government,” he said.Trump has often used tariffs – or simply the threat of them – as a way to retaliate against countries for decisions outside trade policy. Last year, he threatened a tax on imports from Mexico and Canada until the two countries agreed to implementmeasures on border security.Despite challenges from the supreme court, Trump has persisted in implementing tariffs globally, claiming that they will help boost US jobs and manufacturing. The tariffs he announced yesterday would impose a 10% levy on the EU, and were designed to clamp down on what Trump claimed were unfair labor practices.The EU has cracked down on a handful of large tech companies since before the start of Trump’s presidency after passing the Digital Markets Act, meant to help regulate competition among digital media companies.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsEuropean UnionDonald TrumpTariffsUS politicsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: US surpasses 2025’s record number of measles infections as cases climb | MMR | The Guardian
description: The latest milestone, a recorded 2,318 infections, makes 2026 the worst year for measles in the US since 1991
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: The latest milestone, a recorded 2,318 infections, makes 2026 the worst year for measles in the US since 1991
Content: Health department staff members enter the Andrews county health department measles clinic carrying doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, on 8 April 2025, in Andrews, Texas.Photograph: Annie Rice/APView image in fullscreenHealth department staff members enter the Andrews county health department measles clinic carrying doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, on 8 April 2025, in Andrews, Texas.Photograph: Annie Rice/APMMRUS surpasses 2025’s record number of measles infections as cases climbThe latest milestone, a recorded 2,318 infections, makes 2026 the worst year for measles in the US since 1991Marina DunbarFri 24 Jul 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has officially surpassed last year’s record number of measles infections, marking the highest case count since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000.New figures from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released on Friday show the country has recorded 2,318 measles cases in 2026, overtaking the 2,289 cases reported during all of 2025 – with five months still remaining in the year. The country crossed the2,000-case thresholdlast month before climbing even higher in July.The latest milestone makes 2026 the worst year for measles in the US since 1991. Large outbreaks inSouth Carolina,UtahandArizonahave infected hundreds of people, while additional clusters have emerged in several other states.CDC cuts leave US less prepared for disease outbreaks, former officials warnRead moreThe growing outbreak makes it increasingly likely that the US could be entering a period in which measles once again becomes a regularly circulating disease, capable of sickening thousands of people each year.International health officials arescheduled to meetin November to decide whether the US and Mexico should lose their measles-free status. The US achieved elimination of local measles transmission in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, butcoverage has declinedin recent years, falling below the 95% level considered necessary to prevent outbreaks.Even as reported cases continue to rise, the true scope of the outbreak may never be fully known. Public health officials and disease researchers have long said official totals are incomplete because some infected people never seek medical care.Experts say reversing the current trend would require a nationwide effort to increase vaccination rates, but such an undertaking appears unlikely under the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long history ofdownplayingthe importance of immunizations and grosslyoverstatingtheir risks.The American Academy of Pediatrics, which has sharply criticized the Trump administration’s approach to vaccines, described the new record as “an avoidable crisis that disproportionally hurts children”.“These thousands of cases represent real people in communities across the country, including babies hospitalized with pneumonia, students who have missed weeks of school, and parents forced to miss work to stay home and care for sick children,” thestatementsaid. “We should not accept this as our new normal. Unless we reverse this trend, America’s children will continue to pay the price.”The measles surge comes as the US continues to face multiple public health threats, includinghantavirus,screwworm,Ebola,cyclosporiasis,whooping coughandbird flu, highlighting growing concerns about the nation’s ability to prevent, detect and contain infectious disease outbreaks, especially as the Trump administration has cutstaffing and fundingto several preventive and response programs.Former top CDC officials say the rapid dismantling of the US public health system at every level has left the country ina weaker positionthan it was before the Covid pandemic.Explore more on these topicsMMRHealthUS healthcareVaccines and immunisationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nutrients in our food are declining. Can regenerative agriculture save it? | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: Approach focuses on rebuilding soil health, increasing biodiversity and restoring natural ecosystems
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Approach focuses on rebuilding soil health, increasing biodiversity and restoring natural ecosystems
Content: The calcium content in carrots fell by more than a quarter between the mid-1970s and the late 1990s, according to the US Department of Agriculture.Photograph: Marcio José Sánchez/APView image in fullscreenThe calcium content in carrots fell by more than a quarter between the mid-1970s and the late 1990s, according to the US Department of Agriculture.Photograph: Marcio José Sánchez/APVegetablesNutrients in our food are declining. Can regenerative agriculture save it?Approach focuses on rebuilding soil health, increasing biodiversity and restoring natural ecosystemsHugh ThomasFri 24 Jul 2026 08.34 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the last few decades, the nutrient content of our crops has been declining. In the late 90s,the US Department of Agriculture foundthe vitamin C content of lemons had decreased by almost a third over the previous 22 years. Calcium in carrots, an important source especially for non-meat eaters,had reduced, on average, by more than a quarter. Vitamin A in bananas wasdown by57%. The mineral content of wheat has declined bybetween 20-30%since the 1960s.A number of reasons have been suggested for this worrying decline, ranging from new varieties of crop that are bred to grow quicker and bigger to thehigher carbon dioxide levelsin the air causing plants to produce more sugars and starches (they grow faster but they produce fewer nutrients). A wide range of fixes have been suggested,from GM cropsto synthetic soil amendments, or underground farms.One group of agricultural researchers, however, argues that the answer to declining nutrients may be more straightforward than that: regenerative agriculture. This “focuses on building organic matter and ecosystems in the soil”, says Francesca Brkic. “The question is, does that therefore deliver more nutrition?”Her work, in conjunction with the University of Lincoln, explores how regenerative agriculture affects nutrient density. The researchers sampled a number of products and found that iron in kale could be up to 22 times higher in samples from regenerative farms compared with conventional ones, while selenium (an antioxidant) in dried peas was eight times higher and folate (good for red blood cells) in carrots was up to 20,000 times greater.Brkic says: “Organic had to be our minimum baseline, because regen doesn’t have a certifiable standard. But while organic as a concept focuses on not doing harmful things, it doesn’t specify that you are doing positive things.” Regenerative farms, in this case, were defined by those using cover crops and grazing animals, while abstaining from ploughing the land and using insecticides or other pesticides.View image in fullscreenFungicide and insecticide are sprayed on a field of bell pepper plants in Florida.Photograph: Design Pics Inc/AlamyThe way soil is treated by modern farming may be part of the problem. Ploughing and heavy use of chemicals – fertilisers, herbicides and pesticides – disturb and even destroy the soil’s mycorrhizal networks, which we are only just coming to understand but allow plants to pull in nutrients from the earth.Dr David Montgomery, a US geologist and the co-author of the book What YourFoodAte,says we need regenerative agriculture to right the wrongs of the “degenerative” farming that helped sustain a postwar population boom but wrecked soil health in the process.“It was the microbial truckers and miners in our soils that got put off the job by conventional agriculture,” he says. “Regenerative practices that treat soil as an ecosystem can return those miners and truckers to the job.” Montgomery and his wife, Anne Biklé, a biologist,undertook a studyin 2022, albeit on a much smaller scale, noting some correlation between regenerative agriculture and higher nutrient density in food crops in the US.Other studies support these findings. A largeliterature reviewby Newcastle University in 2015, for example, found that a switch to eating organic fruit, vegetable and cereals – and food made from them – would provide additional antioxidants equivalent to eating between one to two extra portions of fruit and vegetables a day. The Bionutrient Institute multi-year study framework tested thousands of samples and found that thestrongest positive correlationfor high nutritional value was the biological activity and overall health of the soil.View image in fullscreenA farmer in Cambridgeshire points out soil health at a farm that follows regenerative agriculture practices.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianBut other research has not reached similar conclusions. Reviews by the UK and French food standard agencies found some differences, but concluded that they were small. A large-scale review by Stanford University also found that although some organic foods did contain higher levels of minerals and nutrients, with phosphorus in particular higher across the board, the results were still highly variable and in some cases insignificant.Regenerative agriculture has plenty of critics. It is much less reliant on mechanisation and agrochemicals and can require more human labour (therefore is often considered less cost-effective). It is also susceptible to greenwashing (increasingly prevalent, asstudies have shown) and, in the context of nutrition, medical professionals say they already have enough of a challenge getting their patients to eat enough fruit and veg without the extra cost.One sceptic, the physician Dr Naheed Ali, notes the phenomenon of “dietary displacement”, wherein an individual perceives a food to have more nutritional value than it actually has because of its sustainable or regenerative claims, and as a result, may eat much less of it. “This belief,” Ali says, “can lead to inadequate intake of important macronutrients and micronutrients. In my practice, I see examples of this type of thinking frequently.”View image in fullscreenThere are concerns consumers may perceive a food to have more nutritional value than it does because of its sustainable or regenerative claims.Photograph: Ceri Breeze/AlamyOn top of that, some soil scientists, such as ProfKen Giller and his colleagues, think it is “unlikely” that regenerative agriculture can be implemented in a way that reliably feeds the world’s 8.3 billion people and counting while reaping environmental benefits.Montgomery disagrees. “I’m confident regenerative can scale [up] because it’s not dependent on particular practices or equipment. What it’s dependent on is a particular philosophy – the idea we build soil health as the north star of agriculture,” he says.Perhaps that is the central lesson from this research; there is potentially some glorious gold to be found in farming practices that improve soil health, both for biodiversity and for nutrition.How can we integrate that into the way food systems, and society at large, already operate? “Just imagine what we could do,” says Brkic, “if we made a few tweaks to our soil and agriculture practices and the impact that that would have on us.”Explore more on these topicsVegetablesFoodFarmingNutrition (Science)Nutrition (Life and style)AgricultureClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rare heron seen at Somerset estate where river has been allowed to run free | Birds | The Guardian
description: Black-crowned night heron one of many species thriving at Holnicote Estate where river ‘reset’ has transformed area into lush oasis
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Black-crowned night heron one of many species thriving at Holnicote Estate where river ‘reset’ has transformed area into lush oasis
Content: Rare night heron spotted on Somerset estateBirdsRare heron seen at Somerset estate where river has been allowed to run freeBlack-crowned night heron one of many species thriving at Holnicote Estate where river ‘reset’ has transformed area into lush oasisSteven MorrisFri 24 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA rareblack-crowned night heronhas been spotted on an estate in the south-west of England where an innovative river “reset” is transforming the area into an oasis for birdlife.The heron was caught on camera in a jungly corner of the Holnicote Estate, where conservation experts have been restoring the landscape by allowing a river to return to its natural course.As well as the heron, charismatic birds includingwhite-tailed eagles, white storks and cranes have been seen at the National Trust estate.View image in fullscreenHolnicote Estate, where conservation experts have been restoring the landscape by allowing a river to return to its natural course.Photograph: James Beck/National Trust/PABen Eardley, restore nature project manager forSomersetcoast and countryside, said it had been incredible to see the heron. “It’s rare to see this wetland species in the UK and so exciting that we observed one on our estate cameras on three consecutive days,” he said.Eardley believes that more birds were congregating becauseso much of southern England is dry, while parts of Holnicote remain wet and lush.“Everywhere else is parched, so we’re seeing lots of wildlife utilise it and lots of interesting bird species arrive. It’s proving a real refuge.”View image in fullscreenHolnicote’s night heron, pictured, was spotted close to a camera set up to provide a livestream of the area.Photograph: National TrustAs well as birds, the estate is providing a home or hunting grounds for water voles, otters, pine martens and grass snakes.The black-crowned night heron typically grows up to 66cm (26in), roughly half the length of the grey heron, which is commonly seen in the UK.It has grey plumage, yellow legs and a black “cap” from which trail long white plume feathers. As its name implies, it is mainly active at night.The bird is widespread across Africa, Asia, the Americas and mainland Europe. According to the British Trust for Ornithology, the first confirmed night heron breeding in the UK was recorded in Somerset in 2017but it is categorised as a scarce visitor.Holnicote’s night heron was spotted close toa camera set up to provide a livestreamof an area wherebeavers have been introducedto play a part in the landscape restoration.View image in fullscreenA black-crowned night heron in Romania.Photograph: Pal Hermansen/National Trust/PAEardley said there were trout, sticklebacks, eels and European bullhead fish in the water there. “When we set up the camera, we weren’t sure how popular it would be but people have really got into it. The night heron appeared front centre.”Over the past 500 years,England has lost approximately 90% of its wetlands. Work is being done through organisations and partnerships to restore, enhance, increase and connect the lost habitats.For centuries the River Aller at Holnicote had been carefully controlled by landowners and farmers,largely confined to a narrow channel.View image in fullscreenA pond at Holnicote Estate, Somerset, which was recently created to encourage and benefit wildlife.Photograph: Nick Upton/National TrustInspired by schemes in the wilds of Oregon in north-west US, a stretch of the river was liberated,allowing the water to spill out and find its own way, creating smaller streams, more pools and boggy areas, better for flora and fauna, with the slower water flow making flooding less likely.Eardley said it had led to a surge in creatures including reptiles, amphibians and insects – which in turn attracted predators.While the night heron and white-tailed eagles –which have been re-introducedon the Isle of Wight after being driven to extinction in the UK – have been seen close to the beavers’ home, the cranes and storks have frequented the wider estate. “The birds are very visible indicator of an ecosystem getting more diverse.”Explore more on these topicsBirdsThe National TrustSomersetEndangered speciesEnglandConservationRiversnewsShareReuse this content

title: What can the Galápagos Islands’ animals teach us about the threats of El Niño? | Environment | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: the archipelago at the centre of the extreme weather phenomenon could help scientists predict how other marine ecosystems will adapt to our warming climate
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: the archipelago at the centre of the extreme weather phenomenon could help scientists predict how other marine ecosystems will adapt to our warming climate
Content: Plunged into a hot bath … marine iguanas are just one of the animals dealing with rising ocean temperatures in the Galápagos Islands.Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPlunged into a hot bath … marine iguanas are just one of the animals dealing with rising ocean temperatures in the Galápagos Islands.Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty ImagesDown to Earth newsletterEnvironmentWhat can the Galápagos Islands’ animals teach us about the threats of El Niño?In this week’s newsletter: the archipelago at the centre of the extreme weather phenomenon could help scientists predict how other marine ecosystems will adapt to our warming climateDon’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up herePatrick GreenfieldFri 24 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ocean waters around theGalápagos Islandsare hot. Very hot. Observed for centuries in the Pacific by fishers, the El Niño weather phenomenon begins when the prevailing trade winds slow, allowing warm water to spread east along the coast of South America. Right now, the pattern is in full flow and will build from this year into next, likely bringing record temperatures to an already overheating world.If 2026 is not the hottest year on record, 2027 surely will be – and the Galápagos archipelago is in the centre of this climate crisis.More on the consequences of this, after this week’s most important reads.Essential reads‘It’s only going to get worse’: wildfires forcing firefighters to make impossible choicesMillions face long-term coastal flooding risk in UK without climate action, scientists warnSlowdown in Arctic ice melt ends after largest winter decline on recordIn focusView image in fullscreenCan’t beat the heat … the population of Galápagos penguins falls sharply during El Niño years.Photograph: Gareth Codd/Getty ImagesIn normal conditions, the water in the eastern Pacific is cold: Galápagos penguins and fur seals live on the islands, species more commonly associated with ecosystems closer to the poles. The archipelago is the only place in the world where you can see penguins swimming next to coral reefs.The arrival of El Niño always signals an abrupt change, effectively giving the marine ecosystem a hot bath: water temperatures rise fromaround 18C to above 30C, causing a population crash in many fish species as nutrients disappear from the water. The populations of sea birds such as Nazca boobies, penguins and blue-footed boobies also go into freefall, while marine iguanas starve en masse. When temperatures drop in a La Niña year, marine life explodes once again.This pattern has played out for so long that many species on the islands have adapted to such oscillations. Iguanas in the Galápagos can shrink their body skeletons in El Niño years to increase their chances of survival, and regrow them when normal conditions return. But climate change presents a fresh evolutionary challenge as El Niños become more frequent and more extreme in a warming climate. There are fears among scientists that these extremes will drive some species into extinction in the coming decades.“The Galápagos Islands has some of the highest temperature variability of any ecosystem in the world,” says Jon Witman, a professor emeritus of ecology at Brown University, who has been studying the cycles in the Galápagos for years. “Things are always going up and down with the El Niño-La Niña cycle. There’s an almost total collapse of the marine system during El Niño, and it comes roaring back duringLa Niña. But how much stress can an ecosystem take?”In the face of future climate extremes, the ecosystem that inspired the theory of evolution has a key role in helping researchers understand how plants and animals will respond. Witman was part of a team that recorded an ulcerative skin disease outbreak in many fish species during the 2015-16 El Niño, with knock-on effects across the food network. During the severe 1982-83 El Niño, several endemic species on the Galápagos went extinct, including the Galápagos damselfish. Witman and his team are bracing themselves for what the 2026-27 El Niño will bring.“The main question I have is if these climate shocks become so frequent that the ecosystem passes a tipping point and switches to another state of perhaps low productivity and biodiversity,” says Witman. “That happens with ecosystems. They get pushed so far that they end up in an entirely new state. In that sense, it’s kind of a natural laboratory for the future.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is not all doom and gloom. These islands have long proved resilient to extremes, and Witman says he is quietly optimistic about what they will be able to withstand, even as the Earth continues to heat.“We are in a new zone. It’s worrisome, but studying the ecosystem gives me hope,” he says. “In my work studying corals, I have definitely seen changes in the composition of reefs. But they have been towards more resilient species that can recover after extreme El Niños.”Read more:‘Super El Niño’ is officially here, scientists say. What can we expect?El Niño is back with a vengeance – and fears of ‘Godzilla’ strength may be the least of our worries‘We are waiting with bated breath’: experts alarmed as BoM says gathering El Niño could be strongest on recordTo read the complete version of this newsletter –subscribe to receive Down to Earthin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentDown to Earth newsletterGalápagos IslandsClimate crisisEl Niño southern oscillationLa NiñaExtinct wildlifenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Most people arrested during Henry Nowak protests had been reported for domestic abuse | UK news | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Hampshire police data reveals 22 of 37 detained had been accused or convicted of intimate partner violence
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Exclusive: Hampshire police data reveals 22 of 37 detained had been accused or convicted of intimate partner violence
Content: The outburst of violence in Southampton last month came after a demonstration outside the city centre’s police station.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAView image in fullscreenThe outburst of violence in Southampton last month came after a demonstration outside the city centre’s police station.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAUK newsMost people arrested during Henry Nowak protests had been reported for domestic abuseExclusive: Hampshire police data reveals 22 of 37 detained had been accused or convicted of intimate partner violenceNic Murray andRajeev SyalFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost people arrested during violent protests after the sentencing of Henry Nowak’s murderer had previously been reported to the police for domestic abuse, the Guardian can disclose.Data released by Hampshire police under freedom of information laws shows that 22 of 37 people (59%) detained inSouthamptonafter Vickrum Digwa was jailed for life have been reported for crimes associated with intimate partner violence.Protests took place on 2 June after police bodycam footage was released showing Nowak, 18, handcuffed as he lay dying after being stabbed by Digwa, who had falsely accused him of racism. Nowak repeatedly said he had been stabbed.Digwa stabbed Nowak with a large blade he claimed to carry as part of his Sikh faith, before falsely telling police he had been the victim of a racist attack, leading officers to initially arrest the white teenager rather than his killer.The footage led to claims from Nigel Farage and others that it was evidence of “two-tier policing” and “anti-white prejudice” within police forces.Demonstrators initially gathered outside a city centre police station, with several hundred people then attempting to march towards the murder location and the street where Digwa’s family lived. During prolonged violent disorder, 12 police officers were injured, and nearby properties and vehicles were damaged.View image in fullscreenTwelve police officers were injured during the clashes with protesters in Southampton last month.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersHarry Varney, 34, claimed he attended the public gathering to pay his respects to Nowak, but was later filmed swearing at police and punching their riot shields. He was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment.In 2023, he pleaded guilty to assault by beating after pinning his partner against a bedroom wall, bruising her neck. He claimed she deserved to be beaten by a previous abusive ex-partner and continued to threaten her after this attack.She said in a written statement read out in court: “I suffer with flashbacks, anxiety attacks and nightmares. I also now struggle with my social life trusting people. I can’t be left alone with a man without feeling scared.”Dillon Crawford, 29, was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment after throwing a brown bin and a metal chair “with some force” at police officers during the disturbances. He has 19 previous convictions, including for domestic abuse offences. During one incident, he broke a partner’s front teeth, punching her unconscious, and, after she woke up, told her he had put bleach in her hair.Andrew Summerhayes, 38, was seen throwing a wheelie bin at police during the disorder. He was sentenced to three years and two months for violent disorder and possession of an offensive weapon.Hampshire police confirmed that 33 people had now been charged for their involvement in the public disorder. The force has referred itself to the police watchdog, with two officers who attended the scene beinginvestigated for potential gross misconductby the Independent Office for Police Conduct. The investigation is considering potential failures to identify that Nowak needed urgent medical help and the decision to arrest and handcuff him before providing first aid.The Guardianpreviously revealedthat two out of every five arrested for participating in riots in 2024 had been the subject of a domestic abuse report before their involvement, with one in five subsequently being reported for domestic abuse.Farah Nazeer, the chief executive of Women’s Aid, said: “Over the last two years, we have seen recurrent anti-migrant protests that have erupted into violence, with many of those arrested also carrying convictions for domestic abuse or other crimes against women and girls. It is not surprising that someone who is violent in public may also be violent at home, as there is a proven correlation between the two.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “Violence against women and girls is a national emergency. We will continue to deploy the full power of the state to bring perpetrators to justice and prevent harm before it occurs.“Our violence against women and girls strategy sets out how we willpursue and manage domestic abuse perpetrators, including through the rollout of new domestic abuse protection orders.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsViolence against women and girlsSouthamptonPoliceHampshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s generations of decline’: can Andy Burnham really end rough sleeping? | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: Outreach workers on the frontline of England’s homelessness crisis react to PM’s flagship policy pledge
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Outreach workers on the frontline of England’s homelessness crisis react to PM’s flagship policy pledge
Content: A rough sleeper in south London. Burnham’s pledge has been welcomed by homelessness charities but with some scepticism.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA rough sleeper in south London. Burnham’s pledge has been welcomed by homelessness charities but with some scepticism.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianHomelessness‘It’s generations of decline’: can Andy Burnham really end rough sleeping?Outreach workers on the frontline of England’s homelessness crisis react to PM’s flagship policy pledgeUK politics live – latest updatesJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentFri 24 Jul 2026 09.31 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is close to midnight as two outreach workers from Spear, a homelessness charity in south London, shine their torches around bushes on the edge of a park in Twickenham.Suddenly they alight on an array of sleeping bags, airbeds, toilet rolls and plastic bags stuffed with belongings – a rough sleeping encampment that has popped up in the last two days.“We are seeing numbers going up which is really not what we want,” said Peter Bancroft, the operations manager at the charity. “And it is everyone from individuals with complex mental health and substance use issues, to people who have either had a relationship breakdown or lost their job and fallen behind with their rental payments.”In a bold first pledge in his first speech as prime minister,Andy Burnham promised to eradicate rough sleepingin England, allocating an extra £340m of funding.The move was welcomed by homelessness charities, but with some scepticism:Boris Johnson saidhe would end rough sleeping when he was prime minister, andKeir Starmer vowedto halve long-term rough sleeping during his time in office.Yet rough sleeping numbers have risen to 4,793, the highest on record.View image in fullscreenA makeshift shelter in Tooting, south London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianOn their shift, Spear outreach workers are following up nine referrals for new rough sleepers who have been spotted throughout Wandsworth and Richmond in the past 48 hours, as well as checking on the people they already know and speaking to others they spot on the way.Their journey takes them into graveyards, parks, front gardens, shop doorways and car parks, where people have been spotted sleeping in tents, in cars and on the ground. Some people are happy to chat to the workers – they accept water, the offer of a mobile phone and a housing assessment – but others turn down all offers of help.Two people with drug addiction issues sleeping in a haphazard tent in the corner of a graveyard had emergency council accommodation until two weeks ago, but they didn’t use it and it was revoked.Bancroft said: “I would love to be able to say homelessness services can deal with this, but I’ve been playing the game a long time now and I know the best results have been in partnership with other services.View image in fullscreenA rough sleeping site in Twickenham, west London.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“You’ve got to get drug and alcohol services, mental health services, social services, all onboard, everybody working collaboratively to wrap around the person or it just falls apart. Ultimately, my dream is to be out of a job because that would mean we’ve solved it, but it’s not easy.”The details on Burnham’s rough sleeping plans are still unclear but it is likely he will build on the success of hisA Bed Every Night schemein Manchester, which departed from the norm by allowing all rough sleepers to access support – even those without local connections or recourse to public funds.It also provided individuals with case workers to deal with multiple issues, not just housing, and it ran alongside aHousingFirst pilot scheme targeted at the most complex rough sleeping cases, which guided more than 300 people into long-term tenancies.There is a growing consensus that funnelling lots of vulnerable rough sleepers, many with complex needs, illnesses and addictions, into communal living spaces such as hostels and houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) often pushes people back into homelessness.View image in fullscreenRay, who experienced homelessness after sudden sight loss.Photograph: Grey HuttonSocial housing is still being built at a painfully slow rate in England – Burnham has pledged the “biggestcouncil housebuilding programmesince the postwar period”, but his housing minister, Angela Rayner, has since acknowledged the country is still very far off this building pace.Francesca Albanese, the executive director of policy and social change at Crisis, said: “For a long time inEnglandwe’ve just been maintaining the status quo, so putting lots of money into hostels, emergency and temporary accommodation – managing homelessness not ending it.“What we need is to get people off the streets into permanent homes, not into temporary accommodation. Housing First is the most evidence-led intervention we know that works to end rough sleeping so we need to see that rolled out nationally. We know about Andy’s track record and there’s real optimism this can be done.”Ray, 53, spent four years drifting between sofa surfing, street homelessness and temporary accommodation that was “barely nicer than a prison cell” in Liverpool after experiencing sudden sight loss. It was only when he was given support from Crisis and finally offered a social home that he was able to turn his life around.“The biggest thing for me is the government should be opening front doors again for people to come into and not putting all the pressure on charities,” he said. “I thinkAndy Burnhambrings positivity to this and a different outlook. Housing is a right and shouldn’t be a fight. But this is not about one individual, it’s about a country that’s been in decline for generations.”View image in fullscreenA homeless person sleeping outside Westminster magistrates court in central London.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThursday briefing: ​Now he has the power to do it, can Andy Burham really end homelessness in the UK?Read moreAs well as the wider cost of living crisis, there are a range of policies thought to be driving up rough sleeping. Local housing allowance rates have been frozen which has increased the gap between what benefits cover and what landlords are charging, pushing more people into rent arrears.Charities also said an increasing number of people on the streets are people who have left prison, or asylum seekers who have been granted refugee status and moved out of Home Office accommodation.Any attempt to eradicate rough sleeping must deal with all these issues, experts said, not forgetting that a lot of rough sleepers – especially women – are not represented in the national statistics.Lucy Campbell of the Single Homeless Project said: “If Andy Burnham is serious about ending rough sleeping, he needs to be the first political leader who’s not going to shy away from saying, actually, the figures are much higher than we think they are.“And we cannot expect generic homelessness initiatives to work the same for men as they do for women and the LGBTQ community.”Explore more on these topicsHomelessnessHousingAndy BurnhamLabourSocial exclusionPovertyCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform councillors told to call donations inquiry ‘establishment stitch-up’ | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Party briefing notes say: ‘Daily routine of hit jobs and smears will not deter us from winning next general election’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Party briefing notes say: ‘Daily routine of hit jobs and smears will not deter us from winning next general election’
Content: Police are investigating donations worth £500,000 made to Nigel Farage’s party by the mother the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenPolice are investigating donations worth £500,000 made to Nigel Farage’s party by the mother the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAReform UKReform councillors told to call donations inquiry ‘establishment stitch-up’Party briefing notes say: ‘Daily routine of hit jobs and smears will not deter us from winning next general election’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 24 Jul 2026 13.12 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has instructed its councillors to describe a police investigation into donations from the mother of George Cottrell as an establishment stitch-up, as polling showed the party’s popularity plummeting.Internal briefing documents circulated to the party’s councillors included instructions to respond to questions about aMetropolitan police investigationinto party donations with: “It is now clear that the establishment will try anything to stop us”, theTimes revealed on Thursday.Local government representatives were also instructed to respond to questions with: “The British people are tired of the establishment media doing anything they can to stop Reform. A daily routine of hit jobs and smears will not deter us from winning the next general election and fixing broken Britain.”Police areinvestigating donations worth £500,000made to Reform UK by Fiona Cottrell, the mother of the crypto-gambler and convicted fraudster “Posh George”, who is a close friend of Farage.The Guardianrevealed in Aprilthat the Reform UK leader had received a£5m giftfrom the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election, which iscurrently subject to standards inquiry. The Conservativeshave also asked HMRC to investigatewhether Farage should have paid tax on the £5m gift. Farage is alsosubject to another inquiryover allegations that he breached parliamentary rules by being financially supported by Cottrell.View image in fullscreenGeorge Cottrell beside Farage on the campaign trail in 2024, when the Reform leader was doused in milkshake.Photograph: James Manning/PAHow to Launder Money But Not Like Me, by George Cottrell (as imagined by John Crace)Read moreNew polling by YouGov shows that NigelFarage’s popularity has plummeted, falling to the joint lowest level in the decade it has been tracked by the pollster. Only 22% of people have a positive view of Farage, while 68% see him in a negative light – a net favourability rating of -46.YouGov said the figure was on a par with figures recorded by Boris Johnson after the first “partygate” revelations had broken (-42 in early December 2021) and Keir Starmer just before his resignation (-45).The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, is also enjoying popularity levels higher than those of any Conservative leader for more than five years, according to the survey.Separate polling byMore in Commonindicated that Burnham’s personal approval rating is already higher after a week in office than Starmer ever achieved. The new prime minister has a net approval rating of +13, with a blitz of voter-pleasing policies appearing to have given a boost to the former mayor of Greater Manchester.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow could Britain look under proportional representation? See the results for your areaRead moreIn addition, YouGov’slatest voting-intention pollfo the Times and Sky News showed that Labour and the Tories are now within touching distance of Reform UK. Labour appears to be enjoying a “Burnham bounce”, with the party at its most popular since January.It shows Labour just two points behind Reform – with Farage’s party on 23% of the vote, Labour on 21% and the Conservatives on 20%.YouGov gives Labour its highest figure recorded by the pollsters since January, up five points from the 16% low recorded for the party four times between March and early May this year.The polling continues to show a tightening between the three parties. In the aftermath of May’s local elections, Reform UK polled a 28% vote share, giving them an 11-point lead over any other party.In his first cabinet meeting, Burnhampromised to lead a “cost of living government”,and has used a string of early morning announcements this morning to grab the public’s attention.His first major announcement since taking office was a cut toVAT on electricity billsfrom October, beforecapping bus fares at £2and giving pubs, clubs and live music venuesa 20% discount on their business rates billsas part of a £100m aid package. Burnham has faced questions abouthow these measures will bepaid for, but the new administration insists all measures are fully funded.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: British-born man living in US since age of nine held by ICE under threat of deportation | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Connor Read, who is married and has two children, was detained in June during residency permit interview
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Connor Read, who is married and has two children, was detained in June during residency permit interview
Content: Connor Read, 29 with his wife, Jaelin, 25.Photograph: HandoutView image in fullscreenConnor Read, 29 with his wife, Jaelin, 25.Photograph: HandoutICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)British-born man living in US since age of nine held by ICE under threat of deportationConnor Read, who is married and has two children, was detained in June during residency permit interviewJamie GriersonFri 24 Jul 2026 08.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA British-born man who has lived in the US since he was nine years old has been held in an ICE detention facility for more than a month and a half under threat of deportation, it has been reported.Connor Read, 29, was taken by ICE agents after he was invited to a green card (residency permit) interview in Tampa,Florida, on 3 June, and separated from his wife, Jaelin, 25, and his three-year-old twin sons Ryder and Ozzie.Originally from Chatham, in Kent, Read moved to the US in 2007 as a child with his mother and stepfather. He attended American schools and only returned to the UK once.According tothe Times, he was subject to a removal order in 2011 but at the age of 16 was grantedDeferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (Daca) status, a policy that provides deportation relief and work permits to eligible individuals who entered the US as children.But while under Daca status Read reportedly gained minor convictions, including for possession of narcotic equipment, possession of liquor and resisting an officer, that have now led to him being deemed a “criminal illegal alien” by theTrump administration.View image in fullscreenFederal agents standing guard at Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility, in Newark, New Jersey.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianThe Times reported that because of the narcotic charge, at the age of 22, Read was unable to renew his Daca status. He met Jaelin on a dating app in 2020, when his immigration status was unsettled. Having married, the couple tried to apply for a green card.On 3 June, Read was invited to attend a green card meeting at the federal immigration building inTampa. In the interview room, four ICE agents arrested him and removed him from the building. Immigration officials told Jaelin Read that her husband would not be coming home.He was taken to Pinellas county jail, in Florida, where he spent eight days in a shared cell, and was then flown to an ICE detention centre in Louisiana. He is appealing against his final removal order but has been told a decision may take up to six months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS immigration agents arrested a record number of people in June, data showsRead moreAn ICE spokesperson told the Times: “Connor Michael Read, a criminal illegal alien of the United Kingdom, was arrested on 3 June 2026 by the ICE law enforcement in Tampa, Florida.“His criminal history includes convictions for possession of narcotic equipment, possession of liquor and resisting an officer. He was issued a final order of removal, issued by an Orlando, Florida, immigration judge from January 2011.“Read entered the United States on 21 November 2007, through the Orlando international airport as a non-immigrant with an F-2 visa, as a dependent of an F-1 non-immigrant student. Read’s status was contingent upon his parent’s status as a student. After a violation of the terms of their visa, Read was placed into removal proceedings.“Under President Trump and [homeland security] secretary Mullin, ICE is targeting the worst of the worst. Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the US.”Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationUS politicsUS immigrationFloridaTampanewsShareReuse this content

title: Masked men invading and taking Amazon communities ‘hostage’ in organised crime surge, say local leaders | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
description: Delegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western Amazon
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Delegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western Amazon
Content: Masked gunmen entered homes in the Brazilian village of Apiwtxa, within the Amazon Forest, earlier this month.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APView image in fullscreenMasked gunmen entered homes in the Brazilian village of Apiwtxa, within the Amazon Forest, earlier this month.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APAmazon rainforestMasked men invading and taking Amazon communities ‘hostage’ in organised crime surge, say local leadersDelegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western AmazonJonathan WattsFri 24 Jul 2026 07.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndigenous leaders on the Brazilian-Peruvian border have said their communities are being “taken hostage” by organised crime groups who are running rampant across the region, destroying rainforest, building roads and trafficking drugs.Earlier this month, masked men armed with semi-automatic weapons entered homes in Apiwtxa, a village in the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory, intimidating people and searching for targets.The Asháninka people, who have faced threats from intruders for decades because of their efforts to protect the forest and eject narco smugglers, say this is the worst danger they have faced, prompting an emergency delegation to Brasília this week to appeal for support from the government of the president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.“Either the state steps in to provide protection, or communities will start organising to defend themselves – and that would be disastrous,” said Francisco Piyãko, the general coordinator of the Organisation of Indigenous People of the Juruá River, who is part of the delegation. “We are not facing a local conflict. We are facing the expansion of transnational criminal networks into Indigenous territories that currently represent one of the last barriers against the illegal occupation of this region of the Amazon.”View image in fullscreenThe Asháninka Indigenous people are seeking protection from the Brazilian government.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APThe petition of the Asháninka people comes amid growing concerns about the nexus of drug trafficking and environmental crime, which Brazilian climate scientistCarlos Nobre has describedas the greatest new threat to the Amazon Forest.The Brazilian side of the border is in Acre state, where the forest is still relatively healthy compared with the Peruvian side, which has experienced heavy logging and violence. Acre has sometimes been a perilous area for environmental and land defenders. One of the country’s most celebrated forest campaigners,Chico Mendes, was shot dead there in 1988. After that, there was a period of relative peace in Acre, compared with other countries in the Amazon or other Brazilian states such as Pará. More recently, however, there has been a rise in tension, much of it from the outside. Isolated Indigenous communities from Peru have beenincreasingly crossing the border to escapeconfrontation with loggers and drug cartels.Apiwtxa was the last Indigenous village visited by the British journalist Dom Phillips before he was murdered in the neighbouring Brazilian border state of Amazonas in 2022 while researchingillegal extractivist activitiesin another area menaced by arms and drug smugglers.View image in fullscreenSunrise on the Amônia River, which runs through the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory in Brazil.Photograph: Nicoló Lanfranchi/The GuardianAccording to the Asháninka petition to the Brazilian government, the most recent intrusion into Apiwtxa involved five heavily armed, Spanish-speaking men arriving on the evening of 6 July at the home of one of the Asháninka leaders, who was out of the village at the time. “They were clearly poised to attack with lethal intent,” said one member of the community. It was the second time in several days that masked gunmen had entered the village looking for leaders.Frightened villagers took their children into one building for protection and notified the authorities. The army arrived at midnight, by which time the would-be assassins had disappeared back into the forest, leaving only tracks.“For us, this was a threat unlike any other, because they came right into our home – they entered our house,” said Piyãko. “We realise that the context we’re living in now isn’t just about drug trafficking; you can see it’s a movement involving everything from wildcat mining and illegal mining to illegal logging, drug trafficking and other issues.”View image in fullscreenFrancisco Piyãko, general coordinator of the Organisation of Indigenous People of the Juruá River, is part of the delegation to Brasília.Photograph: Martín Mejía/APThe Asháninka delegation in Brasília is calling for a permanent security presence along the border to prevent the free movement of drug traffickers, illegal loggers and the illicit construction of “virus roads” that push into the forest without environmental oversight. They also want greater protection for their leaders and operations to combat organised crime in the area.The neighbouring Peruvian department of Ucayali has the widest network of illegal roads in the Peruvian Amazon, providing transport for gangs involved in environmental crime, gold, money laundering and drugs. In the past five years, coca cultivation in Ucayali has tripled.The Igarapé Institute, a public security thinktank,has saidthat organised crime – which often intersects with narcotics and illegal extraction of natural resources – needs a more robust response by governments across the region: “It is increasingly clear that the fight against organised environmental crime in the Amazon ultimately demands better intelligence and strategic prioritisation. The goal must be to strengthen Brazilian state authority to deter and repress crimes and those who commit them.”Piyãko said this was now a matter of urgency. He added: “If the Peruvian and Brazilian governments joined forces and wanted to resolve the situation, they could. Because they have the means to combat this.”“If the state doesn’t protect these territories, they will be dominated by this criminal system, or the people will be forced to defend themselves on their own. This could lead to very serious situations, because as the net tightens around these territories, tensions rise.”Explore more on these topicsAmazon rainforestAmericasIndigenous peoplesBrazilPeruDrugs tradeLogging and land-clearingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel planning ‘extensive’ military operation in West Bank after settler attack | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed and several hurt after armed settlers entered village with military support
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed and several hurt after armed settlers entered village with military support
Content: People in mourning at a hospital in Nablus, where the bodies of four Palestinian people were taken.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APView image in fullscreenPeople in mourning at a hospital in Nablus, where the bodies of four Palestinian people were taken.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APWest BankIsrael planning ‘extensive’ military operation in West Bank after settler attackFour Palestinians and two Israelis killed and several hurt after armed settlers entered village with military supportAndrew Roth,Sufian Taha,Quique Kierszenbaumand agencies in JerusalemFri 24 Jul 2026 12.54 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 05.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael has said it is preparing a major military operation in theWest Bankafter four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed during a confrontation that began after armed settlers entered a Palestinian village with support from the Israeli military.Several more people were seriously injured at the scene after a scuffle broke out over an Israeli settler’s weapon and the military opened fire, according to residents. Dozens more have been reported wounded in ensuing settler attacks on neighbouring Palestinian towns.The shooting in the Palestinian village of Tell, near Nablus, is the deadliest attack in the West Bank this year and during the reprisals on nearby Palestinian towns, settlers set fire to houses and attacked local people. At least eight more Palestinians had reportedly been hospitalised, most with gunshot wounds.The Israeli military announced it was preparing for an “extensive” operation in the West Bank, with troops surrounding the town of Nablus and reports of security forces entering the hospital to arrest those wounded in the violence.The military said it planned to apprehend “dozens of Palestinians” involved in the incident, which it said it was treating as a terrorist attack, although video from the scene indicated the clash was not premeditated and involved a struggle over a weapon held by an armed settler.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers outside a hospital in Nablus. There are reports of security forces entering hospitals to arrest those wounded in the violence.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APIsrael’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, and defence minister, Israel Katz, said in a statement: “The security forces must be allowed to act freely and with full force against terrorism.” They called for more troops in the West Bank and the razing of the homes of the accused in Tell, as well as the collection of weapons and revoking of work permits in the village.Netanyahu also called for the building of new settlement outposts in the area and the legalisation of existing outposts. Unauthorised settlements are illegal under Israeli law.The head of Israel’s Democrats party, Yair Golan, said Netanyahu and Katz’s response showed a “clear intent to set the area ablaze”. The Palestinian foreign ministry condemned what it described as a “massacre committed by settlers in partnership with the occupation forces in the village of Tell”.Walid Zidan, the head of Tel village council, told Agence France-Presse that about 20 Israeli settlers had entered the village at about 8.30am local time. “Villagers came out to defend their homes and property. Clashes and physical altercations broke out between the residents and the settlers,” Zidan said.“Israeli soldiers were present and together with the settlers began opening fire … It was the settlers who stormed the village, with the intention of killing, vandalising and setting property on fire,” he said.View image in fullscreenFamily members of one of the four Palestinians who died in the clashes mourn outside a hospital in Nablus, in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Jaafar Ashtiyeh/AFP/GettyVideo footage showed an armed settler approaching several Palestinian men near the village and pushing them back with his rifle, after which a scuffle broke out and one of the Palestinian residents reached for the gun. It is unclear who shot the settler, who was named as Benayahu Mellet, 32, a security guard from the nearby Israeli settlement Havat Gilad.The Israeli military said in its statement it had come to the aid of the settlers, who were taking an “unauthorised and uncoordinated hike” in the village. They claimed that in the struggle over the weapon, a Palestinian resident of the village had taken the rifle and opened fire. The military said Maj Yuval Ezra, 27, a battery commander in an artillery regiment, was also killed in the clash. It was not immediately clear who had shot him.The Palestinian health ministry in Ramallah said the four Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces. All four were said to be cousins from the same family and have been named as Farouk, Ibrahim, Jawad and Imran Ramadan.IDF accused of working with settlers after latest deadly West Bank raidRead moreViolence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has flared in recent days and Israeli settlers have called for attacks to “erase” Tell.The far-right and pro-settler Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said the villages of Tell, Iraq Burin and Beit Furik “need to look exactly like the refugee camps in Nablus and Tulkarm”, referring to the mass demolition campaign that displaced tens of thousands in the West Bank towns last year.Itamar Ben-Gvir, Netanyahu’s far-right national security minister, said he would call for the villages in the West Bank to “be treated like Beit Hanoun in Gaza”, which has been devastated in bombing raids, and said he would demand that Israel bomb and bulldoze Palestinian houses.Israel’s defence and finance ministers recently announced plans for new illegal settlements in Gaza, and the country’s military commander for the region has described violent outposts as his “security partners”.All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.Palestinian health officials said they were treating four injured Palestinians, three in critical condition. Israel’s rescue service said two injured Israelis were airlifted out of the West Bank.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahunewsShareReuse this content

title: Indian Cockroach activist ends hunger strike after 26 days as protests spread | India | The Guardian
description: Sonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stall
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Sonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stall
Content: A Cockroach Janta party supporter takes part in a protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA Cockroach Janta party supporter takes part in a protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/GettyIndiaIndian Cockroach activist ends hunger strike after 26 days as protests spreadSonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stallHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiFri 24 Jul 2026 10.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 23 Jul 2026 20.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheCockroach activist Sonam Wangchukhas ended a 26-day hunger strike, as youth-led protests continued to erupt across India and leaders of the movement said there was no breakthrough in talks with the government.Wangchuk had been fasting since June in solidarity with the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), a new youth-led movement that has been holding mass protests calling for government accountability and the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over exam paper leaks. The leaks affected 2 million students in May and have been linked to more than a dozen suicides.On Friday morning, Wangchuk posted that he had ended the hunger strike inDelhiafter striking a “hard bargain” with the government.View image in fullscreenSonam Wangchuk posted a video from hospital, saying he had received assurances his conditions would be met by the government.Photograph: Sonam Wangchuk/X/ReutersIn a video from his hospital bed, he said he had been assured in writing that accountability in the examination system would be taken up on the parliament floor and that there would be no cases registered against young people who took part in mass protests in Delhi on Monday.After 26 days without food, Wanghuck appeared weak but in lively spirits. The hunger strike has long been a powerful tool of protest inIndia– repeatedly used by Mahatma Gandhi in the fight for Indian independence. Gandhi’s longest hunger strike was 21 days.After Wangchuk ended his hunger strike, Modi urged the activist to follow doctors’ advice and regain the weight he had lost.The CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, thanked Wangchuk for his “courage and sacrifice” and said the protests would continue until Pradhan resigned. “We won’t let Sonam ⁠sir’s sacrifice go in vain,” Dipke added.On Friday, CJP leaders said the government had agreed to meet them in a “neutral location” to discuss their demands.However, in the aftermath of the meeting, the CJP’s spokesperson, Ashutosh Ranka, said that no resolution had been agreed and the government had requested more time to consider their key demand, the resignation of Pradhan.0:51‘Cockroach’ movement: thousands march in anti-government protest in New Delhi“We hope the government will dismiss Dharmendra Pradhan at the earliest, or that he will resign, so that we can bring ⁠this matter to a conclusion,” said Ranka.The senior government minister JP Nadda confirmed that talks between the two sides would resume on Saturday.Anger, defiance and a hunger strike: India’s Cockroach movement protests – in picturesRead moreAs talks stalled on Friday, thousands of protesters continued to gather at CJP’s protest site in Delhi, in an unprecedented show of support for the dissenting movement. Tens of thousands more are expected to turn up over the weekend.Authorities shut down 17 metro rail stations near the protest site. In a move that was criticised by human rights groups, the government also ordered telecom companies to block mobile internet services in the area. However, it did little to stem the tide of people turning out.“It feels so positive out here,” said Afreen Ali, 21, a student at Delhi university, who stood among the crowds. “I’m feeling so mesmerised to see all my Indian brothers, my sisters, my youth, everyone out here protesting for their rights and for their education. It was the blood of our freedom fighters that brought us independence, and we are here to fight for that country.”Protests erupted across India on Friday as part of the countrywide callout, with demonstrations in Bengalaru, Mumbai, Pune, Thiruvananthapuram and Kolkata.On the ground at India’s ‘Cockroach’ protestThe protests represent the biggest youth challenge to Modi since he came to power in 2014. ‌Opposition parties have echoed the youth movement’s demands and have ‌disrupted the monsoon session of parliamentthat began this week.On Thursday, Modi saidspecial courts would be set up to prosecutethose behind exam paper leaks, his first public response to the crisis. “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future ⁠of our youth!” he posted on social media.But the CJP rejected the proposal, saying what courts do after paper leaks is just one aspect of the problem. “But ​Modi-ji, tell us why are paper leaks happening in this country in the ​first place?” said Ranka.“Fast-track ​courts are set up in this country for every other issue, but whether those fast-track courts have actually solved those issues – you know the answer to that question, ​and so do we.”View image in fullscreenA supporter of India’s Cockroach Janata party (CJP) stands next to graffiti of a cockroach holding a pen at the protest site at Jantar Mantar in Delhi.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersLater in the day, Modi ‌said on social media that the government ​would announce more strict actions against paper leaks at ​a cabinet meeting on Friday.After top Bollywood stars were hit with criticism for staying silent about the protests, some of India’s biggest actors, including Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt and Kareena Kapoor, released social media posts saying it was heartening to see students come together to fight for a cause – though stopped short of criticising the Modi government.Explore more on these topicsIndiaDelhiSouth and central AsiaProtestNarendra ModinewsShareReuse this content

title: Guyanese authorities confirm death of 72 people in sinking of coastal ferry | Guyana | The Guardian
description: Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 were rescued as efforts continue to salvage the ship and recover all bodies
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 were rescued as efforts continue to salvage the ship and recover all bodies
Content: Rescuers pick up survivors after the 87-year-old MV Barima capsized off the Essequibo coast.Photograph: Bishop Juan Edghill/ReutersView image in fullscreenRescuers pick up survivors after the 87-year-old MV Barima capsized off the Essequibo coast.Photograph: Bishop Juan Edghill/ReutersGuyanaGuyanese authorities confirm death of 72 people in sinking of coastal ferryOf the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 were rescued as efforts continue to salvage the ship and recover all bodiesAssociated Press in GeorgetownFri 24 Jul 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe confirmed death toll from the recent capsizing of a state ferry offGuyana’s coast has risen to 72, with more bodies recovered as a multinational team struggle to salvage the partially submerged vessel.Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 people were rescued. The government has estimated that 100 may have died in the accident, which would make it the worst marine tragedy on record for the South American nation.The prime minister, Mark Phillips, said late on Thursday that crews have widened the search area and are determined to find all those who were aboard so loved ones can bury them with dignity.Huge search operation after passenger ferry sinks off coast of GuyanaRead more“The government ofGuyanacontinues to stand in solidarity with all those affected during this difficult time and will ensure that every available resource is deployed until the operation is brought to a safe and dignified conclusion,” he said.The 87-year-old MV Barima departed the capital, Georgetown, on Saturday and was headed to Port Kaituma when it began taking on water and capsized in Atlantic waters off the Essequibo coast.Phillips said the ferry was not insured, and the government is paying for the funerals and other related expenses.Divers from countries including Brazil and Trinidad and Tobago are trying to salvage the vessel, with officials saying they hope to inspect it for any possible damage that could shed light on what happened.Police have launched a criminal investigation and detained three people so far, including the rescued captain and a crew member the authorities say tested positive for marijuana.Also detained is the marine superintendent responsible for overseeing the loading of the ferry. The government maintains it was under capacity in both people and cargo, but survivors have told reporters that they believe the vessel was overloaded.The ship’s manifest listed 116 passengers and 17 crew, but authorities believe as many as 179 people were aboard.A growing number of Guyanese are questioning why it took so long to rescue people, with some survivors telling the Associated Press that they spent hours in the water.Phillips has asked for patience and said officials are awaiting the conclusion of an investigation. Its findings will be reviewed by a commission of inquiry, which has not yet been established.Asked why an 87-year-old ferry was still in service, the government said it had acquired a new vessel from India in recent months to replace the MV Barima, but was waiting on the completion of a new pier at Port Kaituma needed to accommodate it.The MV Barima was last dry docked in 2024 for major repairs and was scheduled for additional work in October.Explore more on these topicsGuyanaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Paramount agrees to pause $110bn Warner Bros merger as case plays out | US news | The Guardian
description: Twelve states led by California had obtained temporary restraining order blocking merger from closing for 28 days
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Twelve states led by California had obtained temporary restraining order blocking merger from closing for 28 days
