Content: Paramount Studios in Los Angeles, California, on 29 April 1024.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenParamount Studios in Los Angeles, California, on 29 April 1024.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUS newsParamount agrees to pause $110bn Warner Bros merger as case plays outTwelve states led by California had obtained temporary restraining order blocking merger from closing for 28 daysGuardian staff and agenciesFri 24 Jul 2026 16.36 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 16.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParamount ⁠Skydance ⁠has agreed to ​pause its $110bn acquisition ⁠of ​Warner ‌Bros ‌Discovery until a ‌ruling on several states’ challenge ‌to the deal, or ​until 1 June ⁠2027, according ​to court ​papers ​filed ​on Friday.A group of 12 US states headed byCaliforniaobtained a temporary restraining order this week that blocked the merger from closing for 28 days, pending the outcome of a motion for a preliminary injunction.The states allege that the deal should be blocked because it will reduce competition in the cable and theatrical markets.A Warner-Paramount merger would bring together two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood, as well as a host of TV networks, titles filling streaming libraries and news operations. That would include Warner’s HBO Max and CNN coming under the same roof of Paramount-owned CBS, movies including Top Gun and the Paramount+ streaming service.The ⁠delay could cost Paramount Skydance, controlled by the Ellison family, about $7m a ‌day in fees ‌it agreed to payWarner Bros‌shareholders if the merger does not close by 30 September. Similar merger ​challenges have taken an ​average ‌of eight ​months for ​a judge to rule on, a Reuters review of recent cases found.Journalists at CBS News and CNNhave expressed concernsabout the possibility of the networks being merged and the likely resulting job losses. Press freedom groups have also voiced fears over political influence around the deal.David Ellison and his father, Larry, a longtime Trump associate, havereoriented the CBS networkin an editorial direction more favorable to the president, especially under the leadership of CBS News’s embattled editor-in-chief, Bari Weiss.However, David Ellisonpledged in Marchthat CNN’s editorial independence would be protected amid speculation that he could put Bari Weiss in charge of the cable network.At the time the deal wasapproved by the Trump administration in June, Elizabeth Warren, the progressive Democratic senator,said in a social media postthat the development was “terrible news for every American who doesn’t want Trump-aligned billionaires to control what they watch and how much they pay”, adding that the merger “has reeked of corruption and influence-peddling”.In a statement, Paramount said: “Today’s agreement is a significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence.”It added: “This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers and good for creators – a conclusion dozens of competition authorities around the world have already reached … We look forward to proving our case at trial.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsParamount PicturesWarner BrosMergers and acquisitionsLaw (US)US justice systemCalifornianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Netflix has to evolve’: can the upstart survive the end of the binge-watch era? | Netflix | The Guardian
description: Streaming pioneer that transformed TV faces slowing growth and battle for viewers’ attention from YouTube
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Streaming pioneer that transformed TV faces slowing growth and battle for viewers’ attention from YouTube
Content: Netflix revolutionised the TV industry when it offered viewers the chance to watch an entire season of House of Cards.Photograph: Netflix/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNetflix revolutionised the TV industry when it offered viewers the chance to watch an entire season of House of Cards.Photograph: Netflix/Kobal/ShutterstockNetflix‘Netflix has to evolve’: can the upstart survive the end of the binge-watch era?Streaming pioneer that transformed TV faces slowing growth and battle for viewers’ attention from YouTubeMark SweneyFri 24 Jul 2026 12.00 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Netflix offered viewers the chance to binge on an entire season of House of Cards itrevolutionised the TV industryand started on a path to becoming the world’s most popular streaming service.Almost 15 years on, however, the upstart’s strategy of pumping its service with an avalanche of content and an almost-as-rapid penchant for mercilessly cancelling shows has viewers reaching for the remote.A recent analysis of a number of Netflix’s top shows, such as One Piece, Beef, The Night Agent and Avatar: The Last Airbender,revealed audience declines of 30% to 70%in their second seasons and further declines in their third.Last week, Netflix said it wouldscale back the viewership datait releases to once a year, following the scrapping of the quarterly reporting of subscriber growth last year, further fuelling fears that its years of juggernaut-like engagement growth may have passed its peak.“We’ve been saying to TV producers to be careful, it might be tempting to take the big money being offered to make a show forNetflix, but the saying goes that it’s often the case of ‘one and done’ – you’re cancelled,” says one senior TV industry executive. “What is happening with binge model audiences has been clear for years now. Fifteen years ago it was a means to an end, creating a market leader, but look how different the world is today. Netflix is looking out of date.”View image in fullscreenThe Night Agent, starring Luciane Buchanan and Gabriel Basso. Analysis revealed an audience decline in its second and third seasons.Photograph: Dan Power/NetflixWhile there is a popular perception that Netflix is quicker to cancel shows than its competitors, research from Ampere shows that it is a facet of the streaming model. A look at cancellations of scripted programmes made last year shows that across all the big streamers this usually occurred after series two or three.Netflix has announced the fate of about 180 unscripted and scripted shows annually over the last three years, with a cancellation rate averaging about 22%, with a similar ratio seen across the other global streaming players.The reason streaming cancellation rates seem so high is largely because they are, but only compared to traditional broadcasters. For example, an analysis of the rate of cancellations last year at the BBC shows that a scripted show was typically cancelled after its fifth or sixth season, a lifespan typical across major traditional broadcasters.“I remember always having to defend the weekly broadcast model by saying there is value in deferred pleasure,” says Peter Fincham, a former senior executive at the BBC and ITV who is a co-chief executive of the production company Expectation. “Linear broadcasting is biased towards recommissioning, because you have a schedule. And there are plenty of examples of a series that has shown some promise, but maybe not done quite as well as hoped, building over time. In the world of streamers, which is much more data driven, it is much less sentimental.”Netflix does dabble with how it releases some content, such as its flagship franchise Stranger Things, which has been released in multi-episode tranches, and Love is Blind as a weekly drop.View image in fullscreenNetflix’s competitor Disney+ had success using the traditional TV-style slower-burn drip-feed for its hit Rivals.Photograph: Disney+However, competitors such as Disney+, HBO Max and Apple TV have had huge success using the traditional TV-style, slower-burn drip-feed for hitssuch as Rivals,The Pittand Widows Bay respectively.Investors started showing concern about Netflix’s hit content pipeline when it stunned the market by making an $83bn (£62bn) bid to buy Warner Bros Discovery’s (WBD) studios and streaming business.While it was positioned by bosses as a rare chance to pick up a trove of assets – including the Hollywood studio behind franchises including Harry Potter, Superman and Batman, as well asHBO, home to shows including Game of Thrones, The White Lotus and Succession – that bid marked the first time Netflix had hoped to bolster its content firepower through an acquisition.With the mega-franchise Stranger Things and Squid Game coming to an end, and the new hit Wednesday not scheduled to return to screens until next year, investors worry the move was instigated in recognition of a need to shore up a patchy content slate to keep viewing in growth mode.The company’s share price has tumbled 40% over the last year.Emarketer forecasts that time spent on the streamer in the US, by far and away Netflix’s largest market, will grow just two minutes this year to 36 minutes, and just one minute in each of 2027 and 2028.View image in fullscreenStranger Things, season 5. The mega franchise is coming to an end.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix/PABut again, while investors have reacted to a perceived engagement problem at Netflix, that appears to be a factor at rivals too. Emarketer forecasts that the amount of time spent by viewers on Disney+ will only increase by 1 minute this year, half that of Netflix.Profits at Disney’s streaming operations nearly doubled year on year in its most recent quarterly results, reporting its first double-digit streaming margin. Nevertheless, an analyst at Wells Fargo recently suggested Disney shouldget out of streamingand focus on producing and licensing to boost a share price down almost a quarter over the past year.Almost a decade ago, the founder of Netflix, Reed Hastings, quipped that the market opportunity was so vast that his biggest competitor wasn’t rivalsbut sleep, as viewers flocked to binge-watch its hosepipe of content. However, while Netflix has enjoyed golden years as a first-choice streamer it faces newer competitors in the battle for consumers’ attention.And when it comes to screen time,YouTubehas become a force to be reckoned with. Last year, average daily viewing on YouTube passed Netflix for the first time, according to a report by Digital-i. The 20 market report found that while YouTube viewing rose from 87.2 minutes to 99.1 minutes per day on average, Netflix fell from 100.5 to 93.4 minutes per account.Figures from eMarketer also put TikTok in the attention competition mix, with average daily viewing per user in the US at 57 minutes. However, it is YouTube’s drive into the living room that marks it out as the biggest threat to the existing streaming hegemony.Last year, YouTube said TV screens officiallyovertook mobile phones and desktop computersas the primary device for viewing the platform’s content in the US, a milestone that was alsoreached in the UKas four- to 15-year-olds joined older demographics that had already made the jump to television formost of their viewing on the video platform.UK data from the audience body Barb showed that TV sets became the first-choice device for YouTube viewing for over-55s in October 2023, for those between 35 and 54 in April 2024, and for 16- to 34-year-olds in December 2024.Sky owner announces £1.6bn takeover of ITV’s broadcasting armRead moreYouTube’s combined share of UK television and streaming viewing is now second only to the BBC – 18.3% to 20.55% – according to Barb’smost recent figures for June.And in terms of content, viewers have moved beyond videos of cats on skateboards and gamers’ videos of themselves playing Minecraft. Digital-i estimates that the share of viewing to long-form content on YouTube, that is videos more than 20 minutes long, is about 68%.Netflix itself acknowledged the YouTube threat when it was bidding to take over WBD, as is Sky and ITV in theirargument to gain takeover clearance.Paramount, rival and ultimate victor for WBD, claimed that a Netflix deal would give it too much dominance over the streaming market in the US. Netflix countered by saying that as a video-platform YouTube should be included as a competitor in the market.“The problem is Netflix isn’t distinctive any more, it is now just part of the firmament,” said the senior TV executive. “It is not head and shoulders above everyone else any more, and is no longer the first choice destination for discovery, and I think that is massive. Everyone else has changed and evolved, why hasn’t Netflix?”Explore more on these topicsNetflixMedia businessTV streamingTelevision industryHBOYouTubeDisney+featuresShareReuse this content

title: Mass job cuts loom at VW as profits fall steeply on China sales slump | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Carmaker expects to sell 3% fewer vehicles this year as it pushes through a programme that could eliminate 100,000 roles
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Carmaker expects to sell 3% fewer vehicles this year as it pushes through a programme that could eliminate 100,000 roles
Content: A rally of VW employees and union members in the grounds of the companys’s headquarters. The German words read ‘We’re fighting for you.’Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenA rally of VW employees and union members in the grounds of the companys’s headquarters. The German words read ‘We’re fighting for you.’Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Pool Reuters/APVolkswagen (VW)Mass job cuts loom at VW as profits fall steeply on China sales slumpCarmaker expects to sell 3% fewer vehicles this year as it pushes through a programme that could eliminate 100,000 rolesMark SweneyFri 24 Jul 2026 06.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolkswagen has reported a steep fall in profits and cut its revenue forecast amid a sales slump inChina, as the German carmaker pushes through a brutal cost-cutting programme that includes axeing up to 100,000 jobs.VW said it expects sales revenue to fall by up to 3% this year, a reversal of a previous forecast for a 3% increase on last year’s €321.9bn (£275.3bn), because of a sales slump in the highly competitive Chinese market.The sales slump will increase pressure on the world’s second-largest maker of vehicles to cut costs. Earlier this month VW’s supervisory board rejected the plans by thechief executive, Oliver Blume, to shut four factories in Germany, as the manufacturer confirmed it wasraising the job cuts target to 100,000, double the number already agreed by unions.Tesla stock suffers double-digit drop on carmaker’s worst day in yearsRead moreVolkswagen’s operating profit fell by 9.5% to €3.5bn in the second quarter, below analysts’ estimates of a small increase to €3.9bn, as Blumebattles with unionsto push through a restructuring programme.On Friday the company said the proposed additional job cuts would mostly be in administrative positions across its global business.The plans also include reducing Volkswagen’s model line by up to half.Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which include Audi, Bentley, Skoda, Seat, Porsche and Cupra, and has been hit hard bygrowing – and cheap – Chinese competitionand the struggle to shift to electric cars.In the first half of this year, Volkswagen delivered 6.3% fewer cars globally, about 4.1m, mostly because of its travails in China.Volkswagen sales in China have fallen by more than 31% in the first half, against increases inEuropeand North America.“The extent to which western carmakers are being squeezed out of the Chinese car market by domestic operators is laid bare by Volkswagen’s latest update,” said Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlume said on Friday that Chinese carmakers had sharply increased exports, which was adding pressure in Europe. The restructuring was essential to make the company “more innovative, faster, more attractive and robust”.Volkswagen’s share price fell 1.5% after the release of its latest financial results and is down 66% over the past five years.“After nearly four years at the wheel as chief executive, Oliver Blume is likely to come under increasing pressure,” Mould said. “His plan to steer Volkswagen back on to a growth path involves drastically cutting costs, including by slashing the company’s headcount. There are also plans to reduce the number of models and sell off non-core assets to make Volkswagen a more efficient machine. Pushing these through may be difficult given likely opposition from unions, and whether they are enough to win over the market is an open question.”The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers, with BMW last month cutting its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryManufacturing sectorGermanyEuropeJob lossesChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Every sentence will be put under pressure’: how we make our Long Reads unputdownable | Magazines | The Guardian
description: From plot twists to stunning visuals, our flagship long-form journalism can be as gripping as any beach read. To mark the publication of the summer issue of the Guardian Long Read magazine, we look at the craft that goes into making the stories so compelling
Author: Gautam Malkani
Headline: From plot twists to stunning visuals, our flagship long-form journalism can be as gripping as any beach read. To mark the publication of the summer issue of the Guardian Long Read magazine, we look at the craft that goes into making the stories so compelling
Content: Illustration: Klaus Kremmerz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Klaus Kremmerz/The GuardianInside the GuardianMagazines‘Every sentence will be put under pressure’: how we make our Long Reads unputdownableFrom plot twists to stunning visuals, our flagship long-form journalism can be as gripping as any beach read. To mark the publication of the summer issue of the Guardian Long Read magazine, we look at the craft that goes into making the stories so compellingGautam MalkaniFri 24 Jul 2026 10.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor thelatest issue of the Guardian Long Read magazine, the brief for the cover was simple: something that evokes the pleasure of summer reading.“With these magazines, there’s always a front-and-back reveal,” explains Chris Clarke, who has art directed all four issues of the magazine, which collates some of our finest long-form journalism. “For this summer issue, we lean into the joy of undistracted reading: on the front, a woman sits in a boat, reading, as the tide comes in. On the back, she is still there, still reading, except the tide has gone out and the boat is beached on the sand.”View image in fullscreenThe cover of The Guardian Long Read magazine,  volume 4Photograph: Klaus Kremmerz/The GuardianThe imagery evokes how a long read can be an immersive experience. You dive in. You feel the pull of the story. You get swept along. You definitely don’t ask an AI chatbot to start spitting out sip-sized summaries.The cover illustration also positions the summer issue as a perfect beach read. “We tried to make it look like something you’d want to take on holiday with you on the plane or the train,” says David Wolf, the Guardian’s Long Read editor.The beach read vibe highlights how some of our Long Reads can be as gripping as any page-turner you pick up at the airport. The craft that goes into making them compelling begins long before the writing stage. “When a journalist suggests an idea for a piece, we sometimes have to tell them that it sounds more like a subject than a story,” says David. “Whereas we’re looking for stories that have, at their core, a substantial, intellectually interesting or important subject. So, for instance, it should be a narrative with one, or a small number of, main characters, and a starting point and an end point. It should have conflict, scenes, maybe some twists – all the things you would associate with movies or novels. But of course, the pieces need to be scrupulously accurate as well.”View image in fullscreenThe back cover of the magazinePhotograph: Klaus Kremmerz/The GuardianWhen a writer submits a first draft, the first part of the editing process involves asking those same fundamental questions again, before any sentence-by-sentence work can begin. “Sometimes in an initial draft, the beat-by-beat of what happens is gripping, but you step back and ask: what did it add up to? Why does it matter? Other times, it has a lot of substance but not enough movement or unexpected moments.”View image in fullscreenThe contents pageIllustration: Klaus Kremmerz/The GuardianIt takes an average of five to six months and several more drafts before a Long Read is ready to publish. “Although it’s very common for it to be nine months to a year,” says David. “Sometimes we’ll ask the writer to build out a particular angle, which can mean going away and developing new sources to get new information.”He highlights a deeply reported story in the new magazine about the beer baron Humphrey Smith, who died in June. It’s full of details that could only come from months of painstaking work and the cultivation of dozens of sources. “It also has quite an unusual ending, and we were five or six drafts in before we came up with the idea for a ‘Rosebud’ moment,” he says. “There are an infinite number of ways to tell a story and we’re trying to hit on the dream version – to make it the best thing out there on that topic. Something that will stand the test of time.”View image in fullscreenSome pages from volume four of The Guardian Long Read magazineIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianThat shared goal helps everyone involved persevere through what can be a gruelling editing process. “People often expect there’ll be more friction than there is,” says David. “But writers generally find it exciting to have someone scrutinise their work and take it really seriously. Every sentence will be put under pressure. We try to anticipate our readers’ queries or puzzlements, and we’re always asking, are we being fair? Are we looking at it from every possible angle?”double quotation markFun stories are often the hardest to do - you need a writer who will fully embrace it and take it seriously in an almost pathological wayOne challenge is to keep rereading a piece as a reader would, with fresh eyes. “When I feel as if I’ve read it too many times, I share it with Clare Longrigg and Yohann Koshy, the other editors on the desk. It’s great to discuss it with other people who are really smart and will bring their own perspective to it. The other thing I do is, I print out a hard copy and make a note of the parts of the story that I’m gulping down and the parts where I’m having to drag myself through it – if I’m having that experience that suggests something needs fixing.”View image in fullscreenSome pages from volume four of The Guardian Long Read magazinePhotograph: Christian Gralingen/The GuardianThe obsessive attention to detail isn’t just about accuracy and journalistic integrity: it also makes for stories that genuinely stay with you. For instance, the new issue contains a fascinating Long Read about vending machines by Tom Lamont. “I absolutely love pieces like this that get into incredible detail about how an industry that’s in front of our noses the whole time actually works,” says David. The previous issue of the magazine contained an equally memorable story about the paper towel and hand dryer industries. “Ostensibly, those two stories are fun, light subjects. But the writers who took them on are absolutely brilliant, and they reported those stories with as much care and attention to detail as they would a so-called serious story. Fun stories are often the hardest to do - you need a writer who will fully embrace it and take it seriously in an almost pathological way.”Video: Lisa SheehanLike all the stories in the magazine, Tom Lamont’s vending machine article also looks stunning. When it was first published online and in the newspaper in 2022, it was accompanied by photographs of vending machines from around the world. For this summer’s magazine version, illustrator Lisa Sheehan has produced bespoke images of vending machines with the headline and snippets from the article emblazoned on crisp packets.Republishing Long Reads in the magazine gives the design team a chance to reimagine how to visually present them – with a larger canvas and more time to work on them. Chris, who is the Guardian’s editorial creative director and worked with art director Suzanne Lemon on this issue, explains how the designers approach things differently in print: “Often, the visual element commissioned for a Long Read digitally works exactly as it needs to in that space. On a website, its difference is what helps it stand out among everything around it. With the magazine it becomes much more about flow, pace and rhythm; how all of these stories sit together, and how one piece leads into the next.”View image in fullscreenSome pages from volume four of The Guardian Long Read magazineIllustration: Michelle Thompson/The GuardianAs with the front and back covers, the original artwork for each story is a crucial aspect of the care that goes into each issue. “We take the subject really seriously. The writer takes the subject really seriously. So then the reader takes the subject really seriously. And the designers are doing the same,” says David.“The hope,” says Chris, “is to stop the reader with large, punctuated moments, but never at the expense of the read. Everything surrounding the magazine has been built for the pleasure of reading.”The summer issue of the Long Read magazine is out now.Click hereto orderExplore more on these topicsMagazinesInside the GuardianNewspapers & magazinesJournalism booksDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was 100% the moment I lost innocence’: how a childhood stop-and-search led to the British debut movie of the year | Movies | The Guardian
description: When Imran Perretta was young, he was abruptly pulled by police into a van for questioning. That experience, as well as the death of his mother, inspired him to make Ish, a coming-of-age tale set amongst the British Muslim community. He talks about trauma, designing toilets and making Luton look magnificent
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: When Imran Perretta was young, he was abruptly pulled by police into a van for questioning. That experience, as well as the death of his mother, inspired him to make Ish, a coming-of-age tale set amongst the British Muslim community. He talks about trauma, designing toilets and making Luton look magnificent
Content: ‘I have to dedicate my life to doing the things that I want to do’ … Imran Perretta.Photograph: Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty Images for BFIView image in fullscreen‘I have to dedicate my life to doing the things that I want to do’ … Imran Perretta.Photograph: Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty Images for BFIMoviesInterview‘It was 100% the moment I lost innocence’: how a childhood stop-and-search led to the British debut movie of the yearCath ClarkeWhen Imran Perretta was young, he was abruptly pulled by police into a van for questioning. That experience, as well as the death of his mother, inspired him to make Ish, a coming-of-age tale set amongst the British Muslim community. He talks about trauma, designing toilets and making Luton look magnificentFri 24 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImran Perretta always knew that the title of his debut feature film would be “Ish” – short for Ishmail, the name of the 12-year-old boy from Luton at the heart of his story. Only later did people point out the similarity to other coming-of-age films with three letters in the title: Kes by Ken Loach, and Satyajit Ray’s Apu trilogy. Now, as the reviews trickle in, the comparisons to Kes and Apu keep coming. Like them, Ish is a poetic film that grabs you by the heart and pulls you into a child’s perspective on the world.The response has been lovely, says Perretta, and a relief. “It’s nice that people have compared Ish to those films rather than Kidulthood. I did worry about that.” Why, because it features kids speaking in slang and getting into scrapes? He nods. “I always say that I don’t read reviews, but of course I’ve read every single one. I can’t help myself. And we’ve been really lucky; the reviews have been amazing. A couple have been middling. Then you read them, and the subtext is: ‘I thought it was going to be like Kidulthood.’”Perretta is just back from a trip to Poland for the opening of a new exhibition of his work. Yesterday he was atTate Britainin London, tweaking the sound on his 2019 video installation The Destructors, about the lives of young Muslim men, which has just gone on show at the gallery. He is in the process of buying his first home and has two small children. “I’m knackered,” he says with a grin, chatting a mile a minute, no sign of tiredness.He grew up in Streatham, south London, the son of a British Italian dad who worked as a music journalist. His mother, who was born in Bangladesh, was a child protection social worker: “She was super political, a firebrand.” She died from cancer when he was 21. Perretta studied architecture for three years, before switching to art. During Covid in 2020, when the Turner prize was cancelled, he was one of 10 artists to receive £10,000 bursaries. But it never crossed his mind that he could direct a film, he says: “Not in a million years did I think I would ever get to do that. That’s something that happens to other people.” It was the head of BBC Film at the time, Rose Garnett, who approached him to write a film treatment after seeing The Destructors at a gallery in London.View image in fullscreenPerretta’s 2019 video installation The Destructor is currently on show at Tate Britain, London.Photograph: Andy Keate for Turner BursariesIsh is partly autobiographical, based on the first time Perretta was stopped and searched by police aged 13. This was in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks in a climate of increasing Islamophobia. “My mate got away. They pulled me into a van and just started asking me loads of weird questions,” he remembers. “I was so young, I didn’t really understand what was going on. It was incredibly traumatic. That was 100% the moment in my childhood when I lost my innocence. Because I understood how I was seen outside my family home, outside school, outside the community, all these protected spaces. In that moment, I understood I was seen as a deviant or some sort of threat.”It politicised him, says Perretta. “That kind of made me. From that point I had something to make work about. If I look at everything I’ve done for years, making work that is viewed by the public on the walls of a gallery or whatever, it all comes from that moment of seeing oneself as other people see you.” He co-wrote Ish with theIrish playwright and scriptwriter Enda Walsh.View image in fullscreenFarhan Hasnat as Ish.Photograph: Venice film festivalLike all brilliant coming-of-age films, Ish is culturally specific but also universal. It’s set in Luton, following 12-year-olds Ish (Farhan Hasnat) and his best mate Maram (Yahya Kitana) as they roam about during the holidays. It’s their last summer of boyhood: they are still young enough to build dens in the woods and pick blackberries. Ish’s mum has just died, and at home his family are dazed by grief. Maram, who is already a foot taller than Ish and has the beginnings of a moustache, is hanging around with older boys, getting in trouble.The stop and search, when it happens, is shocking – watching a child being grabbed from the street, forcefully and without parental consent. When I say this to Perretta, he points out therecent case of Child Qand accounts of interviews conducted with children under the government’s anti-extremism Prevent strategy without a parent or teacher in the room. “It happens to children from certain backgrounds more than others. I wanted to explore what it means to drag children into the adult world before their time.”All the kids in Ish are played by first-time actors. The casting process took six months, auditioning about 900 local boys. Unbeknown to the film-makers, the pair who got the roles of Ish and Maram had been friends since they were toddlers. Their bond shines through on screen; the chemistry is unfakeable. “It was just about getting out of their way, letting them do what they do naturally, which is basically wind each other up,” Peretta says.Ish was shot in Luton over five weeks in the summer of 2024. Perretta’s wife, a secondary school teacher, grew up down the road, and he has been visiting the area for years. Perretta says that commuter towns take a lot of stick. Luton in particular has frequently been in the news for negative reasons, as the home town of Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (AKA Tommy Robinson) or labelled as a centre of Islamic extremism. “But at the heart of it was just a community going about their business,” he says.He shot the film in luminous monochrome. Why, I ask? “What I figured is black and white didn’t negatively aesthetise Luton. It gave it grandeur. It made the concrete feel like marble. When you shot in colour, you immediately felt the fact that it had been at the sharp end of austerity.”View image in fullscreen‘Life’s too short to design toilets’ … Imran Perretta.Photograph: Capital Pictures/AlamyFilming days were short to comply with laws to protect child actors. “When you film with kids, there’s an egg timer. They can only be on set for six hours.” The key, he says, was not to be too precious about nailing it. “We just didn’t have the time.” That sounds stressful, I suggest. Perretta shrugs good-naturedly. “I would like to say that I’m fairly unflappable in those situations. It sounds sort of trite, but when you’ve looked after someone that’s dying, a film set is not that bad. I refuse to get to wound up about that sort of thing.” He smiles. “It’s an extraordinary thing to make a film. On a personal level it’s extremely important. But on the scale of all the things that can happen in life, it’s not really.”Perretta says his mother getting ill is what set him on the path to becoming an artist. “After she died, I thought: I have to dedicate my life to doing the things that I want to do.” He was 18 when she was diagnosed with cancer, and he was one of her carers, along with his dad and his younger sister. “That was my first degree. And after my mum died, I was working in an architect’s practice and thought: Life’s too short to design toilets.” Is that what he was doing, designing toilets? “Literally. I was working on the team that was spacing toilet cubicles. I won’t tell you where – it’s a high-profile architect.” He lasted a week. “I was like: Nah, I’m good.”Nostalgia review – Tarkovsky’s yearning cine-poem is deeply mysterious and profoundRead moreWhen his mother was sick, he had visited the Serpentine gallery in London to watch Blue, Derek Jarman’s final film, first released in 1993 months before his death from an Aids-related illness. “It was so extraordinary seeing that film. I stayed there for hours. I’d never had any experience of contemporary art before, other than school trips to the Tate. I was spellbound by it. I thought: ‘Oh God, I need to do that.’ I just need to run at the things that make me angry and scared, and make work about them. That was the beginning.” He grins. “And here we are.”Ish is in UK and Irish cinemas nowExplore more on these topicsFilmTate BritainDerek JarmaninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: If Deadpool wants to be a true Marvel superhero, is it time he grew up and stopped joking around? | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ryan Reynolds’ sarcastic superhero is rumoured to be in Avengers: Doomsday – but how is he going to fit in the MCU proper when he spent all of his previous film mocking it?
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Ryan Reynolds’ sarcastic superhero is rumoured to be in Avengers: Doomsday – but how is he going to fit in the MCU proper when he spent all of his previous film mocking it?
Content: Ryan Reynolds in Deadpool & Wolverine, the most popular Marvel film in years.Photograph: Jay MaidmentView image in fullscreenRyan Reynolds in Deadpool & Wolverine, the most popular Marvel film in years.Photograph: Jay MaidmentWeek in geekMoviesIf Deadpool wants to be a true Marvel superhero, is it time he grew up and stopped joking around?Ben ChildRyan Reynolds’ sarcastic superhero is rumoured to be in Avengers: Doomsday – but how is he going to fit in the MCU proper when he spent all of his previous film mocking it?Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.46 EDTShareHow do you solve a problem like Deadpool in the Marvel Cinematic Universe?Deadpool & Wolverinefound a way: rather than integrate the bloodthirsty, fourth-wall-breaking merc with a mouth into the rather more sanitised world of Thor, Iron Man and Spider-Man, Shawn Levy’s 2024 film chose to lampoon it from the outside instead. Why bother to make everyone’s favourite chimichanga-munching mutant fit when you can make the fact that he doesn’t the entire joke? Why become another cog in the Marvel machine when you can stand beside it, point out the loose screws and watch the box-office greenbacks roll in like it’s Christmas 2019?Deadpool & Wolverine made $1.3bn worldwide, becoming the second highest grossing film of 2024 and the highest grossing R-rated film ever. But it did absolutely nothing to introduce Ryan Reynolds’ potty-mouthed antihero into the MCU, unless one counts the several thousand jokes about Kevin Feige. By the end of the movie,Deadpoolseems no closer to becoming the saviour of Marvel than Happy Hogan is to wielding Mjolnir. He remains a sarcastic observer from the sidelines, less a vital MCU character than its resident heckler.Which makesthis week’s newsthat Reynolds is to embark on a sequel intriguing, to say the least. Because really, about what exactly? How do you make another Marvel movie when you have systematically pulled the whole enterprise apart? How could Deadpool emerge as the hero of Avengers: Secret Wars, and perhaps sacrifice himself to stop Doctor Doom from folding the multiverse into one vast Latverian theme park, when he has already treated Marvel continuity as something to be rummaged through for disposable cameos?Is Deadpool waiting in the wings? Watch the new Avengers: Doomsday trailerNobody has much inkling of how another Marvel-era Deadpool film might pan out. Butsome reports suggestthe character will play a role in the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday, albeit most probably not as part of the titular superhero combo.A new trailer for Doomsday, released earlier this week, does little to clarify matters. Reynolds is nowhere to be seen, but Channing Tatum’s Gambit, introduced in memorably bizarre fashion in Deadpool & Wolverine, features prominently. Patrick Stewart’s Professor X and Ian McKellen’s Magneto appear to be caught up in the film’s multiversal collision course, while Rebecca Romijn’s Mystique is once again prowling around in blue body paint. All of them belong to the same sprawling, hopelessly tangled 20th Century Fox-era mutant continuity that Deadpool calls home. It’s not hard to imagine Reynolds is hovering somewhere nearby, waiting to burst through the scenery and complain about Robert Downey Jr’s salary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBest in an ensemble? … Reynolds with Hugh Jackman as Wolverine.Photograph: Jay Maidment/APAnd yet if Wade Wilson is capable of becoming more than just the man shouting jokes from the cheap seats, if he is eventually to be seriously integrated into the MCU, he will at some point need to stop mocking the Fox-era mutants who appear to be caught up in no less than saving the known multiverse.Reynolds has recently suggestedthat Deadpool works best as part of an ensemble, but that is only interesting if the other characters are allowed to matter. A reunion with Gambit and other assorted denizens of Charles Xavier’s mansion cannot simply become another procession of cameos to be mocked, dismembered and discarded. At some stage Deadpool must stop treating the Fox universe as a box of comedy props, and confront the possibility that its destruction might genuinely mean something to him.That need not mean sanding off the obscenity or forcing Wade to deliver a solemn speech about responsibility beneath a swelling Alan Silvestri score. The first two Deadpool films occasionally managed to create genuine feeling without requiring their hero to stop being a complete clown. But if he is to play any meaningful role in the end of the multiverse, the joke cannot always be that superhero stories are stupid and the whole enterprise is one enormous corporate fever dream. The most popular Marvel movie in the last four years may have done its best to persuade us we should not be watching Marvel films in the first place, but there are only so many times Reynolds can trot out a glorified SNL sketch about how silly superhero flicks are and persuade us all that he has actually made a movie.Sooner or later Deadpool has to stop sneering at the apocalypse and try to do something about it.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekDeadpoolAvengers: DoomsdayScience fiction and fantasy filmsComics and graphic novelscommentShareReuse this content

title: 72 Hours review – Kevin Hart drags down Netflix midlife crisis comedy | Kevin Hart | The Guardian
description: The overexposed actor falls flat in another disappointing vehicle that fails to make the most of its neat bachelor-party-with-a-twist concept
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The overexposed actor falls flat in another disappointing vehicle that fails to make the most of its neat bachelor-party-with-a-twist concept
Content: Kam Patterson, Marcello Hernández, Kevin Hart and Ben Marshall in 72 Hours.Photograph: Alan Markfield/NetflixView image in fullscreenKam Patterson, Marcello Hernández, Kevin Hart and Ben Marshall in 72 Hours.Photograph: Alan Markfield/NetflixKevin HartReview72 Hours review – Kevin Hart drags down Netflix midlife crisis comedyThe overexposed actor falls flat in another disappointing vehicle that fails to make the most of its neat bachelor-party-with-a-twist conceptAndrew LawrenceThu 23 Jul 2026 21.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google72 Hours is Kevin Hart’s midlife crisis comedy. He stars as Joe, a 40-year-old New York marketing executive whose once-reliable Midas touch has worn off. He’s no longer the office’s go-to translator of youth culture, yet he remains on the verge of a promotion – the final hurdle standing between him and happily-ever-after with his longtime girlfriend (Teyana Taylor), a doctor weighing an opportunity that could pull her away from the life they’ve built together in the city.Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender review – engaging TV-to-movie adventureRead moreAll the while, crude texts and memes flood his phone from a random group chat populated by a pack of twentysomething guys planning a bachelor party in Miami – an annoyance that quickly becomes his ticket back to relevance. Joe not only drops everything to join these perfect strangers for the weekend; he upgrades the whole affair, picks up the tab and supplies the booze in hopes of harvesting content for his struggling campaign. It would be a fine set-up if it weren’t such an obvious metaphor for Hart’s own showbiz career.There was a time, in the not-too-distant past, when the kids were crazy for the 47-year-old Hart. Dave Chappelle had a whole bit in one of his standup specials about taking his son to see Hart perform live and the professional jealousy he felt watching the boy fan out over the guy, as if his own father wasn’t also one of the biggest names in comedy. The running joke with Hart was that he looked kid-sized next to other celebrities, a physical mismatch that fueled a towering Napoleon complex.He invited audiences to laugh at his shortcomings as he ascended from the comedy club circuit to bit parts in movies like The 40-Year-Old Virgin and Little Fockers before becoming a leading man in his own right and starring opposite Will Ferrell and The Rock. What’s more, Hart was an underdog story: a scrappy Philadelphia kid whose first shot at movie stardom came as the lead in Soul Plane, a mega-flop he hustled to outgrow.Just when Hart seemed too big to fail – no longer just a go-to headliner but the king of all media – the headwinds blew in again. He was involved in twoheadline-grabbing traffic incidents, one of which resulted in hisarreston drunk-driving charges, caughtcheating on his pregnant wifeand lost a dream job hosting the Oscars after old tweets in whichhe made homophobic comments resurfaced. But the bigger threat to Brand Hart has been overexposure. Him selling you a movie, then selling you the credit card to buy a ticket to that show or, perhaps, seats to his next cash-grab atthe state-sponsored comedy festival in Riyadh. The idea that there doesn’t seem to be anything Hart won’t sell was reinforced by a recent Netflix roast that saw him laugh along as Shane Gillis, Tony Hinchcliffe and other white comedians deliveredracially charged jokesnot just about him but about George Floyd – a man whose memorial service Hartmemorably attended.72 Hours, which marks the eighth collaboration between Hart and the Ride Along director Tim Story, was supposed to be the comedian’s chance to turn the page from that controversy, as well as the legal battles ragingwithin his embattled media company. Instead, the 105-minute picture offers the starkest proof yet of just how far Hart has fallen out of step with the times – the polished version of the unfiltered gen Z collaborations he has manufactured withDruski and Kai Cenat.In place of those wildly popular internet personalities, Hart has ensconced himself among Hollywood’s freshest faces: SNL it-kids Marcello Hernández (as alpha-bro Nick), Ben Marshall (as lovesick Hunter) and Kam Patterson (as the lovable himbo Freshman), along with Mason Gooding – son of Oscar winner Cuba Gooding Jr and the young bachelor in question. And the chemistry within the group-chat clique is genuinely compelling. The guys might have an affection for crude memes and coarse language, but they also check in with one another emotionally before they party and preserve their shared memories in a physical scrapbook – a level of sincerity that doesn’t compute with Joe’s understanding of this supposedly terminally online generation.A story about the four of them tangling with the bachelorette party quartette that drugs them and robs them blind would have been a much richer avenue for 72 Hours’ Cobra Kai-heavy writing team to explore. Instead, Hart turns the film into a platform for his longstanding grievances against cancel culture and political correctness while slipping into hackneyed versions of Puerto Rican and Chinese stereotypes. The R-rated script only makes matters worse by writing Joe, a 40-year-old, like someone twice his age – the kind of guy who downs two bottles of Pepto before a night of binge drinking and uses the latest wearable tech to surreptitiously capture footage of his new friends for his marketing campaign.The meta-joke about an actor trapped inside his own midlife-crisis character doesn’t merely fall flat; it underscores the movie’s fatal flaw: 72 Hours would have far more potential if Hart weren’t in it at all. The insecurities that once made him relatable aren’t comic any more. They’re sad.72 Hours is now available on Netflix on 24 JulyExplore more on these topicsKevin HartComedy filmsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Devil Wears Prada 2 to Eleanor the Great: the seven best films to watch on TV this week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Miranda and Andy reunite to save Runway magazine in the jolly couture-drenched sequel, plus Scarlett Johansson’s moving comedy about a twinkly eyed 94-year-old liar
Author: Simon Wardell
Headline: Miranda and Andy reunite to save Runway magazine in the jolly couture-drenched sequel, plus Scarlett Johansson’s moving comedy about a twinkly eyed 94-year-old liar
Content: Fashion face-off … Meryl Streep as Miranda and Anne Hathaway as Andy in The Devil Wears Prada 2.Photograph: 20th Century Studios/PAView image in fullscreenFashion face-off … Meryl Streep as Miranda and Anne Hathaway as Andy in The Devil Wears Prada 2.Photograph: 20th Century Studios/PAThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekTelevision & radioThe Devil Wears Prada 2 to Eleanor the Great: the seven best films to watch on TV this weekMiranda and Andy reunite to save Runway magazine in the jolly couture-drenched sequel, plus Scarlett Johansson’s moving comedy about a twinkly eyed 94-year-old liarSimon WardellFri 24 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekThe Devil Wears Prada 2Miranda Priestlyis back– and the last 20 years haven’t diminished the fashion magazine editor’s hauteur one iota. But in David Frankel’s couture-drenched comic sequel her former callow assistant, Anne Hathaway’s Andy, is now an award-winning investigative journalist. Hired by the owner to improve Runway’s reputation, she can take all that Meryl Streep’s disdainful Priestly throws at her. This time round, the main conflict is with the internet, as declining print sales and clickbait competition threaten the publication’s future. It’s a jolly, aspirational outing, buoyed by scene-stealers Stanley Tucci and Emily Blunt, even if the gags are largely from the preloved rack.Wednesday 29 July, Disney+LurkerView image in fullscreenEasy-going … Archie Madekwe and Théodore Pellerin in Lurker.Photograph: MubiAt first sight, Alex Russell’sintense dramais about a pop singer stalked by an obsessive fan. Théodore Pellerin’s LA clothes shop worker Matthew talks himself into the entourage of the apparently easy-going Oliver (Archie Madekwe), a British musician on the up. As he sidles from obsequious gofer to would-be documentary profiler, Matthew’s neediness is embarrassing going on excruciating – but it also flatters Oliver. And as their relationship develops over weeks, the power balance between them shifts drastically.Saturday 25 July, 6.15pm, Sky Cinema PremiereMonsterView image in fullscreenHeartbreaking … Hinata Hiiragi (left) and Soya Kurokawa in Monster.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyJapanese film-makerHirokazu Kore-edahas long been a brilliant illuminator of children’s fractured, often inarticulated lives. This 2023 Cannes winner is another compelling look into their inner worlds, framed as an episodicmystery. First, we see events from the point of view of Sakura Ando’s single mother Saori, who thinks her son Minato (Sōya Kurokawa) is being bullied by his teacher, Mr Hori (Eita Nagayama). But then we get Hori’s side of the story and, crucially, Minato’s; what emerges is a heartbreaking tale of friendship and difference.Saturday 25 July, 10.25pm, BBC FourEleanor the GreatView image in fullscreenMoving … June Squibb in Eleanor the Great.Photograph: prScarlett Johansson’sdirectorial debutmay be not what you’d expect from the Black Widow: a moving comedy revolving round the lies a 94-year-old woman tells about the Holocaust. June Squibb plays the twinkly eyed Eleanor, who relocates from Florida to live with her daughter in New York after her longtime best friend/housemate Bessie dies. Partly through grief and loneliness – but also to keep the memories alive – Eleanor begins to pass off Bessie’s tales of surviving Nazi atrocities as her own.Sunday 26 July, 6am, 2pm, 4.10am, Sky Cinema Premiereskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe New BoyView image in fullscreenMystical … Cate Blanchett and Aswan Reid in The New Boy.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThe Australian state’s former policy of separating Indigenous children from their parents, to assimilate them into western culture, gets a sideways take in Warwick Thornton’s mystical period drama. Aswan Reid stars as a blond-haired Indigenous boy found in the outback and taken to a Benedictine orphanage run by Cate Blanchett’s unconventional Sister Eileen. It’s an alien world to him, but when he displays miraculous powers, Eileen sees in him a very Christian divinity.Tuesday, 11.05pm, BBC TwoPrimateView image in fullscreenBrutal horror … Primate.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyA brutally efficienthorrorfrom Johannes Roberts that employs all your favourite slasher movie tropes – remote location, invincible foe, gut-wrenching dismemberings, final girl – but makes the serial killer a chimp. Ben was the test subject of a linguistics professor who has recently died, and can communicate using sign language; he now lives with her widower Adam (Troy Kotsur) and teenage daughters, Lucy (Johnny Sequoyah) and Erin (Gia Hunter). But a mongoose bite turns the cute ape into a rabid menace and the family’s Hawaiian clifftop home into a deathtrap.Wednesday, Paramount+NormalView image in fullscreenPacking heat … Brendan Fletcher, Bob Odenkirk and Reena Jolly in Normal.Photograph: Magnolia Pictures/APIf you’ve seen Bob Odenkirk in black ops caperNobodyyou’ll know what to expect from Ben Wheatley’sspry thriller. He plays Ulysses Richardson, the temporary sheriff of the small town of Normal, Minnesota. There’s nothing normal about Normal, of course, which Ulysses discovers when a bank heist goes wrong and he realises it’s not the robbers he has to be worried about. The slapstick gunplay of Wheatley’s own Free Fire mingles with the deadpan drama of Fargo and the still delicious incongruity of Odenkirk packing heat.Friday, 8.25am, 8pm, 1.10am, Sky Cinema PremiereExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekDrama filmsThrillersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I know what it’s like to be vulnerable’: musician This Is Lorelei AKA Nate Amos on addiction and finding peace | Music | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter and Water from Your Eyes guitarist was unstoppably prolific, despite a growing dependence on substances. Now sober, he reflects on his new album and the songs that helped him turn his life round
Author: Jazz Monroe
Headline: The singer-songwriter and Water from Your Eyes guitarist was unstoppably prolific, despite a growing dependence on substances. Now sober, he reflects on his new album and the songs that helped him turn his life round
Content: Basement tracks … Nate Amos.Photograph: Eve AlpertView image in fullscreenBasement tracks … Nate Amos.Photograph: Eve AlpertMusicInterview‘I know what it’s like to be vulnerable’: musician This Is Lorelei AKA Nate Amos on addiction and finding peaceJazz MonroeThe singer-songwriter and Water from Your Eyes guitarist was unstoppably prolific, despite a growing dependence on substances. Now sober, he reflects on his new album and the songs that helped him turn his life roundFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor most of his life, Nate Amos made music just to get through the day. There was plenty of it: dozens of self-produced albums and EPs uploaded – since his This Is Lorelei project launched in 2012 – to what was then a plucky, independent platform called Bandcamp. Now 35, he is perhaps the quintessential Bandcamp artist: part bedroom-pop whiz, part alt-country troubadour, part indie rock rascal with a big, heavy heart. His peers treat him like a lost folk hero from a bygone era.Amos is sitting in the basement of a cafe in Camden Town, north London, cradling an iced matcha; coffee makes him “feel like shit”, he says, and he no longer indulges such foibles. The title of one of those Bandcamp albums, OK N8, is tattooed on his knuckles. A friend inked it a few years ago, soon after Amos got sober. “Exactly when you’re not supposed to be making decisions like getting a tattoo on your hand,” he jokes. His active blue eyes dance around behind a golden-brown fringe and an unruly, woodchip beard. In a tough spot he will swing back in his chair and search for answers that always seem to be hiding beneath the table. But each time he stumbles upon the truth, he looks up with a hungry smile.Amos recorded his new album, The Singer in My Band, at the Brooklyn apartment he moved into in 2017. It had a “punk house vibe” then, but as housemates moved on, he gradually took over the place. The home studio setup allows him to work fast, the only way he knows. He may speak in a slow drawl, but his torrential work ethic belies any affinity with slackerdom. He finished the new record before signing to Matador, but kept its existence a secret from the label (also home to his other band, art-rock misfits Water from Your Eyes). “I sent them the completed album within half an hour of signing the contract,” he says, stirring his bright green drink with a straw. “I was like: ‘Actually, it’s done!’”The Singer in My Band is alarmingly jaunty – an outlier in a bric-a-brac catalogue that has noodled from sad chamber pop to murky post-punk to midsize indie anthems. He knocks out twangy riffs, hearty harmonies and bunnyhopping basslines that hark back to his childhood under the spell of his bluegrass-maestro father, Bob Amos. Had he made something so ripe and bucolic a decade ago, you might have assumed it was a joke.In truth, Amos has always had a country soul. He was born in Denver but felt more at home in rural Vermont, where his family holidayed and eventually moved to a house on the side of a mountain. He was 14 then, and getting sick of school. “I lashed out, like teenagers do,” he says wryly. By 16, he was skipping classes to hang out on dirt roads, smoke weed and absorb the influence of more seasoned truants. Daunted by the busyness of impending adulthood, he spent the best part of six months tripping on psychedelics. “I did a pretty good number on myself.”He graduated, somehow, and settled in Chicago in his early 20s. Music fascinations proliferated. He made psychedelic beats for rappers, throttled electric guitars in bands, occasionally shuttled around to play bluegrass with Dad. This Is Lorelei emerged from the chaos, with songs that burbled like Animal Collective one month and thrashed like Hüsker Dü the next.He was still well acquainted with vices he now lumps together as “substance issues”. Looking back, he sees his all-consuming focus on music and drugs as a way to defer a brewing storm. “You find ways to be excited when you’re younger, and for me that was through drugs. I settled into what, at the time, I was sure was going to be a pattern of just being a lifelong addict.”Despite courting a hectic social life, he craved peace and quiet – the kind he left behind in Vermont. “People say they’re born in the wrong generation: they’re talking about the 60s or whatever. I honestly feel like I would have been a happier person working on a farm 300 years ago.” The closest he could get was “drowning out bad noise through substances, dumbing myself down to a point where it felt like things were simple”.View image in fullscreenBranching out … Amos with Rachel Brown in Water from Your Eyes.Photograph: Adam PowellThat bad noise re-emerged in his music. He was briefly banned from the online distributor Distrokid for uploading so many epic drone dirges he was flagged as a bot. A deluge of similarly experimental work was themed around “technology corrupting nature”, he says, but he portrays it less as an art concept than as a symptom of anxiety and depression. “The beauty was in the unknown, because I was having such a hard time with the known.”His shaggy, lurking presence at shows became a source of intrigue to Rachel Brown, a fellow music obsessive in Chicago’s DIY scene. They became a band and, once he got a haircut, a couple. As Water from Your Eyes, the duo ran a long-distance operation making silly, stoned electropop while Brown studied film and television at New York University. In 2017, Amos left Chicago to join them. The band and friendship survived their breakup two years later.At the time, Amos responded to their split by mainlining Blink-182’s All the Small Things on repeat. Its quick hooks and stupid charm felt like a signal in a world of noise. Still his low mood lingered. Doctors prescribed heavy medication that sometimes helped, sometimes dragged him deeper into a funk. In 2020, he started dating Al Nardo, now his fiance and a live member of both bands. He gave up drink and hard drugs a year later. Weed filled the void, so another year later, he quit that too. “It felt like my brain was on fire for three months,” he remembers. “I would do push-ups until I collapsed.” He made music for 12 hours a day, terrified that if he stopped, he would relapse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA documentary on lifelong drinker Shane MacGowan, of all people, finished the repair job that Blink-182 had improbably started. Watching an a cappella Sinéad O’Connor cover MacGowan’s distraught folk ballad The Song With No Name, Amos rediscovered pure folk melody. “I grew up surrounded by bluegrass and folk music,” he recalls, “so I felt like a sleeper agent being activated.”His tunes got more hummable, his lyrics more acute. In 2024, he released Box for Buddy, Box for Star, his first sober album. One song, Where’s Your Love Now, features a line so suffering and simple that it seemed to go missing from the songbook of one of his ancestors, such as Elliott Smith or Wilco: “That hole in my chest still wishes you all the best.” The track has since been covered – separately – by two of the era’s eminent indie songwriters, Cameron Winter and Waxahatchee.‘Your favourite album is not as cool as any dinosaur’: set sail with New York art rock duo Water From Your EyesRead moreAmos still gets “pretty constant visual hallucinations” from his tripping teens. “It can take me by surprise,” he says, “but for the most part I don’t really notice them any more.” He dabbles in weed but is long past the period when, as he puts it on the new record, he “wouldn’t trade a good night for a better day”. He hopes This Is Lorelei will be a “safe space” for the similarly afflicted: “Use this as the platform and then check it at the door.” Is it a safe space for him to do the same? “It was … before people started listening.” He laughs. “Water from Your Eyes fans will come up to me like: ‘Yo, sick guitar playing.’ From Lorelei fans, I’ve had some crazy trauma-dumping situations.”Not that he resents the attention – it just makes him cautious. “I know what it’s like to be vulnerable and then encounter art that can change the way you think about things … but the idea of being responsible for that art is really scary. I don’t fully understand why, out of all the people I know, I’m the one who is given this opportunity.” His gaze burrows back under the table. Something down there makes him chuckle. “I will try my best,” he says finally. “I promise I’ll try my best.”The Singer in My Band is released on 11 September on Matador.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Strokes: Reality Awaits review – a perfect marriage of mayhem and melody on their best album in years | Music | The Guardian
description: Allying the crackpot strangeness of Julian Casablancas’ side projects with his band’s gift for pop minimalism, the New Yorkers are on playful, joyous form
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Allying the crackpot strangeness of Julian Casablancas’ side projects with his band’s gift for pop minimalism, the New Yorkers are on playful, joyous form
Content: Tighter than ever … the Strokes.Photograph: Johann RashidView image in fullscreenTighter than ever … the Strokes.Photograph: Johann RashidMusicReviewThe Strokes: Reality Awaits review – a perfect marriage of mayhem and melody on their best album in years(RCA/Cult)Allying the crackpot strangeness of Julian Casablancas’ side projects with his band’s gift for pop minimalism, the New Yorkers are on playful, joyous formShaad D'SouzaFri 24 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere’s a sentence no old-head Strokes fan wants to hear: to understand Reality Awaits, the stalwart NYC group’s seventh album and first in six years, you first have to understand the Voidz. Julian Casablancas’s otherband has been taking up more and more of his time in recent years, much to the chagrin of fans who may have dipped into the group’s painfully, awkwardly proggy2014 debut Tyrannyand decided to just let the old legend have his fun (away from their own speakers, of course). Anyone who decided to listen further will have found that the Voidz have turned into a great, crowd-pleasing, safely experimental zone for Casablancas to pull out some of the most energised, goofy work of his career. If you’re thinkingI come to this guy for cool,notgoof,I don’t know what to tell you: this is a man who spends interviewsdiscussing his theoriesabout ancient Sumerian culture.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Reality Awaits by the Stokes.Photograph: Richard PrinceThe2018 Voidz record Virtueis a high point of Casablancas’s entire catalogue: a gentle stylistic mixed bag that covers winsome pop-rock, yacht rock, bedroom pop and much more. That album seemed to clear the decks for the Strokes’ last record,2020’s The New Abnormal, on which they sounded the most like their 2001 selves since Is This It. That album is now the definitive Strokes album for gen Z – go to any Strokes show and watch the younger contingent light up during The Adults Are Talking – but it didn’t presage a long-term back-to-basics route for Casablancas and co. On Reality Awaits, by sheer force of will, he fuses the crackpot strangeness and, ahem, fondness for AutoTune of the Voidz with the Strokes’ minimalism and pop melodicism.The Strokes: Going Shopping – videoIt’s this combination that gets you some of Casablancas’s funniest, most interesting performances in years: warbling unintelligibly about John Legend and Josh Groban; borderline screaming the phrase “and in a hundred thousand years from now!” in order to fit it neatly to an old-timey Strokes melody; singing sweetly about “starting again” on Going to Babble On, one of the most winsome, heartfelt Strokes songs since their debut. It’s worth emphasising, once again, that Casablancas is no longer the louche chronicler of downtown cool that he once was. But he’s still a totally compelling frontman and, even with a tighter-than-ever rhythm section, the hot-burning core of this band.The Strokes’ 20 greatest songs – ranked!Read moreIf Casablancas sometimes sounded like he was going through the motions on The New Abnormal, Reality Awaits retrofits the madcap experimentalist side of the Voidz to cleaner, more tuneful production; the result is playful and frequently joyful. Going Shopping rides a simple, insistent yacht rock groove that allows Nick Valensi to noodle with increasing intensity as Casablancas sings about being a “seven-foot zombie”, while the dubby The Fruits of Conquest revives the sinister 80s sleaze of 2011’s Angles with a little more conviction.Inevitably, Reality Awaits suffers from the same sense of clumsiness that’s touched most recent Casablancas projects. Here, it arrives in the form of Tyrants of the Mellow Moon, the album’s formless, ambling closer. Unlike the rest of the record, which is content to gambol in pop structure, Tyrants feels unwieldy and leaden, threatening to drag down what is otherwise one of the band’s most nimble outings in years. Here, Casablancas’s AutoTuned warblings feel oppositional to the band’s moody soundscape; it feels like the first time, amazingly, on the whole record that his Voidziness is threatening to eclipse his Strokesiness. But that the two sides can align so thoroughly, and so pleasurably, is itself a victory – for years, it’s felt like the Strokes have been his cash-grab project. Now, it feels like there’s a whole lot more road left for the group to explore.Explore more on these topicsMusicThe StrokesIndiePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the ramshackle, soulful twang of Twisted Teens and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: The New Orleans country-punk duo are on a hot streak, about to release their third album in a year, and the crunchy, literate hooks keep coming
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: The New Orleans country-punk duo are on a hot streak, about to release their third album in a year, and the crunchy, literate hooks keep coming
Content: Twisted Teens, a ragtag, deeply charismatic band from Louisiana.Photograph: Bobbi RichView image in fullscreenTwisted Teens, a ragtag, deeply charismatic band from Louisiana.Photograph: Bobbi RichAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the ramshackle, soulful twang of Twisted Teens and the week’s best new tracksThe New Orleans  country-punk duo are on a hot streak, about to release their third album in a year, and the crunchy, literate hooks keep comingShaad D'Souza,Ben Beaumont-Thomas,Claudia EfeminiandLaura SnapesFri 24 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromNew OrleansRecommended if you likeParquet Courts, Sheer Mag, Royal HeadacheUp nextHoly Cross Tigers out later this yearNot one but two of the year’s best albums so far are authored by a ragtag, deeply charismatic band from Louisiana named Twisted Teens, who bear Pynchonian names – Caspian Hollywell and RJ “Razor Ramone” Santos – a console steel guitar and, in Hollywell’s case, one of rock’s greatest, most soulful voices in many years. Virtuosic when it counts, ramshackle when necessary, Twisted Teens feel like they could slot nicely on to a bill with Parquet Courts and the late, greatRoyal Headache– crunchy, literary rock bands who seemed to shyly conceal their music’s anthemic nature.Twisted Teens broke through earlier this year with their second album Blame the Clown, a set of 12 country-punk tracks that’s hooky and effusive enough to give any major-label pop record released this year a run for its money. A couple of weeks ago, they released its followup, the rangier and slightly more introspective Florida Water Blues, and before the year’s out they’ll have dropped Holy Cross Tigers, a release schedule befitting a band on a hot streak.The pair’s origin story is foggy – the most one can glean from interviews is “they were neighbours, then Santos travelled cross-country to buy a steel guitar” – which feels appropriate for this kind of grimy, mythic music, which is raw and self-consciously handmade. Part of that feeling can be put down to Hollywell’s voice, a gritty and pockmarked thing which he uses to great effect, interspersing deadpan meditations on life and love with a rich, almighty howl that’s ostentatious but unpretentious. In other words, Twisted Teens are two of 2026’s true originals – a breakout band whose kooky, ultra-clarified vision outstrips the hype.Shaad D’SouzaThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenClub-ready … John Glacier.Photograph: Ayanna AllenJohn Glacier – Bond GirlThe peerless UK MC’s most club-ready cut to date: a hip-house track with a Detroit-ish bassline, topped with Glacier airily pronouncing her fashion bona fides.BBTJeffrey Silverstein–Portland WorksSilverstein was raised in New Jersey, based in the Pacific Northwest and, here, inspired by a Sheffield factory – yet this radiant cosmic Americana smear of pedal steel, acoustic and honeyed synths exudes pure wild west.LSProtomartyr – Sounds We Cannot HearWith a central riff like a siren sounding through a hurricane of hail, this is an enormous return for the Detroit post-punks, who as usual get to the heart of today’s ennui and horror.BBTNamesblissxPaul Stephan–Run ItThe two London MCs engage in a back and forth of fluid flows on brotherhood, faith and dreams, over a stuttering, saxophone-laced beat by producer T.o.CEMurex–Flock of Swans Fly inV’sFrom her thrillingly innovative debut album, the Swedish artist offers the delightful vision of sprites playing hide-and-seek around a glitching harp.LSChad Hugo–Jumpupw!nya (ftTierra Whack and Leikeli47)The non-Pharrell half of the Neptunes brings every ounce of his considerable production nous and sense of funk to these aerobic breakbeats, with both guest MCs on equally oxygenated form.BBTCole Pulice – The Limits of the FrameEven when deconstructing their trademark sax – this track was somehow made without using the mouthpiece or breath – Pulice makes reliably soothing, detail-laden sound miasmas to take a moment in.LSSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Unsayable by Michael Cunningham review – The Hours author on the insecurities that powered his creative life | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The American novelist and screenwriter’s memoir covers sex work, Virginia Woolf and Hollywood success
Author: Alex Clark
Headline: The American novelist and screenwriter’s memoir covers sex work, Virginia Woolf and Hollywood success
Content: Michael Cunningham.Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMichael Cunningham.Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty ImagesBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewUnsayable by Michael Cunningham review – The Hours author on the insecurities that powered his creative lifeThe American novelist and screenwriter’s memoir covers sex work, Virginia Woolf and Hollywood successAlex ClarkFri 24 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an eight-year-old in comfortable, solid, suburban California,Michael Cunninghamfelt compelled to make art before he quite understood what it was, or could do: a painting of souls ascending to heaven, for example, in which paradise resembled the Griffith Park Observatory and the dead were all depicted in profile because their creator felt unequal to the challenge of full faces. There was also a cigar box covered in gold-sprayed macaroni and a clay representation of the animals on Noah’s Ark – anything, in fact, that would challenge the painting of a placid white chicken that hung in a gilt frame on his parents’ wall.If Cunningham moved on fairly rapidly from the visual arts, either sparing or denying us the fruits of a more fully formed talent, it wasn’t because the impulse to create had withered. Rather, it was that the experience of making material art had functioned as a temporary outlet, being less painful, less embarrassing – both emotions he ascribes to his young, sensitive self – than attempting to capture the world in words.Unsayable, an intriguing combination of memoir and writing guide, asks us to consider what causes those feelings of embarrassment and pain, and what powers them. Do they proceed, almost inevitably, from the gap between language and the vast, mysterious terrain it tries to describe? Cunningham’s writerly insecurity, from childhood to maturity, seems to live in that gap, and to feel it as an ever-present judgment on his endeavours, impossible to expunge. Success is no antidote and, he points out, might even contribute to a feeling of isolation from other writers, or a quickening fear of a return to obscurity.View image in fullscreenNicole Kidman as Virginia Woolf in The Hours.Photograph: Paramount/AllstarCunningham did become successful, and extremely so, when in 1998 he publishedThe Hours, a triple-stranded, time-shifting riff on Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway; his celebrity increased four years later, when Stephen Daldry and David Hare released a film adaptation starring Nicole Kidman, Meryl Streep and Julianne Moore. Several novels and 25 years later, he was to return to a similar structure – compressed time and multiple interior monologues – in Day. “I don’t work on an epic scale”, he tells us in this book, “though my ambitions run to more epic proportions than I like to admit.” This, one might say, is the tension at the heart of modernism, perhaps Cunningham’s greatest stylistic influence: the attempt to render the grandeur of consciousness that also shows us its fragility, how easily it evaporates on examination.Fragility and contingency recur throughout Unsayable. Cunningham might never have discovered Woolf unless he’d found himself secretly smoking at high school alongside a cool girl called Natalie, whom he desperately wanted to impress, despite his increasing suspicion that heterosexuality was not available to him. He’d overheard her mention Allen Ginsberg and asked what she was reading now. “It’s funny you should ask,” she replied. “I’m being just so completely transformed by Virginia Woolf.” Pretty soon, he was too.There are plenty of observations that feel like familiar territory when it comes to writers on writing, most of them of the “fail again, fail better” variety. But where Cunningham is most engaging, and in a much more offbeat way, is in his repeated depictions of himself – mostly younger, but not always – as a man anxious to fit in, to lay claim to experiences that are far more recherché, more daring, than he really is. His flair for pace is no hindrance, and the chapter that begins, with no prior ground-laying, “During my senior year at Stanford, I started going to San Francisco on weekends to work as a rent boy” is a brilliant evocation of bravado, precarity and pathos.So, too, are the episodes and people about whom he won’t write: his beloved sister, for instance, or – beyond a series of respectful vignettes – an elderly and gracious gay couple who befriended him when he briefly lived in Provincetown, who fed him delicious dinners and gasped delightedly in mock horror at his mildly exaggerated tales of sexual abandon. After their deaths, he wonders about the extent to which they had chosen their lives, or whether they had adapted to what, at the time, society would allow them to have. It’s a few pages, but so touching, so unsentimental, so enlarging a view of these two incidental men that you feel sure that Cunningham made the right choice, all those years ago, when he shelved the gold pasta cigar box.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
