title: Lucy Caldwell: ‘Even your text messages fizz after reading James Joyce’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The author on the power of folktales, being inspired by Ulysses – and the book that every woman should read
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The author on the power of folktales, being inspired by Ulysses – and the book that every woman should read
Content: ‘I didn’t read any DH Lawrence until I was in my 40s’ … Lucy Caldwell.Photograph: Neil HainsworthView image in fullscreen‘I didn’t read any DH Lawrence until I was in my 40s’ … Lucy Caldwell.Photograph: Neil HainsworthThe books of my lifeBooksLucy Caldwell: ‘Even your text messages fizz after reading James Joyce’The author on the power of folktales, being inspired by Ulysses – and the book that every woman should readLucy CaldwellFri 24 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryThe summer my middle sister was born, my mum and I would walk to the shops at Cherryvalley, in east Belfast, to do her messages, and she’d buy me the latest issue of Storyteller, illustrated tales from around the world. It came with a cassette tape of actors reading the stories, a ding to tell you when to turn the page. My favourite was a Japanese folktale called The Goblin Rat. I was only just two, but I listened to it, entranced and terrified, until I could recite it by heart.My favourite book growing upSusan Cooper’s The Dark Is Rising series. I first read them aged 10 – I’ve read the title book every midwinter since, and read them last year with my own then-10-year-old son. They tell a haunting story of the age-old battle between the forces of dark and light, weaving in Arthurian legend, shot through with an adult melancholy that makes them as compelling now as then.The book that made me want to be a writerJennifer Johnston’s How Many Miles to Babylon? We read it in English when I was 13 and our homework was to write an extra chapter. I spent every spare minute that week writing mine – the intoxicating feeling of tuning in to another world, until that world becomes more real than your own.Thebook I came back toI’ve always loved Dubliners by James Joyce, but first read Ulysses in paroxysms of undergraduate anxiety about not “getting” the references. Years later, I bought an edition with no footnotes, no endnotes, just the novel itself – it was, and continues to be, one of the most glorious reading experiences of my life. Even your text messages fizz after you’ve been reading Joyce.The book I rereadClarissa Pinkola Estés, Women Who Run With the Wolves. She’s a Jungian psychoanalyst and a cantadora, a keeper of the old tales, and this book is about the secret gifts and power of mythology, the paths to your inner psyche, reclaiming your wildness. I’ve read it in my 20s, 30s and 40s, and different stories have sung out to me each time. Every woman should read this book.The book I could never read againI love Rosamond Lehmann but I’ve never been able to get past the part in The Echoing Grove where two sisters try, ineptly and at agonising length, to bludgeon a rat to death.The book I discovered later in lifeAs teenagers, we’d dare each other to leave the school library copy of Lady Chatterley’s Lover open on the “dirty bits” – where the spine was broken. But I didn’t actually read any DH Lawrence until I was in my 40s, and I’m so glad I came to that book later in life, as a wife, as a mother. It’s not the explicitness of the sex that’s shocking – it’s the ardency of the longing, the abandon of his rhythms. That would have been wasted on me before.The book I am currently readingI’ve just finished Helen Bain’s debut, The Daffodil Days, which I loved – an account of Sylvia Plath’s last year, told backwards, in an intricate series of stories by people momentarily close to her. It’s hard to know what to follow it up with, but I have high hopes for Courttia Newland’s The Art of Opposition, a book of essays “on hope, resilience and creative expression beyond the mainstream”, by a writer I know to be a formidably sharp and compassionate thinker.My comfort readIt’s not that the stories themselves are comforting – far from it – but I reread Lorrie Moore’s Self-Help. There’s such pleasure in knowing that each story, like Philip Larkin’s definition of poetry, is a perfect verbal device to take you through its experience.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: ‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angst | Games | The Guardian
description: Going by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havoc
Author: Chris Schilling
Headline: Going by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havoc
Content: One for sorrow … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothView image in fullscreenOne for sorrow … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothSummer games previewsGames‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angstGoing by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havocChris SchillingFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid the gleeful anarchy of Bad Magpie’s debut trailer, there’s a striking note of melancholy. The game’s protagonist – a wounded corvid that creates havoc wherever she goes – calls out forlornly as a flock of her kind passes above, with a conspicuous gap in their formation.Milktooth games designer and co-founder Daisy Fernandez has had this particular image in her head for years. Lying in the grass one afternoon during the 2020 lockdowns, she looked up and saw a V-shaped pattern in the sky, poignantly incomplete. “It really stuck with me,” she says. “I posted about it online and someone told me about a ‘missing man’ formation, which is an aerial salute to a fallen pilot.”View image in fullscreenDistraction tactics … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothAlready, Fernandez and her then colleagues George Batchelor and Catherine Unger at State of PlayGames(South of the Circle) had been batting around ideas for a game of their own. Unger – whose brilliant artwork can currently be seen in SFB Games’ The Mermaid Mask – pitched an idea to the group. “It was a fairytale about a duck that falls in love with a star and goes on a quest to bring it gifts,” Batchelor says. “This was 2019, and because the duck was white …”The implication is clear. Any game featuring a mischievous bird was always going to draw comparisons toUntitled Goose Game, but back then the visual resemblance to House House’s Bafta winner encouraged the team to consider a different path.The star and the central quest remained, but as time went by it was clear that a magpie was a much better fit for a story about a character seeking out shiny objects as a distraction from her abandonment issues. They may have had to reverse-engineer it, Fernandez says, but it has come to feel like the ideal choice: “You know, ‘One for sorrow, two for joy …’ – that almost sounds like an anthem for the co-dependent.”View image in fullscreen‘Some surprisingly inefficient outcomes’ … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothThe game, then, is designed to be something of a collectathon – one that could be read as a meta-commentary on the way games distract us from broader existential worries. And not just in the playing, either. “One thing George and I talk about quite a bit is that making a game is the best form of avoidance, because there are endless tasks you can throw yourself into,” Fernandez says, cheerfully adding that her death anxiety “is the quietest it’s ever been” as development continues.All of which risks making a game in which you set fields of flowers aflame, launch fireworks through car windows and chase a frowning computer monitor with a trumpet in your beak, sound awfully serious. Yet there’s a thrilling through-line of experimental chaos, that Batchelor says has been somewhat inspired by Zelda: Breath of the Wild. “It means we do get some surprising outcomes,” he says. “And some surprisinglyinefficientoutcomes,” Fernandez quips.That has led to a few happy accidents, as the studio builds a sandbox that feels truly reactive to the player’s input, bolstered by Eli Rainsberry’s deft audio design that gives each object its own sonic palette. “We’re testing the whole time, so we get to see what [players] want to do and try to accommodate that – or at least make a joke that gestures at it,” Batchelor says. For all that the scope has crept, there have been a few judicious cuts: a keenness to “degoosify” the game, as Fernandez puts it, led to a model village being removed, House House having got there first.They needn’t have worried. Bad Magpie is very much its own bird – not least thanks to its higher dynamic tonal range. “There’s this expression in screenwriting that if you want to make someone laugh, you make them cry first, and vice versa,” Fernandez says. “Pixar’s so good at that – every time there’s a devastating moment there’s a slapstick beat seconds later, and you’re so relieved to laugh.” Batchelor nods in agreement: “People really picked up on that emotional beat of seeing the magpie alone. Just that one shot helped validate how it’s going to feel in the final game.”Bad Magpie is in development for PC and Xbox Series X/S.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsShareReuse this content

title: Bedlam dreamscapes, digital-age aliens and a summer pastoral – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The terrifying visions of Richard Dadd, UFOs, aliens and Van Gogh’s troubled peasant woman
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The terrifying visions of Richard Dadd, UFOs, aliens and Van Gogh’s troubled peasant woman
Content: Creepy baby … detail from Puck by Richard Dadd, 1841.Photograph: Simon Critchley/© Harris Museum and Art GalleryView image in fullscreenCreepy baby … detail from Puck by Richard Dadd, 1841.Photograph: Simon Critchley/© Harris Museum and Art GalleryArt Weekly newsletterArt and designBedlam dreamscapes, digital-age aliens and a summer pastoral – the week in artThe terrifying visions of Richard Dadd, UFOs, aliens and Van Gogh’s troubled peasant woman –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 24 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekRichard Dadd: Beyond BedlamTerrifying creatures of the night and surreal dreamscapes galore – and those are just the “sane” canvases this Victorian artist painted before he was confined to Bedlam, where his visions became truly unsettling.Royal Academy, London, 25 July to 25 OctoberAlso showingFelicity PowellDreamlike images across many media by this artist who died in 2015 after documenting her own cancer.Richard Saltoun Gallery, London, until 3 OctoberAutopsyUFOs, the Roswell “alien” and the inaccessibility of truth in the digital age provide suitably strange fodder for Paul McCarthy, Chino Moya and many more.Seventeen Gallery, London, until 15 AugustElizabeth Blackadder: A Life in ColourTapestries by this colour-loving Scottish artist are accompanied by her paintings and drawings.Dovecot Studios, Edinburgh, until 14 NovemberClare Woods: Garden Without SeasonsPastoral and horticultural new paintings that delve into nature in a show that suits the season.Pitzhanger Manor and Gallery, London, from 29 July until 8 NovemberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Jem SouthamRay Exworth spent his life filling Cornish sheds with breathtaking sculptures – but wouldn’t let anyone in to view them. Now, after his death, his secret body of work has been revealed.Read the full articleWhat we learnedAt 100, painter, sculptor and performance artist Ken Turner is still smashing the system … and the occasional TeslaSheffield’s Designers Republic lit up the north with their work for Aphex Twin, Pulp … and PringlesTrent Park House museum reveals the story of its wartime ‘secret listeners’The Manifesta biennale brings radical community spirit to struggling German townsThe artful work of hundreds went into dazzling textiles show Entangled and WovenJessica Morgan has taken ‘a big pay cut’ to become Tate’s new directorMasterpiece of the weekHead of a Peasant Woman by Vincent van Gogh, about 1884View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Imagedoc/AlamyWhen Vincent van Gogh gave up his early attempts at art dealing, teaching and missionary work to learn to paint, he saw art as a social vocation. Instead of saving the poor by preaching he would help them by depicting their harsh lives. This peasant woman is one of the folk he painted from life in Nuenen in the south Netherlands in his first really ambitious art project: a passionate attempt to document rural poverty that culminated in his famous 1885 painting The Potato Eaters. He sees sadness and distraction in her eyes as she patiently sits for him, her individual presence heightened by the vague background that leaves nothing to look at but the figure. Van Gogh suggests a tension between her workaday appearance and a richer, more elusive inner life. He would later embrace expressionism and wild colour in search of ways to open that subjective realm of the soul.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shechter II: In the Brain review – a thrilling release of rave and ritual | Dance | The Guardian
description: Hofesh Shechter’s latest doesn’t break new ground, but its exceptional dancers throw themselves into a moody, pulse-quickening celebration of communal movement
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Hofesh Shechter’s latest doesn’t break new ground, but its exceptional dancers throw themselves into a moody, pulse-quickening celebration of communal movement
Content: Transcendent … Shechter II: In the Brain at Queen Elizabeth Hall, London.Photograph: Todd MacDonaldView image in fullscreenTranscendent … Shechter II: In the Brain at Queen Elizabeth Hall, London.Photograph: Todd MacDonaldDanceReviewShechter II: In the Brain review – a thrilling release of rave and ritualQueen Elizabeth Hall, LondonHofesh Shechter’s latest doesn’t break new ground, but its exceptional dancers throw themselves into a moody, pulse-quickening celebration of communal movementLyndsey WinshipFri 24 Jul 2026 06.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may be 38 years since the second summer of love, three decades since the dance music boom of the early 90s, but on the contemporary dance stage, rave is still peaking. In recent years, you’ve barely been able to move for dancers letting loose to repetitive beats, in tribal gatherings and transcendent ones.Hofesh Shechter’s dance has always had that rhythmic pull of the dancefloor – he writes his own beat-driven music, after all – but while the early works were more angst-fuelled, now he seems happy to get lost in music. Shechter’s latest, In the Brain, has been developed from a piece called Cave made forMartha Graham Dance Companyin 2022. It’s danced by his junior company, Shechter II, a collection of some of the best young dancers under 25, selected from around the world. They have that hungry energy of youth, and they lay it all out on the floor.In the Brain is not an all-out party, though. It has its quiet moments, its slow build, its not-always-enlightening detours (into a brief swing dance, and a couples’ slow dance, to name two). The feel is subterranean, not least because of Tom Visser’s lighting. Visser is king of the dim glow in all its subtle shades – maximum atmosphere with minimum drama – and Shechter’s score is similarly dusky and moody, rather than party bangers. (There’s also additional music from German techno duo Âme.)View image in fullscreenRecognisably Hofesh … Shechter II: In the Brain.Photograph: Todd MacDonaldMore than anything, In the Brain is recognisably Hofesh: the hunch of the shoulders, the arms raised to the sky, the ritualised groups moving as one – it’s a style that’s inspired many others. This piece isn’t rushing into new territory, but part of the appeal of Shechter’s choreography is that you can imagine it feels so good to dance it. There’s a tangible, visceral pleasure, whether that’s the thick, gloopy curves of movement or an almost violent exorcism, flinging out the body’s demons to a pounding bass. It’s dance that doesn’t seem drastically far from natural movement – so the viewer could feel themselves inside it – except there’s no way you could match the skill of these explosive performers. But the power is in the communal nature of the dance, the fellow-feeling, plugged into something bigger than oneself, surrendering to the universal heartbeat of the dancefloor.Until 25 Julyat Queen Elizabeth Hall, LondonExplore more on these topicsDanceHofesh ShechterSouthbank CentrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The World Is Full of Married Men review – Jackie Collins’ bonkbuster as a gloriously filthy puppet show | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Barbies, giant erections and exquisite craftsmanship combine in one of the year’s most outrageously funny and startingly original shows
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Barbies, giant erections and exquisite craftsmanship combine in one of the year’s most outrageously funny and startingly original shows
Content: Enthralling, titillating … The World Is Full of Married Men at Yard theatre, London.Photograph: Emmalisa PaulyView image in fullscreenEnthralling, titillating … The World Is Full of Married Men at Yard theatre, London.Photograph: Emmalisa PaulyTheatreReviewThe World Is Full of Married Men review – Jackie Collins’ bonkbuster as a gloriously filthy puppet showThe Yard theatre, LondonBarbies, giant erections and exquisite craftsmanship combine in one of the year’s most outrageously funny and startingly original showsArifa AkbarFri 24 Jul 2026 06.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDid someone sayJackie Collins, that doyenne of literary raunch and observer of human sexual dynamics? Fantastic! And an adaptation of her first novel, which revealed her formative interest in, and talent for, capturing the drama of love and sex within the bounds of patriarchy, and set in the world of showbusiness (albeit not in the Hollywood Hills but the leafy green film industry of swinging 60s Hampstead)? Great!But played out in miniature, in a series of lit doll’s houses, and mainly acted by repurposed Barbie dolls. What? Who dreamed this up? An experimental adult Swedish company, Malmö Dockteater, and “adult” is quite the understatement. Directed by Erik Holmström, also puppet designer, the dolls come with pubic hair, gigantic erections and heavy, surround-sound breathing. In between the story of a marriage in the doldrums, infidelity and female ambition in an era of predatory film directors and savage casting couches (all conceived decades before Harvey Weinstein and #MeToo), there are eye-watering helpings of nudity, fellatio, cunnilingus, quickies and straight-up bonking. This is puppetry with balls in more waysthan one, which makes the adult content in the current West End puppet production ofAvenue Qlook like The Muppet Christmas Carol.View image in fullscreenAll the better for its left-field weirdness … The World Is Full of Married Men.Photograph: Emmalisa PaulyIt is all the strangerfor being scripted in Swedish and translated by Lulu Raczka back into English. Its two puppeteers,Erik Olsson and Kajsa Ericsson, are followed by videographer Josefin Beischer, whose roving camera relays the action on to a big screen. They voice all the characters, but join in on some parts of the story, dressed as lifesize versions of the dolls. What the actual blazes?And yet it works. More than works. The robust, sexy narrative is recognisably Collins. The miniature lightboxes, designed by Maja Kall, are laden with exquisite period detail, from 1960s wallpaper to intricately designed drinks cabinets, hotel-room shag pads and nightclubs. The sound effects are graphic, especially during the sex scenes. The splicing of puppet world with human actors throws into relief the comedy of it all, but also infuses the dolls with more humanity, somehow. It is an enthralling, titillating and wildly imaginative production.‘I dreamt of a show where the audience becomes horny’: the Swedish puppet play starring bonking barbiesRead moreThe story explores the politics of a long marriage: Linda is a woman in the 1960s stuck in a 50s life of housewifery, boredom and yearning (thinkMad Men’s Betty Draper). David is her philandering husband, having an affair with aspiring actor and model Claudia. There is no sign of Collins’ fabulous creationLucky Santangeloyet, but the women here are still kick-ass and come out on top (David’s sexually voracious secretary is a highlight). Collins was writing in the era of John Updike and a flash of her literary knowingness comes with a fun allusion to hisRabbit, Run series on marriage longueurs, just for those who think she was nothing more than a bonkbuster queen. Despite the nervous giggles that the story inspires, there is so much universal truth in it about sexual relationships and inequality that still feels utterly relevant today.One of the best shows of the year so far, all the better for its left-field weirdness. It sets a precedent for relaying all of Collins’ magnificent back catalogue this way, too. Next stop,The World Is Full of Divorced Women? Bring it on!At theYard theatre, London, until 1 August.Explore more on these topicsTheatreJackie CollinsYard theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s more than backcombing a beehive!’ How tribute acts got massive – and put the live music scene back in the black | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Versions of Amy Winehouse and hundreds of other musicians are generating millions for beleaguered UK venues. But what is the emotional toll for the imitators, and are they pushing out original artists?
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: Versions of Amy Winehouse and hundreds of other musicians are generating millions for beleaguered UK venues. But what is the emotional toll for the imitators, and are they pushing out original artists?
Content: School’s out … Nadine l’Amour, who gave up her job as a teacher to perform as Amy Winehouse under the name the Madnezz of Amy.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSchool’s out … Nadine l’Amour, who gave up her job as a teacher to perform as Amy Winehouse under the name the Madnezz of Amy.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianPop and rock‘It’s more than backcombing a beehive!’ How tribute acts got massive – and put the live music scene back in the blackVersions of Amy Winehouse and hundreds of other musicians are generating millions for beleaguered UK venues. But what is the emotional toll for the imitators, and are they pushing out original artists?Daniel Dylan WrayFri 24 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs peak heatwave sun beams down on to a field in Derbyshire, Amy Winehouse tells the crowd she is in need of hydration – so Robbie Williams fetches her a drink. Elsewhere, members of the public stop the Beastie Boys for selfies, Fred Durst grooves along as Diana Ross covers Al Green, and shirtless teenagers form a circle pit during Korn as a woman sits knitting in a camping chair just behind them. James Brown and Prince turn out to be the same artist – just dressed up in different clothes.These are all scenes from Replika festival last month, which won the Guinness world record for the biggest tribute festival, with 108 acts performing across a very sweaty weekend. The punning deserves an accolade of its own: acts included Catfishing the Bottlemen, Pearl Scam, Wrong Jovi and Iffy Clyro.It is far from the only event of its kind. The UK is inundated this summer, with Fake-Fest, Tribfest, Glastonbudget, Festwich, Tidal Gathering, Could Be Real and numerous others. Similarly, music venues across the country have listings crammed with tribute acts. Dave Bevan, managing director of Alive Network Entertainment Agency – which represents 234 such acts – estimates that there are between 3,000 and 5,000 outfits in operation in the UK.The reason so many of these events and gigs are thriving is because going to see the original artist is often prohibitively expensive, especially during a cost of living crisis, while these gigs offer cheap access to live music, with songs you are guaranteed to know and love. Replika charges £100 for a weekend ticket. Its organiser, James Dean, says: “Our festival is targeted at low- to middle-income families who have very little disposable income. Compare that with the costs of going to Wembley Stadium for a single concert.” This is echoed by one group of young lads I speak to at the festival: “It’s cheap, local and a laugh.”View image in fullscreen‘I don’t think I’ve ever been busier’ … Dan Budd who performs as a Robbie Williams tribute act.Photograph: HandoutDan Budd, who has performed as Robbie Williams for the last 14 years, is disarmingly good on stage, full of the requisite swagger and cheekiness, plus he has the same Stoke accent and even has matching real tattoos. “I don’t think I’ve ever been busier in terms of bookings,” he says. “I haven’t got a free Saturday night until September 2027.”Dean tells me that the very top acts in the game will pull in £10,000-£15,000 a show. Budd won’t give me specific figures but says: “Put it this way, I’m 36 and mortgage-free.”Similarly, Nadine l’Amour – who performs as Amy Winehouse under the name the Madnezz of Amy – is flying. She set foot on stage as Winehouse for the first time in December 2024 but, by April 2025, she had quit her job as a secondary school teacher to do it full-time. Like Budd, L’Amour has replicated Winehouse’s tattoos, though she is such a fan that they were done years before she got into the tribute game.“There are 14- and 15-year-old girls singing every single word,” she says of her shows. “I have young people saying: ‘I never got to see Amy, but watching you on stage, I feel like that’s the closest thing I’ll ever get.’”It is not just individuals such as L’Amour and Budd who are benefiting. According to the charity Music Venue Trust (MVT), at a time when half the UK’s grassroots music venues make no profit, tribute artists are helping to keep the entire sector afloat.“There is an elitist attitude about them, but these acts really do keep parts of the live music infrastructure moving,” says Nathan Clark, owner of the Brudenell Social Club in Leeds, one of the most well-respected and thoughtfully curated independent music venues in the country. Despite its buzzy reputation for cutting-edge newcomers and international indie stars, tribute bands play a significant role there. “Not every gig has to be about discovering the future,” he says. “The key is balance: tribute bands should support original music, not replace it.”View image in fullscreenAndrea Pattison performs as Dolly Parton at this year’s Replika festival.Photograph: James BeckThere is no hard data on the precise financial impact of tribute acts. MVT’s chief executive, Mark Davyd, guesses that they make up about 25-30% of all bookings in independent venues across the UK. The Night Time Industries Association also states there is no authoritative number, but a spokesperson says tribute acts contribute “many millions of pounds each year” to the live music industry.Dean had an independent survey carried out on his festival’s economic impact over the last 10 years – including associated local spending on travel, hotels, supermarkets and so on – and it came out at about £8.5m. Given the number of touring tribute bands, festivals, gigs and events, he estimates a number that could stretch into hundreds of millions of pounds overall across the same 10-year span.One reason this huge sector is being overlooked and undocumented is because it is often seen as a bit feeble or regressive. “People, especially in the mainstream music industry, look at us as nonstarters,” says Dean. “We’re not really taken seriously.” But tribute acts are no longer just dodgy Elvis impersonators with wayward pitch. “We’ve had a couple of Take That tributes who were able to sing a lot better than Robbie Williams and Gary Barlow,” says Dean; Clark points out that Graham Sampson of the Smyths, a Smiths tribute band, can probably hold a note better than Morrissey.View image in fullscreen‘Back to Black puts a very big lump in my throat’ … Nadine L’Amour, pictured at the Jam House in Birmingham.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianSuch skill and dedication in mirroring others can bring with it an emotional toll. “Four or five years into it, I had a bit of a breakdown,” says Budd. “I couldn’t keep up with being one person in my private life and then going into Robbie mode and then having to switch it off again. It was like a split personality.” But Budd has found a way around it, performing a different set every night to keep it fresh, merging deep cuts with hits, and also being less gung-ho about inhabiting Williams. “As I’ve matured, I go on stage as Dan and I sing the songs in his style and manner,” he says.When you love the act you are portraying, it can be more than just a gig. “There are a couple of songs that send me back to a time in my life that was quite dark,” says L’Amour. “Back to Black puts a very big lump in my throat when I sing that. It’s not only remembering my pain, but also the pain that Amy felt.” At Replika, L’Amour dedicates that song, very movingly, to a friend who has recently died. “As hard as it is to sing, it’s nice to dedicate that song to my friend who I lost to mental health,” she tells me later. “And that was also down to losing the person that she loved, and drinking and everything that was involved in that.”View image in fullscreenActing up … (from left) Xenna as Taylor Swift, a tribute to Lainey Wilson, Carrie Underwood (Beth McCann), JC as Chappell Roan and Pink-Ish at Replika with the Guinness World Record adjudicator.Photograph: James BeckL’Amour says that while some people – such as Replika’s Prince-James Brown combo – moonlight in numerous tribute acts, she could only ever do Winehouse because of the significance of the material. “This is more than sticking on eyeliner, backcombing the beehive and putting on really expensive, uncomfortable shoes,” she says. “It’s a feeling. That gut-wrenching first love that kicks you in the stomach; having your heart broken beyond repair. But then being able to pour that out to the audience and feeling that love come back. It’s way more than a tribute for me.”Tribute acts also have a domino impact on other areas in the industry. “It may not always be treated as culturally prestigious but it creates employment,” Clark says. “It drives paying musicians, designers, promoters, venues.” He points to the Smyths having a four-night run coming up at his venue. “What original bands at this grassroots level can do four nights and sell them out?” he asks. “Very few. Those four shows allow us to take the risk on booking something else.”View image in fullscreenRecord breaking  … this year’s Replika festival won the Guinness World Record for the biggest tribute festival with 108 acts.Photograph: James BeckTribute bands also tend to bring in “exponentially higher” bar revenue for venues, according to Davyd, as gigs are usually held at the weekend and are often attended by groups of people. Clark agrees: “A tribute show is often more of a social night out: people are relaxed, they know the songs, they sing together … it’s like a celebration. For independent venues, that matters. Bar income is a major part of how grassroots venues survive.”Davyd points out that tribute acts “fill up the programme” in smaller towns “where there is an absence of touring acts”, which is a mixed blessing. Yes, they allow people to see live music in places bigger acts ignore, but does their success make it harder for acts starting out who are writing and performing their own material? “Any experience with live music is really important for social interaction, community cohesion and a whole bunch of reasons,” he says. “But we really need to be concerned about generating the next wave of great British talent. I would prefer there was more space for that. Tribute bands are an important part of the grassroots sector but we wouldn’t like them to become the sole reason venues are open.”‘The whole ecosystem is collapsing’: inside the crisis in Britain’s live music sceneRead moreWhat is clear at Replika festival is that while, for many, these bands are vehicles for pure nostalgia, comfort and familiarity – big Oasis choruses, indelible Beatles hooks and sugary 00s pop – they are also a first gateway to music. It is genuinely endearing watching battle-jacket-clad children navigating their first mosh pit and working out the rhythms and etiquette, as a fake Limp Bizkit turns a sizeable tent into an explosion of bouncing bodies. And it is a dream come true for the band members, too, who seem blown away by the response. The turntablist shouts out to his parents in the audience, his adrenaline clearly pumping, as he declares: “They keep telling me to get a real job – but look at me now!”Explore more on these topicsPop and rockMusic industryFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Plus-size models and £5 tickets: Sinéad O’Dwyer’s runway show puts inclusivity first | Fashion | The Guardian
description: V&A event celebrates all shapes and sizes as wider fashion industry stalls on body diversity
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: V&A event celebrates all shapes and sizes as wider fashion industry stalls on body diversity
Content: Sinéad O'Dwyer’s Fashion in Motion show took place at the Victoria and Albert Museum.Photograph: Peter Kelleher/Peter Kelleher/V&AView image in fullscreenSinéad O'Dwyer’s Fashion in Motion show took place at the Victoria and Albert Museum.Photograph: Peter Kelleher/Peter Kelleher/V&AFashionPlus-size models and £5 tickets: Sinéad O’Dwyer’s runway show puts inclusivity firstV&A event celebrates all shapes and sizes as wider fashion industry stalls on body diversityLauren CochraneFri 24 Jul 2026 12.31 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVisitors to London’s Victoria and Albert Museum on Friday afternoon to watchSinéad O’Dwyer’s Fashion in Motion show would have encountered something a little different. The cast of performers and models wore everything from underwear to skirt suits and sequins, and sometimes danced interpretively on the catwalk to a performance by the band Jeanie and The White Boys, but most notably came in all shapes and sizes.O’Dwyer’s work has pushed against fashion’s insistence on a thin body type since she appeared atLondonfashion week in 2021. If most brands make the samples for clothes shown on the catwalk based on a size 4-8, she uses a size 18. She has won awards for her work, as well as celebrity fans including Cardi B and Björk.View image in fullscreenFashion in Motion was open to the public, who could buy a ticket for £5.Photograph: Peter Kelleher/V&AFriday’s event – unlike a lot of fashion shows – was open to the public, who could buy a ticket for £5. O’Dwyer says this more inclusive attitude suits her brand. “In terms of the ethos [of the brand], it’s a lot more appropriate for everyone than the luxury fashion system, which actually doesn’t really want everyone.”For a few years, O’Dwyer was part of a wider shift towards body diversity in fashion – with Paloma Elsesser the first plus-size model of the year at the Fashion Awards in 2023, for example – but progress has stalled. TheSize Inclusivity Report, produced by Vogue Business every season since 2023, found that for autumn/winter 2026, 97.6% of models were “straight-size”, or a UK 4-8.View image in fullscreenO’Dwyer said her brand is ‘a lot more appropriate for everyone than the luxury fashion system, which actually doesn’t really want everyone’.Photograph: Peter Kelleher/V&AFashion’s focus on the thin has been controversialsince the early 20th century, with women’s bodies long subject to trends – slight with a small bust as an ideal in the flapper 20s, slender and leggy in the youth-obsessed 60s, athletic and curvy in the aerobicised 80s. The current rollback to thinness can be seen as part of a wider trend away from diversity.“It coincided with Trump coming into power,” saysJeanie Annan-Lewin, a stylist. “There are fewer people of any minority across the board and that’s the same thing that’s happening in fashion.”Emma Matell, the casting director who worked on O’Dwyer’s show and has also worked for Lueder and Tolu Coker, agrees. “It’s becoming more and more apparent that we’re back to wanting women to both metaphorically and physically take up less space,” she says.The impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is also part of the story. “[They] mean cultural figures are shrinking, the general population, in many respects, is shrinking,” says Lucy Maguire, the features director at Vogue Business. “It’s brought back a reverence for thinness that was always underlying in fashion.”London remains the one fashion week that consistently features more body diversity – even if straight-size models still made up 92.7%, according to the Size Inclusivity Report. As well as O’Dwyer, Mark Fast and Chopova Lowena will probably have a more diverse range at their shows in September.View image in fullscreenSinéad O’Dwyer’s Fashion in Motion. London fashion week consistently features more body diversity, according to in the Size Inclusivity Report.Photograph: Peter Kelleher/V&A“Sinéad and a few other young designers are carrying a huge amount of effort that the rest of the industry seems unwilling to make,” says Matell. “But I think that also comes down to the rebellious spirit of London. To me, being inclusive is the most punk thing you can do.”The difficulty and cost of changing long-established manufacturing methods to make clothes in bigger sizes is central to the problem of body diversity in fashion. But O’Dwyer believes even just seeing models of all sizes on the luxury stage has power. “Luxury is very deeply embedded in everything, even if you don’t know anything about luxury,” she says. “That’s what I definitely experienced as a young person. I didn’t know why I wanted to be size 6, but I really wanted to be size 6.”Friends Elenor Rowland and Orla McEvoy, both 14, watched Friday’s show – their first interaction with fashion. Rowland said she was glad for the diverse casting “because a lot of the time there’s not much representation for different body types … It probably makes lots of people think: ‘Oh, I’m not that size. Maybe I should be.’”View image in fullscreenO’Dwyer’s work has pushed against fashion’s insistence on a thin body type since she appeared at London fashion week in 2021.Photograph: Peter Kelleher/V&AIn the UK, size 16 is the average. Annan-Lewin sees fashion’s continued focus on the very thin to be a missed commercial opportunity. “I find it really strange that we just go ‘no, if you’re plus-size, you don’t have any disposable income, you don’t want to buy anything luxury. You just need to go and get fast fashion,’” she says.Maguire points to a survey conducted by Vogue Business that found “34% of mid-size and 68% of plus-size respondents felt alienated by the fashion industry due to their size, compared to 17% of straight-size respondents … Brands need to represent different bodies in order to not alienate this consumer who has really huge spending power.”To change things, all argue that financial support for brands trying to increase size diversity is needed. Annan-Lewin is clear it’s time for action. “I feel like I talk about things all the time, and it’s great, but water is wet,” she says. “What are we going to do about this? If we can’t get that fatphobia out of here, then nothing is going to move forward in any way, shape or form.”Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion industryWeight-loss drugsWomenLondonV&AnewsShareReuse this content

title: From high heels to ‘Zara death pants’: how fashion falls foul of women’s safety | Women's health | The Guardian
description: A physio, a tailor and a historian on the style trends that can put women in hospital and how to avoid the dangers
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: A physio, a tailor and a historian on the style trends that can put women in hospital and how to avoid the dangers
Content: High heels are the most common cause of fashion injuries to women.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHigh heels are the most common cause of fashion injuries to women.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianWomen's healthFrom high heels to ‘Zara death pants’: how fashion falls foul of women’s safetyA physio, a tailor and a historian on the style trends that can put women in hospital and how to avoid the dangersChloe Mac DonnellFri 24 Jul 2026 12.01 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Buyer beware” is one of the oldest principles in English law. Now, a pair of wide legged trousers from Zara is bringing the phrase back to the forefront of shoppers’ minds.On social mediathe £25.99 wide-legged trousersfrom the high-street retailer have earned the moniker “Zara death pants” thanks to a slew of videos showing wearers tripping over the leg of the trousers and injuring themselves.“These Zara pants need to come with a warning because now I have a fractured knee,” wroteone TikTok userbelow a video of them leaving hospital in a wheelchair.Some videos show wearers face-planting on pavements while others highlight bloodied knees and elbows, bruised limbs and broken fingernails.Lucy McDonald, a spokesperson for the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy and a physiotherapist at Restart, said that throughout her career she had treated injuries, including fractures and ligament tears, due to “fashion pieces that cause difficulty in movement and balance”. The most common culprits are high heels, but long trousers also feature.Despite the social media posts alerting wearers to the risks of Zara’s “lethal trousers” they continue to be a bestseller.View image in fullscreenZara’s flowing wide-leg trousers continue to be a bestselller despite socia media posts.Composite: ZaraIt is not just Zara championing the wide leg; the style has been spotted at brands from M&S to Mango and Next. At John Lewis, searches for the style are up 61% year on year, while linen versions are up 225%. This echoes the catwalk, with designers including Victoria Beckham and Stella McCartney showing long fits.On its website, Zara describes the trousers as being “longer than usual” with “a loose fit”. The accompanying imagery shows the fabric pooling around the model’s feet. In the sizing description, the total length of a size small is 108cm, while the large measures 109cm. Zara did not respond to a request for comment about its wide-legged trousers.Ruby Slevin, a tailor and the founder of Banshee of Savile Row, said the trip issue stemmed from the length of the in-seam.During the design process most high street brands use a “fit model”, a model with specific proportions who tries on the clothes to test for size and movement. To reduce costs, rather than hiring fit models some brands use a stationary mannequin that mirrors their typical sizing baseline.The national average height for women in the UK is 162.5cm (5ft 4in) but most fit models hover around the 178cm mark.“Fit models are not an accurate indication of an everyday woman,” Slevin said. “The length has to be in proportion to the person who is wearing it otherwise it is going to end up being problematic.”To ensure this, Slevin said, the client’s hip measurement should be used as a guide to how wide the trousers should be cut. “A person who is 5ft 5in cannot wear the same width of trousers as someone who is 5ft 10ins. It’s like wearing a pair of shoes that are the wrong size. It’s not safe.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe suggested high street shoppers should take trousers to a local tailor or drycleaner to have them adjusted.View image in fullscreenLindsey Wixson, modelling here for Chanel in 2012, had to take a career break five years later because of various catwalk injuries.Photograph: Christophe Karaba/EPAVirginia Hill, a fashion historian, said wide-legged trousers first became popular in the 1920s when women began to wear house pyjamas. She pointed to a rich history of fashion clothing being impractical or hazardous. The hobble skirt, introduced by the Parisian designer Paul Poiret in 1910, featured such a tight hem around the lower legs that women could only shuffle. One headline from the time read: “Skirts are so tight around the ankle that locomotion is seriously impeded and speed is impossible.”In 1927, the American dancer Isadora Duncan was killed when her silk scarf became entangled in the wheels of the open-top car she was travelling in.In 2009 the model Abbey Lee Kershaw tore a ligament when she fell while wearing high heels on the Rodarte catwalk, while Lindsey Wixson revealed that numerous catwalk injuries over her modelling career, including a linear tear on her big toe, had forced her to take a year off work in 2017.Macdonald said the most common fall injury was a fractured wrist because people put their hands out to break their impact. A foot getting caught in fabric could lead to torn ligaments, and hip issues were also common but the severity depended on how the person landed and the state of their bone health.Injuries could take anywhere from six weeks to nine months or more to heal. “At the very least you will end up with a whopping big bruise,” Macdonald said. “My advice is very simple: do not wear anything that could increase your risk of falling.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthWomenHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: The best gaming chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play in 2026 – tested | Games | The Guardian
description: Whether you’re on PC or a console, take your setup to the next level with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Whether you’re on PC or a console, take your setup to the next level with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs
Content: Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian DesignThe FilterGamesReviewThe best gaming chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play in 2026 – testedWhether you’re on PC or a console, level up your setup with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairsThe best games of 2026 so farKeith StuartFri 24 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Comfort is crucial to the gaming experience. It’s hard to focus on blasting aliens or taking Stoke to the Champions League final if your bum has gone to sleep because you’ve been sitting on an old chair for three hours. We’re spendingmore time playing games than ever before, so good posture matters. If you have set up a dedicated gaming space, then a rickety seat just won’t cut it.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.From luxurious ergonomic thrones to cheap-and-cheerful bucket seats, the options available are bewildering. So I set out on an epic quest: to find the most comfortable, durable and stylish gaming chairs. Here’s what I discovered.At a glanceBest gaming chair overall:Secretlab Titan Evo£469 at SecretlabBest budget gaming chair:ThunderX3 Solo 360£169.99 at OverclockersBest mid-range gaming chair:ThunderX3 Core£249.95 at OverclockersBest for combining gaming and working:Herman Miller x Logitech G Embody£1,331.25 at Herman MillerBest for improving posture:Anthros the Chair$1,949 at AnthrosWhy you should trust meI have been playing video games for 40 years (gulp), and writing about them for my entire career as a journalist. I spend most of my waking hours sitting with a joypad in hand, and as a sufferer of lower back pain too (gee, I wonder why?), being comfortable while I’m “working” is vital. I’m also a veteran reviewer of gaming technology, including joypads, monitors, keyboards and headsets. In short, I know what people need from their games hardware.How I testedI’m paid to sit and play video games all day (and often into the night), so that’s exactly what I did to test the chairs here. I started by noting how easy or challenging they were to assemble, how sturdy they felt and their level of adjustability. I also judged how cool they looked as part of my gaming setup.I tested 10 gaming chairs over five days each, spending up to four hours a day sitting on them, playing a variety of games, from restful puzzlers to intense shooters and complex flight sims. I also sought the opinions of my sons, who are also keen gamers, and my wife – who isn’t at all interested in games, but who works from home, so was able to assess each model as an occasionaloffice chair.Once the testing process was finished, the chairs were donated to the video games accessibility charity,SpecialEffect, so that other people will get to enjoy them while blasting noobs in Fortnite.The best gaming chairs in 2026Best gaming chair overall:Secretlab Titan EvoSecretlabTitan Evo£469£469 at SecretlabWhat we loveGorgeous looks and lots of room for loungingWhat we don’t loveExpensive and the seat is very firmView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£469 at SecretlabSecretlab is a cool upmarket brand, beloved of many game streamers. Inside the box, the Titan Evo was packaged so neatly and stylishly, it felt as if I was unwrapping a giant iPhone. Although there are a lot of parts, I assembled it in less than 20 minutes, thanks to the poster-sized quick-start guide. My sample came in a sleek, matt-black leatherette finish, but there’s also a fabric version, plus a range of tasteful colours and designs to choose from. It comes in three sizes; I chose the XL because I like a LOT of space.Why we love itAs a natural contrarian I wanted to dislike this much-hyped chair, but I couldn’t.The Titan is solid, beautiful and futuristic, looking like it’s been removed from the bridge of some extraordinarily luscious starship. The controls for the armrests and recline functions are well placed, with adjustments available to tweak the curvature and height of the lumbar support. The seat is capacious enough for lounging, and the leatherette is soft to the touch.My wife found the seat too firm, and while I agreed initially, after a few days I realised it was helping me stay alert over long gaming sessions. Now, everything else feels like sitting on a marshmallow. (As an aside, I have also tried the newEvo NanoGen edition, which you may find offers a bit more give.)The Titan Evo is neither cheap nor as ergonomically advanced as the Herman Miller or Anthros, yet it was the chair I looked forward to sitting in and really enjoyed using.It’s a shame that …the warranty is only three years. You can extend it to five years by posting a photo of your chair on social media, but I dislike the idea of customer support being incentivised in this way.Dimensions (XL version):78 x 70 x 145cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:50cm, 46-55.5cmAdjustments:lumbar support, armrests, recline, tilt lockBrand’s sustainability claims:90% of packaging is recycled paper content. Chair has modular design: if a component wears out over time, it can be replacedSecretlabTitan Evo£469£469 at SecretlabWhat we loveGorgeous looks and lots of room for loungingWhat we don’t loveExpensive and the seat is very firmBest budget gaming chair:ThunderX3 Solo 360ThunderX3Solo 360from£169.99£169.99 at Overclockers£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s well-priced yet sturdy and comfortableWhat we don’t loveMay not suit gamers over 6ftView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£169.99 at Overclockers£199.99 at AmazonA lot of so-called “ergonomic” gaming chairs at the sub-£200 price point are made with squeaky faux leather, plastic parts and sport brash designs – but not the Solo 360. Its slim build and muted grey and black colour options look sophisticated and are backed up with a solid steel construction. There are four variations –Racer,Mesh,Modernand theLoft Air Lightversion I tested – all in different materials.Why we love itAs well as being quick and easy to assemble, I was surprised by how comfortable the Solo 360 is, even over long periods – a view shared by my wife. The armrests are adjustable for both height and angle, and I welcomed the synchronous tilt, which reclines the back and the seat together for a laid-back feel, while your feet stay firmly on the ground. For less than £200, the ThunderX3 is a chair you can use for gaming, working and – possibly – sleeping.It’s a shame that …the seat is rather low, and although the back is curved for lumbar support, the position wasn’t suitable for someone of my height (I’m 6ft 3in). However, this all makes it a good choice for shorter gamers.Dimensions:72-86 x 70 x 127-140cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:48cm, 45-53cmAdjustments:seat height, tilt, armrests, backrest resistanceBrand’s sustainability claims:armrests and wheels made of plastic contain 30% recycled materials. Metal products use approximately 70% recycled materials. Most components apart from leather, fabric and foam are recyclable. Spare parts availableThunderX3Solo 360from£169.99£169.99 at Overclockers£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s well-priced yet sturdy and comfortableWhat we don’t loveMay not suit gamers over 6ftBest mid-range gaming chair:ThunderX3 CoreThunderX3Corefrom£249.95£249.95 at Overclockers£249.95 at AmazonWhat we loveSupportive, with an innovative designWhat we don’t loveChallenging to build and adjustView image in fullscreen£249.95 at Overclockers£249.95 at AmazonWidely acclaimed by the gaming press, the ThunderX3 Core is a chunky, comfortable chair with a large winged back that envelops you. The chair offers several adjustability options, including the same synchronous tilt feature as the Solo, so the backrest and seat move together for ultimate comfort. I also appreciated the ability to slope the seat downwards, to really lean into the action yet take the pressure off the backs of my knees after hours of play.Why we love itThe fabric version of the seat has the smoothest upholstery of all the chairs here – a really lovely soft feel. It also features a lumbar panel on the rear that moves with you as you lean from side to side, for excellent support while playing shooters and driving sims, for example. I didn’t like this feature as much for working, though.It’s a shame that …although it’s easy to assemble, the heads of its hex screws are way too shallow and vulnerable to stripping. Also, the adjustment controls are awkwardly positioned and the armrests rattle a bit.Dimensions:70 x 70 x 129-139cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:45-50cm, 46-56cmAdjustments:height, tilt, armrestsBrand’s sustainability claims:see ThunderX3 Solo 360 aboveThunderX3Corefrom£249.95£249.95 at Overclockers£249.95 at AmazonWhat we loveSupportive, with an innovative designWhat we don’t loveChallenging to build and adjustBest for combining gaming and working:Herman Miller x Logitech G EmbodyHerman MillerEmbody£1,331.25£1,331.25 at Herman MillerWhat we loveSupportive chair with excellent build qualityWhat we don’t loveExpensive if you’re just playing games in itView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£1,331.25 at Herman MillerThe Embody is Herman Miller’s premium gaming chair – and it shows. Whether you’re leaning into the screen or tilting back for a chilled session, its strong aluminium frame and high-end fabrics, including heat-dissipating composite particles, combine to keep you comfortable and cool. Available in a range of understated colours to suit more mature tastes, it arrives fully assembled – I was seated and playing Arc Raiders within 10 minutes of it being delivered.Why we love itThe Embody is an impressively svelte chair. It has a narrow silhouette and a lower back than many of its competitors; there’s no headrest, nor does it offer some of the more intricate adjustments, such as 4D armrests or precise lumbar control. But it doesn’t need to – its clean, precise, ergonomic design gently encourages you to sit comfortably and correctly without you even realising.Therearelevers allowing you to tilt fully, extend the seat depth or alter the back to fit your spine, but I didn’t have to spend ages getting everything right. The armrests are perfectly placed, the seat allows plenty of movement, and my spine felt cushioned, even when I spent all day in it – which made it great for work, too.It’s a shame that …it’s expensive – but worth the money, if you’ll be using it for hours daily and it’s doubling as ahome office chair. It comes with an impressive 12-year warranty, and when it does finally give up, the company claims it is up to 96% recyclable.Dimensions:74.9 x 38.1-45.7 x 106.7-114.3cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:38.1-45.7cm; 43.2-55.9cmAdjustments:seat height, seat depth, tilt and back fit, armrest height and widthBrand’s sustainability claims:corporate sustainability programme. Worn parts replaced free under warranty (outside that, UK customers are pointed to third-party suppliers). Made from 44% recycled materials. Chair is up to 96% recyclable at end of lifeHerman MillerEmbody£1,331.25£1,331.25 at Herman MillerWhat we loveSupportive chair with excellent build qualityWhat we don’t loveExpensive if you’re just playing games in itBest for improving posture:Anthros the ChairAnthrosThe Chair$1,949$1,949 (about £1,455)What we loveDesigned with deep medical knowledge of back painWhat we don’t loveExpensive, but you get what you pay forView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian$1,949 (about £1,455) at AnthrosThe Anthros is a serious piece of ergonomic equipment with intricately adjustable, well-placed controls for tilt, height and back support. Designed to stabilise your pelvis in order to alleviate back pain, its creators are as obsessed with posture as an overbearing Victorian governess – but in a good way. Indeed, the team used to design wheelchairs, so they know about ensuring long-term comfort.Customers are even offered a complimentary video session with an expert in order to calibrate it properly. The chair frame comes in black or white, with a range of colours, textures and designs available for the rear of the backrest. It ships in two sections, so there’s little assembly.Why we love itAs with the Herman Miller and Secretlab models, the Anthros offers a firm sit, with just the right amount of padding to keep glutes and upper thighs comfy. The back is made of two sections, one providing pelvis support, and the other gently cushioning your upper back – this part actually moves with you slightly as you lean left or right, which ensures you’re always in optimum contact with the chair. The decompress mode lets you tilt back and relax while still maintaining a healthy position.After using it for a couple of weeks, I felt I was much better at sitting properly and experienced less of my usual pain when getting up. Whether I was bolt upright for hours writing articles, or wildly slamming about playing Call of Duty, it quite literally had my back.It’s a shame that …it’s already pricey, but with US-only distribution pushing UK shipping costs to $307.71 (about £230) right now, it’s a significant investment. However, if you struggle with back pain, it’s excellent as a gaming and office chair.Dimensions:66 x 67 x 101.9-110.9cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:38.7-46.6cm, 48-59cmAdjustments:tilt, seat height, upper and lower backBrand’s sustainability claims:most parts are potentially recyclable (although it may be a struggle due to a lack of processing streams in the UK). Spare parts available. 12-year warrantyAnthrosThe Chair$1,949$1,949 (about £1,455)What we loveDesigned with deep medical knowledge of back painWhat we don’t loveExpensive, but you get what you pay forThe best of the restX Rocker Tempest RGBX RockerTempest RGBfrom£169£169 at Dunelm£169.99 at VeryWhat we loveA fun, comfy chair with basic featuresWhat we don’t loveThe components feel cheapView image in fullscreen£169 at Dunelm£169.99 at VeryBest for:tweens and teensThe Tempest is clearly aimed at a younger market, with sports car styling and fun LED panels that light up in a variety of colours. It was easy to assemble and feels pretty comfortable to sit in, with thick padding, a wide seat and rudimentary lumbar support. It’s a decent first gaming chair.It didn’t make the final cut because …the build quality is basic, and there are no adjustment options apart from seat height. I’m not sure how it will hold up with regular use – although the one-year warranty covers replacement parts, and spares can be bought beyond that.Dimensions:69 x 67 x 114.5-122.5cm (WDH);seat depth and height:60cm, 45-53cm;adjustments:height;brand’s sustainability claims:company is FIRA registered and audits factories to ensure best practices.
