It also comes with lumbar and neck pillows, and adjustable arms.It didn’t make the final cut because …the racing car styling is cool, but the construction and materials lack the quality of more expensive models, and some parts were tricky to put together. It’s a decent entry-level gaming chair, but at this price, a dedicated office chair may be a better option for longer sessions and/or back pain sufferers.Dimensions:67 x 68 x 124-132cm (WDH);seat depth and height:50cm, 45-55cm;adjustments:height, recline, armrests;brand’s sustainability claims:corporate sustainability programme. Comes with a two-year manufacturer’s guaranteeCorsairTC100from£199£199 at Currys£204.99 at ArgosWhat we loveLots of width for keen slouchersWhat we don’t loveAssembly is tricky and the armrests don’t rotateNoblechairs LegendNoblechairsLegend£399.95£399.95 at NoblechairsWhat we loveGood comfort; looks cool if you’re into sports carsWhat we don’t loveSeat feels shallow and armrests aren’t greatView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£399.95 at NoblechairsBest for:all-round performanceThe Legend really does look like a sports car seat, with beautifully stitched faux leather fabric (vegan and sustainably made), a high-winged back, and sleek styling. There’s plenty of range to the tilt, and both the lumbar support and armrests are fully adjustable. I found it comfortable over long periods, so it can happily double as an office chair, plus it’s robust – and the company stocks spare parts, if needed.It didn’t make the final cut because …I found the seat too shallow (I’m 6ft 3in) and the armrests uncomfortable, no matter how I adjusted them. There are slightly better options at this price point.Dimensions:52 x 73 x 132-142cm (WDH);seat depth and height:48cm, 48-58cm;adjustments:tilt, armrests, lumbar support;brand’ssustainability claims:solvent- and phthalate-free materials and manufactured with low emissions. Metal parts recyclable. Chairs come with a two-year warranty covering partsNoblechairsLegend£399.95£399.95 at NoblechairsWhat we loveGood comfort; looks cool if you’re into sports carsWhat we don’t loveSeat feels shallow and armrests aren’t greatFractal RefineFractalRefinefrom£454.82£459 at Currys£454.82 at AmazonWhat we loveSturdy and nice seat controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavy, like trying to wheel a Dalek aroundView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£459 at Currys£454.82 at AmazonBest for:solid, sensible build qualityThe Refine is an extremely well-built chair with a minimalist design that would suit the offices of some trendy Gothenburg architecture firm. Everything is easily adjustable, mostly via cool little tabs rather than the usual protruding levers, and the mesh fabric is comfortable and keeps you cool – although my younger son said it felt like sitting in acamping chair. Fractal also offers good after-care support, including spare parts.It didn’t make the final cut because …the seat is a little shallow for taller users even at full extension, and I had to detach the headrest cushion as it was too invasive. Better as a quality office chair that you use occasionally for gaming, rather than the other way around.Dimensions:70 x 70 x134-146.5cm (WDH);seat depth and height:45-50.5cm, 49-61cm;adjustments:recline, height, armrests, lumbar support, headrest;brand’s sustainability claims:one more expensive Fractal Refine model uses Alcantara, a material with recycled elements. The company is moving to plastic‑free packaging. Metal sections can be recycled. Five-year warranty on mechanical parts and a three-year warranty on soft partsFractalRefinefrom£454.82£459 at Currys£454.82 at AmazonWhat we loveSturdy and nice seat controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavy, like trying to wheel a Dalek aroundWhat you need to knowDo you actually need a specific chair for gaming?If you only play console games for a few hours a week in front of a big TV in the living room, a nice slouchy armchair or even a beanbag is fine. However, if you play games at a desk with a monitor and want to feel comfortable, a decent chair is a good investment, especially for long gaming sessions, or if you also work at the desk from time to time.Office chair vs gaming chair: what’s the difference?It’s all about design purpose. An office chair is intended to support posture and productivity for several hours a day and will probably come with ergonomic features that allow you to fine-tune your sitting experience. A gaming chair is designed primarily for shorter-term comfort because, sadly, you’re unlikely to spend as much time playing games as you are working.The design tends to focus on fun and immersion, which is why many look as if they’ve been pulled from a sports car or rollercoaster, featuring high-winged backs, headrests, lots of padding, and seats with raised edges. An office chair is usually conservative and unobtrusive; gaming chairs often sport a bolder look, with bright colours and extravagant design touches.If you’re on a tight budget (£200 or less) and don’t care about flashy looks, an office chair is almost certainly a better choice, as they tend to be more sturdily built and ergonomically designed at this price.For more, read our guide to thebest office chairsWhat do I need to look for?You need a chair that’s right for your size and gaming habits – for good posture, you should be able to plant your feet on the floor with your knees at a 90-degree angle and your upper legs parallel to the floor. If you’re a larger build or move a lot while playing, choose a chair with a wider, deeper seat. If you’re tall or experience back pain, go for an ergonomic model with good lumbar support.Consider the way you play games. If you use a mouse and keyboard, then armrests are a good idea, but if you use a joypad and hold it close to your lap, they may get in the way of your elbows (unless they can be rotated, as chairs such as the Titan Evo, Anthros, Core and Refine allow). If you like to sit back with your feet up, make sure the chair has a deep tilt angle. If you’ll be working in your chair as well as gaming, consider a model with ergonomic features and more space to move about.How much should I spend?Think about how much time you will spend in the chair and how long you expect it to last. From £180, you can buy a comfortable, solidly built gaming chair that will suit most casual to intermediate gamers; from £350, models offer greater adjustability for posture and lumbar support, and are more likely to be built to last.For more, readthe best PS5 games to play in 2026and thebest of 2026 so farAs a veteran technology journalist, Keith Stuart has spent years testing gaming gadgets from headsets to keyboards to full PC builds, so he knows what gamers need. He also spends a disproportionate amount of time sitting down and so is doubly qualified to put gaming chairs through their pacesExplore more on these topicsGamesThe FilterHomesInteriorsHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Panda Bamboo mattress topper review: soothed my pain and improved my sleep – even in a heatwave | Sleep | The Guardian
description: Supportive and surprisingly cool for memory foam, Panda’s flagship topper gave our reviewer some of the best sleep she’s had all summer
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: Supportive and surprisingly cool for memory foam, Panda’s flagship topper gave our reviewer some of the best sleep she’s had all summer
Content: Side sleeper … our review found the Panda supportive, soft and surprisingly cool.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSide sleeper … our review found the Panda supportive, soft and surprisingly cool.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianThe FilterSleepReviewPanda Bamboo mattress topper review: soothed my pain and improved my sleep – even in a heatwaveSupportive and surprisingly cool for memory foam, Panda’s flagship topper gave our reviewer some of the best sleep she’s had all summerThe best mattress toppers – testedJane HoskynFri 24 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.When I was struggling tosleep in a heatwave, diving into a 6ft slab of memory foam didn’t exactly sound like the answer. Memory foam is renowned for trapping heat, and the more “sinky” the foam, the more heat you’d expect it to trap. Less comfort layer, more boiled marshmallow.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.However, the foam used by Panda in its flagship mattress topper genuinely seems to break the mould. It has the cosy feel of conventional memory foam, but it eased my night sweats so well when I tested thebest mattress toppersin summer 2025 that I named it the “best cooling topper”, beating rivals filled with airy wool and microfibre.That test didn’t take place during a record-breaking heatwave, though. Could this topper still keep my temperature under control when the thermometer was reading 32C in my bedroom at 1am? It’s a tall order, but I’m never one to pass up the chance of snoozing in the name of Filter research.In this in-depth review, I have good news and bad news. The bad news is that Panda’s topper – which at £139.95 for a double is less than half the price of the premiumSimba Hybrid topper(£349 RRP for a double) and significantly cheaper than a whole new mattress – won’t actively cool you down. The good news is it helped me achieve some of the best sleep I had all summer, and below I’ll explain why.View at PandaHow I testedView image in fullscreenDegree ceremony: an infrared thermometer was used to test heat retention.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianI test mattress toppers in much the same way that Itest mattresses, namely by sleeping on them. I first reviewed a double-size Panda bamboo topper in summer 2025 and then donated it to charity, so Panda kindly sent me a new model for this 2026 test.I left the topper in the spare room for two days to expand to its full size, then attached it to the medium-firm pocket-sprungPremier Inn Mattress 2.0and slept on it for a week in early July, when our bedroom temperature rarely dropped below 30C at night. Not pleasant, but a good opportunity to put Panda’s claim of a “cooler, comfier sleep” to the test.I was joined for the sleep test by my husband, Alan. We tend to toss and turn at night, so if a mattress or topper can absorb these movements (what’s known as “motion isolation”) and help us sleep in peace, it usually scores extra points with me. Alan also helped me with the more nerdy tests that involved weights, string and a ruler (to measure sinkage), plus an infrared thermometer and Alan’s bottom (to measure heat retention).A mattress topper should be easy to carry and store, especially if you’re unlikely to leave it on your bed indefinitely. Well-made details, such as zips and stitching, are signs of quality, as is a generous stuffing that fills the casing consistently from corner to corner. Other factors such as aesthetics and firmness are more subjective but still important.Price is a key consideration – but I don’t just give kudos for cheapness. Value for money is about getting what you pay for, and not paying over the odds for a brand name or novel features that ultimately add little.What you need to know‘Panda’s memory foam is certainly supportive.’ Video: Jane Hoskyn/the GuardianView at PandaLondon-based bedding company Panda eschews cotton and down in favour of bamboo fibre (hence Panda) in its duvets, bedding, mattresses and toppers – including this one.The topper’s zippable cover is 70% bamboo viscose and 30% polyester, and can be removed for machine washing at 30C. On its underside are thousands of tiny rubberised dots that help stop it sliding around as you get in and out of bed, while each corner features a strong elasticated strap. Surprisingly, Panda’s is the only topper I’ve tested so far with adjustable straps, so you can fit it securely on mattresses of any depth.Inside the cover is a single 5cm layer of high-viscosity polyurethane foam, AKA memory foam. Panda calls the foam in this topper HydroFoam and describes it as “third-generation memory foam”. It’s infused with gel beads designed to regulate temperature, and its open-cell structure aims to counteract memory foam’s tendency to retain heat.Panda describes its topper as “medium-firm and supportive”, with a foam density of 80kg/m3, although it feels far less dense than that. Memory foam tops out at 75kg/m3according to thisdensity chart; 80kg is more like the solid “chip foam” used for gym mats. Panda’s memory foam is certainly supportive, but it’s much more cradling and cosy than a gym mat.The Panda bamboo topper costs from £99.95 for a single to £199.95 for an EU emperor, with a UK double coming in at £139.95. That’s mid-range for mattress toppers, which can be as cheap as theSilentnight Airmax 1000(£38 for a double in the sale at the time of writing), or as pricey as theTempur One(£549), which is close in feel to the Panda. The Panda’s 10-year warranty is at the top end, and you also get 30 nights to sleep on it before deciding whether to keep it.SpecificationsMaterial:memory foam filling; bamboo and polyester fabric coverFirmness:advertised as medium-firm, rated by Alan and me as 6.5/10Depth:5cmCare:unzip cover to wash at 30C; wipe-clean foamFree trial:30 nightsWarranty:10 yearsSustainability credentials:made from renewable bamboo, sourced from managed forests; Oeko-Tex Standard 100 certified to be free of harmful substances; Panda collects and recycles old mattresses for free under“Circle of Life” initiativeWhat we loveView image in fullscreenPurrfect fit … the mattress topper adapted beautifully to side-sleeping.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianAt first, I thought I’d been sent a pillow by mistake. My double topper arrived vacuum-packed in a tiny box (about 1 x 2ft), and even once expanded to full size it was light enough (7.15kg) tomove around and store easily. After wrestling with countless bulky mattresses, it was a joy to be able to unpack it from the shrink-wrap all by myself – without any swearing.Itsqualitywas visible from the off. The memory foam pad fills the fabric cover corner to corner; the zip works smoothly all the way around; the fabric is soft but robust; and the stitching is beautifully finished. These may seem like trivial details, but they show that this product isn’t “fast furnishing”, but something built to last – an impression backed up by its excellent 10-year warranty.Alan and I used the topper’s adjustable straps to attach it securely to the chunky 28.5cm-deep Premier Inn mattress, and slept on it for a week during the soggy, sweltering nights of July. Given the heat, I was surprised by how well I slept. I felt well supported, without too much pressure on my joints or ribs, and the topper’smotion isolationwas exceptional. When Alan turned in bed next to me, I could hear his head turning on the pillow, but there was none of the bounce or ripple you experience when sleeping on a sprung mattress.The topper adapted beautifully to my side-sleeping body, allowing my hips, shoulders and otherpressure pointsto sink and enabling my back to fully relax. I’ve slept on enough saggy hotel beds to know how uncomfortable an overly soft mattress can be, but the topper’s foam washighly supportivewhere needed, lifting me up while cradling my pressure points. I slept well and woke up feeling refreshed and pain-free.In the past I’ve found that an old rib injury can start to niggle on firm surfaces, but there was none of that here. I felt suspended, almost as if I were floating in a dense cloud. If you live with musculoskeletal pain and struggle to get comfy on your existing mattress, this topper could help you sleep more comfortably.Will it help me sleep in the heatwave?View image in fullscreenHot bot: writer Jane’s ‘assistant’ Alan used his rear to test the topper’s temperature pre- and post-use.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianI named the Panda the “best cooling topper” in mymattress toppersroundup after testing it in 2025’s relatively mild conditions. Could it still perform when my bedroom was stubbornly hovering above 30C the following year?No “cooling” mattress or topper can actively cool you down; it’s not like putting your sheets in the freezer. However, what a good cooling topper or mattress can do isstop you from overheating, and in that regard the Panda performs amazingly well. While conventional memory foam tends to trap body heat, Panda’s bamboo fabric and open-cell foam seemed to help keep my temperature under control, even wicking away sweat from my body.To back this up with evidence, I used an infrared thermometer to take the topper’s temperature before and after asking Alan to sit on it for two minutes. Pre-bottom, the bamboo fabric surface was 31.9C, roughly the same as ambient room temperature. Immediately post-bottom, the surface was 34.9C. Thirty seconds later it was 32.5C, and after 90 seconds it had dropped back down to 31.9C. That suggests the foam is able todissipate body heatrather than collect it.I repeated the test on the “temperature regulating” Premier Inn Mattress 2.0 after removing the topper from it, and got similar results. I’d suspected that the Panda would do better on temperature control than conventional memory foam, but I was amazed to find it matching a pocket-sprung mattress.Before celebrating, I had to make sure I didn’t get an identical result from any old surface, so I ran the same test using the “winter” side of theSleepeezee Dual Seasons mattress, which I also have in for review. Sure enough, that mattress retained heat for much longer (as it’s designed to), failing to drop back to room temperature until eight minutes after Alan and his bum had wandered off.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenSinking feeling: ‘Some will find it too soft.’Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianThe sink-in sensation of memory foamtakes some getting used to. When I first began testing mattresses six years ago, I struggled to get comfortable on foam because I was used to much firmer surfaces that made it easier to turn in bed. Also, foamallows less air to circulatearound your body than firmer surfaces do, or mattresses whose upper comfort layers are filled with natural fibres, such as wool.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn my sinkage tests, the middle of the topper’s surface sank 33mm under 7.5kg of weights. That’s similar to a couple of hybrid mattresses I’ve tested, including theEve Wunderflip Hybrid. As such,some will find it too soft, although I found that the Panda topper’s high viscoelasticity (which essentially means that it’s dense but mouldable) made it feel more supportive than that mattress.This mattress topper needs a couple of days to expand to full size before you try sleeping on it – or, indeed, reviewing it. What’s more, itwon’t transform a saggy mattress. As with all the toppers I’ve tested, the mattress you attach it to needs to be at least medium-firm, or the topper will just exaggerate its softness and mould to any dips in its surface.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe topper unzipped, showing the bamboo and polyester fabric cover and memory foam filling.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianThemattress industryisn’t exactly an environmental hero, and memory foam is particularly problematic. Polyurethane foam has an intensive manufacturing process (it’s the UPF of bedding materials) and can only be recycled atspecialised facilities. So far, so unsustainable – but Panda is making more positive efforts than many of the sleep brands I’ve reviewed.Bamboo, which Panda uses, is a renewable resource that releases about35% more oxygenthan trees. All Panda’s bamboo is sourced from managed forests, and its bamboo textiles (viscose and lyocell) are Oeko-Tex Standard 100 certified free of harmful substances.The fabric in this topper is bamboo viscose, which is processed using chemicals and is less green than lyocell. According to Panda’senvironmental impact report, though, all its textiles are produced using a closed-loop process that limits water waste. Its products are also vegan-friendly and packaged in biodegradable cardboard.Panda is the only sleep company I’ve reviewed that doesn’t charge to recycle your old mattress when you buy a new one from them. It will also collect your old Panda mattress for free “when the time comes to part” with it. It says it’s now extended thisschemeto mattress toppers and pillows, too, but there was no offer to collect my old bedding when I tried to check out with a Panda topper on its website.Panda Bamboo mattress topper: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenThe cat’s whiskers: Panda’s bamboo topper is hard to beat for luxurious softness and pressure relief.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianPanda’s topper is the most comfortable memory foam surface I’ve ever slept on. The breathable design does a good job of offsetting foam’s natural heat retention, and its supportive but sumptuous feel could make a real difference for anyone experiencing pain or struggling to get comfy on a mattress that’s too firm.Memory foam can take a little getting used to, and this topper won’t suit everyone. I’m also keen not to overstate its “cooling” powers – it can help avoid nighttime clamminess, but it won’t actively reduce your temperature in a heatwave. It won’t make a saggy old mattress comfortable again, either. If you buy any topper hoping to do that, you’ll have wasted your money.For adding luxurious softness and pressure relief, though, Panda’s bamboo topper is hard to beat, especially for the price. At £139.95 for a double, it’s excellent value, and its 10-year warranty and 30-night free trial make it even easier to recommend.View at PandaPanda Bamboo mattress toppervs…Simba Hybrid topperView image in fullscreenDouble, £314.10 at SimbaSimba’s topper is more than twice the price of the Panda, at £314.10 (sale price at the time of writing) for a double, and is heavier and more bulky to store. But I loved it so much that I made it my overall favourite in our guide to mattress toppers.The 6.5cm-thick Simba contains a layer of thousands of microsprings as well as foam, so it’s essentially a thin bed-in-a-box hybrid mattress with more bounce than you’d expect from a topper. Its foam top layer is less viscous than the Panda’s sink-in foam, so it doesn’t have the same level of cradling pressure relief, but memory foam sceptics may prefer it. Its base layer of high-density foam gives it fantastic support, too.The best mattress toppers for a more comfortable night’s sleep, testedRead moreSilentnight Airmax 1000 mattress topperView image in fullscreenDouble, £38 at SilentnightThe cheapest topper in my roundup is a third of the price of the Panda, at just £38 for a double size (sale price at the time of writing). This hollow-fibre bargain will happily survive anelectric blanketor washing machine. It does a fine job of letting the air flow around your body, too.Silentnight’s topper made my bed look like a bouncy castle at first, but its pillowy surface evens out when you lie on it – and it really is rather comfy. It’s a great buy and will make a hard mattress feel less gruelling, but it won’t do much to soothe joint pain or turn your bed into a sumptuous cosy cocoon like the Panda.Woolroom Deluxe Wool mattress topperView image in fullscreenDouble, £173.99 at WoolroomAnother brilliant temperature controller, this one should be your hot-weather choice if you want to upgrade from hollow-fibre and can’t get on with memory foam. Its silky natural fibre casing contains British wool that’s naturally hypoallergenic and does a brilliant job of insulating your body from the heat of summer and the chill of winter. It doesn’t add much softness, though, which is the usual job of a mattress topper – and at £173.99 (sale price at the time of writing) for a double, it’s an investment.For more ways to sleep better with the Filter:The best mattresses – testedThe best duvets for every seasonThe best pillows for every type of sleeperJane Hoskyn is a features journalist who’s spent three decades rearranging bookshelves and “testing” products while deadlines loom. She would always rather be in the woods, or napping, or napping in the woodsExplore more on these topicsSleepThe FilterHealth & wellbeingHomesInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: DakaDaka’s qvevri – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Orange wine and mezcal mingle in this smoky, Georgian-inspired drink
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Orange wine and mezcal mingle in this smoky, Georgian-inspired drink
Content: DakaDaka's Qvevri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenDakaDaka's Qvevri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: DakaDaka’s qvevri – recipeOrange wine and mezcal mingle in this smoky, Georgian-inspired drinkJack PorterFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsmoky, refreshing highball inspired by Georgia’s amber wines andqvevriwinemaking tradition (large clay vessels buried underground for fermentation). The mezcal works beautifully with the wine, which traditionally has structure and tannin from extended skin contact in those qvevri, and with the hint of citrus. The result is a cocktail that feels ancient and modern at the same time.QvevriServes125ml mezcal– we useQuiquiriqui Espadín, but any will do75ml orange wine, or, if you can get hold of some, Georgian amber wine25mlCocchi Americano, or white vermouth10ml crème de cassis10ml Cointreau10ml simple 1:1 honey syrup5ml fresh lemon juiceSoda water, to top1 strip orange peel, to garnishFill a highball glass with ice, then measure in all the liquids bar the soda. Stir gently to combine, then top with a splash of soda water to taste and garnish with the orange peel (if you’re feeling really fancy, or you’re Georgian, use a strip oftklapi, or fruit leather, instead).Jack Porter,DakaDaka, London W1Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodWineEastern European food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for pineapple and mango paletas | Food | The Guardian
description: These bright, sharp Mexican iced treats are the perfect summer cooler – with a spiky kick
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: These bright, sharp Mexican iced treats are the perfect summer cooler – with a spiky kick
Content: Helen Goh's pineapple and mango paletas.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh's pineapple and mango paletas.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.The sweet spotFoodHelen Goh’s recipe for pineapple and mango paletasThese bright, sharp Mexican iced treats are the perfect summer cooler – with a spiky kickHelen GohFri 24 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first time I encounteredpaletasin Mexico, they felt strangely familiar. They reminded me of the iced treats of my Malaysian childhood: fruit-driven, brightly coloured and made less to indulge than to relieve the heat. What struck me most was the flavour logic shared by both countries, where sweetness is often enlivened with salt, chilli, tamarind or citrus, each sharpening the fruit in its own way and making it seem brighter, cooler and somehow more vivid. Paletas are rarely perfectly smooth; little pieces of fruit suspended in the ice give them texture and interest. These two paletas take different paths from the same base: pineapple – sharp, clean and bright with lime and ginger – and mango – sweeter, rounder and more indulgent, which I’ve spiked with chilli, lime and salt.Pineapple and mango paletasPaleta moulds are easy to find online and in many kitchenware shops, but if you don’t have them, small paper cups and wooden sticks work perfectly well, too.Prep10 minCook15 min, plus coolingFreeze6 hr+Makes10-12For the base syrup70g caster sugarFor the pineapple, lime and ginger paletas600g fresh pineapple flesh, cut into chunks, plus 70g finely diced into 5-7mm pieces1 quantity base syrup(see above)1 tbsp lime juice20g fresh ginger, finely gratedPinch of fine sea saltFor the mango and Tajín paletas500g ripe mango flesh, cut into chunks, plus 70g finely diced into 5–7mm pieces1 quantity base syrup(see above)1½ tbsp lime juiceSmall pinch of fine sea saltTajín or other chilli-lime seasoning, to serveTo make the base syrup, place the sugar and 70ml water into a small saucepan on a medium heat and stir until dissolved. Remove from the heat and cool completely.For the pineapple paletas, blend the pineapple chunks with the cooled syrup, lime juice, ginger and salt until very smooth. Taste – it should seem slightly brighter and sharper than you’d like, as freezing dulls flavour. Pour the fruit puree into the paleta moulds, leaving about 1cm space at the top. Drop a few pieces of the finely diced fruit into each mould, gently nudging them down with a skewer or teaspoon so they’re suspended throughout the mixture. Tap the moulds lightly on the bench to remove air bubbles, then insert sticks and freeze for at least six hours or overnight. To unmould, briefly run the moulds under warm water.For the mango paletas, blend the mango chunks with the cooled syrup, lime juice and salt until smooth. Taste and adjust if needed: mangoes vary enormously in sweetness and acidity, so you may wish to add extra lime. Drop a few pieces of the diced fruit into each mould, gently nudging them down with a skewer or teaspoon so they are suspended throughout the mixture. Freeze and unmould as above. Sprinkle the Tajín over the mango paletas just before serving; this keeps the flavours bright and distinct.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotFruitMexican food and drinkBakingrecipesShareReuse this content

title: I spent years trying to get smaller. Until I decided to get bigger  | Well actually | The Guardian
description: ‘Bulking’, or gaining weight on purpose to get stronger, challenged everything I was once taught to do with my body
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: ‘Bulking’, or gaining weight on purpose to get stronger, challenged everything I was once taught to do with my body
Content: ‘Why would anyone go through all this trouble if they’re not a professional bodybuilder? Building and maintaining muscle is essential for health, especially as we age.’Photograph: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Why would anyone go through all this trouble if they’re not a professional bodybuilder? Building and maintaining muscle is essential for health, especially as we age.’Photograph: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesWell actuallyI spent years trying to get smaller. Until I decided to get bigger‘Bulking’, or gaining weight on purpose to get stronger, challenged everything I was once taught to do with my bodyTell us: what impact have GLP-1s had on your relationships?Madeleine AggelerFri 24 Jul 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 16.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI had been casually lifting weights for a few years when several things changed in quick succession.First, my boyfriend proposed.This wasn’t a surprise – he had already told me he wanted to get married, and I had told him exactly how I wanted him to propose: somewhere public but not crowded, not in a restaurant. Since I spend most of my waking hours hunched over my computer looking like an extra from The Walking Dead, I also wanted to be nicely dressed for the occasion.double quotation markOver the years I had constructed an image of the bride I wanted to be, and that woman was skinnyHe gamely followed instructions and got down on one knee in a quiet gallery of my favorite museum. My cute outfit – an orange wrap dress coupled with dainty purple heels – was only slightly undermined by the fact I cried so hard that my eyes puffed up and snot dripped from my nose.Then came the unexpected part. Planning our wedding sent me into a body-loathing spiral I hadn’t experienced since middle school.37:47After years of not stepping on a scale, I started weighing myself every morning. I tracked calories and counted steps. I ate as little as possible, and when I couldn’t take it any more, I binged until my stomach ached. Part of me knew I had crossed into unhealthy territory, but I was determined to keep trying to lose weight. When my fiance gently expressed concern, I listened, nodded, then ignored him and continued to unravel.It took me a while to figure out what had prompted this change of behavior. I thought my crash diet days were behind me, and I didn’t care that much about weddings. Ours was always going to be lowkey: a small courthouse ceremony followed by two parties at our respective parents’ homes.Eventually, I realized what was driving it. Without consciously doing so, over the years I had constructed an image of the bride I wanted to be, and that woman wasskinny. She was all long, twiggy limbs – think nepo baby supermodel, or a newborn foal. I had internalized a noxious idea: that was the kind of woman who was successful and loved.Despite – or more likely because of – the emotional and physical turmoil I put it through, my body didn’t change. The only thing that did was how I felt about it. Each day, I liked it a little less.‘Why do I need to change?’: the brides saying no to costly pre-wedding glow-upsRead moreIn a matter of weeks, my body would be captured in hundreds of wedding photos. There I would be, looking exactly like myself – not a supermodel. That felt like a crisis, as if my failure to make myself a certain kind of beautiful would undermine the sanctity and magnitude of the day, and disappoint everyone involved. Never mind that I would never think about other people’s weddings in these ugly, vicious terms. I was my only, and favorite, punching bag.Then, a month before we said “I do,” my fiance and I moved into a new apartment building with a really nice gym. For years, I had been making do with a set of stackable dumbbells bought during lockdown. I had used them for about an hour, three to four times a week, and aside from vaguely trying to eat enough protein, I didn’t monitor what I ate.This routine had served me well, but now I had access to heavier weights, barbells, a Smith machine, a functional trainer and big mirrors in which I could check my form. Walking around the gym, I felt like a little country mouse gawping at the bright lights and heavy equipment of the big fitness city.It was exciting. I wanted to see what I could do! Almost immediately, I lifted heavier than I ever had before – and then even heavier than that.My bingeing and restricting had not abated, and my workout performance was mixed. Some days, I moved weights like they were nothing. Others, I could barely budge them.When my wedding day arrived, I didn’t think much about my body. We were married in the courthouse’s basement room with terrible lighting, purple carpet and plastic flowers, and it was perfect. I had a wobble when I saw a picture of myself, where I thought I looked lumpy and ghoulish. But then my husband put his arm around me and smiled, and I felt so happy that I thought I might explode.On the way out, I saw other brides filing into the courthouse: none of them were nepo baby supermodels, all of them beautiful and perfect.Afterwards, discouraged and exhausted by the process of trying and failing to shrink, I decided I would take the opposite approach.Instead of trying to lose weight, I would try to gain weight. I was going to bulk.In lifting parlance, a “bulk” has two parts. The first is eating in a caloric surplus, or eating more calories than your body burns in a day to maintain its current weight. The second is training with progressive overload, which means gradually increasing the difficulty of your lifts by adding weights or reps, in order to build muscle and get stronger.Building muscle is hard. It requires carefully adjusting the dials on a range of behaviors. Youhave toeat enough carbs to fuel your workouts; eat more protein than your body uses in a typical day (the extra protein helps build new muscle); train almost to failure, which means you stop when you cannot complete one more repetition with good form; and practice progressive overload. You should schedule at least one to two rest days a week and get plenty of sleep.It is technically possible to build muscle without increasing your caloric intake. But it’s much harder, and generally only works for people who are new to lifting or who are returning to training after a long hiatus. These are also known as “newbie gains”. But once their bodies adapt, even newbies will eventually require more calories in order to lift heavier.double quotation mark[Bulking] challenges most of what [women] are taught about our bodies, and what we are made to fear about our bodiesCasey Johnston“At the end of the day, energy is king,” says Dr John Tokish, an orthopedic surgeon who specializes in sports medicine.It doesn’t matter if you’re prioritizing protein, he says – if you’re not eating enough calories, your body will start cannibalizing its existing muscle for energy, and you will end up losing muscle instead of building it.Why would anyone go through all this trouble if they’re not a professional bodybuilder? Building and maintaining muscle is essential for health, especially as we age. Strength training has been shown to reduceblood pressure, protectcardiovascular health,improve cognitive functionand alleviate symptoms ofanxiety and depression. It can alsoprevent injuriesand help adults liveindependentlyfor longer as they age.Plus, I truly love lifting. While there is a blunt simplicity to strength training – you pick up something heavy and put it down again – there’s also a beautiful subtlety to it. Tiny, almost invisible adjustments in breath and form can completely change how you move weight. Lifting heavier and with good form required me to develop a physical fluency I didn’t have before. The focus it demanded made my workouts almost meditative. Before each exercise, I tried to empty my mind of everything except what each part of my body needed to do.And because I am vain – and who isn’t? – growing muscle also promised to help me address a more immediate concern: building shoulders the size of bread loaves, and an ass so big and juicy you can see it from space.My bulk would last three months – enough time to see changes.“Three months is enough time for all the pieces [of a bulk] to come together,” says Casey Johnston, author of the health and fitness newsletterShe’s a Beastand the book Physical Education. “It’s sort of like a minimum effective length of time.”For most people, she argues, a month or two is not enough to get dialed into your training and nutrition in a way that will make a meaningful difference.The first thing I had to do was figure out my daily calorie goal. To establish that, I had to figure out roughly how many calories I was burning daily, then add a few hundred more.This turned out to be easier said than done. I consulted multiple online calorie calculators which asked me for my age, sex, height, weight and activity level in order to determine my total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). They all gave me widely different answers. This led to about a week of trial and error – I started at the lower end of the caloric spectrum and when I felt famished, gradually upped the amount I was eating until I thought I had hit a rough surplus.This kind of trial and error is often part of the process, says Turkish. For the average person on the street, he says, the best way to accurately determine your caloric needs is to check your weight, and then use a calorie calculator to track everything you consume and see how your weight fluctuates over the course of weeks. “I do it every day, but you could weigh yourself at the same time every week,” he says. “Then you follow those trends over the course of 12, 15, 18 weeks, and you’ll be good at predicting what your calorie burn versus your calorie surplus is.”For my own sanity, I would not be weighing myself, and instead employing a more vibes-based approach. I would be tracking calories, though, and at first this worried me. Historically, I had only done it in the punishing, restrictive way so many women are taught. But this time was different. Now, I was trying to make sure I got enough – enough calories, enough protein, enough carbs. It felt indulgent to think of the food I could consume, rather than withhold, to reach a goal.double quotation markThe idea of gaining weight on purpose felt scary. But it also felt transgressive and liberatingMy routine eating habits were not a good way to meet these nutritional goals. My meals were often glorified snacks buttressed by other, smaller snacks. This often resulted in me having to wolf down a big bowl of yoghurt after dinner to hit my protein. It felt like my high school days, when I started getting ready for bed only to realize I had forgotten to do my homework.I had to be more intentional, so I started to make my meals meal-sized and had snacks like yoghurt with blueberries instead of a handful of chips gulped down over the kitchen sink.I imagined this would all feel fun. And often, it did. I ate ice-cream sandwiches most days – heaven! – and in the gym, my weights climbed. I hip thrust an amount well above my body weight. I deadlifted nearly twice as much as I had before.But as I ate more, I was also plagued by continuous, roiling anxiety. The slimiest voices in my head screamed, telling me I was making a terrible mistake. Again and again, I demanded that my now-husband tell me how hot he finds me. He would tell me that of course he found me hot, and that he admired what I was doing and was proud of me.To which I’d say: “But also, I’m hot, right?”In a perfect world, this story would be two sentences: I gained weight in order to build muscle, and I loved it. It was easy and uncomplicated, because I know my body does not determine my worth.Sadly, that would be a lie.The reasons for my poor body image are boring and common: the boy in middle school who pointed at my stomach and pretended to vomit; watching hours of The Biggest Loser before my frontal lobe had fully developed; the adult relative who told me, when I was eight, that I should stop eating carbs; reading gossip blogger Perez Hilton every day in 2008 when he calledMischa Barton “Mushy Fartone”because she occasionally had visible cellulite; the college boyfriend who told me that my freshman weight gain put me “at the threshold of attractiveness”.The idea of gaining weight on purpose felt scary. But it also felt transgressive and liberating. What a relief to step off the sisyphean treadmill of weight loss.The people around me were overwhelmingly supportive. Several women, committed lifters themselves, told me they had been intrigued by bulking, but were too nervous to try.What do we mean when we say women can be ‘too muscular’?Read more“The concept of it challenges most of what [women] are taught about our bodies, and what we are made to fear about our bodies,” says Johnston.Johnston did her first bulk in 2016. She had been lifting for a couple of years at that point and her strength had plateaued, but she was nervous.“My fear was that things would spiral out of control,” she says. “What I had always been taught was that if you’re not militantly vigilant about not gaining weight, it happens unpredictably and uncontrollably. The idea of doing it on purpose was completely alien to me.”Eventually, though, her desire to get stronger became greater than her “mortal fear” of gaining weight.“The main thing was I couldn’t believe how different I felt at the gym,” she says. Suddenly, she was easily lifting weights she had struggled with before, and she even found herself sweating less during workouts.Johnston’s bulk lasted about four months, after which she began a “cut”, the common practice of eating in a slight calorie deficit to burn fat and reveal the muscle she had been building. But cutting was “relatively painless” compared with the dieting she had practised before, Johnson explained in a 2022Instagram post, adding that “no one should suffer at the hand of ‘weight loss’.”She has bulked and cut several times since, but is careful to underscore that this is not a requirement for lifting weights.double quotation mark[Bulking] can be unintentionally activating, and loaded with fear, loss of control, and an identity threatRiley NickolsIndeed, you can become the strongest woman in the world without bulking.“I personally have not done a bulk,” says Tamara Walcott, a coach, powerlifter andworld record-holderin multiple lifts. While she regularly programs periods of bulking for her clients, it is not something she does on purpose for herself.“I am a food addict; I will always be a food addict,” she says. At her heaviest, before she ever picked up a weight, Walcott weighed 455lb. Now, she competes at 275lb. “I pretty much eat the same amount of calories I did when I was 400lb, but I’m more strategic about it and I’m using it as fuel, because I know how it gives me energy.”Bulking isn’t for everyone, says Riley Nickols, a sports psychologist and member of the clinical advisory committee for the National Eating Disorders Association (Neda). He warns that people with an extensive history of dieting, and especially those currently navigating eating disorders should probably avoid embarking on the process.“It can be unintentionally activating, and loaded with fear, loss of control, and an identity threat,” he says. “It can activate anxiety, guilt or even shame.”In order to bulk safely, he says, it’s important to keep an eye out for signs that the practice may be shifting from a healthy way to improve performance into an unhealthy fixation on appearance and numbers. These red flags include increased rigidity about food and exercise, fear of deviating from the food and training plan, preoccupation with food and body-specific numbers, compensatory behaviors like extra cardio or avoiding social situations to avoid deviating from the plan.He suggests limiting weigh-ins and mirror checking, and prioritizing performance markers instead, such as strength and recovery. “If the plan starts to control the athlete rather than support the athlete, that’s where we get concerned,” Nickols says.I admitted to Nickols my relationship with food was far from perfect, and I didn’t know if it ever would be. But it also felt important to treat my body in a completely different way than I had in the past. (I also reassured him that I worked with a therapist – one who was a former bodybuilder at that.)“No one has a perfect relationship with anything, and that’s OK,” he said. “You’re curious, but it’s also challenging you.”As the weeks went on, I developed a sense of entitlement in the gym. It’s what I imagine it feels like to be a white man asking for a pay raise: confidence that numbers will just keep going up and up. And they did.Then there was the energy boost. My brain and body hummed along more efficiently. It felt as if I had upgraded from a beat-up 2005 Nissan to a brand new, muscular Toyota Tundra towing a heavy load (my butt).At night, my body seemed to run warmer – all of its systems chugging along, the little muscle factories busy at work. In pictures, I noticed ever-so-slight hints of shoulder muscles.My clothes also fit more tightly. I squeezed into previously comfortable jeans, and my growing glutes made a favorite miniskirt indecent for public wear. At times this filled me with despair. But it was also a relief. The very thing I had spent so much time and energy trying to avoid – gaining weight, getting bigger – was happening, and it was fine. My life didn’t change, except that I had more energy and wore more flowing linen pants.Eventually, something happened that I never thought was possible: eating felt boring. I had never fed myself so consistently and with such care, and now that my body was finally and consistently receiving the fuel and nutrients it needed, it stopped begging me for Nutella and sour cream and onion potato chips. I forgot about the ice-cream sandwiches in the freezer. Occasionally, I groaned when I realized I needed to eat more – a previously unthinkable reaction.Lift, rest, recover: how to start weightliftingRead moreI was happy when the bulk ended (see: tight clothes, food boredom). I stopped tracking my food intake for a while, then went into a slight calorie deficit. Like Johnston had said, it felt very different from any other “diet” I had done in the past. I had to eat enough to maintain the muscle I had built, and I had learned the importance of eating consistently throughout the day, so I rarely felt hungry. The hardest part was not seeing my numbers go up as quickly at the gym. I had gotten spoiled by my own strength.My jeans are still a little tight, and my shoulders and butt are not quite as juicy as I would like them to be, but they’re a little bigger. And gaining weight does not feel like the scary monster under my bed it once was. It’s a tool that can help me get stronger and do cool things.The food noise and body anxiety is still there in the background – two tiresome, unwanted guests who don’t know when it’s time to leave the party. But they are quieter now, or at least I don’t pay them as much attention. A scared, ignorant voice telling you that you’ll be happier if you don’t eat is less persuasive when you’ve experienced the delight of getting strong, feeling energized, and having a hint of shoulder muscles. The external pressures are still there, but it feels satisfying to be doing the opposite of what’s expected of me.Someday, I want to deadlift my own body weight and do pull-ups like the star of an action movie in a training montage. And when that time comes, I will do the calculations, put together a plan and get to work.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyFitnessWomenHealthWeightliftingEating disordersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s become a nepo baby sport’: how secondhand fashion got so expensive | Vintage fashion | The Guardian
description: Thanks to gen Z resellers and platforms like Depop, thrifting has lost its subcultural roots - and ballooned into a $350bn business
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: Thanks to gen Z resellers and platforms like Depop, thrifting has lost its subcultural roots - and ballooned into a $350bn business
Content: A fashion consultant shops at a Goodwill in Los Angeles. Goodwill, North America’s largest thrift chain with 3,400 stores, announced a record $7bn in revenue last year.Photograph: MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fashion consultant shops at a Goodwill in Los Angeles. Goodwill, North America’s largest thrift chain with 3,400 stores, announced a record $7bn in revenue last year.Photograph: MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News/Getty ImagesVintage fashion‘It’s become a nepo baby sport’: how secondhand fashion got so expensiveThanks to gen Z resellers and platforms like Depop, thrifting has lost its subcultural roots - and ballooned into a $350bn businessHannah MarriottFri 24 Jul 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVintage boutique owner Janelle Best has been rummaging in thrift shop bins since the 90s. When she started, she says, there was a stigma about it. “It was either you were a freak, or you were poor – and I was a freak.”How to buy secondhand clothes online that you’ll actually wear – and the best sites to trawlRead moreAt first, she did it to source stage outfits while playing in psych-rock bands. Then, in 2005, she started “casually reselling” on eBay. Ten years later she was trading asDesert Stars Vintageat street markets, and by 2023 she had opened a showroom specializing in upmarket silk dresses in her Williamsburg apartment. Even just a few years ago, she says, she still put in the hours at places like Goodwill. The bins, she says, “were a field day. There were so many fucking bangers.” And then, thrifting became a social media craze, she says, “and the hell gates of high school students flooded in. Twelve people to each bin. Everyone fighting. Suddenly everyone’s a reseller, and instead of these kids intuitively knowing what’s good, they’re on their phones trying to figure out if it’s valuable.”Secondhand clothing has never been more popular. On TikTok, teenage girls post thrift haul videos, gleefully unveiling big bags of clothes acquired for less than $100. Meanwhile, at the top of the fashion food chain, billionaires wear rare vintage pieces to confer status and taste.Many pin the meteoric rise of secondhand clothing to gen Z, who are reportedly more environmentally aware and entrepreneurial than their elders. The real shift, though, is tech, with platforms such as Depop, the RealReal, Vestiaire Collective, Vinted, ThredUp and Poshmark making secondhand buying and selling more accessible than ever.View image in fullscreenA person scrolls through clothing listings on Depop, one of many popular online secondhand fashion platforms.Photograph: Alistair Berg/Getty ImagesThe tipping point was the pandemic, when screen time rocketed and buying and selling online felt like a rare way to “hunt for endorphins”, as writer and dedicated thrifter Linnea Pejcha describes her own Depop habits at the time. Thrifting surged globally by 28% between 2021 and 2022, and has kept growing since. Revenue is not confined to the apps: Goodwill, North America’s largest thrift chain, with 3,400 stores across the US and Canada, announced a record $7bn in revenue last year, with plans to open between 50 and 100 new stores across North America. ThredUp projects the market will reach $367bn by 2029 – growing 2.7 times faster than the overall global apparel market.Theoretically, a boom in reused clothing should be unequivocal good news, given the mountains of fabric sent to landfill each year. But many who have been thrifting for decades are depressed at the changes wreaked on some aspects of the industry as it has mushroomed.double quotation markI think every generation for a long time has thought that they’re discovering [thrifting]Jennifer Le ZotteFor a start, it’s not just plucky rockers selling vintage now. Even some oligarchs are resellers. Client advisers for top fashion brands, the people who deal with shoppers who are spending hundreds of thousands each year, say that some customers have so much swag that they help them, unofficially, to list their wardrobes on secondhand apps as a sales tactic so they can buy new pieces. If they help them “get rid of some of their wardrobe”, says analyst Claudia D’Arpizio, Bain & Company’s global leader of fashion and luxury, “they unlock a lot of potential new buying”.A new report by Bain found that half of luxury shoppers consult an item’s price on the secondhand market before deciding whether to buy new. In high-end vintage, certain brands may be lost to all but the wealthiest collectors, says Best. Cavalli pieces, in particular, have rocketed in price “probably five times in value in four years”. A few years ago, she says, “all of these rich girls started hoarding brands like Cavalli and Blue Marine”.Perhaps none of this is new. Like sex, every generation thinks they invented thrifting, says Jennifer Le Zotte, the author of From Goodwill to Grunge, who teaches at the University of North Carolina, Wilmington. In the past, a lingering sense of stigma – which Le Zotte attributes to antisemitism and germ theory during the earliest days of secondhand clothing, when Jewish pedlars sold clothes from pushcarts in the 19th century – meant thrift felt like “a resource for rebellion, part of an alternative mindset”. That’s how Le Zotte felt herself when she started doing it, in the grunge era, as did the surrealists in the 1920s, andthe Rolling StonesandJimi Hendrixin the 1960s. “I think every generation for a long time has thought that they’re discovering this, this repository of fashionable possibilities.”View image in fullscreenJimi Hendrix performs on stage at the Woburn pop festival in Bedfordshire, England, in August 1968.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesBut this vintage boom is different. While it has been great for business in some ways – and has seen celebrities such as Madonna wearing her clothes – Best says it’s still harder to make a living now, with the rise in prices of gas and shipping. Not to mention the wild competition for popular stock – sometimes, she says, vintage hunting feels like “a nepo baby sport”.Best also has to deal with tariffs. The US market, she says, is now “really dry” so she mainly sources from Italy and France. Yet she has to pay 15% on all imports after Donald Trump got rid of the tariff exemption on imports worth less than $800. She thinks prices are only going to go up: “Because vintage is finite, only so many pieces were made at a certain time, and everyone’s looking for it.”At the cheaper end of the secondhand market, there are widespread complaints from shoppers about prices, which many say have become unfeasibly high for the low-income shoppers who rely on such stores most. Many of those garments are low quality, poorly made fast fashion. Videos calling out inflated prices, posted with titles such as “Goodwill what crack are you smoking??” have become commonplace. One dedicated Reddit community –ThriftGrift– collates examples, some of which are, frankly, distressing: a Carhartt hoodie covered in stains for$12, a $6.99 shirt, which might feel like a bargain until you spot the wasp’s nest attached to the yoke. Some items still have the original tag so you can see, for example, that the pair of peach, pleated pants priced at $8.99 in Goodwill werepriced at $7.99 new. Last month, Goodwill’s western and northern Connecticut branch seemed to confirm its aspirations with the launch of aThrift Tour, offering a “private bus” to three stores, 30 minutes of exclusive early shopping, lunch, a custom T-shirt, a 20% off coupon and the chance to “meet new thrifting besties” for $75.Though the thrift shop workers I spoke to for this feature said that some price rises were associated with inflation – costs of labor, rent, cleaning and display supplies have all zoomed up – much of it is also driven by awareness of the booming resale market. Managers have put cheat sheets of brands to look out for on the wall in backrooms; they use resale prices on eBay or Depop to gauge value; and with the image-searching app Google Lens, they are more likely to find comparable items. The days of finding a bargain at the bottom of a bin might be over.View image in fullscreenPeople sift through used clothes that are sold by the pound at a Goodwill outlet center in Hackensack, New Jersey.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesThe secondhand fashion ecosystem is vast. It ranges from high-end consignment operations, which authenticate, market and sell clients’ items on their behalf, and take a share of the profit (the RealReal is one such example; current wares include a grey leather Hermès Birkin for $32,000), to independent thrift stores in tiny towns where a shopper might still find a donated pair of jeans for a few dollars. In between those price points are vintage stores (the word “vintage” most commonly refers to garments at least 20 years old), which can get very expensive too – particularly in fashion-centric urban centres such as New York City, which often stock rare Y2K pieces such as 00s Jean Paul Gaultier and Dior. Online, dozens of for-profit sites specialise in high street brands – such as ThredUp, which will send a bag to your house to fill with clothes,which they will sell on commission, and sites, from Poshmark to Depop to eBay, where sellers tend to retain more of the profits if items sell, but also do more of the legwork.There are independent thrift stores that operate for profit, many of which buy items from customers as well as sell them, or donate all or part of their profits to charity; small chains which run as non- and for-profit; and large thrift store chains. The largest for-profit thrift chain in North America is private equity-backed Savers, which has more than 300 stores in the US and Canada, andplans to open another 26 this year. The behemoths in thrift clothing, though, are non-profits: Goodwill and the Salvation Army,which has 887 US stores.The big beasts of thrift have their critics. Many of those incensed by high prices call Goodwill “Greedwill” online. Some refer to it as a “corporate thrift store”, despite its philanthropic mission, which centres on helping people get into work, and say that it operates more like a for-profit store than a charity. Central among their complaints is the fact that CEOs and other executives – of which there are many hundreds, because Goodwill is not run centrally, but as 150 autonomous regional operations – earn chunky salaries, usually of about $300,000 to $700,000. In a statement to the Guardian, Goodwill said that, in 2025, it helped “nearly 2 million individuals with job training, placement and other support services”. Some of those job placements were with Goodwill itself, though that too is not without controversy: in 2013 it emerged thatGoodwill was using a loopholedating back to 1938 to pay disabled workers as little as 22 cents an hour. Goodwill has said that while this was legal under section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which allows some people with disabilities to be paid under “a special minimum wage certificate”, it believes “the responsible approach” is to eliminate the use of the certificate in its stores.View image in fullscreenMichael Fitch brings vintage clothing to the sidewalk outside his store, Eclectica, in North Hollywood.Photograph: MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News/Getty ImagesSome of those frustrated with the increasingly professionalised thrift economy put the blame squarely on individual resellers entirely for rising prices. Sheri Pavlović, a sustainable fashion expert who shares tutorials on upcycling garments asRefashionista Sheri, says that this can sometimes get ugly on the shop floor. “I’ve been in thrift stores and seen twentysomething cuties, pulling stuff off racks and saying: ‘We could sell this on Poshmark,’ and then seen older people go up to them and say: ‘You’re the reason why it’s so expensive!’ And it’s like, are you kidding me? These little girlies here have nothing to do with corporate prices!” Rather, Pavlović blames the “suits” running big thrift chains who “are getting a whiff of this being popular, trending”. So they hike the prices because they believe they can, she argues, not because they have to.Robert, who runs a mom-and-pop thrift store in Monterey, California, which serves people on lower incomes, says he has only put its prices up around a quarter of the rate of inflation since the pandemic, despite soaring costs, “because the most important thing for us is customer retention”. He believes the big chains have the scale and brand recognition to charge higher prices, and finds them aggressively competitive: one of them recently put a donation bin near his shop, which has had an impact on donations to his business.It’s not just resellers skimming off items that may be resold for a profit, either. Many thrift stores have multiple ways of doing the same thing: the practice of “picking” – antique and vintage dealers coming in to buy the best stuff – is well known in the industry, and now many organizations do it for their own websites.View image in fullscreenMen’s clothing for sale inside a Goodwill location in Florida.Photograph: Jeff Greenberg/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesOn the price issue, David Eagles, executive vice-president and chief operating officer of Goodwill Industries International, said: “Goodwill does not have one national pricing policy. Prices are set by local Goodwill organizations.” He added: “It is also important to keep the pricing conversation in perspective. We estimate the average retail price per item across the Goodwill network remains below $5. While average item pricing has moved gradually since the pandemic, pricing changes have remained lower than the broader inflationary environment.”double quotation markWhat is good stuff to you is not good stuff to me. I don’t give a shit about the labelSheri PavlovićThe problems with peak thrift, as this time may become known, extend beyond price. Those donating clothing have enjoyed a sense of virtue from the earliest days of the secondhand clothing market, according to Le Zotte. When Goodwill launched at the turn of the century, its model was tailored to a time of high immigration and wealth inequality. Much like ThredUp today, Goodwill would drop burlap bags at middle class homeowners’ houses, to encourage them to part with their old furniture and clothes which they might then feel free to replace, “without being profligate”.In an age of fast fashion, though, that sense of virtue appears to be appeasing our guilt about buying new clothing. A recent Yale University study concluded that participation in secondhand fashion often drives, rather than replaces, the purchase of new garments: while 37.2% of people reported increasing clothing donations between 2020 and 2024, there was also a 38% rise in new clothing purchases. This is all a bit at odds with the “moral social buy-in” Le Zotte says many people report feeling when shopping secondhand: “They think that buying the clothing once it enters the secondhand market isn’t being complicit. I’m not saying that it’s totally misguided, but it’s overexaggerated.”View image in fullscreenShoppers at Vintage Vintage Vintage in Washington DC.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesStill, true believers remain. Liisa Jokinen, who runs Gem, an app that aggregates secondhand clothing, insists that “not everything is expensive – but you need to be patient”. She recommends visiting yard sales, clothes swaps, and places where you can still find fill-a-bag sales and shop-by-the-pound stores in person.Pavlović has abandoned thrifting for now, owing to rising prices, in favor of altering her existing garments to create new items, but she still disagrees with the received wisdom that all the “good” stuff is gone from thrift stores now. “What is good stuff to you is not good stuff to me. I don’t give a shit about the label.” She recommends forgetting the kind of brands shop assistants have been trained to look out for – Zara and Levi’s, for example – and prioritizing personal taste. “When I was thrifting regularly, I was always on the hunt for stuff from the 60s and 70s.”Say less to the dress: why I’m cutting back on secondhand clothes shoppingRead morePat Noecker, owner of Other People’s Clothes, which has four branches in New York City, got what he describes as his “double PhD in thrifting” when he was touring the US as a musician during the 90s and 00s with bands including Liars, “hitting every thrift store in every town”. He says he keeps prices low for the area (as a guide, Zara pieces are sold for $15.98 to $21.98). His business is “profitable, but no one’s buying yachts”. As a store that buys clothing as well, “we price things to move, otherwise we would need a store the size of a football field”.He says his clients range from low-income locals from nearby Williamsburg to celebrities, including the band Geese and the first lady of New York City, Rama Duwaji, who comes in to sell as well as to buy. Her taste is “impeccable. She’s super into it. We absolutely love her.” She once dropped off a pair of the mayor’s shoes (Chelsea boots), which Noecker has hung on to: “I don’t wear them but I keep them in my office as a reminder that we have a really awesome mayor, and I send him good luck through those shoes.”Explore more on these topicsVintage fashionRetail industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Are multi-way clothes the answer to sustainable fashion - or just another excuse to buy more stuff?  | Fashion | The Guardian
description: More and more brands are making clothes that can be adapted by the wearer. But with price points high and fast fashion giants getting in on the act, perhaps we should just stick to wearing our cardigans backwards
Author: Chloë Hamilton
Headline: More and more brands are making clothes that can be adapted by the wearer. But with price points high and fast fashion giants getting in on the act, perhaps we should just stick to wearing our cardigans backwards
Content: Worth the splurge? … SAUV tops sell for $135.Photograph: SAUVView image in fullscreenWorth the splurge? … SAUV tops sell for $135.Photograph: SAUVFashion Statement newsletterFashionAre multi-way clothes the answer to sustainable fashion - or just another excuse to buy more stuff?Brands are making clothes that can be adapted by the wearer. But with fast fashion giants getting in on the act, perhaps we should just stick to wearing our cardigans backwardsDon’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereChloë HamiltonFri 24 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m sitting on my bedroom floor trying to fasten the sleeves back on to a new top that’s just been delivered. I haven’t had an unfortunate accident with scissors; the removable sleeves are a design feature, part of the growing trend for multi-way clothing that is being championed as a win for sustainability – or for anyone moving from air-conditioned office to outside right now. Brow furrowed, I try to attach the puff of red taffeta to the rest of the frilly blouse using the tiny buttons and loops provided. But I’m not having much luck …I enjoy messing around with clothes. Aged 10, I pranced around a sun-drenched Greek holiday in a top that was really a skirt. But a top with sleeves that detach? I’d lose them instantly, I’m sure of it. Even if I didn’t, would my two-tops-in-one actually curb my rabid appetite for new clothes or would it simply feed the beast; another trend to be devoured and then discarded, just like the sleeves?Multi-way clothing – clothing designed to be worn in multiple ways – has come a long way since the zip-off trousers made popular by practical hiking dads (as well as girl band TLC) in the early 2000s, or the “infinity” bridesmaid dressesthat could be worn 72 different ways and were chosen by indecisive (or, perhaps, size-inclusive) brides of the 2010s.View image in fullscreenMake your own … there are plenty of ways to wear our existing clothes more creatively.Photograph: Dan Chung/The GuardianToday, a number of self-proclaimed slow and sustainable brands, including BUCI NYC, Isabella Vrana, Damson Madder and American brand SAUV – the idea for which came about when founder-sisters Margaux and Euxie were forced to split their shared wardrobe as they headed to separate colleges – are creating clothes built to be altered by their wearers. There are reversible cardigans; blouses that can be worn back-to-front; necklines that can be adjusted with a series of hooks and eyes; midi dresses that transform into minis using loops and ribbon ties.The thinking is that the aesthetic of multi-way clothing – doing more with less – encourages creativity, inspiring the wearer to adapt garments to fit their individual need, occasion or style, while promoting sustainability. Because, of course, the benefit (or so say the brands) is that we will be encouraged to buy less stuff: it is the ultimate sustainable magic trick, to turn one item into two or three.For Emily Chan, senior sustainability and features editor at British Vogue, the idea of multi-way clothing is to be celebrated, “if it encourages people to style their garments in different ways, get more wear out of them, and keep them for longer”.View image in fullscreenTo sleeve or not to sleeve? … Damson Madder’s multi-way top.Photograph: Damson MadderOne fan is Jasmain Farara, a 29-year-old social media manager from London.In a clipon her TikTok account, she can be seen undoing the poppers on the full-length sleeves of her plain white SAUV top, transforming it, in seconds, into a simple sleeveless vest. It’s marketed as “the last top you’ll ever buy”, though I asked if she has, in fact, bought more tops since and – spoiler alert – she has.For $135 (about £101),these sets– and other multi-way clothes like them – don’t necessarily come cheap, in case anyone thought the cost of living crisis had led to their boom. For that price, shoppers get the 94% organic cotton popper-sleeved vest as a base and one set of detachable short-capped sleeves. Modular fans can then purchase, separately, other types of sleeves with which to build different tops, like the sartorial version of adding your own toppings to an ice-cream sundae: basic long sleeves for $62 (about £47), for example, or sleeves with a flounce at the cuff for $60 (about £45).But for all of its good intentions, I fear multi-way clothing may, by its very nature, be paradoxical: buy it so you buy less. There is a crushing inevitability, too, to the fact that fast fashion behemoth ASOS is nowgetting in on the action, selling a (95% viscose) top with a modifiable neckline that can be made wider or narrower with buttons, for just £24. This isn’t slow and sustainable, it’s a mass-market cash grab, latching on to the aesthetics of multi-wearability and its eco-friendly optics.Fashion designer and author Orsola De Castro, who co-founded Fashion Revolution, a movement that campaigns for a more sustainable fashion industry, believes multi-way clothing is nothing more than a marketing ploy. “Sustainability-wise, they have absolutely zero merit. They don’t discourage [consumers] from buying new things,” says De Castro. “It is a gimmick; just an added layer that makes you consider the longevity of your clothing but doesn’t necessarily dictate your behaviour.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChan agrees when it comes to trend-driven brands jumping on the bandwagon: fast fashion is fast fashion, whether or not it’s multi-use. “If clothes are treated as throwaway items and not made with the environment or garment workers in mind, it’s not a sustainable choice,” she says.None of this, of course, means we can’t wear clothes in a multi-functional way. Creative people have been doing this forever, without brands marketing it to them. “Who hasn’t worn a cardigan fastened at the back instead of at the front; who hasn’t pinched [their] skirt and somehow tucked it under [their] knickers to change its shape,” De Castro says. “To have it as a pre-designed condition somehow can be restricting rather than liberating.”Back on the bedroom floor, the top is proving fiddly. It’s not long before I discard the sleeves, reuniting them with the top in its packaging, ready to be returned: my life is fiddly enough already. Plus, maybe there is a better way to experiment with multi-way clothing. Only yesterday, in fact, I accidentally wore my dress back to front all day. It cost me nothing – except, perhaps, a little pride.To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content
