title: ‘Full of zesty colour and flavour’: readers’ favourite food festivals in Europe | Food and drink | The Guardian
description: From the Tiramisù World Cup in Italy to street food ‘battles’ in Newcastle, your culinary highlights range from the sublime to the delicious
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From the Tiramisù World Cup in Italy to street food ‘battles’ in Newcastle, your culinary highlights range from the sublime to the delicious
Content: A sculpture made with lemons and oranges for the  Lemon Festival in Menton, France.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAView image in fullscreenA sculpture made with lemons and oranges for the  Lemon Festival in Menton, France.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAReaders' travel tipsFood and drink‘Full of zesty colour and flavour’: readers’ favourite food festivals in EuropeFrom the Tiramisù World Cup in Italy to street food ‘battles’ in Newcastle, your culinary highlights range from the sublime to the deliciousTell us abouta book that inspired you to travel– the best tip wins £200 towards a Coolstays breakGuardian readersFri 24 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSun and citrus in the south of FranceThe town ofMentonon the French Riviera is beautiful at any time of the year but becomes even more of a treat during the annualLemon festival(Fête du Citron, 10-28 February 2027). Its microclimate, courtesy of the Alps to the north blocking colder winds, gives Menton lemons a distinct fragrance, flavour and quality that set them apart. For me, the event transformed a damp cold UK winter into a fortnight of colour, taste and light. There were food tastings, salads made with lemons, tarts, cakes and pies all full of zesty colour and flavour at stalls and markets in the town. There are sculptures made from citrus fruit, parades and exhibitions in the Golden Garden of Light (Jardins Biovès). More than a food festival, it’s a celebration of what nature can give to the world.AprilVeneto’s Tiramisù World CupView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stefano Mazzola/Getty ImagesLast autumn, I discovered there is an annualTiramisù World Cup. I was staying in Treviso (the lovely town near Venice where the dessert originated) during the three-day event featuring tastings, demonstrations from local chefs and a judging contest involving the public. There’s also folk music in the streets, and restaurants offer promotional prices on set meals from about €20 for two courses. In fact, sitting in a mini gondola, prosecco in one hand, bowl of tiramisu in the other, gliding along a canal past ornate houses while the distant snow-capped mountains of the Dolomites sparkled in the sunshine, certainly aided my appetite for food and life.PeterProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.A cheeky celebration in TuscanyView image in fullscreenThe Gota Cotta festival takes place in the village of Colle di Val d’Elsa.Photograph: Silvan Bachmann/AlamyTheGota Cotta festivalin Tuscany (4 October) is a celebration of local meat – pork cheeks. It was a niche product, falling out of favour, but a group of local butchers created the festival to celebrate the local delicacy. It takes over the medieval hilltop town of Colle di Val d’Elsa in Siena province with stalls selling everything from pasta to gelato – all made with pork cheek. There’s also excellent wine and craft beers … all in the most beautiful setting.Rebecca NichollSwitzerland knows its onionsView image in fullscreenModels made from onions on display at the Bern onion fair.Photograph: Alistair Scott/AlamyI stumbled acrossZibelemärit, Bern’s annual onion fair, on a chilly November morning. The old town was packed with farmers selling beautifully braided onions, garlic and seasonal produce. The streets were filled with tempting aromas from stalls frying onion tarts and serving steaming bowls of onion soup and cafes selling sweet onion-shaped pastries. A mug of warmingglühwein was the perfect accompaniment. It was a wonderfully local event and chatting to growers about their harvest made me feel part of a genuine celebration of Swiss farming traditions. Zibelemärit takes place on the fourth Monday in November.SusannaThe Italian town devoted to leeksView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lorenza photography/AlamyYou have to admire the town of Cervere in Piedmont, south of Turin, which is so devoted to its leeks that it has erected a permanent pavilion called the Palaporro (porrois Italian for leek) for its annual festival, calledFiera del Porro Cervere(7-22 November). Book ahead for the sit-down tasting menu, or buy leeky treats such as gratin and risotto to take away, as we did. During thesagra, the town centre is packed with stalls, many heaving with the distinctive bunches of extra-long local leeks. Our favourite part was taking a shuttle bus down to the sandy leek fields in the valley, where enthusiasts explained the traditional cultivation techniques.MarthaFarmers and brass bands in North YorkshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Wise/AlamyMalton is a little village in North Yorkshire that punches way above its size when it comes to food festivals. Theannual festivalis worth a visit in late spring (29-30 May 2027), but so are the monthly farmers’ markets that bring together incredible local suppliers and makers. Plus, there’s a good chance of hearing a top-class brass band while you mooch and taste. Bloomin’ marvellous!Bethskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNewcastle’s battle of the food vendorsView image in fullscreenThe Wylam BreweryPhotograph: Ben Hughes/Food BattlesWylam Brewery’s street vendor food battles in Newcastle upon Tyne showcase local independent eateries serving their bestselling dishes to win a chance at being crowned the culinary King of Newcastle at the finalBattle Royale(28 & 29 August). The competitions are wittily titled, for example Lord of the Wings for the chicken wings competition (23 & 24 October) and Argie Bhaji (27 & 28 November) for Indian street food. The concept is simple: each event offers different cuisines from pizza to pan-Asian to plant-based. The winner of each event is the vendor with the most pre-paid tokens. Set in the idyllicExhibition Park, with DJs playing into the night, locals know not to miss these summer festivals.Carly Bamborough‘A proper northern’ affair in BoltonPhotograph: Paul HeyesBolton food & drink festival(28-31 August) is brilliant because it feels properly northern: busy streets, good smells, live music and families everywhere. It is not trying to be too polished, which is why it works. You can wander from stall to stall, try something different, grab something sweet for the kids and still feel like you are part of the town. The best bit is the atmosphere. Chefs, local businesses, music and people all come together in one place. It is simple, affordable and full of energy. For a family day out, it is hard to beat.Nicholas PearceThe pride of PlymouthView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Roy Perring/AlamyPlymouth Flavour Fest, at the end of May each year, ranks among the finest food gatherings I’ve experienced anywhere. Boutique delicatessens form neat rows, with smartly dressed stallholders presenting produce with infectious pride. Pies, salamis, chillies, confectionery, preserves, hot food – all the good stuff laid out irresistibly. Take a cool bag and budget for things you never knew you needed. Plymouth’s Armada Way is perfect for the event, never claustrophobic when busy. A short stroll takes you to the Hoe, perfect for munching on a treat overlooking one of the finest harbours in the world. Good food brings out the best in people and, for a few hours at least, the world is put to rights.Grant Wyness‘Ireland’s culinary playground’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Valerie O’Sullivan/Visit IrelandEvery October, the charming fishing town of Dingle transforms into Ireland’s ultimate culinary playground. TheDingle food festival(2-4 October) brings more than 60 venues to life for the famous Taste Trail, where pubs, galleries and shopfronts serve up local seafood, artisan cheeses and much more. Add bustling market stalls, cookery masterclasses and workshops, live street music and a strong zero-waste ethos, and you’ve got a weekend that celebrates the best of Irish food, drink and hospitality, all with Irish small-town warmth.John O’KellyView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsFood and drinkReaders' travel tipsTop 10sEurope holidaysFood festivalsFestivalsUnited Kingdom holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I hunt for missing hikers in remote mountains | Walking | The Guardian
description: Since I started doing search and rescue five years ago, I have found seven survivors. Sadly, the number I find dead is higher
Author: Chi-hui Lin
Headline: Since I started doing search and rescue five years ago, I have found seven survivors. Sadly, the number I find dead is higher
Content: ‘There’s the initial shock, and then the immediate pivot to logistics’: Petr Novotny in Puli, Taiwan.Photograph: An Rong Xu/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘There’s the initial shock, and then the immediate pivot to logistics’: Petr Novotny in Puli, Taiwan.Photograph: An Rong Xu/The GuardianExperienceWalkingExperience: I hunt for missing hikers in remote mountainsSince I started doing search and rescue five years ago, I have found seven survivors. Sadly, the number I find dead is higherPetr NovotnyFri 24 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2012, I was a student and had arrived in Taiwan from the Czech Republic. I soon discovered something that interested me far more than my studies: the mountains of Taiwan. I would leave the campus to explore untouched trails near Taipei. I was obsessed with old maps, often looking for routes that had vanished from modern ones, and hiking paths that no one had taken for decades.I stayed in Taiwan because of my love for the mountains – there are more than 250 peaks that exceed 3,000 metres. Among the local hiking community, I became known for my speed and knowledge of remote regions.In October 2021, after a typhoon, I heard about a man who had gone missing. I decided to look for him. I hiked for 13 hours, but had no luck. When the man had been missing for more than a week, I received a message from his brother. He had heard about me and asked if I would carry out a search. The fire department was also looking for him.Over the next three days, I covered 67km with a 6,800-metre elevation gain. I moved back and forth across the peaks, searching for any sign of life. After two weeks, the fire department called off the search.When he’d been missing for 29 days, the family began to lose hope. We decided on one final attempt. This time, I knew I was close. I started finding fragments of fabric and discarded gear. I was terrified.double quotation markThe emotional fallout hits me long after I’ve left the mountainView image in fullscreenPhotograph: An Rong Xu/The GuardianWhen I finally found him, the scene was harrowing. His body was wedged between rocks in the water; he had been dead for weeks. He was an experienced hiker but had underestimated the weather. A stream crossing must have turned fatal, washing him into a side creek where he became trapped between the rocks. I told him I would take him home.As soon as I got a signal, I called my wife, Eva. She usually delivers the news – good or bad – to the families who hire me. His family gathered eight men, who went with me to bring the body back. We cleared a platform so a helicopter could airlift him out.The family paid me 300,000 NTD (£7,200) to thank me, plus a 15,000 NTD (£360) day rate. They were devastated, but they finally had an answer. Now, each year, when his family returns to the mountain to pay their respects, they stop by my place.I filmed the search and posted it on YouTube. It went viral. Since then, I’ve received many requests. I don’t always say yes, but I usually step in if the authorities aren’t making progress.Sometimes, I carry out search and rescue operations alongside the fire department; other times, I continue after they have called off the search.Every search begins at my computer, poring over maps and analysing data. I ask the family to provide the missing person’s last-known phone signal location and any CCTV footage from the trailhead car park – this information is invaluable.Eva and I also interview relatives or friends to understand the missing person’s state of mind – whether they were an experienced hiker who took a wrong turn or perhaps an older person who lost their way.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn my time conducting search and rescue, I have found seven survivors. Sadly, the number of those I find dead is higher. Most people die because they don’t have a map downloaded and make the fatal decision to head downhill. The mountains in Taiwan are vertical. Going down into a valley is a death trap. Those who die almost always do so from a fall.I climbed Mount Kilimanjaro on my handsRead moreSearch and rescue is a side job. My full-time work with Eva is hosting theFormosa Trail, a mountain race in Taiwan. It’s rewarding to share the beauty of Taiwan’s mountains with people from all over the world.Finding someone alive brings relief, but seconds later, the mind races: how do we extract them? How do we report it to the authorities? It’s similar when finding a body. There’s the initial shock, and then the immediate pivot to logistics: safe evacuation and next steps. The emotional fallout hits me long after I’ve left the mountain.Doing this has given my life a true sense of purpose. If I save someone or solve a case, it counts for ever.As told to Chi-hui LinDo you have an experience to share? title: I used to be intimidated by roses. But they are not as high-maintenance as you think | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: There are lots of rules about roses, with Instagram adding to the impression they are hard work. But they’re easy to keep when you know how
Author: Alice Vincent
Headline: There are lots of rules about roses, with Instagram adding to the impression they are hard work. But they’re easy to keep when you know how
Content: The key with pruning is to prioritise sturdy growth for the future.Photograph: Mariya Surmacheva/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe key with pruning is to prioritise sturdy growth for the future.Photograph: Mariya Surmacheva/Getty ImagesGardening adviceI used to be intimidated by roses. But they are not as high-maintenance as you thinkThere are lots of rules about roses, with Instagram adding to the impression they are hard work. But they’re easy to keep when you know howAlice VincentFri 24 Jul 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoes your Instagram shout at you? Mine does. Every time I open it up – albeit with increasing reluctance – someone I didn’t previously know existed is sharing a “hack”. It could be for stopping my toddler from throwing a fit in the supermarket or how to button a shirt so I look less old. It’s interesting when gardening suggestions are thrown into the mix. Sometimes they’re nonsense (see growing new spring onions from the bottoms of old ones in saucers of water), sometimes they’re so helpful I stash them away with the unfulfilled intention to watch back in the future.Lately, I’m being shown a lot of stuff about roses. Specifically, deadheading them. Roses are one of those plants that seem more high-maintenance than they are; before I grew them I was convinced they were the preserve of those people who are so serious about gardening that they have a foam kneeler (I still don’t own one of these).double quotation markIf the stem looks good but there are only three leaves on it, cutting above that is a good shoutBut, as a flower grower pal once told me: “You’d have to be Cruella de Vil to kill a rose.” As long as they’re kept vaguely well fed and hacked back in the winter, roses tend to just keep going. I’ve mulched mine all summer, which helps with the hot weather we’ve been having, although I find that after the first couple of years a good root system can handle droughts.Roses do, however, benefit from deadheading – removing the flower heads once the blooms have faded. This encourages the plant to have further flushes of roses through the summer (and sometimes beyond), as it tricks the plant into thinking it needs to keep flowering in order to set seed.There’s a lot of Instagram chat about the five-leaf rule: that when you deadhead a rose you don’t simply snip off the spent bud, but trace the stem down to the nearest clutch of five leaves, and cut just above those, instead. This means you’re promoting strong stem growth for future flowers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMidsummer isn’t the best time for planting, but it’s great for planningRead moreIt’s the strong stem that’s key. There are lots of rules about roses (this is why I thought they were so tricky) but really you just want to prioritise sturdy growth for the future. If the stem looks good but there are only three leaves on it, cutting above that is a good shout. Avoid anything floppy, take the whole lot off instead at the next sturdy stem.I know it may seem a bit savage, but you’ll get new leaf and flower stem growth from where you cut, rather than one gangly long stem. The same applies when you’re harvesting flowers for the kitchen table.As for cutting, good sharp secateurs, ideally clean ones, are the way forward. At the end of summer, when we’ve had enough of deadheading, it’s important to leave rosehips (what the spent flowers turn into) in place, for the birds, insects and autumn interest.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of lightning strikes trigger fresh wildfires in western Canada | Canada | The Guardian
description: At least 90 active blazes in British Columbia in what PM says is one of the country’s most intense seasons on record
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: At least 90 active blazes in British Columbia in what PM says is one of the country’s most intense seasons on record
Content: Smoke rises from wildfire near Quesnel in British Columbia thought to have been started by a lightning strike.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke rises from wildfire near Quesnel in British Columbia thought to have been started by a lightning strike.Photograph: BC Wildfire Service/ReutersCanadaThousands of lightning strikes trigger fresh wildfires in western CanadaAt least 90 active blazes in British Columbia in what PM says is one of the country’s most intense seasons on recordHow dangerous are wildfires and how can we stop them from getting worse?Reuters in TorontoFri 24 Jul 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFresh wildfires have broken out in westernCanadaand forests continued to ⁠burn in Ontario as the country ⁠battled what the prime ​minister, Mark Carney, called one of the most intense wildfire seasons on record.Nearly 34,000 lightning strikes over the past week led to a series of fires ⁠and evacuation orders in southern British Columbia. There were 25 evacuation orders and 90 active wildfires in the province as of Friday morning, and authorities said warming ⁠and drying conditions could cause them to grow.Hugh Murdoch, the incident commander of a cluster of fires near Kimberley, 320 miles (520km) from Vancouver, said: “The weather forecast is far from favourable. There is no significant ​help from mother nature whatsoever in the foreseeable ‌future.”Wildfires fuelled by intense heat and ‌lightning storms attributed to warmer temperatures have burned remote forests across Canada this summer. Smoke from them drifted across large US east coast and midwestern cities last week.View image in fullscreenSmoke from Canadian wildfire smoke hanging in the air over New York last week.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAThere were 139 active wildfires in north-west Ontario, of which 32 were not under control.Environment Canada issued an alert for poor air quality in Banff, Alberta and surrounding areas on Friday but said conditions were expected to improve for most areas over the weekend.Scientists decry Trump’s ‘blame game’ after he claims Canada ‘poisoning’ US airRead moreCarney ‌said in a statement that the federal government would mobilise more than 5,300 firefighters and about 300 water bombers, helicopters and evacuation aircraft to battle the fires. Mexico would also send as many as 200 firefighters in the coming weeks, he added.Thousands of people, including some First Nations communities, have been evacuated this summer. About 2.95m hectares (7.29m acres) of land have been burned this year, above the 10-year ⁠average of about 2.55m hectares. Canada currently has more active wildfires than it did at the same ​time in either of the ​past two years.The country’s forested areas account ​for 28% of the world’s boreal forests.Improving weather in the east has helped Quebec tame ​some blazes with help ‌from firefighters from ​neighbouring provinces, France and the ​US.Stéphane Caron,, of the province’s forest fire prevention agency Sopfeu, said: “The situation in Quebec is under control. We have good weather to help us. We have to make sure that there’s no hotspot on the ground any more because if there’s hot weather and no rain, the fire can be back.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaWildfiresExtreme weatherAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Guyanese authorities confirm death of 72 people in sinking of coastal ferry | Guyana | The Guardian
description: Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 were rescued as efforts continue to salvage the ship and recover all bodies
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 were rescued as efforts continue to salvage the ship and recover all bodies
Content: Rescuers pick up survivors after the 87-year-old MV Barima capsized off the Essequibo coast.Photograph: Bishop Juan Edghill/ReutersView image in fullscreenRescuers pick up survivors after the 87-year-old MV Barima capsized off the Essequibo coast.Photograph: Bishop Juan Edghill/ReutersGuyanaGuyanese authorities confirm death of 72 people in sinking of coastal ferryOf the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 were rescued as efforts continue to salvage the ship and recover all bodiesAssociated Press in GeorgetownFri 24 Jul 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe confirmed death toll from the recent capsizing of a state ferry offGuyana’s coast has risen to 72, with more bodies recovered as a multinational team struggle to salvage the partially submerged vessel.Of the estimated 179 people aboard, 76 people were rescued. The government has estimated that 100 may have died in the accident, which would make it the worst marine tragedy on record for the South American nation.The prime minister, Mark Phillips, said late on Thursday that crews have widened the search area and are determined to find all those who were aboard so loved ones can bury them with dignity.Huge search operation after passenger ferry sinks off coast of GuyanaRead more“The government ofGuyanacontinues to stand in solidarity with all those affected during this difficult time and will ensure that every available resource is deployed until the operation is brought to a safe and dignified conclusion,” he said.The 87-year-old MV Barima departed the capital, Georgetown, on Saturday and was headed to Port Kaituma when it began taking on water and capsized in Atlantic waters off the Essequibo coast.Phillips said the ferry was not insured, and the government is paying for the funerals and other related expenses.Divers from countries including Brazil and Trinidad and Tobago are trying to salvage the vessel, with officials saying they hope to inspect it for any possible damage that could shed light on what happened.Police have launched a criminal investigation and detained three people so far, including the rescued captain and a crew member the authorities say tested positive for marijuana.Also detained is the marine superintendent responsible for overseeing the loading of the ferry. The government maintains it was under capacity in both people and cargo, but survivors have told reporters that they believe the vessel was overloaded.The ship’s manifest listed 116 passengers and 17 crew, but authorities believe as many as 179 people were aboard.A growing number of Guyanese are questioning why it took so long to rescue people, with some survivors telling the Associated Press that they spent hours in the water.Phillips has asked for patience and said officials are awaiting the conclusion of an investigation. Its findings will be reviewed by a commission of inquiry, which has not yet been established.Asked why an 87-year-old ferry was still in service, the government said it had acquired a new vessel from India in recent months to replace the MV Barima, but was waiting on the completion of a new pier at Port Kaituma needed to accommodate it.The MV Barima was last dry docked in 2024 for major repairs and was scheduled for additional work in October.Explore more on these topicsGuyanaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canadian government urged to block Thomson Reuters data deal with US ICE  | Canada | The Guardian
description: US agency is to pay Canadian media company US$125m for use of investigative database to detect ‘immigration fraud’
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: US agency is to pay Canadian media company US$125m for use of investigative database to detect ‘immigration fraud’
Content: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement is a federal law enforcement agency under the Department of Homeland Security.Photograph: Kevin Mohatt/ReutersView image in fullscreenUS Immigration and Customs Enforcement is a federal law enforcement agency under the Department of Homeland Security.Photograph: Kevin Mohatt/ReutersCanadaCanadian government urged to block Thomson Reuters data deal with US ICEUS agency is to pay Canadian media company US$125m for use of investigative database to detect ‘immigration fraud’Olivia Bowdenin TorontoFri 24 Jul 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Canadian federal opposition party leader has called on Mark Carney’s government to block the latest data-sharing deal between US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Canadian media companyThomson Reuters.Avi Lewis, the federal leader of the New Democratic party (NDP), demanded on Tuesday that Ottawa address the contract and further restrict Canadian corporations from doing business with ICE, after Canada’s National Observer news website reported on the deal.“My blood ran cold when I read about this development,” he added in a statement to the Guardian. “Complicity between Canadian corporations and ICE should absolutely be illegal.”Under the US$125m (£94m) deal, ICE will pay the technology and content conglomerate to access its Clear database – which includes property records, social media and geolocation information – in order to identify “voter fraud” and “immigration fraud”, according toreports.In aprocurement documentobtained by 404 Media, Thomson Reuters says it is the only company that allows ICE to have access to the “continuous monitoring” of millions of people.Thomson Reuters’ contracts with ICE date back to 2015, when it first began providing US officials with access to Clear in order to trackpeople for deportation. Critics have long alleged that the databases were being used to facilitate human rights abuses.The latest contract, however, is the first to state that Clear software will be used to support the Trump administration’s objectives of addressing supposed “voter fraud”.In arecent primetime television address, the president repeated false claims about the supposed fallibility of the 2020 US presidential election results, alleging voter fraud, noncitizen voting and a host of other misleading or incorrect statements. Election officials from across the political spectrum lambasted the speech and reasserted the reliability of US elections.Thomson Reuters is owned by the Woodbridge Company, a holding company for the Thomson family, frequently described as the richest family in Canada. The media company also owns the news agency Reuters and the Globe and Mail newspaper.‘Canada is handing people over to ICE’: refugees rejected at border face US detentionRead moreA spokesperson for Thomson Reuters said it did not comment on customer contracts, and referred to a page on the company’s websiteabout Clear.The post says there are “misunderstandings” about the tool, and that it is licensed “exclusively to select businesses, law enforcement and government agencies to help expedite investigative processes in legitimate legal investigations”.The company emphasises that its “investigative solutions are not surveillance tools”.Lewis said the federal government should deny export permits to companies selling equipment to ICE, and pull public subsidies or contracts from any companies that have dealings with the agency. In January, the NDP made similar calls after the fatal shootings of two US citizens by ICE in Minneapolis.“If the Carney government is serious about Canadian economic independence, it should move to block this contract,” Lewis said.The prime minister’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Thomson Reuters contract.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreJoel Bakan, a law professor at the University of British Columbia and author of several books on the unethical behaviour of corporations, said the legal framework did exist in Canada to bar companies from working with ICE.“Companies are not allowed to engage with various rogue regimes, authoritarian regimes, and certainly enemy regimes,” he said. “It’s definitely within the jurisdiction of the government, including the federal government of Canada, to impose various kinds of limitations.”He pointed to Canada’s Special Economic Measures Act, the country’s primary sanctions law, which can authorise the government to restrict trade in relation to human rights violations. “As a matter of realpolitik, I can’t imagine the federal government invoking this against the US, but it is at least arguable that ICE has been involved in such violations,” he said.Explore more on these topicsCanadaThomson ReutersICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Mark CarneyAmericasTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Masked men invading and taking Amazon communities ‘hostage’ in organised crime surge, say local leaders | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
description: Delegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western Amazon
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Delegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western Amazon
Content: Masked gunmen entered homes in the Brazilian village of Apiwtxa, within the Amazon Forest, earlier this month.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APView image in fullscreenMasked gunmen entered homes in the Brazilian village of Apiwtxa, within the Amazon Forest, earlier this month.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APAmazon rainforestMasked men invading and taking Amazon communities ‘hostage’ in organised crime surge, say local leadersDelegation sent to Brasília after gunmen from organised crime group enter homes in western AmazonJonathan WattsFri 24 Jul 2026 07.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 09.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndigenous leaders on the Brazilian-Peruvian border have said their communities are being “taken hostage” by organised crime groups who are running rampant across the region, destroying rainforest, building roads and trafficking drugs.Earlier this month, masked men armed with semi-automatic weapons entered homes in Apiwtxa, a village in the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory, intimidating people and searching for targets.The Asháninka people, who have faced threats from intruders for decades because of their efforts to protect the forest and eject narco smugglers, say this is the worst danger they have faced, prompting an emergency delegation to Brasília this week to appeal for support from the government of the president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.“Either the state steps in to provide protection, or communities will start organising to defend themselves – and that would be disastrous,” said Francisco Piyãko, the general coordinator of the Organisation of Indigenous People of the Juruá River, who is part of the delegation. “We are not facing a local conflict. We are facing the expansion of transnational criminal networks into Indigenous territories that currently represent one of the last barriers against the illegal occupation of this region of the Amazon.”View image in fullscreenThe Asháninka Indigenous people are seeking protection from the Brazilian government.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APThe petition of the Asháninka people comes amid growing concerns about the nexus of drug trafficking and environmental crime, which Brazilian climate scientistCarlos Nobre has describedas the greatest new threat to the Amazon Forest.The Brazilian side of the border is in Acre state, where the forest is still relatively healthy compared with the Peruvian side, which has experienced heavy logging and violence. Acre has sometimes been a perilous area for environmental and land defenders. One of the country’s most celebrated forest campaigners,Chico Mendes, was shot dead there in 1988. After that, there was a period of relative peace in Acre, compared with other countries in the Amazon or other Brazilian states such as Pará. More recently, however, there has been a rise in tension, much of it from the outside. Isolated Indigenous communities from Peru have beenincreasingly crossing the border to escapeconfrontation with loggers and drug cartels.Apiwtxa was the last Indigenous village visited by the British journalist Dom Phillips before he was murdered in the neighbouring Brazilian border state of Amazonas in 2022 while researchingillegal extractivist activitiesin another area menaced by arms and drug smugglers.View image in fullscreenSunrise on the Amônia River, which runs through the Kampa do Rio Amônia Indigenous territory in Brazil.Photograph: Nicoló Lanfranchi/The GuardianAccording to the Asháninka petition to the Brazilian government, the most recent intrusion into Apiwtxa involved five heavily armed, Spanish-speaking men arriving on the evening of 6 July at the home of one of the Asháninka leaders, who was out of the village at the time. “They were clearly poised to attack with lethal intent,” said one member of the community. It was the second time in several days that masked gunmen had entered the village looking for leaders.Frightened villagers took their children into one building for protection and notified the authorities. The army arrived at midnight, by which time the would-be assassins had disappeared back into the forest, leaving only tracks.“For us, this was a threat unlike any other, because they came right into our home – they entered our house,” said Piyãko. “We realise that the context we’re living in now isn’t just about drug trafficking; you can see it’s a movement involving everything from wildcat mining and illegal mining to illegal logging, drug trafficking and other issues.”View image in fullscreenFrancisco Piyãko, general coordinator of the Organisation of Indigenous People of the Juruá River, is part of the delegation to Brasília.Photograph: Martín Mejía/APThe Asháninka delegation in Brasília is calling for a permanent security presence along the border to prevent the free movement of drug traffickers, illegal loggers and the illicit construction of “virus roads” that push into the forest without environmental oversight. They also want greater protection for their leaders and operations to combat organised crime in the area.The neighbouring Peruvian department of Ucayali has the widest network of illegal roads in the Peruvian Amazon, providing transport for gangs involved in environmental crime, gold, money laundering and drugs. In the past five years, coca cultivation in Ucayali has tripled.The Igarapé Institute, a public security thinktank,has saidthat organised crime – which often intersects with narcotics and illegal extraction of natural resources – needs a more robust response by governments across the region: “It is increasingly clear that the fight against organised environmental crime in the Amazon ultimately demands better intelligence and strategic prioritisation. The goal must be to strengthen Brazilian state authority to deter and repress crimes and those who commit them.”Piyãko said this was now a matter of urgency. He added: “If the Peruvian and Brazilian governments joined forces and wanted to resolve the situation, they could. Because they have the means to combat this.”“If the state doesn’t protect these territories, they will be dominated by this criminal system, or the people will be forced to defend themselves on their own. This could lead to very serious situations, because as the net tightens around these territories, tensions rise.”Explore more on these topicsAmazon rainforestAmericasIndigenous peoplesBrazilPeruDrugs tradeLogging and land-clearingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Weather tracker: More than 900 wildfires rage across Canada | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: Fires remain out of control in Northwest Territories and Ontario, while Argentina endures record night-time heat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fires remain out of control in Northwest Territories and Ontario, while Argentina endures record night-time heat
Content: Wildfire devastation in Ontario.Photograph: Chris Young/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenWildfire devastation in Ontario.Photograph: Chris Young/The Canadian Press/APWeather trackerExtreme heatAnalysisWeather tracker: More than 900 wildfires rage across CanadaJames Michelin for MetDeskFires remain out of control in Northwest Territories and Ontario, while Argentina endures record night-time heatFri 24 Jul 2026 04.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTShareRecent hot, dry weather in Canada has triggered hundreds of wildfires across the country. As of Wednesday, more than 900 were burning, scorching about 3m hectares of land. While fires have broken out in several provinces, the greatest concern is in theNorthwest Territories and Ontario, where several remain out of control.Poor air quality has been reported across affected regions, with wildfire smoke carried by winds into the US and even across the Atlantic to northern Europe. The risk of further blazes remains high as North America enters the peak of fire season.Meanwhile, the city of Salta inArgentinarecorded its warmest-ever overnight minimum temperature on Saturday, with the mercury failing to fall below 26C (79F). This reading is particularly remarkable because Argentina is in the middle of winter, when Salta’s average night-time minimum is about 3C.The previous warmest night at this weather station was 22.2C, recorded in January 1953 during the height of summer. This exceptional warmth was driven by the Zonda wind, which develops when westerly airflow crosses the Andes before descending, warming and drying as it sinks back to ground level.This process is known as the Foehn effect, a phenomenon that occurs on the downwind side of mountain ranges around the world. However, the intensity experienced in Salta last weekend was unusual. One contributing factor may have been the rapidly developing El Niño in the eastern Pacific, which would have left the incoming air mass warmer than average, even before it descended on the city.Elsewhere, the strengthening El Niño is also expected to increase typhoon activity in the western Pacific. Tropical Depression 11 formed on Tuesday before developing into Tropical Storm Noul north of thePhilippineson Thursday night. The system is forecast to intensify into a typhoon over the coming days as it tracks between the Philippines and Taiwan, before making landfall on China’s south-east coast on Sunday morning local time as a category 1 storm.Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatWeather trackerWildfiresCanadaAmericasArgentinaEl Niño southern oscillationPhilippinesanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Australian households face prospect of interest rate hike and petrol prices rising above $2 a litre | Reserve Bank of Australia | The Guardian
description: Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel
Content: Crude oil prices are likely to stay elevated for ‘at least a year’ as the US-Iran war enters a new and more dangerous phase, an expert warns.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenCrude oil prices are likely to stay elevated for ‘at least a year’ as the US-Iran war enters a new and more dangerous phase, an expert warns.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPReserve Bank of AustraliaAustralian households face prospect of interest rate hike and petrol prices rising above $2 a litreEconomists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrelGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPatrick ComminsEconomics editorFri 24 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 22.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian households face the prospect of a Reserve Bank interest rate hike and petrol prices above $2 a litre over the coming weeks, economists warn, as the escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel.Financial markets now see an even chance theRBA boardwill deliver a fourth cash rate increase at the next meeting on 11 August.Warwick McKibbin, the director of the ANU’s Centre for Applied Macroeconomic Analysis, said crude oil prices were likely to stay elevated for “at least a year” as the US-Iran war entered a new and more dangerous phase.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Houthis’ blockade of Saudi Arabian oil through the Red Sea and the Ukrainians’ increasingly successful destruction of Russian energy infrastructure had heaped further pressure on global oil supply, McKibbin said.“Getting access to supplies looks different now than it did a few months ago. All the reserves have been run down, particularly in the US. It’s quite a serious situation for the world to be in.”The phasing down of the government’s fuel tax relief to 16 cents a litre and this month’s 37% jump in the international Brent crude benchmark has pushed the cost of unleaded to $1.80 a litre, up from a recent low of about $1.50 at the beginning of the month, according to Motormouth.Graph showing average daily price for a litre of fuel in SydneyJohnathan McMenamin, a senior economist at Barrenjoey, said higher global prices and the end of the remaining fuel excise discount after 2 August meant unleaded would march back above $2 a litre over coming weeks.“That is an uncomfortable level for households, but it isn’t something we are too unfamiliar with,” McMenamin said.Diesel prices are up by about 50 cents in July to about $2.20 a litre in the major East Coast cities.Climbing fuel prices will be another blow to the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation down while managing the damage to the economy from high energy costs.McMenamin believes the central bank will pull the trigger next month – a view he had even before the latest developments in the Middle East.“People will start to see fuel prices go up again, and the concern will be that inflation expectations will once again lift among households and businesses,” he said.“It does matter for how long the oil price is $US100 a barrel – if it’s here for only a couple of days and quickly reverses, then that will provide some relief.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But, clearly, we’ve all lost confidence in where it [the oil price] will be in six months.”Think you have a handle on how Australia’s economy works? Take the RBA’s quiz and find outRead moreWith the economy already slowing sharply, not all economists are convinced that the RBA needs to hike again.Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, said she had never assumed the sharp drop in oil prices during the ceasefire was sustainable, even without a major escalation in the conflict.“But we did think it was going to be just one big spike around March and April, before it settled down. Now it looks like it will be more of a grind, or maybe rolling mini-spikes,” Auld said.Inflation remains too high but is tracking a little below where the RBA had forecast, Auld said, while unemployment was running a little higher. That combination would be enough to keep the RBA on hold while they waited for a slowing economy to take the steam out of price pressures, she said.Auld warned thatnot all Australians will be able to copewith higher borrowing costs and climbing fuel costs.“If you get an intensification of cost of living pressures plus another rate hike, for a certain segment of households that would be a pretty challenging situation and you would start to worry the economic adjustment won’t be so benign.”Explore more on these topicsReserve Bank of AustraliaUS-Israel war on IranAustralian economyEconomicsEnergyOilInterest ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pauline Hanson’s domestic violence comments were no stumble | Pauline Hanson | The Guardian
description: The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence
Author: Ben Smee
Headline: The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence
Content: Pauline Hanson said this week that domestic violence was a ‘two-way street’ and questioned why women did not simply leave abusive relationships.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenPauline Hanson said this week that domestic violence was a ‘two-way street’ and questioned why women did not simply leave abusive relationships.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPPauline HansonAnalysisPauline Hanson’s domestic violence comments were no stumbleBen SmeeThe One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violenceFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastFri 24 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.01 EDTShareFor a decade,Pauline Hansonhas been beating the same drum.Her comments this week –suggesting domestic violence was a “two-way street”and questioning why women did not simply leave abusive relationships – have caused significant concern and beenlabelled “dangerous”by experts and other commentators.But they are not, as they’ve been portrayed, another “gaffe” by the stumbling One Nation leader as she attempts to stabiliseher party’s pollsthat show it might become a new electoral force in Australia.The comments make plain something that has been a driving force for the populist leader since her return to parliament in 2016.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOne Nation’s political ascendancy in recent months has been built on replicating anti-immigrant and hard right pivots in the United States and the UK. Hanson’s own second coming was built on an allyship with groups of anti-feminist men and heavily influenced by domestic violence allegations against her son, Adam Hanson, which she says were false.In 2019, Hanson used parliamentary privilege to call her former daughter-in-law “nasty” and accuse her of making false claims about her son. She has consistently – inside and outside parliament – made claims, rejected by experts and evidence, that suggest women routinely make false allegations of violence for advantage in the family law system.Speaking in 2017, on domestic violence orders, Hanson said: “Women, mostly women, are going around throwing them around left, right and centre.”In 2021 on Sky News, Hanson said: “There are men who have been accused of these things that didn’t, it didn’t happen.One Nation’s rise puts the next election in ‘unknown territory’ – but does Pauline Hanson really have a path to government?Read more“It shows you how lies and perjury are leading to the failure of Australia’s family law system and contributing to the death of 21 men by suicide and the murder of one woman each week.”The “21 men” figure has been repeatedly cited by Hanson, her colleague Malcolm Roberts, and others in One Nation as a campaigning point. The figure comes from a men’s rights organisation, the Australian Brotherhood of Fathers (ABF), and has beendebunked by factcheckers.The ABF have been among Hanson’s biggest cheerleaders since her re-election. Roberts has been particularly close to the group, visiting several times, and recording a special video message for a gathering.One of the first things Roberts did after a federal parliament hearing in 2019 – when he claimed without evidencethere were “many instances” of women making up domestic violence allegations– was to phone the ABF’s founder, Leith Erikson.The ABF has claimed in Facebook posts to have received donations from One Nation, and the political party hasheld community barbecuesin support of the men’s group.The trope that women fabricate violence claims against men is a common grievance of men’s rights groups,but experts saythere is no evidence to support this.Growing political influenceAfter the 2019 election, Hanson’s return to the senate became more than a political curiosity. The Morrison government, four seats short of a senate majority, suddenly needed her support to pass legislation.The government’s sop to Hanson was to accede to her request for a family law inquiry, and to make her the deputy chair (she introduced herself at hearings as the “co-chair”).It is particularly instructive, for all those playing along at home and wondering what One Nation might do with newfound political influence, to understand that the last time Hanson was in a position to ask for something, she chose an inquiry that became a formal platform for misogynists and groups pushing unsupported claims that the system is loaded against men.Hanson livestreamed the hearings to her Facebook page. Commenters called expert witnesses and MPs things like “man-hater” and “dirty snake”.The hearings in March 2020 took place less than a month afterthe murders of Hannah Clarke and her children.Statistically, there’s a reliable way to predict a domestic violence homicide like Hannah Clarke’sRead moreWhen an expert witness, the Griffith University law professor Zoe Rathus, mentioned the case, Hanson responded:“I totally agree that what happened to Hannah and her children was horrendous and should never happen. But it’s on both sides. I have read your report, and it’s all about women. Do you agree that there are men who are aggrieved, men who face domestic violence, men who are taking their own lives?“Do you admit that there are men facing domestic violence?”Rathus responded: “I would prefer if you didn’t ask me whether I ‘admit’ things. I’m not really here to admit things. I’m here to present my research.“The statistics are very clear that domestic violence is something that is very gendered and that violence in the home happens more often by men towards women.”Hanson carried on undeterred.Her comments this week, in the shadow offour more alleged domestic violence homicides, have understandably triggered more backlash because of One Nation’s political ascendancy.As a fringe politician needing only to win a senate quota every six years, Hanson’s views only needed to appeal to a small, angry cohort.The common wisdom is that as One Nation heads for the mainstream – its founder will need to temper her more extreme ideas to keep her coalition of disengaged and aggrieved voters together.But that’s not Pauline Hanson.Ben Smee is Guardian Australia’s Queensland state correspondentIn Australia,domestic and family violence counsellingis available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578.Explore more on these topicsPauline HansonOne NationAustralian politicsanalysisShareReuse this content
