commission on antisemitism and social cohesionUniversity courses covering Israel-Palestine should be audited, Julian Leeser tells royal commissionInquiry’s focus this week is on security for the Jewish community, with the MP telling the commissioner his son is afraid to attend synagogues and eventsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCaitlin CassidyFri 24 Jul 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, has called for universities to undertake an audit of any classes that teach about the Jewish community, Israel orPalestine.Appearing before theroyal commissioninto antisemitism and social cohesion on Friday, Leeser said he had been “very concerned” about antisemitism on university campuses and was not satisfied with how vice-chancellors had addressed the issue after the 7 October 2023 Hamas terrorist attack.“I’ve been particularly unhappy with the responses that I’ve received [from vice-chancellors] in relation to their failure to … audit courses dealing with the Israel-Palestine conflict to ensure that both sides are presented in the best way possible so that students are best prepared to make their own mind up,” he said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThis week, the inquiry focused on security for the Jewish community, hearing a broad consensus that the risk had risen post 7 October.Leeser put a series of recommendations to the commissioner, including for the government to legislate that all universities adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance(IHRA) definitionof antisemitism, instead of their own definitions, as the federal governmentrecently mandated. The IHRA definition is contentious because of concerns it could be used to shut down criticism of Israel.Last year, the chief executive of the Group of Eight, Vicki Thomson, said members had advised that the IHRA definition was “not workable” in an Australian contextas it may limit academic freedom.Leeser said all universities should also undertake “an audit of what’s being taught about Jews and Israel in their classrooms” and remove any “antisemitic materials”. He said universities that taught about the Israel-Palestine conflict should make sure their course materials came from “credible sources” that were “balanced”.Asked how to ensure classroom content was “balanced”, he said people believed they had shown both sides if they had a Palestinian and Israeli perspective, “but one of those perspectives is a full-throated defence by advocates” and “the other perspective is not at all”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHolocaust survivors president says exclusion of Jews from public life has ‘disturbing parallels’ to Nazi GermanyRead moreLast week, the inquiry heard from vice-chancellors of Australia’s largest universities who said they hadsharply changedtheir protest policies since 2023,prompting warningsof restricted academic freedom.Leeser said antisemitism was apparent in “three main vectors” today: “the far right among neo-Nazis, among radical Islamists, and among the academic and cultural left”.The Dor Foundation’s inaugural CEO Tahli Blicblau agreed that “Islamic extremism” and the “extreme-far right” were the most dangerous radical ideologies perpetuating antisemitism, but also took aim at “fringe elements of the far-left and conspiracy movements”. The foundation was launched to combat antisemitism last year.She said the pro-Palestine movement may have some similar ideological drivers as the “radical far left threat” but “the vast majority” of pro-Palestine protesters weren’t motivated by violence towards Jewish people.Blicblau said in an “unprecedented” environment of elevated security risk towards the Jewish community following the Bondi terror attack, greater integration was needed between New South Wales law enforcement and Jewish groups.“If you accept the level of threat is severe … then it follows that the level of integration and engagement between the Jewish community and the law enforcement and intelligence agencies needs to be sufficiently mature to meet the scale of the threat,” she said.Leeser also gave emotional evidence of his experience on 14 December 2025, the day of Bondi terror attack, when he was attending a Hanukkah event in northern Sydney at the time news broke of the fatal shootings. He said his seven-year-old son “cried inconsolably” and asked him “Dad, are we going to be safe?”Leeser said since then, his son had been afraid to attend synagogues and outdoor communal events.“What sort of Australia are we setting up that a seven-year-old child doesn’t feel safe going to a place of worship?” he said. “That’s not the Australia I know and love and it’s not the Australia I want for my children or anyone’s children.”Explore more on these topicsRoyal commission on antisemitism and social cohesionBondi beach terror attackAntisemitismIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Julian Leeser says his son no longer feels safe at Jewish events – as it happened | Australia news | The Guardian
description: This blog is now closed
Author: Catie McLeod
Headline: This blog is now closed
Content: 01.42 EDTJulian Leeser tells royal commission his son no longer feels safe at Jewish eventsCaitlin CassidyBack to the antisemitism royal commission, where the Liberal MPJulian Leeserhas been giving evidence.Leeser has recalled his own experience on 14 December, the day of the terror attack in Bondi.He was attending an outdoor Hanukkah event in northern Sydney at the time.Holding back tears, he says he remembers his son’s fear when the news broke.Leeser had made a speech at the event saying he “recognised that it had been a tough year for the Jewish community, but hoped that things would be better”, when a rabbi pulled him aside and said 50 shots had been fired at Bondi.He told the rabbi they should get down as quickly as possible, because they didn’t know if what had happened at Bondi was more coordinated, and that:double quotation markWhen I came down , it was apparent that people had been killed in the events at Bondi … By that time there were lots of adults who were sharing pictures … And they’re in disbelief.My son at that time was seven and my daughter was three. And my son had overheard the adults talking about the fact that people had been shot and killed in Bondi. And he cried inconsolably … He sat with his legs crossed saying,‘Dad, are we going to be safe?’.This has affected him deeply.Leeser said he couldn’t guarantee to his son that they would be safe. Since then, he has been afraid to attend synagogues and outdoor communal events.double quotation markWhat sort of Australia are we setting up that a seven-year-old child doesn’t feel safe going to a place of worship?That’s not the Australia I know and love and it’s not the Australia I want for my children or anyone’s children.ShareUpdated at01.56 EDT

title: Donald Trump hits Australian exports to US with new higher trade tariff over claims of ‘forced labour’ | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Australia’s trade minister, Don Farrell, says tariff regime is unjustified and inconsistent with free trade agreement with US
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Australia’s trade minister, Don Farrell, says tariff regime is unjustified and inconsistent with free trade agreement with US
Content: Donald Trump has imposed a new 12.5% tariff on Australian exports to the US.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenDonald Trump has imposed a new 12.5% tariff on Australian exports to the US.Photograph: Darren England/AAPAustralia newsDonald Trump hits Australian exports to US with new higher trade tariff over claims of ‘forced labour’Australia’s trade minister, Don Farrell, says tariff regime is unjustified and inconsistent with free trade agreement with USFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerandSarah Basford CanalesFri 24 Jul 2026 03.04 EDTFirst published on Thu 23 Jul 2026 19.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has hit Australian exports with new trade tariffs, claiming the country is not doing enough to combat forced labour, but the Albanese government has demanded he remove them immediately.TheUnited States announced on Friday morning(AEST) that many Australian exports now attract a new 12.5% tariff as part of a broader regime affecting dozens of countries. However the Albanese government says Australia’s three largest export categories – including beef and gold – will avoid the tariff hit.In a statement, the US trade department said Australia was on a list of 54 economies it deemed as having “failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”. Other countries facing a 12.5% tariff include Brazil, China, Egypt, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Russia and Singapore.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailEconomies on a separate list – including the UK, India, Indonesia, Canada and Mexico – will be subject to a lower 10% tariff after the US claimed they had only failed to “enforce” forced labour prohibitions.Friday’s news followed through onan earlier threat from the Trump administrationto level such tariffs, which came after the US supreme court earlier this year struck downTrump’s 10% global tariffs.Trump had responded to that court ruling by immediately announcing temporary trade sanctions, which were due to expire today.Australian government sources had previously told Guardian Australia they believed the forced labour-related tariffs had been levelled as a replacement for the tariffs struck down by the courts.US congresswoman Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat, has denounced the pretext for the new tariffs as a sham.“President Trump isn’t serious about combating forced labor. He’s trying to make an end-run around the Supreme Court and Congress to reimpose his illegal tariffs,” Sánchez wrote on social media.The American trade action document claims “the United States is the only country in the world to adopt, and effectively enforce, a ban on imports made with forced labor”.“President Trump is asking all trading partners to join the United States in eliminating forced labor from global supply chains.”In total the tariffs apply “to the top 60 U.S. trade partners covering 99.4% of U.S. imports”, according to a trade department statement.The Australian trade minister, Don Farrell, immediately called for the US to change course.“These tariffs are unjustified, inconsistent with our free-trade agreement and should be removed,” Farrell said.“Australia’s measures to combat forced labour and modern slavery are among the strongest in the world and we are recognised globally, including in the US, for our leadership.”On the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program, Farrell said has previously had “acrimonious” talks with the US trade chief, Jamieson Greer, over tariffs.“The idea that the Americans should impose this tariff … is just crazy to be honest with you,” he said.“And the idea that India or Pakistan has a better regime, in terms of modern slavery, than Australia is simply incorrect.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe deputy prime minister,Richard Marles, told ABC radio the US actions “make no sense”.“Forced labour is definitely something which needs to be combated around the world, so we support that objective,” he said. “But we have laws, which are amongst the strongest in the world, and we’ve been making that point to the Trump administration.”Trump to impose fresh wave of tariffs on more than 80 countriesRead moreThe US trade action document that sets out the new tariffs includes exemptions for a range of goods including beef; agricultural products such as vegetables and fruits; aircraft parts; certain coal, oil, mineral and chemical products; some metal and steel products; timber products; and machinery.The shadow trade minister, Matt Canavan, claimed the Albanese government had “failed” exporters by not securing lower tariffs, like the UK or Canada.“Australia is subject to a 12.5% tariff rate, the same rate as Russia, China and Venezuela,” the Nationals’ leader said.Canavan said the government had “failed to take meaningful action against forced labour in international supply chains, despite years of warnings”.The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s chief executive, Andrew McKellar, described the move as a “ludicrous decision” and “completely unjustified”.The Business Council of Australia’s head, Bran Black, said the US trade chief’s finding rests on a “narrow claim” without “identifying a single company, enforcement failure, or quantified trade impact”.The National Farmers’ Federation’s chief, Michael Guerin, said the industry was “profoundly disappointed”.“Rather than moving back towards the free and fair trading arrangements that have served both our countries well for two decades, the United States has chosen to further increase barriers to trade, despite Australia’s longstanding record of high standards and responsible trade,” he said.The action, as it pertains to Australia specifically, states that after an investigation, “the Trade Representative has determined to impose 12.5 percent tariffs on products of Australia” except for a limited number of exemptions.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsAustralian politicsAustralian economyLabor partyTariffsTrump tariffsRichard MarlesnewsShareReuse this content

title: More than 200,000 people flee or lock down as wildfires sweep France and Spain | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: ‘Highly unpredictable’ blaze forces evacuation of Cap Ferret on French coast and Spain declares national emergency
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: ‘Highly unpredictable’ blaze forces evacuation of Cap Ferret on French coast and Spain declares national emergency
Content: 1:12Thousands evacuated in south of France as wildfire rages across pine forest – videoWildfiresMore than 200,000 people flee or lock down as wildfires sweep France and Spain‘Highly unpredictable’ blaze forces evacuation of Cap Ferret on French coast and Spain declares national emergencyJon Henleyin Paris andSam Jonesin MadridFri 24 Jul 2026 18.18 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 200,000 people have fled or been ordered to lock down as huge wildfires swept Spain andFranceon Friday, prompting Madrid to declare a national emergency and the French authorities to order the total evacuation, by land and sea, of one of the country’s best-known holiday spots.Authorities in south-west France ordered the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast to be evacuated “village by village” in the face of an “intense, highly unpredictable” wildfire that has burned through more than 19,000 hectares (47,000 acres) of forest.Spain’s government declared its first national emergency for a wildfire as two large blazes merged into one outside Madrid and a third was on the verge of joining them, amid searing heat and tinder-dry conditions across much of southernEurope.Both countries sought EU help. “This is the worst wildfire in our region’s history,” said Madrid’s regional leader, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, describing “an unprecedented situation: a perfect storm of extremely high temperatures and relentless winds”.View image in fullscreenA volunteer guides holidaymakers evacuated from Cap Ferret after they arrive by boat in Arcachon.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/GettyMore than 110,000 people had been evacuated in two days to escape the Cap Ferret fire, the Gironde prefecture said, including thousands of holidaymakers in campsites and rental homes.Boats ferried hundreds off piers on the peninsula on Friday as the blaze threatened to cut off the only access road.Scientists say climate breakdown is triggering more frequent and more extreme weather events,evaporating soilsand waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading tothousands of excess deaths. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate.About 800 firefighters and four water-bombing planes were battling the Gironde blaze north of Arcachon Bay, butthe fire, which began on Wednesdaynear the village of Saumos 25 miles (40km) west of Bordeaux, was not yet stabilised.Map of all the burnt areas near Arcachon Bay in the last 72 hoursNumerous roads in the area, including those leading to Cap Ferret, which contains many villas owned by celebrities and millionaires, were closed to all but essential traffic. Eighty houses had burned.“I’ve seen plenty of fires before, but never one of this intensity,” Jean Mazodier, 86, who owns 150 hectares of forest and was evacuated from his home at 6am, told Le Monde. “Everything’s burned. It’s like losing a child.”A second fire raging in the region, farther south near the popular holiday resort of Biscarrosse, had also burned through more than 2,500 hectares, the Landes prefect, Gilles Clavreul, said on Friday, and led to the evacuation of about 31,000 people.View image in fullscreenWildfire smoke shrouds the sky over Biscarrosse in an ash-grey haze.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA firefighter battles a wildfire spreading in Lège-Cap-Ferret in the Gironde.Photograph: SDIS33/Damien Rembert/EPAView image in fullscreenA firefighter battles flames in Cap Ferret.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersMore than 600 firefighters were struggling to contain that blaze, Clavreul said.“There are a great many new fire starts ahead of the main blaze. The situation is highly dynamic and unfavourable,” he added.In 2022, a wildfireburned more than 30,000 hectaresin France’s south-west, forcing 50,000 evacuations. In parched conditions and fanned by strong winds, the two latest blazes have torn through coastal pine forests with flames up to 10 metres (30ft) high.France’s president, ​Emmanuel Macron, said he had activated the EU’s civil protection mechanism as the country, which has endured three almost back-to-back heatwaves since May, battled numerous wildfires.“We will soon be able to count ‌on reinforcements from two Croatian aircraft, two Portuguese planes, as well as two heavy helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia,” Macron said.View image in fullscreenA helicopter drops water over a burning area as a wildfire flares up again in Pontevès, south-east France.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/GettyFrance’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Friday that 32 wildfires were burning, with 50,000 hectares scorched already so far this year – nearly four times the total by the same date last year.About 800 firefighters were battling a blaze in the south-eastern Var area, where weather conditions were improving, Nuñez said, allowing some firefighting resources to be redeployed to the south-west.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe severity of fires in the EU has broken records for the time of year, data from the European Forest Fire Information System shows.Spain’s government declared a national emergency on Thursday evening after wildfires ⁠threatened areas near the capital and in the neighbouring province of Ávila, leading to the evacuation or confinement of more than 63,000 people.A national emergency, which allows central government to assume overall control of powers and responsibilities that are usually the domain of Spain’s self-governing regions, has only been declared once before, during the countrywide blackout of April 2025.View image in fullscreenPeople spend the night at a sports centre after being evacuated from their homes in Cebreros, Ávila province.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APThe regional government of Madrid requested assistance, describing the situation as one of “extreme gravity”. It said at least four active fires could advance “beyond current extinguishing capacity”. The fires remained uncontained on Friday.Spanish authorities said on Friday afternoon there was “very little time left” before the blaze in Madrid, already made up of two merged fires, combined with the Ávila fire.On Friday night, Madrid’s regional environment minister, Carlos Novillo, said the fire had reached “a critical moment” and was “beyond our extinguishing capability”. He added: “The priority at the moment is protecting people, helping those who have been evacuated, and making the most of windows of opportunity.”José Cobos, who fled his home about 30 miles south-west of Madrid on Friday morning with his wife and three dogs, told Antena 3 television: “The smoke was incredibly thick. You couldn’t breathe.”Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, chaired an emergency response meeting at the Moncloa palace on Friday morning as the state meteorological office warned that the danger of more fires remained very high.View image in fullscreenSmoke plumes rise from wildfires near Madrid.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockHe said the government had deployed “all available resources”, adding: “It will be by your side during the emergency and the recovery.”The prime minister also thanked “all the emergency services that are fighting day and night”. Sánchez is due to visit the affected area on Saturday morning.On Friday morning, Spain’s environment ministry said 29 big forest fires had been recorded so far in 2026, compared with an annual average of nine between January and the end of July per year over the past decade. Forest fires had burned about 114,796 hectares, compared with 25,133 by the same time last year.Spain’s interior ministry has also requested fire-fighting aircraft through the EU’s civil protection mechanism, which aims to strengthen civil protection cooperation between EU countries and 10 additional participating states.Spain’s Guardia Civil force, which polices rural areas, said late on Friday that one man had been arrested and another was under investigation in connection with the forest fire in the Burgohondo municipality of Ávila. It said the two suspects had apparently ignored a ban on the use of heavy machinery, thereby creating “sparks … that may have caused the fire”.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresClimate crisisFranceSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Law student charged after military-grade bomb intercepted near Irish border | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Isobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, remanded in custody after intelligence-led operation against dissident republicans
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Isobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, remanded in custody after intelligence-led operation against dissident republicans
Content: Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Clane, County Kildare, was charged with possession of explosives.Photograph: Damien Eagers/PAView image in fullscreenIsobella Perrie Sullivan, from Clane, County Kildare, was charged with possession of explosives.Photograph: Damien Eagers/PAIrelandLaw student charged after military-grade bomb intercepted near Irish borderIsobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, remanded in custody after intelligence-led operation against dissident republicansLisa O’Carrollin Donegal and agenciesFri 24 Jul 2026 18.18 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 25-year-old law student has been charged in relation to an “extremely significant” bomb intercepted near the UK-Irish border.Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Clane, County Kildare, was charged with possession of explosives at a special sitting of Trim district court on Friday evening.Garda Síochána said in a statement that a second person, a man in his 40s arrested in connection with the investigation, remained detained in relation to offences against the state.Both were arrested after police in Ireland targeting dissident republicans intercepted a vehicle that was allegedly transporting the device, after receiving intelligence information, police said.Members of the Garda Síochána’s special detective unit stopped the vehicle travelling on the N2 south of Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday afternoonRevealing details of the interception on Friday, Garda sources said the bomb was “highly sophisticated”, had been completed and was ready for use. It contained a power unit, a detonator and military-grade explosives they believed to be semtex.Security sources said the probable intended use was as an under-car explosive for an attack in Northern Ireland.Gardaí requested the assistance of the Irish Defence Forces explosive ordnance disposal team, which completed an examination of the vehicle south of Carrickmacross.The Garda commissioner, Justin Kelly, confirmed details of the operation as he spoke to media at a Garda graduation event in County Tipperary on Friday.“To be clear, what we found was an extremely significant seizure,” he said. “So this was an explosive device.“Any seizure of this nature is really concerning. However, we certainly know that there are a small minority of dissident republicans who did not agree with the Good Friday agreement, they did not put weapons and explosives [out of use], they didn’t, you know, go through with the proper process in relation to decommissioning. So that is something that we continue to deal with.”Kelly added: “There’s a small minority of these individuals, I would describe them as radicalised republicans, and this is a threat that we’re going to continue to face for some time in An Garda Síochána.“But what I will say, certainly, it was a significant explosive device. So certainly not just the seizure of components or pieces. This was an explosive device and it would have or could have potentially caused significant damage.”The commissioner confirmed the operation relied on intelligence. “Obviously, this was not a random stop,” Kelly said. “This is an intelligence-led operation, so we certainly do have information in relation to the individuals involved.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA security source said the fact a bomb of that nature had been built and transported to the border was worrying because of the level of skill involved. It required mechanical and electrical knowledge and the sourcing of explosives.They said that “radicalisation of individuals captured by the internet” meant individuals, rather than organised networks, could be at the centre of the incident.Pipe bombs that have been used in the recent past to target members of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) can be “relatively crude” but this bomb appeared to be different and would have needed an initiating device and a timer.The fact that the Garda intercepted the bomb showed its intelligence gathering was working. However, the incident will fuel concerns about the level of counter-terrorism resourcing since the 1998 peace deal.Kelly said: “We work very closely with our colleagues in PSNI and the intelligence services in the UK to deal with this threat. But I want to commend the members of An Garda Síochána who are involved in this operation.”Perrie Sullivan was remanded in custody until a bail hearing on Monday. Bail would only be granted under a series of strict conditions.Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropeNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump threatens EU with ‘substantial’ tariffs over fines of US tech giants | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: After Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Brussels was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayers
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: After Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Brussels was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayers
Content: Donald Trump has lately imposed dozens of new tariffs on countries throughout the world.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump has lately imposed dozens of new tariffs on countries throughout the world.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsTrump threatens EU with ‘substantial’ tariffs over fines of US tech giantsAfter Google fined €890m by EU, US president said Brussels was ‘robbing’ American companies and taxpayersWhat to know about Trump’s new tariffs on more than 80 countriesGaya Guptain WashingtonFri 24 Jul 2026 17.22 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas threatened the European Union with additional and “substantial” tariffs after Brussels imposed a series ofsteep fineson US tech giants.The US president accused Brussels of taking “direct aim” at several American companies including Apple, Meta Platforms, Amazon and Google,writing in a Truth Social post: “The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ forEurope, nor will we allow it to be!”Days earlier, Google was fined €890m ($1bn) by the EU after its search and app store services were found to have breached online competition laws. Last yearApple and Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, were also fined.Trump claimed in his social media post on Friday that the US would “immediately” launch an investigation into the EU’s practice of “‘ROBBING’ American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer,” and said that the EU will “pay a very big price” for its actions.It came just a day after the Trump administrationseparately imposed a sweeping round of tariffson more than 80 countries, including those in the EU.Trump accused of using forced labor as ‘convenient’ justification for tariffsRead moreThe European Commission did not immediately comment on Trump’s threat on Friday. Announcing the fine on Google on Wednesday, it said the tech company had given “preferential treatment to its own services, including shopping, hotels, transport and sports results”.Google welcomed Trump’s intervention on Friday.Jose Castaneda, a spokesperson for the company, said Google had worked hard to comply with the EU’s Digital Markets Act and expressed its concerns about the effects of recent decisions by the European Commission. “We appreciate the engagement by the administration and U.S. government,” he said.Trump has often used tariffs – or simply the threat of them – as a way to retaliate against countries for decisions outside trade policy. Last year, he threatened a tax on imports from Mexico and Canada until the two countries agreed to implementmeasures on border security.Despite challenges from the supreme court, Trump has persisted in implementing tariffs globally, claiming that they will help boost US jobs and manufacturing. The tariffs he announced yesterday would impose a 10% levy on the EU, and were designed to clamp down on what Trump claimed were unfair labor practices.The EU has cracked down on a handful of large tech companies since before the start of Trump’s presidency after passing the Digital Markets Act, meant to help regulate competition among digital media companies.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsEuropean UnionDonald TrumpTariffsUS politicsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: France evacuates Cap Ferret peninsula as Spanish wildfires merge near Madrid – as it happened | France | The Guardian
description: French evacuees using hundreds of mobilised boats or the only road linking the area with the mainland as evacuation also ordered in areas near Spanish capital
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: French evacuees using hundreds of mobilised boats or the only road linking the area with the mainland as evacuation also ordered in areas near Spanish capital
Content: 03.48 EDTFrance orders evacuation of Cap Ferret peninsula as thousands flee wildfiresJakub KrupaThousands of people have been forced to flee parts of south-westFranceamid worsening wildfires that prompted the authorities to order people to evacuate from the Cap Ferret peninsula along the Atlantic coast.A French Civil Security Canadair CL-415 aircraft sprays water on a forest surrounding Cotignac, southeastern France.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesEvacuees have been told to leave the area before 10am, usinghundreds of mobilised boatsor the only road linking the area with the mainland.Holidaymakers from Lege-Cap-Ferret carry their belongings along the pier upon their arrival in Arcachon during an evacuation operation of the entire Cap-Ferret peninsula in southwestern France.Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesMore than10,000 hectares are affected by the two concurrent wildfires,which last night crossed the firebreak established by firefighters.The French authoritiesformally requested the activation of the European Union’s Civil Protection Mechanismto tap into the bloc’s resources as they battle the fires, with Emmanuel Macron saying the situation remained “very intense.”The EU’s crisis commissioner,Hadja Lahbib, confirmed that “following France’s activation of the EU’s civil protection mechanism, the EU is providing assistance and deploying 3 water bomber aircraft.”Dangerous situation is also unfolding in Spain, with the Spanish government declaring a national emergency over wildfires near Madrid and Avila,forcing more than 10,000 people to evacuate.A wall of flames advances as a wildfire burns near Burgohondo, in Ávila province, Spain.Photograph: Mateo Lanzuela/Europa Press/API will bring you all the updates here.It’sFriday, 24 July 2026, it’sJakub Krupahere, and this isEurope Live.Good morning.Share

title: Burnham urged to lobby EU leaders directly to waive EES border controls | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Lib Dems call on PM to push for suspension of ‘bungled, malfunctioning’ system as overseas holiday travel peaks
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Lib Dems call on PM to push for suspension of ‘bungled, malfunctioning’ system as overseas holiday travel peaks
Content: The port of Dover said it was expecting its busiest days of the summer this weekend. French border police have decided not to fingerprint car travellers at ferry ports.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenThe port of Dover said it was expecting its busiest days of the summer this weekend. French border police have decided not to fingerprint car travellers at ferry ports.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PATravel & leisureBurnham urged to lobby EU leaders directly to waive EES border controlsLib Dems call on PM to push for suspension of ‘bungled, malfunctioning’ system as overseas holiday travel peaksGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 24 Jul 2026 11.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has been urged to lobby EU leaders directly to suspend the new entry-exit system, EES, as the peak weekend for overseas holidays begins.About 2.2 million British holidaymakers are expected to head abroad between Friday and Monday, the majority toEurope, with all schools in the UK now on their summer break.Speaking at Heathrow airport on Friday morning, the Liberal Democrats’ foreign affairs spokesperson, Calum Miller, said the prime minister needed to call on EU states to drop the “bungled, malfunctioning border system” until at least September.The EES, which requires non-EU citizens to register on arrival andbe photographed and fingerprinted, has been technically in full force since April afterlaunching last year, but border police have been allowed to relax requirements during extreme delays.View image in fullscreenHolidaymakers queue in traffic at the North Macedonia–Greece border at the start of the summer tourist season.Photograph: Georgi Licovski/EPASome passengers, however, have still missed flights while others have had to queue for several hours.Miller said: “Holidaymakers and hauliers should not be punished by a bungled, malfunctioning border system that is completely out of their control. Andy Burnham needs to pick up the phone to each and every European leader – and persuade them, collectively, to suspend the EES until at least September.”He said a disastrous Brexit deal was “putting millions of Britons at risk of having their holidays ruined by this broken EU border system”.The travel association Abta said Spain would be the main destination for people travelling abroad this weekend, with strong demand also for Greece, Portugal, Italy and Turkey. Its chief executive, Mark Tanzer, said passengers should leave plenty of time for their journeys.“For many heading overseas, this will be the first experience of EES, and for some, though not all, it may take longer than usual to get through passport control,” he said.View image in fullscreenThe EU’s entry-exit (EES) system at Venice airport. Abta advised people to allow plenty of time for their journeys.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/GettyGreece has already indicated it will not impose the additional biometric checks on UK nationals who make up the majority of its incoming non-EU tourists, while problems with technology provided to France means that automated booths at its borders are not working.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has met EU commissioners and her French counterpart, speaking again last week to raise concerns. A government spokesperson said: “While the new EES checks are a matter for the EU, we recognise this is a significant change for British travellers and are doing everything we can to get people away on their summer holidays with as little hassle as possible.”That includes money for EES facilities and management of traffic at the port of Dover. For cross-Channel traffic, the French border posts are in the UK –prompting concerns of tailbacksover the peak getaway period. But French border police have decided not to fingerprint or photograph car travellers at ferry ports or the Eurotunnel terminal and traffic has so far passed smoothly.The port of Dover said it was expecting its busiest days of the summer on Friday and Saturday, with just over 10,000 cars on top of the usual haulage traffic, but that queueing time had not exceeded 40 minutes and had been as little as 10 minutes.Return flights from Europe for UK citizens will be the biggest anxiety. EasyJet urged the EU on Thursday to extend the flexibility to suspend the EES until the end of October.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: Trump switched planes in Turkey earlier this month because of threat from Iran proxy forces – report | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President flew to Ankara onboard Qatari-gifted jet, without advanced defenses, and flew home on old Air Force One
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: President flew to Ankara onboard Qatari-gifted jet, without advanced defenses, and flew home on old Air Force One
Content: Donald Trump boards the Qatari-gifted Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on 1 July 2026.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump boards the Qatari-gifted Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on 1 July 2026.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump switched planes in Turkey earlier this month because of threat from Iran proxy forces – reportPresident flew to Ankara onboard Qatari-gifted jet, without advanced defenses, and flew home on old Air Force OneMarina DunbarFri 24 Jul 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 20.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpswitched aircraft before departingTurkeyearlier this month after US officials determined there was a credible threat from Iranian proxy forces targeting him and Air Force One, according to a new report from theNew York Times.The threat surfaced while the US president was attending theNatosummit. He had arrived in Ankara onboard the new Qatari-donated Boeing 747-8, an aircraft that Trump acknowledged does not have the same advanceddefensive systemsas the older Air Force One.According to the anonymous sources who spoke to the Times, after US officials detected the threat, the Secret Service recommended that Trump change aircraft before leaving the country. He later announced he would depart on the older Air Force One instead.CBS Newsconfirmedthe New York Times reporting later Friday, citing unnamed US officials. According to CBS’s sources, the US Secret Service decided to switch planes after receiving intelligence involving a plan to fire a missile at the president’s aircraft.Trump administration admits canceling clean energy grants to Democratic statesRead moreThe newly reported details about the threat help explain why the White House quickly decided to swap aircraft. They also highlight ongoing security concerns surrounding the donated jet, which Trump had pushed to have ready for use as soon as possible.According to the report, US officials did not believe the Iranian proxy forces were specifically targeting the new Boeing 747-8. Instead, the intelligence indicated the threat was directed at Trump himself and whichever aircraft he was traveling on.The White House has been contacted for comment.Trump’s justice department had previouslysubpoenaedreporters at the New York Times over their coverage of the security risks involving the president’s Qatari-gifted Air Force One replacement, but the justice department hasdropped, for now, those efforts.Earlier this month, it wasreportedthat Trump flew part of the trip home from the Nato summit in Turkey aboard the older Air Force One after arriving on the newQatari-gifted aircraft. At the time, Trump did not provide a detailed explanation for the switch, saying he would use the legacy aircraft “for old time’s sake”. He also said both planes would make a previously unscheduled stop at Royal Air Force Mildenhall, a base used by US troops, before returning to the US.Although Trump did not explain the reason for changing planes at the time, he has previously spoken about threats from Iran against his life, even going so far as to say he leftstanding ordersfor the US military to destroy Iran “at levels they’ve never seen before” if Tehran carries out its longstanding threats to kill him.The revelations also come as Trump reportedly mulls escalating attacks on Iran in the ongoing conflict after a ceasefire deal has recently broken down. ⁠Trump has vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, though he once again left open the door to a diplomatic deal with Iran.“We are talking to ⁠them. I think they’re being serious. I think … ​they are being by far the most serious that we’ve seen them, but that doesn’t mean we get there,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday.He added: “We’re locked and loaded. We’re ready to go.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS national securityTurkeyIranUS-Israel war on IranNew York TimesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US expands Iran attacks as Trump warns Tehran and Houthis over Red Sea strikes | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: No end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: No end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait
Content: Smoke and flames rise after an explosion in Bandar Abbas in Iran’s Hormozgan province before dawn on Friday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersView image in fullscreenSmoke and flames rise after an explosion in Bandar Abbas in Iran’s Hormozgan province before dawn on Friday.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranUS expands Iran attacks as Trump warns Tehran and Houthis over Red Sea strikesNo end to fighting in sight as Revolutionary Guards launch drones at targets in Bahrain, Jordan and KuwaitPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentFri 24 Jul 2026 13.58 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has struck targets across Iran, reaching as far as the Caspian Sea, as Donald Trump threatened “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies inYemenfor extending the war to a second shipping ⁠chokepoint at the entrance to the Red Sea.As Iran retaliated on Friday with missile and drone fire against US bases and allies across the region, the New York Times reportedthat Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire proposaldelivered by the Iraq prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi. This despite the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claiming a day earlier that Iran was begging for a ceasefire. Iraq later disputed the report.Iran’s much improved missile systems pose a real threat to the USRead moreTrump warned China and Russia on Friday against selling weapons toIran, saying he believed assurances from Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin that they were not yet doing so. Iran said it was in consultations with both countries.On his Truth Social network, the US president wrote: “Therefore, two major Countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them – Certainly not in their best interests.”Iran’s military said it had launched drone strikes on Friday morning againstUS militarytargets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait as it appeared there was no end in sight to the fighting. It told civilians across the region to stay 500 metres away from locations where US troops were present.TheHouthis, who control northern and western Yemen, continued to claim a naval blockade on Saudi Arabian ports and ships using the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea.View image in fullscreenHouthi fighters take part in a pro-Iran rally in Sana’a, Yemen, in April.Photograph: Khaled Abdullah/ReutersThe Houthis insisted on Friday that only Saudi-linked trade was under blockade as ships in the Red Sea broadcast messages to the group identifying ownership, flag and crew in the hope of securing a safe passage.The Houthis struck two Saudi tankers on Thursday in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, pushing oil prices up 7% to more than $100 per ​barrel for the first time since May. The attacks forced several other tankers to turn around and head north through the Suez canal, a much longer and more expensive route to reach Asia by sailing around ‌Africa.Shipping insurance costs through the southern Red Sea doubled for some companies on Thursday, sources said. Still, half of the 18 ships exiting Bab el-Mandeb on Thursday were carrying crude oil, including two Chinese supertankers.The number of tankers crossing through the strait of Hormuz fell to just one on Thursday, the lowest figure since 7 May.Trump wrote on social media that he would hold Iran accountable for any further Red Sea attacks, saying “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis themselves”.He told Axios he was considering relaunching major combat against Iran. “They haven’t received enough pain yet,” the US news outlet quoted Truump as saying.Washington and Tehran appear to remain fundamentally at odds over future control of the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, insisted the problem with advancing peace talks was “the American approach”.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi (left), meets his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, in Kyrgyzstan on Friday.Photograph: Russian Foreign Ministry Press Service/APAraghchi said: “Preserving Iran’s interests in the strait of Hormuz is among our principles and we are committed to them. We are neither intimidated by threats nor will we yield to pressure.“As long as the legitimate goals and demands of the Iranian people are not met, it is natural that we continue our efforts.”Iranian officials had earlier suggested that the most recent US proposal involved a temporary arrangement that did not address control of the strait of Hormuz.Pakistan, which has acted as a mediator in the conflict, has also been pushing for fresh talks between the two sides after an initiative by ⁠China.Exploratory discussions took place during ​a visit by Iran’s interior minister, Eskandar Momeni, to Islamabad this week – his second within the last 10 days, sources said.Iranian state media said US missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz. Tehran said it had attacked US military equipment depots at Al-Adiri, officially named Camp Buehring, in northern ​Kuwait, and US troop positions at Camp Arifjan and Camp Doha near Kuwait City. It also said it had significantly damaged a surveillance tower used by the US Fifth Fleet in Bahrain.In an example of how shipping disruption caused by the war affects other countries, ‌Coca-Cola has raised the prices of Diet Coke in India – where it is mainly sold in aluminium cans – by more than 10% as the conflict chokes its supply chain.Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranUS militaryUS foreign policyTrump administrationYemenHouthisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Middle East crisis: US carries out strikes across Iran as Tehran targets American bases in region – as it happened | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies
Author: Mabel Banfield-Nwachi
Headline: Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies
Content: 13.08 EDTThe day so farUS missiles struck targets across Iran on Friday after Donald Trump vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the Middle East war to a second major shipping chokepoint, the mouth of the ⁠Red Sea.US Central Command said it targeted Iranian military command centres, communication networks, drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and maritime capabilities.​Iranian armed forces responded by firing a wave of retaliatory attacks on at US bases in neighbouring Arab countries and warning people there that they may strike non-military buildings used by US personnel.The Iranian army said it used drones to target facilities in Bahrain and Jordan, with attacks also reported in Kuwait and Iraq. The IRGC warned civilians in the Middle East to stay away from US forces, state media reported.The head of Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya central military command, Ali Abdollahi, threatened US military personnel in the region on Friday, saying Iran had “prepared free, one-way tickets to hell for you”. “For every proud citizen of the Islamic Republic of Iran who is martyred, one American service member will be sent to hell,” he was quoted as saying by the state broadcaster.Iranpushed back ona New York Times (paywall) report from Thursdaythat Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire deal presented by the Iraqi prime minister, calling the report “completely diversionary and misleading,” according to state media IRNA.The NYT reported that the proposal was the only one on the table, and Tehran was not interested in a temporary deal which left the question of control of the strait of Hormuz unresolved, citing Iranian officials. Baghdad has also denied the NYT report.Trumpsaid that in recent meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, both leaders assured the US president separately that they would not sell weapons toIran. The US president added: “Two major countries that people speak of often in terms of Iran are, in my opinion, not participating. If they did, it would be very bad for them – certainly not in their best interests.”Share

title: How Chinese tech and Russian tactics are aiding Iran’s bombing of US bases | Iran | The Guardian
description: Increasingly accurate and lethal attacks are revealing weaknesses in stretched defences across the Gulf
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Increasingly accurate and lethal attacks are revealing weaknesses in stretched defences across the Gulf
Content: An Iranian couple rides a motorbike past Iranian missiles, Zolfaghar, on display at Azadi Square in Tehran.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreenAn Iranian couple rides a motorbike past Iranian missiles, Zolfaghar, on display at Azadi Square in Tehran.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAIranAnalysisHow Chinese tech and Russian tactics are aiding Iran’s bombing of US basesDan SabbaghDefence and security editorIncreasingly accurate and lethal attacks are revealing weaknesses in stretched defences across the GulfFri 24 Jul 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 14.22 EDTShareAs the crisis in the Middle East escalates, Iran has been bombing US bases and critical infrastructure in the Gulf with increasing accuracy, helped by Chinese satellite imagery and tactics learned byRussiain Ukraine.Three US soldiers were killedlast Friday in an attack on the Muwaffaq Salti airbase in Jordan, which was being protected by a Thaad air defence system. Satellite imagery later released by Iranian media showed several buildings had been destroyed.It is not clear why the air defence system failed in that incident, which is under Pentagon investigation, but it is a reminder that Iran retains an effective missile capability that its new leadership iswilling to deploy.Almost 100 troops injured in recent weeks, Pentagon admits, as Iran launches reprisals on US alliesRead moreAndreas Krieg, an associate professor at the school of security studies, King’s College London, said a combination of better intelligence, missile navigation, manoeuvrability and coordinated attack planning amounted to “a real transformation”.It was the product, Krieg said, of three years of technological development of Iran’s ballistic missile programme, which remainedroughly 70% intact on US intelligence estimates, despite previous claims from Washington that Tehran’s military capabilities had been obliterated.The first step was to use Chinese satellite imagery to help identify targets at US bases and other sites in the Gulf. The US imposed sanctions on three Chinese companies in May for providing such images.One, Mizar Vision, exposed the presence ofUS militaryaircraft and Patriot and Thaad air defence systems at bases in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the Jordanian base hit last week, and imagery released on social media was widely picked up.Some experts, however, said they were less sure Beijing had been providing intelligence. Sidharth Kaushal of the Royal United Services Institute saidIranhad focused on static targets at US bases, for which commercial imagery was enough.“I haven’t seen anything where Iran has struck a target so dynamic that I’ve looked at this and gone ‘this has got to be foreign aid,’” he said. At the same time, however, questions have been raised about whether US bases, built to withstand attacks from insurgents, are sufficiently hardened against Iranian missile and drone attacks.A string of accurate Iranian attacks on CIA facilities across the Gulf during the bombings made US analysts wonder whether Russia had shared locations with Tehran, but the hypothesis is tentative.Has Trump dragged the US into a forever war in Iran? | Mohamad BazziRead moreThe US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, told Congress this week thatChinaand Russia were helping Iran to some extent. But Donald Trump contradicted him on Friday, saying Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin had personally assured him that they would not sell weapons to Iran.Iran’s ballistic programme relies heavily on Chinese electronics and ammonium perchlorate for rocket fuel, but the finished weapons are considered sophisticated enough to be able to occasionally defeat stretched US and Gulf air defences.Iranian missiles boast complex navigation, using GPS, China’s BeiDou and Russia’s Glonass simultaneously as they launch towards targets, and re-entry speeds, which are several times the speed of sound, always make anti-ballistic defence a challenge.Tehran has also developed “steerable warheads that can adjust their course during descent” on some of its ballistic missiles, Kreig said. Heat-seeking and optical navigation for the terminal phase means they are not vulnerable to electronic jamming because they are not using radio communication.All this is enough to present a serious challenge for US air defences at a time when stockpiles of Patriot and Thaad interceptors have been run down by about half after the 38-day US-Israel bombing campaign in the spring. Add in energy sites, oil refineries and desalination plants and there is a large area to cover.Iran has also evolved tactically in its missile attacks, using methods similar to Russia in Ukraine, where smaller salvoes can be more effective than larger ones, and drones are used to distract air defences, making way for a ballistic attack.Kaushal said he believed it was a case of the two countries’ militaries learning from each other’s experience – “a convergent evolution” – rather than it necessarily being the result of Moscow directly teaching Tehran.Though there is a degree of anti-western understanding between Iran, Russia and China, as well as North Korea, the so called “axis of upheaval” is far from a consistent military alliance.“There is a kind of collaboration there, but it doesn’t produce the kind of massive net benefits that Nato produces,” said Matthew Savill, a defence analyst from the Royal United Services Institute.Explore more on these topicsIranUS militaryUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaChinaRussiaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Israel planning ‘extensive’ military operation in West Bank after settler attack | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed and several hurt after armed settlers entered village with military support
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed and several hurt after armed settlers entered village with military support
Content: People in mourning at a hospital in Nablus, where the bodies of four Palestinian people were taken.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APView image in fullscreenPeople in mourning at a hospital in Nablus, where the bodies of four Palestinian people were taken.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APWest BankIsrael planning ‘extensive’ military operation in West Bank after settler attackFour Palestinians and two Israelis killed and several hurt after armed settlers entered village with military supportAndrew Roth,Sufian Taha,Quique Kierszenbaumand agencies in JerusalemFri 24 Jul 2026 12.54 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 05.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael has said it is preparing a major military operation in theWest Bankafter four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed during a confrontation that began after armed settlers entered a Palestinian village with support from the Israeli military.Several more people were seriously injured at the scene after a scuffle broke out over an Israeli settler’s weapon and the military opened fire, according to residents. Dozens more have been reported wounded in ensuing settler attacks on neighbouring Palestinian towns.The shooting in the Palestinian village of Tell, near Nablus, is the deadliest attack in the West Bank this year and during the reprisals on nearby Palestinian towns, settlers set fire to houses and attacked local people. At least eight more Palestinians had reportedly been hospitalised, most with gunshot wounds.The Israeli military announced it was preparing for an “extensive” operation in the West Bank, with troops surrounding the town of Nablus and reports of security forces entering the hospital to arrest those wounded in the violence.The military said it planned to apprehend “dozens of Palestinians” involved in the incident, which it said it was treating as a terrorist attack, although video from the scene indicated the clash was not premeditated and involved a struggle over a weapon held by an armed settler.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers outside a hospital in Nablus. There are reports of security forces entering hospitals to arrest those wounded in the violence.Photograph: Majdi Mohammed/APIsrael’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, and defence minister, Israel Katz, said in a statement: “The security forces must be allowed to act freely and with full force against terrorism.” They called for more troops in the West Bank and the razing of the homes of the accused in Tell, as well as the collection of weapons and revoking of work permits in the village.Netanyahu also called for the building of new settlement outposts in the area and the legalisation of existing outposts. Unauthorised settlements are illegal under Israeli law.The head of Israel’s Democrats party, Yair Golan, said Netanyahu and Katz’s response showed a “clear intent to set the area ablaze”. The Palestinian foreign ministry condemned what it described as a “massacre committed by settlers in partnership with the occupation forces in the village of Tell”.Walid Zidan, the head of Tel village council, told Agence France-Presse that about 20 Israeli settlers had entered the village at about 8.30am local time. “Villagers came out to defend their homes and property. Clashes and physical altercations broke out between the residents and the settlers,” Zidan said.“Israeli soldiers were present and together with the settlers began opening fire … It was the settlers who stormed the village, with the intention of killing, vandalising and setting property on fire,” he said.View image in fullscreenFamily members of one of the four Palestinians who died in the clashes mourn outside a hospital in Nablus, in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Jaafar Ashtiyeh/AFP/GettyVideo footage showed an armed settler approaching several Palestinian men near the village and pushing them back with his rifle, after which a scuffle broke out and one of the Palestinian residents reached for the gun. It is unclear who shot the settler, who was named as Benayahu Mellet, 32, a security guard from the nearby Israeli settlement Havat Gilad.The Israeli military said in its statement it had come to the aid of the settlers, who were taking an “unauthorised and uncoordinated hike” in the village. They claimed that in the struggle over the weapon, a Palestinian resident of the village had taken the rifle and opened fire. The military said Maj Yuval Ezra, 27, a battery commander in an artillery regiment, was also killed in the clash. It was not immediately clear who had shot him.The Palestinian health ministry in Ramallah said the four Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces. All four were said to be cousins from the same family and have been named as Farouk, Ibrahim, Jawad and Imran Ramadan.IDF accused of working with settlers after latest deadly West Bank raidRead moreViolence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has flared in recent days and Israeli settlers have called for attacks to “erase” Tell.The far-right and pro-settler Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said the villages of Tell, Iraq Burin and Beit Furik “need to look exactly like the refugee camps in Nablus and Tulkarm”, referring to the mass demolition campaign that displaced tens of thousands in the West Bank towns last year.Itamar Ben-Gvir, Netanyahu’s far-right national security minister, said he would call for the villages in the West Bank to “be treated like Beit Hanoun in Gaza”, which has been devastated in bombing raids, and said he would demand that Israel bomb and bulldoze Palestinian houses.Israel’s defence and finance ministers recently announced plans for new illegal settlements in Gaza, and the country’s military commander for the region has described violent outposts as his “security partners”.All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.Palestinian health officials said they were treating four injured Palestinians, three in critical condition. Israel’s rescue service said two injured Israelis were airlifted out of the West Bank.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahunewsShareReuse this content

title: Indian Cockroach activist ends hunger strike after 26 days as protests spread | India | The Guardian
description: Sonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stall
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Sonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stall
Content: A Cockroach Janta party supporter takes part in a protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenA Cockroach Janta party supporter takes part in a protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/GettyIndiaIndian Cockroach activist ends hunger strike after 26 days as protests spreadSonam Wangchuk secures ‘hard bargain’ with Delhi but talks between government and movement leaders stallHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiFri 24 Jul 2026 10.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 23 Jul 2026 20.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheCockroach activist Sonam Wangchukhas ended a 26-day hunger strike, as youth-led protests continued to erupt across India and leaders of the movement said there was no breakthrough in talks with the government.Wangchuk had been fasting since June in solidarity with the Cockroach Janata party (CJP), a new youth-led movement that has been holding mass protests calling for government accountability and the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over exam paper leaks. The leaks affected 2 million students in May and have been linked to more than a dozen suicides.On Friday morning, Wangchuk posted that he had ended the hunger strike inDelhiafter striking a “hard bargain” with the government.View image in fullscreenSonam Wangchuk posted a video from hospital, saying he had received assurances his conditions would be met by the government.Photograph: Sonam Wangchuk/X/ReutersIn a video from his hospital bed, he said he had been assured in writing that accountability in the examination system would be taken up on the parliament floor and that there would be no cases registered against young people who took part in mass protests in Delhi on Monday.After 26 days without food, Wanghuck appeared weak but in lively spirits. The hunger strike has long been a powerful tool of protest inIndia– repeatedly used by Mahatma Gandhi in the fight for Indian independence. Gandhi’s longest hunger strike was 21 days.After Wangchuk ended his hunger strike, Modi urged the activist to follow doctors’ advice and regain the weight he had lost.The CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, thanked Wangchuk for his “courage and sacrifice” and said the protests would continue until Pradhan resigned. “We won’t let Sonam ⁠sir’s sacrifice go in vain,” Dipke added.On Friday, CJP leaders said the government had agreed to meet them in a “neutral location” to discuss their demands.However, in the aftermath of the meeting, the CJP’s spokesperson, Ashutosh Ranka, said that no resolution had been agreed and the government had requested more time to consider their key demand, the resignation of Pradhan.0:51‘Cockroach’ movement: thousands march in anti-government protest in New Delhi“We hope the government will dismiss Dharmendra Pradhan at the earliest, or that he will resign, so that we can bring ⁠this matter to a conclusion,” said Ranka.The senior government minister JP Nadda confirmed that talks between the two sides would resume on Saturday.Anger, defiance and a hunger strike: India’s Cockroach movement protests – in picturesRead moreAs talks stalled on Friday, thousands of protesters continued to gather at CJP’s protest site in Delhi, in an unprecedented show of support for the dissenting movement. Tens of thousands more are expected to turn up over the weekend.Authorities shut down 17 metro rail stations near the protest site. In a move that was criticised by human rights groups, the government also ordered telecom companies to block mobile internet services in the area. However, it did little to stem the tide of people turning out.“It feels so positive out here,” said Afreen Ali, 21, a student at Delhi university, who stood among the crowds. “I’m feeling so mesmerised to see all my Indian brothers, my sisters, my youth, everyone out here protesting for their rights and for their education. It was the blood of our freedom fighters that brought us independence, and we are here to fight for that country.”Protests erupted across India on Friday as part of the countrywide callout, with demonstrations in Bengalaru, Mumbai, Pune, Thiruvananthapuram and Kolkata.On the ground at India’s ‘Cockroach’ protestThe protests represent the biggest youth challenge to Modi since he came to power in 2014. ‌Opposition parties have echoed the youth movement’s demands and have ‌disrupted the monsoon session of parliamentthat began this week.On Thursday, Modi saidspecial courts would be set up to prosecutethose behind exam paper leaks, his first public response to the crisis. “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future ⁠of our youth!” he posted on social media.But the CJP rejected the proposal, saying what courts do after paper leaks is just one aspect of the problem. “But ​Modi-ji, tell us why are paper leaks happening in this country in the ​first place?” said Ranka.“Fast-track ​courts are set up in this country for every other issue, but whether those fast-track courts have actually solved those issues – you know the answer to that question, ​and so do we.”View image in fullscreenA supporter of India’s Cockroach Janata party (CJP) stands next to graffiti of a cockroach holding a pen at the protest site at Jantar Mantar in Delhi.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersLater in the day, Modi ‌said on social media that the government ​would announce more strict actions against paper leaks at ​a cabinet meeting on Friday.After top Bollywood stars were hit with criticism for staying silent about the protests, some of India’s biggest actors, including Salman Khan, Alia Bhatt and Kareena Kapoor, released social media posts saying it was heartening to see students come together to fight for a cause – though stopped short of criticising the Modi government.Explore more on these topicsIndiaDelhiSouth and central AsiaProtestNarendra ModinewsShareReuse this content

title: The ‘cockroaches’ marching on India’s government – podcast | India | The Guardian
description: South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen on the Cockroach movement – and the students driving India’s biggest protests in years
Author: Helen Pidd
Headline: South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen on the Cockroach movement – and the students driving India’s biggest protests in years
Content: Today in FocusIndiaThe ‘cockroaches’ marching on India’s government – podcastMore ways to listenApple podcastsSpotifyRSS FeedDownloadPresented byHelen PiddwithHannah Ellis-Petersen; produced bySaskia Collette,Alex AtackandBrian McNamara; executive producerEli BlockThu 23 Jul 2026 22.00 EDTShare00:00:0000:00:00South Asia correspondentHannah Ellis-Petersenon the Cockroach movement – and the students driving India’s biggest protests in years‘I’ve never seen this many young people out on the streets,’ saysHannah Ellis-Petersen.For days, tens of thousands of Indians have been marching under the banner of the Cockroach Janta party.The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent tellsHelen Piddthe protesters are reclaiming a slur after India’s chief justice reportedly referred to unemployed young people as ‘cockroaches’ and ‘parasites’. Their anger erupted after leaks of exam papers forced millions of students to resit tests. The scandals have also been linked to dozens of suicides in recent years.Since then, the movement has gathered momentum, with protests against corruption and unemployment, and demands, at the very least, for the resignation of the education minister.It is perhaps the biggest challenge to Narendra Modi’s government in years. But will this week’s concessions be enough to keep the Cockroach movement off the streets?Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAExplore more on these topicsIndiaToday in FocusSouth and central AsiaStudentsProtestNarendra Modi

title: Existing care workers could be exempt from UK’s tough new immigration rules  | Social care | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sector
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sector
Content: Ghanaian nurse Evans Sarbeng with resident Phyllis Padham at St Cecilia’s nursing home in Scarborough.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenGhanaian nurse Evans Sarbeng with resident Phyllis Padham at St Cecilia’s nursing home in Scarborough.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverSocial careExisting care workers could be exempt from UK’s tough new immigration rulesExclusive: Andy Burnham thought to be considering waiving stricter right to remain rules for people already working in the sectorKiran StaceyandPatrick ButlerFri 24 Jul 2026 14.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands of care workers could be exempted from the home secretary’s plans to toughen up the immigration system under proposals being considered by Andy Burnham as he looks for ways to relieve pressure on the social care sector.The prime minister will give a speech next week spelling out his determination to start creating a National Care Service before the next general election as he looks to accelerate the process set up by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.In a highly personal speech, Burnham will talk about his experience of the care system through his father, Roy, who has Alzheimer’s, and announce that he is bringing forwardLouise Casey’s review into the sector, which was due to conclude in 2028.He is now also considering granting widespread exemptions from Shabana Mahmood’s plans to make it harder for people to achieve settled status in the UK.The measure is not likely to be included in next week’s speech but could come later in the year once theHome Officehas considered responses to a public consultation on the issue.One person briefed on the plans said: “Andy is determined to do something about the social care system, and quickly. This is highly personal for him, and he will talk about why he wants to push some of it through before the election, even if that comes at a political price.”Burnham has put reform of the social care system near the top of his list of priorities, having tried and failed to do so as health secretary more than 15 years ago.Hetold broadcastersthis week: “I think it’s about being prepared to grasp the nettle. I’ve got personal experience of the system. My dad has Alzheimer’s, and you see what the staff have to put up with. It’s not their fault. The system’s broken.”He added: “You can’t leave social care like this. And this is part of my criticism of Westminster. It has flinched over the years from these big decisions.”The prime minister has previously argued for replacing inheritance tax with a 10% levy on all estates once a person dies to pay directly for a universal care system, but those proposals were scrapped after the Conservatives labelled them a “death tax”.People inEnglandget state-funded care if they have less than £23,250 in assets, but those with more must pay the entire cost themselves.Meanwhile, social care providers say they are financially stretched and increasingly unable to provide the services for which they have been contracted given the low value of their contracts with local authorities.Many have complained bitterly about the likely impact of Mahmood’s plans to double the length of time it takes migrant workers to qualify for settled status, known as indefinite leave to remain, which could disproportionately affect the care sector.Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, the country’s biggest union, said: “Vulnerable people and those with complex needs won’t get the help they deserve unless ministers focus on recruitment and retention. That means dropping plans to push migrant care workers out of the UK.”Mahmood has said she will consider exemptions to the new ILR (indefinite leave to remain) rules, though carving out those on social care visas would make a significant dent in the numbers affected.The Home Officehas grantedabout 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more coming as their dependants.Burnham is understood to be considering exempting those already in the country from the changes but allowing them to be applied to new entrants.While the changes are not likely to be included in his speech next week, he is set to lay out some short-term fixes to alleviate the burden on the sector.They could include putting more money into the £9bn Better Care Fund, a ringfenced pot of money designed to be used to boost social care where doing so would relieve pressure on the NHS.One option he is understood to be looking at is increasing the fund to offer patients free short-term care once they leave hospital in an attempt to prevent them having to go back into acute care.The prime minister will also leave the door open to levying extra taxes to pay for a new system in the longer term, saying that funding options should be considered as part of Lady Casey’s review.My generation shouldn’t be scared of a care tax – we’re paying one already | Gaby HinsliffRead moreCasey was commissioned by the former health secretary Wes Streeting to publish an interim report this year and a final one in 2028 but those close to the process say she could now simply accelerate her final report instead.Burnhamtold the Guardianlast month he would like to see the review published by the end of the year, though sector experts said this is likely to prove overambitious.Casey has said the UK faces a “moment of reckoning” over its longstanding failure to match sufficient resources and action to the demands of growing numbers of frail elderly people and disabled adults.She has been scathing of the way patients with dementia or Alzheimer’s are undermined by institutional fights over whether a person qualifies for free NHS care or is means-tested and charged for social care, and smoothing the fault lines between the services is expected to be a key focus of the review.Casey will launch a public consultation in the next two weeks calling for a “challenging conversation” with the public this summer.Sources said she wants to answer a series of questions including who should qualify for social care, how far families should provide care for loved ones, and how far individuals should pay for care.Explore more on these topicsSocial careImmigration and asylumEnglandHome OfficeShabana MahmoodPublic services policyAlzheimer'snewsShareReuse
