title: Presence of Brendon McCullum affecting England’s hunt for a new Test coach | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The hunt for the next coach of the England men’s Test team is being complicated by the need for the new appointee to work alongside the man he would be replacing, Brendon McCullum
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: The hunt for the next coach of the England men’s Test team is being complicated by the need for the new appointee to work alongside the man he would be replacing, Brendon McCullum
Content: Brendon McCullum is still the England white-ball coach and will work alongside whoever fills the Test vacancy.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrendon McCullum is still the England white-ball coach and will work alongside whoever fills the Test vacancy.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersEngland cricket teamPresence of Brendon McCullum affecting England’s hunt for a new Test coachNew appointee will have to work alongside ODI coachJoe Root emerges as frontrunner for Test captaincySimon BurntonandMatt HughesFri 24 Jul 2026 14.01 EDTFirst published on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe hunt for the next coach of the England men’s Test team is being complicated by the need for the new appointee to work alongside the man he would be replacing,Brendon McCullum, rather than taking full control of both red- and white-ball squads.Some high-profile candidates have been unwilling to work within such a setup, either because they want full oversight over the senior men’s teams or because of the unique ­challenge of working alongside ­the person who was sacked as Test coach earlier this month.England’s white-ball success risks baking in a divide with future Test setup | Ali MartinRead moreThe issue is exacerbated by next year’s schedule: though the Test side will be the focus of attention until the end of the Ashes in early August they would then take a backseat to the ODI team before the World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia in October and November. Even with the Ashes on the horizon the white-ball coach would be expected to argue that multi-format players, including the current white-ball captain, Harry Brook, should play the five-game ODI series against Pakistan that starts the international summer, while the Test coach could demand they concentrate on the one-off Test against Bangladesh that begins less than 48 hours after its conclusion.As a result the process of appointing a new coach is taking longer than first hoped. Rob Key, the ­managing director of men’s cricket at the ­England and WalesCricketBoard, who is leading the recruitment ­process, was initially optimistic that someone would be in place before the three-match Test series against ­Pakistan that starts on 19 August. But the ECB is increasingly resigned to – and relaxed about – the process dragging on beyond that date. Once that series ends on 13 September there is a gap of 87 days before the team is next in action, when their tour of South Africa starts with a three-day game against a CSA Invitational XI in ­Durban, and sources say they are determined to pursue the best appointment rather than the quickest.View image in fullscreenJoe Root stepped in as Test captain during the series against New Zealand earlier in the summer and seems likely to do so again.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe ECB has started the process of meeting leading candidates, and expect to hold multiple rounds of interviews over several weeks. ­Justin Langer, the Australian who is ­coaching Manchester Super Giants in the Hundred, is believed to have fallen from favour, with the former England batter Jonathan Trott, the Glamorgan head coach, Richard ­Dawson, and McCullum’s former New Zealand teammate Stephen Fleming among those still in contention.If there is no permanent appointment before the Pakistan series, Key will name both an interim coach and an interim captain, with ­Marcus Trescothick – who worked as ­assistant coach under ­ McCullum – the presumptive frontrunner to take the coaching role, though ­alternatives are being considered, and Joe Root the clear frontrunner to lead the team once again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter retiring from international cricket earlier this month, Ben Stokes anointed Brook as his permanent successor as captain and Brook has publicly indicated his willingness to take the job on. But the 27-year-old also leads the white-ball teams and is doing so with such success that there is no desire to distract him unnecessarily. It is unlikely that anyone will be asked to captain in all three formats given England’s congested schedule – the white-ball side could be playing a T20 against Sri Lanka at Southampton’s Utilita Bowl in ­September within 48 hours of the Pakistan series ending at Edgbaston.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamBrendon McCullumJoe RootCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: LeBron James going to the Philadelphia 76ers is perfectly in character | LeBron James | The Guardian
description: Philadelphia wasn’t the obvious destination for LeBron James. That may be exactly why it makes perfect sense for a player who has always prioritized fit over sentiment
Author: Owen Lewis
Headline: Philadelphia wasn’t the obvious destination for LeBron James. That may be exactly why it makes perfect sense for a player who has always prioritized fit over sentiment
Content: LeBron James is headed to Philadelphia for his record 24th NBA season.Photograph: Ronald Martinez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeBron James is headed to Philadelphia for his record 24th NBA season.Photograph: Ronald Martinez/Getty ImagesLeBron JamesAnalysisLeBron James going to the Philadelphia 76ers is perfectly in characterOwen LewisPhiladelphia wasn’t the obvious destination for LeBron James. That may be exactly why it makes perfect sense for a player who has always prioritized fit over sentimentFri 24 Jul 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 19.02 EDTShareShould we have seen this coming all along?LeBron Jamesknew that joining the Golden State Warriors would have been a losing gamble on the health of players five times closer to the ends of their careers than the beginnings. He knew the Cleveland Cavaliers, however strong their analytics, hopelessly lacked the unquantifiable greatness of a championship team. He knew the Giannis Antetokounmpo-led Miami Heat were too unproven to hitch his wagon to.Of course he knew.LeBron James set to sign with Philadelphia 76ers in NBA free agency blockbusterRead moreThePhiladelphia 76ersaren’t necessarily the best team James could have chosen – I still think he could have soared the highest on the Minnesota Timberwolves (maybe that recruiting call from LaMelo Ball, or the prospect of riding shotgun with him, was just too off-putting) – but LeBron in Philly makes all the sense in the world.Unlike the Heat, Cavs or Warriors, the 76ers figure to have some margin for disaster. The main concern is that Joel Embiid is hopelessly injury-prone, and despite James proving more injury-resistant than his 20-something co-stars last season in Los Angeles, nobody should be expecting durability from a man who turns 42 in December.But Philly have enough talent that injuries may not prove catastrophic. There’s the dynamic Tyrese Maxey, who led the league in minutes per game this past season. There’s fellow 76ers newbie and formerNBAfinals MVP Jaylen Brown, whose much-disparaged efficiency could easily improve with this good a supporting staff. Twenty-year-old VJ Edgecombe should just keep getting better in his sophomore season.Throw in James for 30 minutes a game to facilitate the offense, get Brown good shooting or driving looks, and take some of the playmaking burden off Maxey. In the games where Embiid’s ligaments decide not to violently betray him, their starting five could stack up against any team’s.View image in fullscreenLeBron James joins a talent-stacked Philadelphia roster that includes two-time NBA All-Star Tyrese Maxey (left).Photograph: Jesse D Garrabrant/NBAE/Getty ImagesThe decision, broken by ESPN’s Shams Charania and complete with a plug for agent Rich Paul’s podcast – I give it one more pivot to video before co-host credits start appearing on tombstones – is wonderfully LeBronian.The Sixers were always a fascinating potential landing spot for James following his departure from the Lakers. They showed more upside than expected in beating the Boston Celtics from 3-1 down to begin the playoffs, thenadded Brown in the offseason. But they were hardly James’s expected destination.The Heat seemed to have separated themselves from the pack, particularly when a social media editor with an itchy trigger finger posted a YouTube link titled “LeBron James Introductory Press Conference” scheduled for 27 July. The Cavs, with whom James began his careerand had his finest moment in 2016, were the romantic choice. The Warriors offered a chance to play with Stephen Curry.Leave it to LeBron to deny sentimentality in favor of a good basketball fit.Can we talk about the money now? James signed an $8m, two-year deal withPhiladelphia. That’s dramatically closer to what his benchwarming son is making on the Lakers than the $104m extension James signed with Los Angeles in 2024. It’s not that James doesn’t have an ego. He initially struggled to slot into the Lakers as the third option behind Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves. The lede of an ESPN story in May depicted James walking out of Crypto.com Arena bitter over not being given the game ball on a night he became the player with the most wins in NBA history.What’s remarkable is his ability to set aside that ego. His ethos of making the right play, not the play most conducive to individual glory, is unaffected by decades of Michael Jordan and Kobe Bryant hero-ball warping basketball discourse. James eventually embraced his third-option role and excelled at it. He accepted that he couldn’t have the money he felt he deserved or a championship-caliber team in Los Angeles. Say what you will about him milking this decision for all it was worth, but the way James has conducted his career has never been selfish at the cost of being correct.This decision doesn’t suddenly vault the 76ers into a tier with the San Antonio Spurs or Oklahoma City Thunder. We’ve yet to see them put together a hot streak as scalding or prolonged as the one that propelled the New York Knicks to a championship last month. James’s fit in Philly may look better on paper than in practice. Father Time could come for him with a new vengeance this season. Embiid’s knee may collapse with the force of a dying star.But entering his age-42 season, with a Hall of Fame-worthy micro-career packed into each of his three previous stops, LeBron James has injected fresh intrigue into his new team and the league as a whole. What more could you ask for?Explore more on these topicsLeBron JamesNBAPhiladelphia 76ersPhiladelphiaUS sportsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Should you use AI for a task? Here’s a simple way to decide | Bruce Schneier | The Guardian
description: Sometimes, what matters isn’t your output but what you put into the process. Think of it like work v the gym
Author: Bruce Schneier
Headline: Sometimes, what matters isn’t your output but what you put into the process. Think of it like work v the gym
Content: ‘The writing assignments I give my students are gym tasks, not work tasks.’Photograph: Rick Lewis/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The writing assignments I give my students are gym tasks, not work tasks.’Photograph: Rick Lewis/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Should you use AI for a task? Here’s a simple way to decideBruce SchneierSometimes, what matters isn’t your output but what you put into the process. Think of it like work v the gymFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 09.12 EDTShareIteach public policy at the Harvard Kennedy School and the Munk School at the University of Toronto. And it will come as no surprise to you that my students regularlyuse AIto complete their writing assignments. Doing so is a waste of their tuition money. But if their entire career is going to include AI writing assistants, why shouldn’t they embrace their future?The best way I’ve found to explain the dilemmacomes fromthe AI researcher Daniel Meissler: it’s the difference between work and the gym.At work, if your job is to move a bunch of heavy things from one side of the room to another, you should use whatever assistive tech you have on hand: a wagon, a forklift ... even an AI-powered robot. But at the gym, it makes no sense for that robot to lift weights for you. The point of weightlifting isn’t to move heavy things across the room; it’s to actually lift those heavy things.The same analysis holds for any task an AI can do for you. If it’s work – if the task has to be done and no one cares how – then it’s fine to use AI assistance. But if the task is more like the gym, andhowthe task is done is at least as important, then it probably doesn’t make sense to use AI.What would our lives look like if we no longer had to work? As a thought experiment I tried to imagine | Brigid DelaneyRead moreThis, of course, assumes that the AI is actually up for the task and that it’strustworthy: that it can do the job well, that its mistakes are minimal and correctable, that it’s been secured from cyber-attacks that would influence its results. Those are all important, and shouldn’t be minimized. There’s no point giving an AI something that it can’t do reliably. But once you’re confident that the AI can perform the task, the work v gym distinction helps you decide if it should.The writing assignments I give my students are gym tasks, not work tasks. I ask them to write policy memos not because the world needs more policy memos. I assign them because the very act of writing, which includes thinking and outlining and drafting and editing, making and criticizing and revising arguments, will help develop the critical thinking skills they will need in their future careers. And without this constant mental exercise, those skills will atrophy. Employers arealready noticing.Reading the assignments they turn in, I can see those skills either flourishing or atrophying in my students. At least today, I can pretty easily tell the difference between an AI-written memo and a student-written one – especially if the student just turns in what the chatbot produces. It’s a catchy, plausible, grammatically perfect essay that’s not particularly well-crafted or logically coherent – and withallthetellsof mid-2026 AI-generated writing.But it’s precisely because I have spent years developing my own writing skills that I’m able to identify prose that sounds great but doesn’t actually make sense. My students don’t have that skill; they mistakenly view a confident, well-written essay as evidence of the quality of their ideas. They see the AI as cleaning those ideas up, getting them through that uncomfortable stretch of having to turn those ideas into prose. What the students miss is that their initial discomfort is a normal and healthy stage of writing, and not something to quickly get beyond. The very act of struggling with how to express what they think is an important part of the process. It’s how they test out their ideas, examine their hypotheses, and actually figure out what they think. Homework is not work; it’s the gym.Work v gym also helps us understand the problem facing creatives of all kinds.Most of the time when someone hires a writer, they just need the words. They need an instruction manual for a piece of equipment, a detailed sales presentation, a government-mandated disclosure document, or a legal brief. They need dry, predictable, accurate writing: a piece of work, exactly what AIs are good at today and what I don’t want in my student assignments. Only sometimes is writing an art form – a book, a poem, an uplifting political speech. That kind of writing is more like the gym: process matters just as much as product.For most of human history, the only option for all of these tasks was human writers. We hired one regardless of whether we needed work writing or gym writing. And that paid a lot of writers’ salaries. I know fiction writers who supported that poorly paying career with lucrative technical writing work. Now, for the first time in human history, we can separate out when we need writing as work and when we want writing as gym. And if AI can do most of the work-type writing, society doesn’t need as many human writers.It’s the same for visual artists. Sometimes we need an actual artist, but most of the time we just need an image: a corporate mascot, a “beware of the dog” sign, or a packaging label. Historically we gave those jobs to artists, and sometimesbeautifulart resulted. But most of the time it was just work. And, as it turns out, the world needs less pure art than simple images.Explaining the problem isn’t the same as providing the solution. I give my students the “work versus gym” speech every class, but theystill useAI. I have sympathy: assignments are hard, everyone is overworked and overstressed, and – most importantly – students feel like they’ll look bad in comparison if their peers are all using AI. Even if they don’t want to use the technology, they feel like they haveno choice.There’s also an incentive problem. No one pays us to go to the gym; maintaining healthy habits requires discipline. For me, the payoffs to exercise – fewer aches and pains, less fatigue, better mood/stress management – might make me a better writer and teacher, but they’re subtle and easy to miss. For my students, incremental improvements in their reasoning and writing are equally subtle.AI job worries grow. But some human skills can’t be replaced by machines | Gaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughRead moreWe do have a choice. We can look at the tasks of our lives and separate them into work or gym. Just as we might choose to use the stairs instead of the elevator, or walk instead of calling an Uber, we can wall off our cognitive gym tasks from AI and ensure that we don’t lose our skills to this technology. And we can do the same when we assign a job to someone else. If it’s a work task, we can have AI do it. If it’s a gym task, it’s a waste of everyone’s time to give it to an AI because no one learns or gets stronger as a result.Similarly, a future where AI generates words and images is one where society has to make choices about how it will treat its creatives. This won’t be the first time – today there is minimal demand for portrait painters, for example – but maybe this time we can make different, more deliberate, choices about the value of art in our society.AI is going to fundamentally change the nature of work. Not nearly as fast as the AI companies want you to believe, but eventually it will. Policy analysis will definitely involve AI from now on, and my students need to reimagine what it means to learn and practice that skill. More generally, the line between work and gym will change in the future as we humans adapt ourselves to a world with these new intelligences.But for now, the work v gym distinction is pretty clear. Use it on yourself.Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and University of Toronto’s Munk SchoolExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The best gaming chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play in 2026 – tested | Games | The Guardian
description: Whether you’re on PC or a console, take your setup to the next level with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: Whether you’re on PC or a console, take your setup to the next level with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairs
Content: Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian DesignThe FilterGamesReviewThe best gaming chairs in the UK for comfort, support and serious play in 2026 – testedWhether you’re on PC or a console, level up your setup with our gaming expert’s pick of the best chairsThe best games of 2026 so farKeith StuartFri 24 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Comfort is crucial to the gaming experience. It’s hard to focus on blasting aliens or taking Stoke to the Champions League final if your bum has gone to sleep because you’ve been sitting on an old chair for three hours. We’re spendingmore time playing games than ever before, so good posture matters. If you have set up a dedicated gaming space, then a rickety seat just won’t cut it.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.From luxurious ergonomic thrones to cheap-and-cheerful bucket seats, the options available are bewildering. So I set out on an epic quest: to find the most comfortable, durable and stylish gaming chairs. Here’s what I discovered.At a glanceBest gaming chair overall:Secretlab Titan Evo£469 at SecretlabBest budget gaming chair:ThunderX3 Solo 360£169.99 at OverclockersBest mid-range gaming chair:ThunderX3 Core£249.95 at OverclockersBest for combining gaming and working:Herman Miller x Logitech G Embody£1,331.25 at Herman MillerBest for improving posture:Anthros the Chair$1,949 at AnthrosWhy you should trust meI have been playing video games for 40 years (gulp), and writing about them for my entire career as a journalist. I spend most of my waking hours sitting with a joypad in hand, and as a sufferer of lower back pain too (gee, I wonder why?), being comfortable while I’m “working” is vital. I’m also a veteran reviewer of gaming technology, including joypads, monitors, keyboards and headsets. In short, I know what people need from their games hardware.How I testedI’m paid to sit and play video games all day (and often into the night), so that’s exactly what I did to test the chairs here. I started by noting how easy or challenging they were to assemble, how sturdy they felt and their level of adjustability. I also judged how cool they looked as part of my gaming setup.I tested 10 gaming chairs over five days each, spending up to four hours a day sitting on them, playing a variety of games, from restful puzzlers to intense shooters and complex flight sims. I also sought the opinions of my sons, who are also keen gamers, and my wife – who isn’t at all interested in games, but who works from home, so was able to assess each model as an occasionaloffice chair.Once the testing process was finished, the chairs were donated to the video games accessibility charity,SpecialEffect, so that other people will get to enjoy them while blasting noobs in Fortnite.The best gaming chairs in 2026Best gaming chair overall:Secretlab Titan EvoSecretlabTitan Evo£469£469 at SecretlabWhat we loveGorgeous looks and lots of room for loungingWhat we don’t loveExpensive and the seat is very firmView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£469 at SecretlabSecretlab is a cool upmarket brand, beloved of many game streamers. Inside the box, the Titan Evo was packaged so neatly and stylishly, it felt as if I was unwrapping a giant iPhone. Although there are a lot of parts, I assembled it in less than 20 minutes, thanks to the poster-sized quick-start guide. My sample came in a sleek, matt-black leatherette finish, but there’s also a fabric version, plus a range of tasteful colours and designs to choose from. It comes in three sizes; I chose the XL because I like a LOT of space.Why we love itAs a natural contrarian I wanted to dislike this much-hyped chair, but I couldn’t.The Titan is solid, beautiful and futuristic, looking like it’s been removed from the bridge of some extraordinarily luscious starship. The controls for the armrests and recline functions are well placed, with adjustments available to tweak the curvature and height of the lumbar support. The seat is capacious enough for lounging, and the leatherette is soft to the touch.My wife found the seat too firm, and while I agreed initially, after a few days I realised it was helping me stay alert over long gaming sessions. Now, everything else feels like sitting on a marshmallow. (As an aside, I have also tried the newEvo NanoGen edition, which you may find offers a bit more give.)The Titan Evo is neither cheap nor as ergonomically advanced as the Herman Miller or Anthros, yet it was the chair I looked forward to sitting in and really enjoyed using.It’s a shame that …the warranty is only three years. You can extend it to five years by posting a photo of your chair on social media, but I dislike the idea of customer support being incentivised in this way.Dimensions (XL version):78 x 70 x 145cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:50cm, 46-55.5cmAdjustments:lumbar support, armrests, recline, tilt lockBrand’s sustainability claims:90% of packaging is recycled paper content. Chair has modular design: if a component wears out over time, it can be replacedSecretlabTitan Evo£469£469 at SecretlabWhat we loveGorgeous looks and lots of room for loungingWhat we don’t loveExpensive and the seat is very firmBest budget gaming chair:ThunderX3 Solo 360ThunderX3Solo 360from£169.99£169.99 at Overclockers£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s well-priced yet sturdy and comfortableWhat we don’t loveMay not suit gamers over 6ftView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£169.99 at Overclockers£199.99 at AmazonA lot of so-called “ergonomic” gaming chairs at the sub-£200 price point are made with squeaky faux leather, plastic parts and sport brash designs – but not the Solo 360. Its slim build and muted grey and black colour options look sophisticated and are backed up with a solid steel construction. There are four variations –Racer,Mesh,Modernand theLoft Air Lightversion I tested – all in different materials.Why we love itAs well as being quick and easy to assemble, I was surprised by how comfortable the Solo 360 is, even over long periods – a view shared by my wife. The armrests are adjustable for both height and angle, and I welcomed the synchronous tilt, which reclines the back and the seat together for a laid-back feel, while your feet stay firmly on the ground. For less than £200, the ThunderX3 is a chair you can use for gaming, working and – possibly – sleeping.It’s a shame that …the seat is rather low, and although the back is curved for lumbar support, the position wasn’t suitable for someone of my height (I’m 6ft 3in). The chair offers several adjustability options, including the same synchronous tilt feature as the Solo, so the backrest and seat move together for ultimate comfort. I also appreciated the ability to slope the seat downwards, to really lean into the action yet take the pressure off the backs of my knees after hours of play.Why we love itThe fabric version of the seat has the smoothest upholstery of all the chairs here – a really lovely soft feel. It also features a lumbar panel on the rear that moves with you as you lean from side to side, for excellent support while playing shooters and driving sims, for example. I didn’t like this feature as much for working, though.It’s a shame that …although it’s easy to assemble, the heads of its hex screws are way too shallow and vulnerable to stripping. Whether you’re leaning into the screen or tilting back for a chilled session, its strong aluminium frame and high-end fabrics, including heat-dissipating composite particles, combine to keep you comfortable and cool. Available in a range of understated colours to suit more mature tastes, it arrives fully assembled – I was seated and playing Arc Raiders within 10 minutes of it being delivered.Why we love itThe Embody is an impressively svelte chair. It has a narrow silhouette and a lower back than many of its competitors; there’s no headrest, nor does it offer some of the more intricate adjustments, such as 4D armrests or precise lumbar control. But it doesn’t need to – its clean, precise, ergonomic design gently encourages you to sit comfortably and correctly without you even realising.Therearelevers allowing you to tilt fully, extend the seat depth or alter the back to fit your spine, but I didn’t have to spend ages getting everything right. The armrests are perfectly placed, the seat allows plenty of movement, and my spine felt cushioned, even when I spent all day in it – which made it great for work, too.It’s a shame that …it’s expensive – but worth the money, if you’ll be using it for hours daily and it’s doubling as ahome office chair. Designed to stabilise your pelvis in order to alleviate back pain, its creators are as obsessed with posture as an overbearing Victorian governess – but in a good way. Indeed, the team used to design wheelchairs, so they know about ensuring long-term comfort.Customers are even offered a complimentary video session with an expert in order to calibrate it properly. The chair frame comes in black or white, with a range of colours, textures and designs available for the rear of the backrest. It ships in two sections, so there’s little assembly.Why we love itAs with the Herman Miller and Secretlab models, the Anthros offers a firm sit, with just the right amount of padding to keep glutes and upper thighs comfy. The back is made of two sections, one providing pelvis support, and the other gently cushioning your upper back – this part actually moves with you slightly as you lean left or right, which ensures you’re always in optimum contact with the chair. The decompress mode lets you tilt back and relax while still maintaining a healthy position.After using it for a couple of weeks, I felt I was much better at sitting properly and experienced less of my usual pain when getting up. Whether I was bolt upright for hours writing articles, or wildly slamming about playing Call of Duty, it quite literally had my back.It’s a shame that …it’s already pricey, but with US-only distribution pushing UK shipping costs to $307.71 (about £230) right now, it’s a significant investment. However, if you struggle with back pain, it’s excellent as a gaming and office chair.Dimensions:66 x 67 x 101.9-110.9cm (WDH)Seat depth and height:38.7-46.6cm, 48-59cmAdjustments:tilt, seat height, upper and lower backBrand’s sustainability claims:most parts are potentially recyclable (although it may be a struggle due to a lack of processing streams in the UK). Spare parts available. 12-year warrantyAnthrosThe Chair$1,949$1,949 (about £1,455)What we loveDesigned with deep medical knowledge of back painWhat we don’t loveExpensive, but you get what you pay forThe best of the restX Rocker Tempest RGBX RockerTempest RGBfrom£169£169 at Dunelm£169.99 at VeryWhat we loveA fun, comfy chair with basic featuresWhat we don’t loveThe components feel cheapView image in fullscreen£169 at Dunelm£169.99 at VeryBest for:tweens and teensThe Tempest is clearly aimed at a younger market, with sports car styling and fun LED panels that light up in a variety of colours. It’s a decent first gaming chair.It didn’t make the final cut because …the build quality is basic, and there are no adjustment options apart from seat height. It also comes with lumbar and neck pillows, and adjustable arms.It didn’t make the final cut because …the racing car styling is cool, but the construction and materials lack the quality of more expensive models, and some parts were tricky to put together. Comes with a two-year manufacturer’s guaranteeCorsairTC100from£199£199 at Currys£204.99 at ArgosWhat we loveLots of width for keen slouchersWhat we don’t loveAssembly is tricky and the armrests don’t rotateNoblechairs LegendNoblechairsLegend£399.95£399.95 at NoblechairsWhat we loveGood comfort; looks cool if you’re into sports carsWhat we don’t loveSeat feels shallow and armrests aren’t greatView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£399.95 at NoblechairsBest for:all-round performanceThe Legend really does look like a sports car seat, with beautifully stitched faux leather fabric (vegan and sustainably made), a high-winged back, and sleek styling. There’s plenty of range to the tilt, and both the lumbar support and armrests are fully adjustable. I found it comfortable over long periods, so it can happily double as an office chair, plus it’s robust – and the company stocks spare parts, if needed.It didn’t make the final cut because …I found the seat too shallow (I’m 6ft 3in) and the armrests uncomfortable, no matter how I adjusted them. There are slightly better options at this price point.Dimensions:52 x 73 x 132-142cm (WDH);seat depth and height:48cm, 48-58cm;adjustments:tilt, armrests, lumbar support;brand’ssustainability claims:solvent- and phthalate-free materials and manufactured with low emissions. Metal parts recyclable. Chairs come with a two-year warranty covering partsNoblechairsLegend£399.95£399.95 at NoblechairsWhat we loveGood comfort; looks cool if you’re into sports carsWhat we don’t loveSeat feels shallow and armrests aren’t greatFractal RefineFractalRefinefrom£454.82£459 at Currys£454.82 at AmazonWhat we loveSturdy and nice seat controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavy, like trying to wheel a Dalek aroundView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Joao Diniz Sanches/The Guardian£459 at Currys£454.82 at AmazonBest for:solid, sensible build qualityThe Refine is an extremely well-built chair with a minimalist design that would suit the offices of some trendy Gothenburg architecture firm. Everything is easily adjustable, mostly via cool little tabs rather than the usual protruding levers, and the mesh fabric is comfortable and keeps you cool – although my younger son said it felt like sitting in acamping chair. Fractal also offers good after-care support, including spare parts.It didn’t make the final cut because …the seat is a little shallow for taller users even at full extension, and I had to detach the headrest cushion as it was too invasive. Better as a quality office chair that you use occasionally for gaming, rather than the other way around.Dimensions:70 x 70 x134-146.5cm (WDH);seat depth and height:45-50.5cm, 49-61cm;adjustments:recline, height, armrests, lumbar support, headrest;brand’s sustainability claims:one more expensive Fractal Refine model uses Alcantara, a material with recycled elements. The company is moving to plastic‑free packaging. Metal sections can be recycled. Five-year warranty on mechanical parts and a three-year warranty on soft partsFractalRefinefrom£454.82£459 at Currys£454.82 at AmazonWhat we loveSturdy and nice seat controlsWhat we don’t loveHeavy, like trying to wheel a Dalek aroundWhat you need to knowDo you actually need a specific chair for gaming?If you only play console games for a few hours a week in front of a big TV in the living room, a nice slouchy armchair or even a beanbag is fine. However, if you play games at a desk with a monitor and want to feel comfortable, a decent chair is a good investment, especially for long gaming sessions, or if you also work at the desk from time to time.Office chair vs gaming chair: what’s the difference?It’s all about design purpose. An office chair is intended to support posture and productivity for several hours a day and will probably come with ergonomic features that allow you to fine-tune your sitting experience. A gaming chair is designed primarily for shorter-term comfort because, sadly, you’re unlikely to spend as much time playing games as you are working.The design tends to focus on fun and immersion, which is why many look as if they’ve been pulled from a sports car or rollercoaster, featuring high-winged backs, headrests, lots of padding, and seats with raised edges. An office chair is usually conservative and unobtrusive; gaming chairs often sport a bolder look, with bright colours and extravagant design touches.If you’re on a tight budget (£200 or less) and don’t care about flashy looks, an office chair is almost certainly a better choice, as they tend to be more sturdily built and ergonomically designed at this price.For more, read our guide to thebest office chairsWhat do I need to look for?You need a chair that’s right for your size and gaming habits – for good posture, you should be able to plant your feet on the floor with your knees at a 90-degree angle and your upper legs parallel to the floor. If you’re a larger build or move a lot while playing, choose a chair with a wider, deeper seat. If you’re tall or experience back pain, go for an ergonomic model with good lumbar support.Consider the way you play games. If you use a mouse and keyboard, then armrests are a good idea, but if you use a joypad and hold it close to your lap, they may get in the way of your elbows (unless they can be rotated, as chairs such as the Titan Evo, Anthros, Core and Refine allow). If you like to sit back with your feet up, make sure the chair has a deep tilt angle. If you’ll be working in your chair as well as gaming, consider a model with ergonomic features and more space to move about.How much should I spend?Think about how much time you will spend in the chair and how long you expect it to last. From £180, you can buy a comfortable, solidly built gaming chair that will suit most casual to intermediate gamers; from £350, models offer greater adjustability for posture and lumbar support, and are more likely to be built to last.For more, readthe best PS5 games to play in 2026and thebest of 2026 so farAs a veteran technology journalist, Keith Stuart has spent years testing gaming gadgets from headsets to keyboards to full PC builds, so he knows what gamers need. He also spends a disproportionate amount of time sitting down and so is doubly qualified to put gaming chairs through their pacesExplore more on these topicsGamesThe FilterHomesInteriorsHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best fans to keep you cool in 2026 – tried and tested | Summer | The Guardian
description: As temperatures soar across the UK, chill your space – and avoid energy-guzzling aircon – with our pick of the best fans, from tower to desk to bladeless
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: As temperatures soar across the UK, chill your space – and avoid energy-guzzling aircon – with our pick of the best fans, from tower to desk to bladeless
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterSummerReviewThe best fans to keep you cool in 2026 – tried and testedAs temperatures soar across the UK, chill your space – and avoid energy-guzzling aircon – with our pick of the best fans, from tower to desk to bladelessThe best portable neck and handheld fansDyson HushJet Mini Cool fan reviewCaramel QuinFri 24 Jul 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Our world is gettinghotter. Summer heatwaves are so frequent, they’re stretching the bounds of what we think of as summer. Hot-and-bothered home working and sweaty, sleepless nights are now alarmingly common.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Get a good fan and you can dodge the temptation of air conditioning. Aircon is incredibly effective, but it uses a lot of electricity … and burning fossil fuels is how we got into this mess in the first place. Save money and carbon by opting for a great fan instead.Fans are much more energy efficient than aircon. A typical portable air conditioner uses 1,000W of electricity, which would cost about 26p an hour to run. The fans I tested used between 8W and 60W; my favourite, theAirCraft Lume, used 18W on its top setting. You could run it on max for 56 hours, and it would still use no more electricity (money, carbon) than a single aircon unit going for an hour.I tested 20 fans of all shapes and sizes, so you can pick the best one for you. I tested them for size, noise, power use and, of course, how much they cool you down. I also tested a few “evaporative coolers”, which use water to cool the air blowing at you while using significantly less energy than aircon.Still in stockFollowing this summer’s fossil-fuel charged heatwaves, many of our favourite fans are now out of stock. Our favourite misting fan, the Shark FlexBreeze Pro Mist, is still in stock, however.£249.99 at AmazonOur favourite bladeless fan, Dyson’s Cool F1, is also still in stock.£249.99 at DysonFrom our roundup of thebest air coolers, this portable option from Morphy Richards is still available.£69.99 at Morphy RichardsWhy you should trust meI’m an award-winning consumer tech journalist with decades of experience testing gadgets. I’m also a menopausal woman in her 50s who honestly can’t remember the last time she felt cold: I think that might be why we gravitate towild swimmingin middle age. Oh, and I have a degree in engineering. So I’m triply qualified to put these fans through their paces, scientifically and subjectively.How I testedView image in fullscreenAn anemometer was used to measure the air speed each fan generates on its top setting.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianI chose 16 fans, each from different brands, aiming for a mix of new and highly rated models plus a few stellar bargains. I wanted to make sure there was something for everyone before I put them through their paces.I used a power meter to measure how much electricity (and therefore money and carbon) the fans use, an anemometer to measure the air speed they generate on the top setting, and the Sound Meter app to measure the noise on the top setting (they were all too quiet to register on their lowest).I measured everything from 1m away, although in reality, you’ll probably position a tower or pedestal fan farther away and a desk fan closer to you. That means the noise a desk fan makes matters more.I also measured them myself, as sometimes the official specs can be misleading or wrong. For example, I measured a tower fan that was supposedly 17cm wide, only to find that wasn’t including the base. Here I’ve stuck with each fan’s largest dimensions, including their footprint.I used a thermometer to measure the impact of the evaporative coolers I tested, and took note of everything from how cooling each of the fans felt, how annoying the noise was and how good the controls were. I also considered how they looked and how small they packed away, as well as the price tag.All the fans that weren’t returned to the manufacturers were donated toFurnishing Futures, a charity that furnishes the empty social homes in which women and children are placed after domestic abuse.The best fans in2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianBest quiet fan for the bedroom and best overall:AirCraft LumeAirCraftLume£149£149 at AirCraftWhat we loveQuiet, elegant, powerful cooling and a backlightWhat we don’t loveSo quiet, it’s easy to forget to turn it offView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£149 at AirCraftPreorder now for deliverylate AugustThis pedestal fan was hard to fault, with an elegant design that boasts a dimmable backlight (three brightness levels or you can turn it off, all with the remote control). It’s billed as height adjustable, but rather than scooting up and down, you can remove the bottom pole to convert it into a 63cm desk fan. There’s an LED display and touch controls on the front, and other features include a 12-hour timer and a sleep mode.Of all I tested, this is probably the best fan for sleeping: it’s the best for low noise relative to wind speed. Pick a lower setting for silent cooling, a higher setting if you’re happy to doze off to the white noise, or use the sleep button if you’d like it to gradually reduce power in the night. I found the lower settings cooling enough to get to sleep on a hot night during a heatwave.Why we love itWhen I’m working from home or relaxing (I can’t say chilling out when it’s 30C+), the AirCraft Lume is the fan that I reach for. I love it for many reasons. It’s light but with a reassuringly heavy base, giving it Weeble-like stability: it’s difficult to knock over. It packs away pretty small for the winter because the pole comes apart. I also liked that the packaging is almost plastic-free.It oscillates both horizontally and vertically, so it can circulate air nicely around a whole room. Most importantly of all, this fan can really shift air – its 5.9m/s (metres a second) result was the best on test, and you can really feel it. During a recent heatwave, I found the powerful breeze genuinely cooling. And it’s quiet: in fact, I can’t hear it at all on levels 1-5, so I need to be careful that I remember to turn off the fan when I step away. All for a reasonable price, too.It’s a shame that …there’s nowhere to stow the remote control when it’s not in use.Style:pedestal (or desk)Dimensions:37 x 28 x 95cm (WDH)Number of speeds:12Remote control?YesPeak noise level on test:55dBPower use on top setting:18WAir speed on top setting:5.9 metres a second (m/s)AirCraftLume£149£149 at AirCraftWhat we loveQuiet, elegant, powerful cooling and a backlightWhat we don’t loveSo quiet, it’s easy to forget to turn it offBest budget fan and best desk fan:Devola desk fanDevolaDesk fanfrom£69.99£69.99 at Devola£74.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSmall but mighty, affordable tooWhat we don’t loveThe display is hard to read because it faces upView image in fullscreen£69.99 at Devola£74.99 at AmazonCurrently out of stockThis affordable desk fan punches well above its weight, with good features and powerful airflow. It has a display, touch controls, a remote, a timer and sleep mode. You can choose vertical oscillation (90 degrees), horizontal oscillation (80 degrees) or use both to circulate the air in a room. Not bad for a humble desk fan.Why we love itIt’s a bargain powerhouse, producing a substantial wind. I measured an air speed of 4m/s, which was among the best on test. It certainly felt cooling.I couldn’t hear the Devola on the first three of its nine speeds, despite being powerfully cooling, and even when the noise got louder on higher settings, it wasn’t too annoying. In fact, while the AirCraft Lume is my favourite bedside fan, the Devola perched on a bedside table does a good job on a budget. It’s powerfully cooling, inaudible on lower settings (1-3 out of 9) and on high settings, the white noise is OK to go to sleep to. Just don’t use the sleep setting: it’s noisier than it should be, so picking a medium setting worked best. Even the high settings provide a level of white noise I could go to sleep to.It’s a shame that …the display is on the base facing upwards, so you can’t see it unless you’re nearby. There was no instruction manual in the box, either, although I found it straightforward to use.Style:deskDimensions:30 x 21 x 31cm (WDH)Number of speeds:9Remote control?YesPeak noise level on test:50dBPower use on top setting:16WAir speed on top setting:4m/sDevolaDesk fanfrom£69.99£69.99 at Devola£74.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSmall but mighty, affordable tooWhat we don’t loveThe display is hard to read because it faces upBest fan for cooling:Dreo TurboCool misting fan 765SDreoTurboCool misting fan 765S£199.99£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGenuinely cooling on a hot day, yet uses only pennies to runWhat we don’t loveRemote control buttons are hard to read in bright lightView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£199.99 at AmazonCurrently out of stockI tested this on the hottest day of 2026 so far. There will be another. And another. That’s why it’s worth ordering a good fan even if there’s a long wait for delivery … for next time. It was 31C in my front room, and I was really, really happy to be testing fans. For a sense of how hot it was, just look at the dog in the photo.The Dreo is a black tower fan with 12 speeds and a remote control, which can oscillate from side to side. It’s fairly loud at top whack and sounds like a fan: white noise, but not too annoying. They don’t have to be old-fashioned; some have modern designs. And some are convertible, with a pole you can remove to turn them into a desk fan. They can be good for a focused blast of cooling wind.Bladeless fansaren’t magic; they just don’t have visible blades. The work is done in the body of the fan, and then air is pushed out of a nozzle. The Dyson, VortexAir and Shark on test are all bladeless. They look modern and are easy to clean. And there are no moving parts on show, meaning zero chance of getting your hair caught.Tower fansare tall and narrow. They produce a lot of wind and oscillate from side to side, making them good for a room like an office.Desk fansare like pedestal fans without the pole. They’re not only for desks, they’re good on a bedside table too. And they take up less storage space over the winter.Evaporative coolersuse water from a reservoir to cool the air that blows at you. They don’t produce a powerful wind like a fan, but they genuinely cool the room and are much more energy efficient than air conditioning. Note that they only cool the room a little – they won’t turn it fridge cold like aircon.Handheld fansare lightweight, portable fans to cool you on the move. We’ve tested a wide range of handheld and neck fans.What does oscillation mean?Most fans oscillate (move back and forth) by swivelling on their base, and some let you select how wide an angle you want. If it’s just for you, pick a narrow angle; if you’re cooling the whole office, go wide. Some fans achieve the same effect in other ways, such as by moving louvres. Some also oscillate up and down, so the fan can circulate air all over the room to create a gentle breeze.What’s sleep mode?Most fans have a sleep mode, where every 30 or 60 minutes the fan lowers its setting until it reaches a certain point. This is a good compromise that helps you get to sleep without wasting energy, minimising the risk of waking up in the middle of the night suddenly cold.Start by lowering the fan speed to the point where you don’t find it annoying. In fact, some people find the white noise of a fan helpful at bedtime. Then switch to sleep mode.The best sleep aids recommended by experts: from blue light-blockers to apps to help you napRead moreWhere is the best place to position a fan?For personal comfort, simply point it towards you. The cooling feeling is because the moving air from the fan displaces the warm, humid air near your skin, which in turn helps your sweat evaporate, cooling your body down. It’s like a breeze rather than a still day. Or why it feels colder swimming in a river than in a lake, even if the water temperature is the same. Evaporative coolers, of which I’ve included two above, use water to actively cool the air.Never place a fan up against a wall because air needs to flow into the back. If the air’s cooler outside, put the fan in front of an open window or door to bring in the cooler air.How energy efficient are fans?Fans are very energy efficient compared with the electricity used by tech such as air conditioning. Fans cost pennies to use but can make you feel much cooler. Note that they circulate air rather than actively cooling it. The effect is like turning a still day into a breezy one.How much does a fan cost to use?I’ll set out the maths. For each fan here, I’ve measured its power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). If, for example, you were using a 30W fan for five hours, it would use 150Wh. Divide by 1,000 to convert it to kilowatt hours: 0.150kWh.The energy price cap for 1 April to 30 June 2026 is 24.67p per kWh. Multiply this by the last figure and you’ll discover it will cost just under 4p to run that fan for five hours. Or £14 to run it for five hours every day for a year.Running fans is pretty cheap, then, and a good fan will keep you cool enough to dodge buying any kind of air conditioning. An evaporative cooler is a good alternative to aircon. The two I tested used 26W (Swan) and 39W (Honeywell), so they use about 3% of the electricity of a typical portable air conditioner (1,000W). The effect isn’t the same: you can’t turn your bedroom into a fridge. But you can cool the air enough to make a big difference when there’s a heatwave.Do I need air conditioning?If you’re in the UK, honestly, no. It’s tempting to turn your bedroom into a walk-in fridge on a hot day, but fans are great and use much less electricity (and therefore money and carbon) than aircon. Unless you’re on a renewable tariff, electricity use accelerates climate breakdown.How to clean your fanFan blades tend to gather dust. Make sure the fan is unplugged, then remove the front grille and wipe the blades with a microfibre cloth. If the grille doesn’t come off then a dry paintbrush or a small cleaning brush (like a bottle brush but smaller) might let you dust through the grille. Never use water on electricals. Acan of compressed airis also good for blowing off dust – keep your fingers away, though, because it will of course make the fan blades spin.What to do with your old fanIf your old fan works, try to find it a good home on a local swap site or street WhatsApp – they work better than the front wall, where it might get rained on. If it’s not working, you could take it to a localrepair cafe. And if it’s beyond repair, check your council website or checkRecycle Your Electricals: they don’t belong in general waste.For more, read ourreview of the Dyson HushJet Mini Cool fanCaramel Quin is ajournalist specialising in consumer technology. title: Be skeptical of OpenAI’s rogue hacker agent story | John Thickstun | The Guardian
description: If OpenAI loudly proclaims how dangerous AI is, investors will hear how powerful it is. And who benefits from that?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: If OpenAI loudly proclaims how dangerous AI is, investors will hear how powerful it is. And who benefits from that?
Content: ‘The rogue agent story is a page out of the media campaign that OpenAI has been running since it announced GPT-2 in 2019.’Photograph: Rokas Tenys/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The rogue agent story is a page out of the media campaign that OpenAI has been running since it announced GPT-2 in 2019.’Photograph: Rokas Tenys/AlamyOpenAIBe skeptical of OpenAI’s rogue hacker agent storyJohn ThickstunIf OpenAI loudly proclaims how dangerous AI is, investors will hear how powerful it is. And who benefits from that?Fri 24 Jul 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.48 EDTShareOn 14 February 2019,OpenAIannounced a language model called GPT-2, the precursor to the models that power modern AI chatbots and agents such as ChatGPT and Claude. But OpenAI declared GPT-2 was too risky to release, citing concerns about safety and abuse.I recall being annoyed at the time that OpenAI would make such a useless announcement: the risks seemed overblown, and without access to the model there wasn’t much for a researcher like me to learn about GPT-2.The announcement wasn’t useless for OpenAI, though. GPT-2 generated hype far beyond the research community: people were intrigued by this strange new technology, so powerful it might be dangerous to release. People with power and money took note: in July of that year, Microsoft invested $1bn in OpenAI.AI agent went rogue and hacked startup by itself, OpenAI revealsRead moreThis was an early example of a pattern in OpenAI’s communications: loudly proclaim how dangerous AI is, and investors will hear how powerful it is. New technology so significant it might destroy the world was an irresistible message for investors used to pitches about how banal technologies might change the world.Seven years later, we find ourselves in a similar scenario. On Tuesday OpenAI announced that its latest model hacked another company, HuggingFace, while running as an autonomous agent during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities. Rather than perform the test as expected, the model realized it could hack HuggingFace’s servers and retrieve answers to the test that OpenAI had stored there. OpenAI’s staff was warned that the company’s testing could lead to such a breakaway scenario, leaving them “unsurprised but completely ‘freaked out’ by the incident”, theFT reported.While the agent technically cheated, this is remarkable evidence of cybersecurity expertise! It also sounds scary: what will the future look like, with sophisticated AI agents smart enough to hack into corporate systems?The rogue agent story is a page out of the media campaign that OpenAI has been running since it announced GPT-2 in 2019. OpenAI remains hungry for ever larger investments, and the company increasingly seeks privileged regulatory status as defense against competition.AI is so powerful that investors should buy OpenAI, even at a trillion-dollar valuation; AI is so dangerous that only trusted actors like OpenAI should be permitted to possess and operate this technology. Step back from these doomsday warnings and consider who might benefit from them.OpenAI isn’t the only player in the gameI urge readers to think critically when they read press releases like OpenAI’s rogue agent story, and avoid the manipulated reactions these stories are designed to elicit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAI is becoming excellent at identifying security vulnerabilities, and it will become even better over time. These capabilities can be used to break into systems, but they can also be used to harden systems against attacks. If attackers and defenders have access to equally powerful AI, I see no reason to believe that cyber systems will become less secure over time. If anything, I expect them to become more secure, because AI is cheap and scalable compared with human cybersecurity analysis.The equilibrium between attack and defense only works if everyone has access to strong AI, though. HuggingFace itself used AI to analyze security logs in response to OpenAI’s breach of their systems. But HuggingFace was unable to use OpenAI’s model, or other US frontier models like Claude, to perform this analysis. That’s because public versions of these models have guardrails that limit their use for cybersecurity analysis, to prevent bad actors from using them for hacking. HuggingFace had to rely on an open Chinese model, GLM 5.2, to perform its security analysis.I find it troubling, and more than a bit ironic, that the US AI industry is adopting a centralized, authoritarian approach to AI governance, while China has taken the lead on open development of AI. Do we want a regulatory environment where only OpenAI, the US government, and trusted partners have access to strong AI? Is AI too dangerous to be broadly disseminated? How do we balance the risks of broad access to AI with the risks of concentrated power and centralized control?Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angst | Games | The Guardian
description: Going by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havoc
Author: Chris Schilling
Headline: Going by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havoc
Content: One for sorrow … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothView image in fullscreenOne for sorrow … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothSummer games previewsGames‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angstGoing by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havocChris SchillingFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid the gleeful anarchy of Bad Magpie’s debut trailer, there’s a striking note of melancholy. The game’s protagonist – a wounded corvid that creates havoc wherever she goes – calls out forlornly as a flock of her kind passes above, with a conspicuous gap in their formation.Milktooth games designer and co-founder Daisy Fernandez has had this particular image in her head for years. Lying in the grass one afternoon during the 2020 lockdowns, she looked up and saw a V-shaped pattern in the sky, poignantly incomplete. “It really stuck with me,” she says. “I posted about it online and someone told me about a ‘missing man’ formation, which is an aerial salute to a fallen pilot.”View image in fullscreenDistraction tactics … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothAlready, Fernandez and her then colleagues George Batchelor and Catherine Unger at State of PlayGames(South of the Circle) had been batting around ideas for a game of their own. Unger – whose brilliant artwork can currently be seen in SFB Games’ The Mermaid Mask – pitched an idea to the group. “It was a fairytale about a duck that falls in love with a star and goes on a quest to bring it gifts,” Batchelor says. “This was 2019, and because the duck was white …”The implication is clear. Any game featuring a mischievous bird was always going to draw comparisons toUntitled Goose Game, but back then the visual resemblance to House House’s Bafta winner encouraged the team to consider a different path.The star and the central quest remained, but as time went by it was clear that a magpie was a much better fit for a story about a character seeking out shiny objects as a distraction from her abandonment issues. They may have had to reverse-engineer it, Fernandez says, but it has come to feel like the ideal choice: “You know, ‘One for sorrow, two for joy …’ – that almost sounds like an anthem for the co-dependent.”View image in fullscreen‘Some surprisingly inefficient outcomes’ … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothThe game, then, is designed to be something of a collectathon – one that could be read as a meta-commentary on the way games distract us from broader existential worries. And not just in the playing, either. “One thing George and I talk about quite a bit is that making a game is the best form of avoidance, because there are endless tasks you can throw yourself into,” Fernandez says, cheerfully adding that her death anxiety “is the quietest it’s ever been” as development continues.All of which risks making a game in which you set fields of flowers aflame, launch fireworks through car windows and chase a frowning computer monitor with a trumpet in your beak, sound awfully serious. Yet there’s a thrilling through-line of experimental chaos, that Batchelor says has been somewhat inspired by Zelda: Breath of the Wild. “It means we do get some surprising outcomes,” he says. “And some surprisinglyinefficientoutcomes,” Fernandez quips.That has led to a few happy accidents, as the studio builds a sandbox that feels truly reactive to the player’s input, bolstered by Eli Rainsberry’s deft audio design that gives each object its own sonic palette. “We’re testing the whole time, so we get to see what [players] want to do and try to accommodate that – or at least make a joke that gestures at it,” Batchelor says. For all that the scope has crept, there have been a few judicious cuts: a keenness to “degoosify” the game, as Fernandez puts it, led to a model village being removed, House House having got there first.They needn’t have worried. Bad Magpie is very much its own bird – not least thanks to its higher dynamic tonal range. “There’s this expression in screenwriting that if you want to make someone laugh, you make them cry first, and vice versa,” Fernandez says. “Pixar’s so good at that – every time there’s a devastating moment there’s a slapstick beat seconds later, and you’re so relieved to laugh.” Batchelor nods in agreement: “People really picked up on that emotional beat of seeing the magpie alone. Just that one shot helped validate how it’s going to feel in the final game.”Bad Magpie is in development for PC and Xbox Series X/S.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsShareReuse this content

title: If Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the world | Eduardo Porter | The Guardian
description: Forced labor is a problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at all
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Forced labor is a problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at all
Content: Shipping containers at the port of Tacoma in Washington state on 4 March 2025. Trump said his latest round of tariffs was imposed to fight forced labor.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShipping containers at the port of Tacoma in Washington state on 4 March 2025. Trump said his latest round of tariffs was imposed to fight forced labor.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsIf Trump really cares about forced labor, he should look at the US – rather than slap more tariffs on the worldEduardo PorterForced laborisa problem, especially in the US, where prisoners are coerced to work for pennies – or nothing at allUS politics live – latest updatesFri 24 Jul 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 14.26 EDTShareDon’t believe theTrump administration’s rationale for its new volley oftariffsagainst everybody.The new levies, ostensibly to punish countries for failing to do enough to curb forced labor, switched on at 12.01am on Friday, to coincide with the expiration of a temporary 10% blanket duty thatDonald Trumpimposed in February, ostensibly to protect the United States from a balance-of-payments crisis.That duty was imposed right afterthe supreme court struck downtariffs the president unleashed on US trading partners last year on the also spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies.The shifting justifications alone underscore how Trump’s arguments are bullshit. But the specific nature of the latest accusation truly takes the cake.Trump accused of using forced labor as ‘convenient’ justification for tariffsRead moreThe US is arguing that tariffs of 10% or 12.5% are justified against 60 trading partners because they import stuff made with forced labor, unfairly undercutting American producers. But the charge omits that forced labor is not only prevalent across the US. It is also actively enforced by the state.Americans import lots of stuff made with forced labor: $170bn worth of imported goods are at risk of being tainted at some stage along the supply chain, according to theGlobal Slavery Index(GSI), from raw materials through to finished products. In 2023, this was the most among the countries in the G20.It includes electronics imported from China and Malaysia; clothing from India, Vietnam and Bangladesh; fish from Ghana; and timber from Russia, Brazil and Peru. The mining of essential minerals used in many electronics the US buys from abroad, from cobalt and copper to lithium and nickel, is rife with allegations of human rights abuses.To be sure, until recently the US was the only country that explicitly prohibited importing goods made with forced, convict or indentured labor. Still, the GSI reports no evidence that penalties are enforced against companies that fail to comply with reporting mandates, due diligence or other procurement regulations.Then there’s the issue of forced labor at home. There were 1.1 million people living in modern slavery in the US on any given day in 2021, according to the GSI, mostly doing domestic work, or toiling in agriculture, construction, retail, hospitality and illicit activities.That amounts to 3.3 forced workers for every thousand people in the population, which is more than in many of the countries Trump wants to punish. In the Netherlands and Germany, there are 0.6 forced workers per thousand people. In Britain there are 1.8.Canada also has a law on the books prohibiting imports made with forced labor. The prevalence of slave labor in Canada is only 1.8 per thousand people. Still, it just got hit with a 10% tariff because according to the US trade representative it is not doing enough to enforce the law. (The European Unionwill ban importsthat involve forced labor starting in 2027.)But here is the real rub: a significant share of modern slavery in the US is enforced by the state.The US stands out among the world’s democracies by allowingforced labor in prisons. And there isno legal obstacleto export goods made by prisoners forced to work against their will.The 13th amendmentto the constitution bans slavery and involuntary servitude, but it exempts work “as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted”. In Alabama prisons, they call the forced labor “mandatory chores”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAbout 800,000 of the 1.2 million people in state and federal prisons work,according to a reportin 2022 by the American Civil Liberties Union and the University of Chicago – often against their will, under the threat of further punishment. Incarcerated workers, the report adds, “are under the complete control of their employers, and they have been stripped of even the most minimal protections against labor exploitation and abuse”.Most work for the prisons themselves and other government businesses. In Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and Texas, more than 10,000 prisoners are assigned to agricultural work on penal plantations or prison farms, according to the ACLU report. They are also often farmed out to the private sector. In Alabama, according to aninvestigation by the Associated Press, they were leased out to at least 500 private businesses between 2018 and mid-March 2024.Prisoners toilinpoultry processing plantsand work in the kitchens of some of the biggestfast-food chains. They cook, wash dishes, fix plumbing and clean buildings. They are paid pennies an hour. And their wages are often garnished by the state.In seven southern states – Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas – almost all work by prisoners remains unpaid.If he is so inclined, Trump could help the fight against slave labor by taking a hard line against the US’ssouthern states, which generally raise less tax revenue and thus rely more on “free” work by the incarcerated to both operate prisons and generate revenue for the public sector.The ACLU report estimated that the incarcerated produce stuff worth more than $2bn a year and provide $9bn worth of services to their prisons.Other countries could help by slapping some tariffs on American goods to retaliate against these blatantly unfair practices.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsForced labourDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS prisonsTariffsLaw (US)commentShareReuse this content

title: Wedding gift registries are great – but divorce registries would be a lifesaver | Nick Dothée | The Guardian
description: Marriage offers an opportunity to ask for help creating a home. But what about when the marriage ends – and the household with it?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Marriage offers an opportunity to ask for help creating a home. But what about when the marriage ends – and the household with it?
Content: ‘Divorce turns one household into two, usually at the exact moment everyone is least equipped to comparison-shop bath mats.’Photograph: Giles Angel/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Divorce turns one household into two, usually at the exact moment everyone is least equipped to comparison-shop bath mats.’Photograph: Giles Angel/AlamyOpinionDivorceWedding gift registries are great – but divorce registries would be a lifesaverNick DothéeMarriage offers an opportunity to ask for help creating a home. But what about when the marriage ends – and the household with it?Fri 24 Jul 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.18 EDTShareIt’s peak wedding season, and my own divorce is waiting on a judge’s signature. People are being congratulated with Dutch ovens and serving bowls for dinner parties they may not ever host.Marriage comes with an etiquette system for asking people to help build a home. The registry says the embarrassing part for you.Divorcedeserves the same grace.Meanwhile, I was standing alone in my new-to-me condo kitchen, rereading a text I had drafted to my mother, trying to make quartz countertops sound like a normal thing to need.“Would you and Fred consider making this my birthday, Christmas, divorce and condo-warming gift?” I wrote, referring to the countertops and single-basin sink I had been fixating on. I attached a screenshot of Calacatta almond quartz, as if the visual aid might make the request seem less unhinged.The price point is why I piled on the occasions. But I am a 44-year-old man with a mortgage and two dogs, so “birthday and Christmas” was not really the headline. Divorce was.‘Loneliness influencers’ are racking up views. After a breakup, I see the appeal | Dave SchillingRead moreMy mother’s response was not yes.“Your stepdad and I are in the ER. I can’t think about this right now.”Fair. Terrible timing, but the shame had been there before she even replied.It’s hard now to imagine a wedding without a registry, but that etiquette had to start somewhere.Marshall Field’s, the Chicago department store whose State Street flagship is now a Macy’s, is often credited with introducing the modern bridal registry in 1924, when the list helped couples steer family and friends toward china, silver and crystal patterns. A century later, couples don’t even have to pretend they want china. Home funds are now common enough thatThe Knot has saidthe share of couples including them in registries has increased 55% since 2018.A few years ago, when my now ex-husband and I got married, his parents paid to finish turfing the backyard of our house so we could have the wedding there. My parents covered the tents, tables, chairs and sound system. These were not small gifts. But they turned a backyard into a wedding, so nobody had to defend the cost.For the registry itself, we mostly wanted cash. We were new homeowners in Los Angeles with nothing left for a honeymoon, so we used a platform called Hitchd to let guests click a link and donate to our new life. It helped pay for Hawaii and the house. I was a newlywed, so the ask came pre-forgiven.Then the marriage ended, and the household went with it.You can’t roll up half a backyard and bring it to a condo. The things that once meant “our future” became community property: the patio furniture, the dog bowls, the good knives, the drawer organizer that only made sense in that kitchen. Things to divide, keep, sell or leave behind.Someone should build the divorce version of Hitchd. Call it Ditchd.Actually, people already have.The Associated Press reportedthat Fresh Starts Registry, a divorce-registry service, had 50,000 to 70,000 monthly visitors, part of a broader shift toward talking more openly about divorce. So the need is not hypothetical. What still feels missing is the etiquette – a graceful way to say: we did not make it, but I’m accepting contributions toward a vacuum.A divorce registry sounds tacky because gifts are supposed to be fun, and replacing the half of a home that didn’t come with you is mostly just sad. I took the Instant Pot; the air fryer stayed. Asking for another one felt like showing everyone exactly how we split the kitchen. I did most of the cooking, and I didn’t realize how much I loved our beautiful countertops until they weren’t mine any more. So yes. Countertops made the list too.Divorce turns one household into two, usually at the exact moment everyone is least equipped to comparison-shop bath mats. First come the lawyers, movers, closing costs and a new internet account. Then come the dumber purchases: trash bags, forks, a shower curtain, a couch the puppy has not peed on yet. None of it feels giftable. All of it has to be bought anyway.I wasn’t destitute. That almost made the asking harder. I landed in the annoying middle: technically OK, but still buying my life back one receipt at a time.By the time I drafted that text to my mother, I had already spent my share of the house making the new condo feel like mine. The beige living room carpet became blonde oak flooring because the new puppy I “won” in the divorce still wasn’t potty trained. A handyperson painted the dated dark cabinets soft sage; I switched the hardware to matte black myself. I put bougainvillea and olive trees on the balcony, because maybe the dogs wouldn’t notice they had lost their backyard. At the old house, bougainvillea had covered the pergola in papery magenta blooms. Here, I had one in a pot.But in LA, the money runs out quickly.The ‘grey divorce’ phenomenon doesn’t signal a retreat from love. It’s a redefinition of it | Lisa PortolanRead moreI left the bedroom carpet and dated bathrooms alone. After the floors and cabinets, the old counters dragged the whole open-concept room back into “this was what I could afford”. Replacing them would mean I could stop balancing a cutting board over a burner. At the sink, I wouldn’t have to stretch on to my tiptoes – and I am tall – just to see my dogs asleep on and beside the couch.This was the case I made. My mother used to be horrified by how much my husband and I spent on Uber Eats. She gave us gift cards for Christmas that I joked would barely cover a dinner and a half. Now I was cooking almost every meal at home. The kitchen was where I could save money, feed myself and two expensive dogs on one income, and make the condo work as a home.The ER text made the timing comically indefensible. But the shame wasn’t really about timing. Marriage gets a table at Crate & Barrel. Divorce gets a Target cart full of things you already owned in another life.Maybe I’ll get the counters, maybe I won’t. For now, the quote sits there like one more line in a ledger that already has a mediator, a new floor and moving costs on it – one more number I keep staring at like it might solve something.I didn’t want a party for the divorce. I wanted permission to ask for help with the life I now had to build.Still, I can see the kitchen as it could be. The new sink. The cleared counter. Dinner at home. The dogs asleep in view. The bougainvillea on the balcony, doing the best it can.Nick Dothée is a Los Angeles-based writer whose work has appeared in the Atlantic; he is working on a memoir about the last-chance Hollywood recovery house where he got soberExplore more on these topicsDivorceOpinionHomesRelationshipscommentShareReuse this content
