If you do not rebuild it as it was imagined, you lose all of its integrity – and you do nothing more than celebrate the incompetence of its temporary custodians that led to its demise.”The entire sorry debacle began with a small fire breaking out at an end-of-year student show in 2014, when an aerosol canister of expanding foam placed near a hot projector caused flammable gases to ignite. It could and should have been contained, but Mackintosh’s arrangement of timber-lined voids and ducts contrived to spread the flames. Nonetheless, almost all of the building was saved, and a £35m restoration commenced. Weeks before its completion in 2018, the building was gutted by a second fire.View image in fullscreenDouble destruction … the 2018 fire.Photograph: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service/PACosily familiar to patrons of museum gift shops, it’s perhaps hard to envisage just how radical and unsettling Mackintosh’s art and architecture were in his day. A temperamental dandy who took his cue from movements in fin de siècle Europe – art nouveau, Japonism, symbolism – his oeuvre was a zinging riposte to the conventions of Victorian neoclassicism. “How absurd it is to see modern buildings made in imitation of Greek temples!” he fulminated in 1893. “We must clothe modern ideas in modern dress.”Mackintosh experienced extreme reversals of fortune. In 1900, his fame was such that during a trip to Vienna, “Toshie” and his wife, artist Margaret Macdonald, were feted as Caledonian heroes by the secessionist movement and cheered through the streets in a flower-decked cart. But the first world war sundered connections with Europe and a slow decline into poverty and obscurity ensued. By 1928, Mackintosh was dead of mouth cancer at 60, induced by his penchant for drinking and smoking, a grimly bohemian end to a fitfully stellar life.View image in fullscreen‘If you do not rebuild it as it was imagined, you lose all of its integrity’ … the interior basement level of the Mackintosh building in 2023.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAIf the Mac is not to be rebuilt as it was, there are precedents for a strategy of what might be described as “curated decay”, mixing new and old parts to relate the wider story of the building. Gutted by wartime bombing, Berlin’s neoclassicalNeues Museumlay in ruins for more than 40 years until an evocative scheme by David Chipperfield, abetted by conservative specialist Julian Harrap, transformed its fortunes. The city’s Reichstag building, remodelled by Norman Foster, retained graffiti scrawled by victorious Russian soldiers.Yet the glory of the Mac is the fact that it is all of a piece, from door handles to furniture, stained glass to light fittings, all minutely considered by Mackintosh as an exemplary Gesamtkunstwerk, or total work of art. Its double destruction has been a disaster, but, at present, its rebirth as a hugely costly phoenix from the flames feels as far away as it ever was.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureGlasgowGlasgow School of ArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can’t paper over the cracks of history. It will haunt you’: Gugu Mbatha-Raw on her race-horror thriller  | Television | The Guardian
description: She paved the way for Bridgerton, lit up Black Mirror’s most joyful episode – and now she stars in a grisly supernatural horror about slavery. The Belle star talks about Possession, partying with Prince and why she loves to shake things up
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: She paved the way for Bridgerton, lit up Black Mirror’s most joyful episode – and now she stars in a grisly supernatural horror about slavery. The Belle star talks about Possession, partying with Prince and why she loves to shake things up
Content: ‘It’s hard to talk about slavery’, says Gugu Mbatha-Raw.Photograph: David ReissView image in fullscreen‘It’s hard to talk about slavery’, says Gugu Mbatha-Raw.Photograph: David ReissTelevisionInterview‘You can’t paper over the cracks of history. It will haunt you’: Gugu Mbatha-Raw on her race-horror thrillerEmma LoffhagenShe paved the way for Bridgerton, lit up Black Mirror’s most joyful episode – and now she stars in a grisly supernatural horror about slavery. The Belle star talks about Possession, partying with Prince and why she loves to shake things upFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGugu Mbatha-Raw seems blissfully immune to the heat. London is pushing 40C on one of those heatwave mornings when everyone is wearing the weather: damp collars, flushed faces, hair slicked to foreheads. Arriving at the cafe of the central London hotel where we meet, however, the star looks as if she’s stepped in from an altogether different climate. Dressed in a pristine white linen two-piece, makeup free, hair scraped back, she carries herself with a composure that makes everyone else’s perspiration seem faintly melodramatic.She is, in every sense of the word, cool. This impression is only reinforced as we settle in for some small talk and she mentions that she’s been to the hotel once before.“I stayed here during the premiere of Belle – gosh, almost 15 years ago now,” she says. Then, almost as an afterthought: “And Prince performed at the afterparty.” She laughs at the look on my face. “It was incredible,” she says. “Just completely surreal.” It’s the sort of global cut-through all British actors dream of, and an anecdote that perhaps feels slightly out of place in the orbit of Mbatha-Raw’s career. SinceBelle– Amma Asante’s luminous 2013 period drama about Dido Elizabeth Belle, the real-life mixed-race daughter of an enslaved African woman raised in the English aristocracy –Mbatha-Raw has become one of Britain’s most fascinating actors.View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw as Claudia with Sheldon Shepherd as Cudjoe East in Possession.Photograph: Des WillieFrom playing the lead in Charlie Brooker’s acclaimed queer Black Mirror episodeSan Juniperoand starring in Jennifer Aniston and Reese Witherspoon’s workplace #MeToo drama The Morning Show to leading Apple TV’s identity-bending psychological thrillerSurfacein which she plays a woman recovering after a suicide attempt, the 43-year-old has consistently chosen projects that are intellectually and politically ambitious – roles one might summarise as having “something to say”.“I don’t want to do the same thing all of the time,” Mbatha-Raw tells me. “It’s fun for me to go from a period drama to a romantic drama to a comedy – it keeps me stimulated.”That instinct is precisely what drew her to Possession, Sky’s new supernatural thriller. Mbatha-Raw plays Claudia, a Bristol lawyer dispatched to Jamaica after a white plantation owner’s wealthy descendant dies suddenly, leaving his fortune not to his family but to a Jamaican man nobody can seem to track down. Claudia is assigned the case partly because, as one colleague bluntly puts it, having a Black, half-Jamaican lawyer would be “better optics”. But the legal work slowly gives way to something far more unsettling: the ghosts of Britain’s colonial legacy – both literal and metaphorical – intrude upon the present.“I was fascinated by Claudia because she’s caught between her professional obligations and her own personal history,” says Mbatha-Raw. “[She goes] from this relatively detached, brittle, ambitious career woman who was quite numb to her heritage and disconnected from her Jamaican background to becoming more grounded and rooted.”The story slips between modern Jamaica and the brutal realities of plantation slavery. But the enslaved do not remain confined to history: the enigmatic Cudjoe East, the man at the centre of the inheritance dispute, claims to be an enslaved man cursed centuries earlier to wander the Earth. In the past, a plantation mistress keeps grisly relics – locks of hair, severed ears – to perform magic on the bodies of those she enslaved. Present-day characters find themselves possessed by the spirits of enslavers, while Claudia struggles to resist being claimed herself.Filmed on location, much of the show’s richness comes from the vision of its Jamaican director,Storm Saulter, whose work has long explored the country’s layered histories and identity. The island is rendered in full polyphonic Technicolor: music and traditional masquerade rituals punctuate the narrative, while Obeah – the African-Caribbean spiritual practice of contacting ancestors, long feared by colonial authorities for its association with resistance and rebellion – becomes one of the show’s recurring motifs.“We wanted everything to feel as real as possible – the beauty of the colour, music and smells of Jamaica, but also its darkness,” says Mbatha-Raw. “We filmed at a real plantation house – all the scenes in the grounds, with enslaved people working on the land – real people lived and died there. Driving up the hill towards the house, you could really feel the weight of history.”View image in fullscreenLegal action … Mbatha-Raw in Possession.Photograph: Des WillieThe show belongs to the same lineage as Jordan Peele’sGet Out– racially conscious horror, in which the supernatural is merely a conduit for the far more terrifying legacy of racism. It is a provocation about reparations, colonial wealth and Britain’s historic relationship with slavery. In one pointed exchange, Claudia and the son of the plantation owner discuss the fact that the British government compensated former slave owners after abolition – a debt underwritten bytaxpayers until 2015– while those who had been enslaved received nothing. These are conversations that feel particularly pointed with the rise of far-right nationalism and racism in the UK and beyond. Is this something she was conscious of when making the show?“It’s uncomfortable to talk about reparations, it’s hard to talk about slavery and how we make peace with that history,” she says. “I think that’s what makes [the show] so compelling,” she continues. “You can’t just paper over the cracks of history. If we don’t deal with it, it will find ways of haunting us.”More than a decade separates Possession and Belle, but the two projects feel in conversation with one another in their meditations on empire.View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw with Sarah Gadon in Belle.Photograph: Cinematic/Alamy“It’s funny because it wasn’t like a huge blockbuster film,” she says when I ask how the movie changed her life. “But it was my first lead role, and it opened up lots of opportunities for me. And it was an important story to tell. A lot of people didn’t know that mixed-race characters existed in history – certainly not of any status, because you never saw them in movies unless they were a slave or being brutalised in some way.”Before we meet, she tells me she took a walk through Hampstead Heath to Kenwood House, once the stately home where Dido lived. “I wanted to immerse myself in that history again before speaking to you,” she says. Looking back now, she believes Belle helped widen ideas about who gets to exist in Britain’s period dramas.“I do think Belle helped pave the way for a show like Bridgerton,” she adds. “Just having Black and brown people visible is a huge change in the last 10 years or so.” Belle also marked the beginning of her friendship with Oprah, who was an early champion and offered to help with its US marketing; the pair have remained in touch ever since.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolitics has never been optional in Mbatha-Raw’s life. She was born in 1983 in Witney, a town just outside Oxford. Her father was a student anti-apartheid activist and ANC campaigner who fled South Africa to avoid imprisonment on Robben Island, eventually rebuilding his life with support from the UN’s Refugee Agency.“I remember we would talk about politics at the dinner table, but when you’re South African, you don’t know any different,” she says.She grew up an only child, living with her mother, a British nurse. Her parents split when she was young, but her father remained in her life. Ballet was her first love, as well as music – she trained with the National Youth Music Theatre before going on to Rada.As a young, biracial aspiring actor – particularly one growing up outside of London – has she ever felt held back by her race? She demurs.“There were certainly some roles that would have been closed off to me, like those early Regency-era roles, but the industry is changing in a really positive direction,” she says.She does mention that early on in her career, an older – white – actor suggested she change her name to something easier to pronounce. It was advice she politely ignored.“I love my name, it’s what makes me who I am,” she says. “I don’t think it’s that hard to pronounce. Plus, it translates to ‘our pride’ in Zulu, so changing that would feel so wrong – the opposite of what it means!”View image in fullscreenMbatha-Raw with Boris Kodjoe in Undercovers.Photograph: Chris Haston/Everett Collection Inc/AlamyAfter graduating from Rada in 2004, Mbatha-Raw built her career the old-fashioned way: on stage. In 2005, she appeared in Antony and Cleopatra before landing one of her first major roles opposite Andrew Garfield inRomeo and Juliet at Manchester’s Royal Exchange. Supporting screen roles in Bad Girls, Marple and Doctor Who followed, before a celebrated turn as Ophelia opposite Jude Law’sHamlet in the West Endand on Broadway. JJ Abrams saw the production and cast her in his American spy drama Undercovers, opening the door to Hollywood. For years she lived peripatetically, dividing her life between sets in the US and London. For now, she is London-based again.Her move coincided with a broader exodus of Black British actors across the Atlantic. Daniel Kaluuya has spoken about not getting roles in the UK “because of the colour of my skin”; David Oyelowo has talked of being “pushed out” because of the racial “glass ceiling”, as has David Harewood. Blockbuster names such as Cynthia Erivo and Damson Idris have found some of their biggest roles in the US, fuelling a long-running debate about whether Britain’s film and television industry truly nurtures its Black talent.“It’s definitely something I’ve heard, but it hasn’t been my personal experience,” she says when I ask about this. “I didn’t go to the US looking for opportunities; I got offered a role in Hollywood because of the work I’d already done here – and that’s not really something you turn down. I was very lucky.”Mbatha-Raw is thoughtful and politically engaged, but I get the sense she would rather speak through her characters. “I wouldn’t ever want to tell people what to think or experience,” she says. “Maybe Possession will inspire people to think about the more thought-provoking conversations around slavery, the idea of reparations and the complexity of that. But mostly, I just hope people find it entertaining.”Possession starts on 6 August on Sky Atlantic at 9pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionSlaveryDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s more than backcombing a beehive!’ How tribute acts got massive – and put the live music scene back in the black | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Versions of Amy Winehouse and hundreds of other musicians are generating millions for beleaguered UK venues. But what is the emotional toll for the imitators, and are they pushing out original artists?
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: Versions of Amy Winehouse and hundreds of other musicians are generating millions for beleaguered UK venues. But what is the emotional toll for the imitators, and are they pushing out original artists?
Content: School’s out … Nadine l’Amour, who gave up her job as a teacher to perform as Amy Winehouse under the name the Madnezz of Amy.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSchool’s out … Nadine l’Amour, who gave up her job as a teacher to perform as Amy Winehouse under the name the Madnezz of Amy.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianPop and rock‘It’s more than backcombing a beehive!’ How tribute acts got massive – and put the live music scene back in the blackVersions of Amy Winehouse and hundreds of other musicians are generating millions for beleaguered UK venues. But what is the emotional toll for the imitators, and are they pushing out original artists?Daniel Dylan WrayFri 24 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs peak heatwave sun beams down on to a field in Derbyshire, Amy Winehouse tells the crowd she is in need of hydration – so Robbie Williams fetches her a drink. Elsewhere, members of the public stop the Beastie Boys for selfies, Fred Durst grooves along as Diana Ross covers Al Green, and shirtless teenagers form a circle pit during Korn as a woman sits knitting in a camping chair just behind them. James Brown and Prince turn out to be the same artist – just dressed up in different clothes.These are all scenes from Replika festival last month, which won the Guinness world record for the biggest tribute festival, with 108 acts performing across a very sweaty weekend. The punning deserves an accolade of its own: acts included Catfishing the Bottlemen, Pearl Scam, Wrong Jovi and Iffy Clyro.It is far from the only event of its kind. The UK is inundated this summer, with Fake-Fest, Tribfest, Glastonbudget, Festwich, Tidal Gathering, Could Be Real and numerous others. Similarly, music venues across the country have listings crammed with tribute acts. Dave Bevan, managing director of Alive Network Entertainment Agency – which represents 234 such acts – estimates that there are between 3,000 and 5,000 outfits in operation in the UK.The reason so many of these events and gigs are thriving is because going to see the original artist is often prohibitively expensive, especially during a cost of living crisis, while these gigs offer cheap access to live music, with songs you are guaranteed to know and love. Replika charges £100 for a weekend ticket. Its organiser, James Dean, says: “Our festival is targeted at low- to middle-income families who have very little disposable income. Compare that with the costs of going to Wembley Stadium for a single concert.” This is echoed by one group of young lads I speak to at the festival: “It’s cheap, local and a laugh.”View image in fullscreen‘I don’t think I’ve ever been busier’ … Dan Budd who performs as a Robbie Williams tribute act.Photograph: HandoutDan Budd, who has performed as Robbie Williams for the last 14 years, is disarmingly good on stage, full of the requisite swagger and cheekiness, plus he has the same Stoke accent and even has matching real tattoos. “I don’t think I’ve ever been busier in terms of bookings,” he says. “I haven’t got a free Saturday night until September 2027.”Dean tells me that the very top acts in the game will pull in £10,000-£15,000 a show. Budd won’t give me specific figures but says: “Put it this way, I’m 36 and mortgage-free.”Similarly, Nadine l’Amour – who performs as Amy Winehouse under the name the Madnezz of Amy – is flying. She set foot on stage as Winehouse for the first time in December 2024 but, by April 2025, she had quit her job as a secondary school teacher to do it full-time. Like Budd, L’Amour has replicated Winehouse’s tattoos, though she is such a fan that they were done years before she got into the tribute game.“There are 14- and 15-year-old girls singing every single word,” she says of her shows. “I have young people saying: ‘I never got to see Amy, but watching you on stage, I feel like that’s the closest thing I’ll ever get.’”It is not just individuals such as L’Amour and Budd who are benefiting. According to the charity Music Venue Trust (MVT), at a time when half the UK’s grassroots music venues make no profit, tribute artists are helping to keep the entire sector afloat.“There is an elitist attitude about them, but these acts really do keep parts of the live music infrastructure moving,” says Nathan Clark, owner of the Brudenell Social Club in Leeds, one of the most well-respected and thoughtfully curated independent music venues in the country. Despite its buzzy reputation for cutting-edge newcomers and international indie stars, tribute bands play a significant role there. “Not every gig has to be about discovering the future,” he says. “The key is balance: tribute bands should support original music, not replace it.”View image in fullscreenAndrea Pattison performs as Dolly Parton at this year’s Replika festival.Photograph: James BeckThere is no hard data on the precise financial impact of tribute acts. MVT’s chief executive, Mark Davyd, guesses that they make up about 25-30% of all bookings in independent venues across the UK. The Night Time Industries Association also states there is no authoritative number, but a spokesperson says tribute acts contribute “many millions of pounds each year” to the live music industry.Dean had an independent survey carried out on his festival’s economic impact over the last 10 years – including associated local spending on travel, hotels, supermarkets and so on – and it came out at about £8.5m. Given the number of touring tribute bands, festivals, gigs and events, he estimates a number that could stretch into hundreds of millions of pounds overall across the same 10-year span.One reason this huge sector is being overlooked and undocumented is because it is often seen as a bit feeble or regressive. “People, especially in the mainstream music industry, look at us as nonstarters,” says Dean. “We’re not really taken seriously.” But tribute acts are no longer just dodgy Elvis impersonators with wayward pitch. “We’ve had a couple of Take That tributes who were able to sing a lot better than Robbie Williams and Gary Barlow,” says Dean; Clark points out that Graham Sampson of the Smyths, a Smiths tribute band, can probably hold a note better than Morrissey.View image in fullscreen‘Back to Black puts a very big lump in my throat’ … Nadine L’Amour, pictured at the Jam House in Birmingham.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianSuch skill and dedication in mirroring others can bring with it an emotional toll. “Four or five years into it, I had a bit of a breakdown,” says Budd. “I couldn’t keep up with being one person in my private life and then going into Robbie mode and then having to switch it off again. It was like a split personality.” But Budd has found a way around it, performing a different set every night to keep it fresh, merging deep cuts with hits, and also being less gung-ho about inhabiting Williams. “As I’ve matured, I go on stage as Dan and I sing the songs in his style and manner,” he says.When you love the act you are portraying, it can be more than just a gig. “There are a couple of songs that send me back to a time in my life that was quite dark,” says L’Amour. “Back to Black puts a very big lump in my throat when I sing that. It’s not only remembering my pain, but also the pain that Amy felt.” At Replika, L’Amour dedicates that song, very movingly, to a friend who has recently died. “As hard as it is to sing, it’s nice to dedicate that song to my friend who I lost to mental health,” she tells me later. “And that was also down to losing the person that she loved, and drinking and everything that was involved in that.”View image in fullscreenActing up … (from left) Xenna as Taylor Swift, a tribute to Lainey Wilson, Carrie Underwood (Beth McCann), JC as Chappell Roan and Pink-Ish at Replika with the Guinness World Record adjudicator.Photograph: James BeckL’Amour says that while some people – such as Replika’s Prince-James Brown combo – moonlight in numerous tribute acts, she could only ever do Winehouse because of the significance of the material. “This is more than sticking on eyeliner, backcombing the beehive and putting on really expensive, uncomfortable shoes,” she says. “It’s a feeling. That gut-wrenching first love that kicks you in the stomach; having your heart broken beyond repair. But then being able to pour that out to the audience and feeling that love come back. It’s way more than a tribute for me.”Tribute acts also have a domino impact on other areas in the industry. “It may not always be treated as culturally prestigious but it creates employment,” Clark says. “It drives paying musicians, designers, promoters, venues.” He points to the Smyths having a four-night run coming up at his venue. “What original bands at this grassroots level can do four nights and sell them out?” he asks. “Very few. Those four shows allow us to take the risk on booking something else.”View image in fullscreenRecord breaking  … this year’s Replika festival won the Guinness World Record for the biggest tribute festival with 108 acts.Photograph: James BeckTribute bands also tend to bring in “exponentially higher” bar revenue for venues, according to Davyd, as gigs are usually held at the weekend and are often attended by groups of people. Clark agrees: “A tribute show is often more of a social night out: people are relaxed, they know the songs, they sing together … it’s like a celebration. For independent venues, that matters. Bar income is a major part of how grassroots venues survive.”Davyd points out that tribute acts “fill up the programme” in smaller towns “where there is an absence of touring acts”, which is a mixed blessing. Yes, they allow people to see live music in places bigger acts ignore, but does their success make it harder for acts starting out who are writing and performing their own material? “Any experience with live music is really important for social interaction, community cohesion and a whole bunch of reasons,” he says. “But we really need to be concerned about generating the next wave of great British talent. I would prefer there was more space for that. Tribute bands are an important part of the grassroots sector but we wouldn’t like them to become the sole reason venues are open.”‘The whole ecosystem is collapsing’: inside the crisis in Britain’s live music sceneRead moreWhat is clear at Replika festival is that while, for many, these bands are vehicles for pure nostalgia, comfort and familiarity – big Oasis choruses, indelible Beatles hooks and sugary 00s pop – they are also a first gateway to music. It is genuinely endearing watching battle-jacket-clad children navigating their first mosh pit and working out the rhythms and etiquette, as a fake Limp Bizkit turns a sizeable tent into an explosion of bouncing bodies. And it is a dream come true for the band members, too, who seem blown away by the response. The turntablist shouts out to his parents in the audience, his adrenaline clearly pumping, as he declares: “They keep telling me to get a real job – but look at me now!”Explore more on these topicsPop and rockMusic industryFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Prince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Sacha Baron Cohen’s doofus voice of yoof has been making fresh mischief with new film Who Iz I? But who will he catch out this time? And what does his fictional hometown make of his return?
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Sacha Baron Cohen’s doofus voice of yoof has been making fresh mischief with new film Who Iz I? But who will he catch out this time? And what does his fictional hometown make of his return?
Content: ‘If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed, I iz here wif de hookup’ … Sacha Baron Cohen dressed as Ali G departs the Wimbledon tennis tournament where he attended the men’s singles final earlier this month.Photograph: Eleventh Hour Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed, I iz here wif de hookup’ … Sacha Baron Cohen dressed as Ali G departs the Wimbledon tennis tournament where he attended the men’s singles final earlier this month.Photograph: Eleventh Hour Photography/AlamyMoviesPrince William? David Cameron? JD Vance? Celebrities brace – and Staines celebrates – ahead of new Ali G filmSacha Baron Cohen’s doofus voice-of-yoof has been making fresh mischief with new film Who Iz I? But who will he catch out this time? And what does his fictional hometown make of his return?Catherine ShoardFri 24 Jul 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Wimbledon lawn tennis championships are not generally a hotbed of crime. Yet this year, unprecedented infringements ocurred. Eleven players were fined a total of £34,000 for “audible obscenities” and “racquet abuse”. Meanwhile, a spectator at the men’s singles final called a heckler a “bumbaclat” before inviting them to fight,badgeredPrince William to repay a drugs debt of £1,400 allegedly owed to him by Prince Harry from his days at Eton, and attempted to sell illegal substances to those seated near him – and beyond. “If u iz at dis borin wimbledore final lookin 2 get grand slammed,” he posted on Instagram, touting for business, “I iz here wif de hookup.”The culprit was Ali G, real name Alistair Leslie Graham, AKA the malapropism-dropping home counties wide boy played by Sacha Baron Cohen, kitted out for the occasion in trademark skullcap and gold chain, plus custom Wimbledon jacket, traditional crossed rackets replaced with cannabis leaves. Security released him without penalty, but thereprimandwas captured on scores of smartphones – including one held by Cohen himself.View image in fullscreenAli G at the tournament.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImageSuch footage is likely to find its way into a movie that will be released worldwide on 23 October and whoseexistence was only revealed four days before the Wimbledon incident. This week, a title was announced – Ali G: Who Iz I? – as well as the fact the film is to be the directorial debut of its star: a new development in the career of one of the UK’s most audacious, ambitious – and powerful – comedy actors, apparently taking greater agency over his projects as hisown political engagement intensifies. (The appalled reaction to his recent Netflix comedy Ladies First, which he neither wrote nor directed, suggests this is a sage move.)It also makes sense logistically: Ali G is a character who would energetically embrace selfie-mode shooting, which presumably streamlines a film crew considerably. Meanwhile the absence of a US theatrical release for the first Ali G film, 2002’s Indahouse, means targets in America would be easier to hoodwink.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueCohen first rose to fame as the tracksuit-wearing naïf and committed cultural appropriator in 1998, when Ali G was introduced as the “voice of the yoof” on Channel 4’s The 11 O’Clock Show. His own show followed in the early 2000s, constructed around interviews with unsuspecting subjects including Buzz Aldrin (whom he called Buzz Lightyear and asked if he was “ever jealous of Louis Armstrong”), Naomi Wolf (whom he complimented by telling her she’s attractive enough to be a sex worker) and Tony Benn. The late MP was outraged by the character’s dismissal of striking workers in 1984 as lazy skivers; Cohen later told Benn he was the only interviewee who had “dealt seriously with his loud, sexist, materialist image of youth”. (Benn’s letter of reply ended with the words: “You’re my main man.”)Although Cohen declared both Ali G andBorat– his Kazakh TV presenter and the star of a 2006 film that was a commercial and critical hit – retired in 2007, both have since returned. Borat was resurrected in 2020, forBorat Subsequent Moviefilm, intended by Baron Cohen as an intervention in the impending US presidential election. As with his 2018 seriesWho is America?, it secured a number of high-profile and highly-embarrassing scalps – most notably Rudy Giuliani, who was caught with his hand down his trousers in a hotel room with an actor pretending to be Borat’s 15-year-old daughter.Before his recent reappearance, Ali G was last seen presenting an award at the 2016 Oscars: a surprise even to the show’s producers, who understood Cohen would appear as himself. The ruse involved the star feigning food poisoning then locking himself and then-wife Isla Fisher in a disabled loo for 40 minutes to change into his costume.View image in fullscreenCritical approval … Borat Subsequent Moviefilm (2020).Photograph: Courtesy of Amazon StudiosWhile Ali G Indahouse was a scripted comedy concerning the character’s inadvertent role in the downfall of the government, indications are that its sequel will be closer to the more politically intentionalBoratfollowup, returning Ali G to his origins as an interviewer whose dubious views prompt his subjects to reveal their own.The film was shot in secret – as was 2009’s Brüno, in which Baron Cohen skewered the fashion industry – but some of the leaked locations in the UK and US give early clues as to whom Cohen may have had in his crosshairs.Last summer, there were sightings of the character in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire - home to the likes of David Cameron, Rebekah Brooks, Ellen DeGeneres and Jeremy Clarkson. The town was also, during the dates Ali G was spotted, playing host to US vice president JD Vance and his family, there to enjoy a Cotswolds holiday.Vance travelled with a considerable security detail, so it remains uncertain how close Cohen would have been able to get, had he been in pursuit.The Sun ran a photograph of the charactersporting a Rastafarian beret while filming at a nearby wildlife park in Burford. A source told the paper: “He was with a whole film crew and was in full character. He seemed very comfortable in the role. I was amazed, I thought to myself, ‘that’s Ali G’.”A crew member on the film to whom the Guardian spoke said an NDA prevented them from comment, but added: “I CAN tell you that it’s gonna be big. And packed full of laughs.”Ali G at the Oscars in 2016.Representatives for Kellie Bright, Charles Dance and Martin Freeman, all of who had roles in the original film, did not respond to enquiries, but the actor Adam Deacon confirmed he was not returning, “even though I would have loved to be a part of it”. He added that he could also do a “perfect” Borat accent so would be happy to be kept in mind for further films featuring that character too. “I’m a massive fan of what Sacha creates and I hope the new movie is a success.”In the first film, Deacon played a member of the East Staines Massiv, the rivals of Ali G’s less-than-intimidating gang from the other end of town. The Surrey commuter town wasscepticalabout the fame bestowed on it by the Ali G connection, and in 2010, a group spearheaded by the Spelthorne business forum lobbied the borough council to change the town’s name to Staines-upon-Thames inan attempt to add distance. The area, said Alex Tribick, chair of the forum at the time, “is really rather nice and it has some fantastic natural beauty around it”.He added: “Staines has had some adverse press further to that with it being portrayed as an urban wasteland off the end of the M25. The purpose of the exercise is to improve the image of Staines, rebrand it, and denote its greatest natural resource.”The then MP for Spelthorne, Kwasi Kwarteng, supported the move – which was duly voted through by the local council in 2011 – saying “if anyone knows anything about Staines, then one would know that Ali G is a million miles from it. It’s a very charming place actually.”Yet in his Thursdayvideoannouncing the title and release date, Ali G announces himself as “representing the westside of Staines-upon-Thames” – suggesting the area is unlikely to shake off the association any time soon.View image in fullscreenRepresenting for the West Staines Massiv in Ali G Indahouse (2002).Photograph: Film Four/AllstarHappily, the sitting Spelthorne MP, Lincoln Jopp, said he welcomed news of the return of the town’s prodigal son. “I can’t believe Ali G is coming back!” he said. “I loved Ali G Indahouse; it’s hilarious.Sacha Baron Cohenis a genius.”Jopp, who specified to the Guardian that his constituency includes the “West Staines Massiv”, added that the town was “a great place. We can take a bit of mickey-taking, trust me. Booyakasha!”Posts on local Facebook forums suggest resurgent grassroots support for the character putting the town on the map. “Oh happy days, loved the film,” wroteBlossom Welch, while longtime Staines resident Joanna Barlow added: “Loved Ali G not ashamed saw the show being filmed thought it was hilarious.”However one user,Bettafisheye, demurred, venturing that Ali Gis “like a bad smell that never leaves. I just say I’m from Laleham now. If u say Staines it’s like being around a constipated dog talking through there arse.”Explore more on these topicsFilmSacha Baron CohenPrince WilliamBoratBorat Subsequent MoviefilmfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was 100% the moment I lost innocence’: how a childhood stop-and-search led to the British debut movie of the year | Movies | The Guardian
description: When Imran Perretta was young, he was abruptly pulled by police into a van for questioning. That experience, as well as the death of his mother, inspired him to make Ish, a coming-of-age tale set amongst the British Muslim community. He talks about trauma, designing toilets and making Luton look magnificent
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: When Imran Perretta was young, he was abruptly pulled by police into a van for questioning. That experience, as well as the death of his mother, inspired him to make Ish, a coming-of-age tale set amongst the British Muslim community. He talks about trauma, designing toilets and making Luton look magnificent
Content: ‘I have to dedicate my life to doing the things that I want to do’ … Imran Perretta.Photograph: Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty Images for BFIView image in fullscreen‘I have to dedicate my life to doing the things that I want to do’ … Imran Perretta.Photograph: Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty Images for BFIMoviesInterview‘It was 100% the moment I lost innocence’: how a childhood stop-and-search led to the British debut movie of the yearCath ClarkeWhen Imran Perretta was young, he was abruptly pulled by police into a van for questioning. That experience, as well as the death of his mother, inspired him to make Ish, a coming-of-age tale set amongst the British Muslim community. He talks about trauma, designing toilets and making Luton look magnificentFri 24 Jul 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImran Perretta always knew that the title of his debut feature film would be “Ish” – short for Ishmail, the name of the 12-year-old boy from Luton at the heart of his story. Only later did people point out the similarity to other coming-of-age films with three letters in the title: Kes by Ken Loach, and Satyajit Ray’s Apu trilogy. Now, as the reviews trickle in, the comparisons to Kes and Apu keep coming. Like them, Ish is a poetic film that grabs you by the heart and pulls you into a child’s perspective on the world.The response has been lovely, says Perretta, and a relief. “It’s nice that people have compared Ish to those films rather than Kidulthood. I did worry about that.” Why, because it features kids speaking in slang and getting into scrapes? He nods. “I always say that I don’t read reviews, but of course I’ve read every single one. I can’t help myself. And we’ve been really lucky; the reviews have been amazing. A couple have been middling. Then you read them, and the subtext is: ‘I thought it was going to be like Kidulthood.’”Perretta is just back from a trip to Poland for the opening of a new exhibition of his work. Yesterday he was atTate Britainin London, tweaking the sound on his 2019 video installation The Destructors, about the lives of young Muslim men, which has just gone on show at the gallery. He is in the process of buying his first home and has two small children. “I’m knackered,” he says with a grin, chatting a mile a minute, no sign of tiredness.He grew up in Streatham, south London, the son of a British Italian dad who worked as a music journalist. His mother, who was born in Bangladesh, was a child protection social worker: “She was super political, a firebrand.” She died from cancer when he was 21. Perretta studied architecture for three years, before switching to art. During Covid in 2020, when the Turner prize was cancelled, he was one of 10 artists to receive £10,000 bursaries. But it never crossed his mind that he could direct a film, he says: “Not in a million years did I think I would ever get to do that. That’s something that happens to other people.” It was the head of BBC Film at the time, Rose Garnett, who approached him to write a film treatment after seeing The Destructors at a gallery in London.View image in fullscreenPerretta’s 2019 video installation The Destructor is currently on show at Tate Britain, London.Photograph: Andy Keate for Turner BursariesIsh is partly autobiographical, based on the first time Perretta was stopped and searched by police aged 13. This was in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks in a climate of increasing Islamophobia. “My mate got away. They pulled me into a van and just started asking me loads of weird questions,” he remembers. “I was so young, I didn’t really understand what was going on. It was incredibly traumatic. That was 100% the moment in my childhood when I lost my innocence. Because I understood how I was seen outside my family home, outside school, outside the community, all these protected spaces. In that moment, I understood I was seen as a deviant or some sort of threat.”It politicised him, says Perretta. “That kind of made me. From that point I had something to make work about. If I look at everything I’ve done for years, making work that is viewed by the public on the walls of a gallery or whatever, it all comes from that moment of seeing oneself as other people see you.” He co-wrote Ish with theIrish playwright and scriptwriter Enda Walsh.View image in fullscreenFarhan Hasnat as Ish.Photograph: Venice film festivalLike all brilliant coming-of-age films, Ish is culturally specific but also universal. It’s set in Luton, following 12-year-olds Ish (Farhan Hasnat) and his best mate Maram (Yahya Kitana) as they roam about during the holidays. It’s their last summer of boyhood: they are still young enough to build dens in the woods and pick blackberries. Ish’s mum has just died, and at home his family are dazed by grief. Maram, who is already a foot taller than Ish and has the beginnings of a moustache, is hanging around with older boys, getting in trouble.The stop and search, when it happens, is shocking – watching a child being grabbed from the street, forcefully and without parental consent. When I say this to Perretta, he points out therecent case of Child Qand accounts of interviews conducted with children under the government’s anti-extremism Prevent strategy without a parent or teacher in the room. “It happens to children from certain backgrounds more than others. I wanted to explore what it means to drag children into the adult world before their time.”All the kids in Ish are played by first-time actors. The casting process took six months, auditioning about 900 local boys. Unbeknown to the film-makers, the pair who got the roles of Ish and Maram had been friends since they were toddlers. Their bond shines through on screen; the chemistry is unfakeable. “It was just about getting out of their way, letting them do what they do naturally, which is basically wind each other up,” Peretta says.Ish was shot in Luton over five weeks in the summer of 2024. Perretta’s wife, a secondary school teacher, grew up down the road, and he has been visiting the area for years. Perretta says that commuter towns take a lot of stick. Luton in particular has frequently been in the news for negative reasons, as the home town of Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (AKA Tommy Robinson) or labelled as a centre of Islamic extremism. “But at the heart of it was just a community going about their business,” he says.He shot the film in luminous monochrome. Why, I ask? “What I figured is black and white didn’t negatively aesthetise Luton. It gave it grandeur. It made the concrete feel like marble. When you shot in colour, you immediately felt the fact that it had been at the sharp end of austerity.”View image in fullscreen‘Life’s too short to design toilets’ … Imran Perretta.Photograph: Capital Pictures/AlamyFilming days were short to comply with laws to protect child actors. “When you film with kids, there’s an egg timer. They can only be on set for six hours.” The key, he says, was not to be too precious about nailing it. “We just didn’t have the time.” That sounds stressful, I suggest. Perretta shrugs good-naturedly. “I would like to say that I’m fairly unflappable in those situations. It sounds sort of trite, but when you’ve looked after someone that’s dying, a film set is not that bad. I refuse to get to wound up about that sort of thing.” He smiles. “It’s an extraordinary thing to make a film. On a personal level it’s extremely important. But on the scale of all the things that can happen in life, it’s not really.”Perretta says his mother getting ill is what set him on the path to becoming an artist. “After she died, I thought: I have to dedicate my life to doing the things that I want to do.” He was 18 when she was diagnosed with cancer, and he was one of her carers, along with his dad and his younger sister. “That was my first degree. And after my mum died, I was working in an architect’s practice and thought: Life’s too short to design toilets.” Is that what he was doing, designing toilets? “Literally. I was working on the team that was spacing toilet cubicles. I won’t tell you where – it’s a high-profile architect.” He lasted a week. “I was like: Nah, I’m good.”Nostalgia review – Tarkovsky’s yearning cine-poem is deeply mysterious and profoundRead moreWhen his mother was sick, he had visited the Serpentine gallery in London to watch Blue, Derek Jarman’s final film, first released in 1993 months before his death from an Aids-related illness. “It was so extraordinary seeing that film. I stayed there for hours. I’d never had any experience of contemporary art before, other than school trips to the Tate. I was spellbound by it. I thought: ‘Oh God, I need to do that.’ I just need to run at the things that make me angry and scared, and make work about them. That was the beginning.” He grins. “And here we are.”Ish is in UK and Irish cinemas nowExplore more on these topicsFilmTate BritainDerek JarmaninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angst | Games | The Guardian
description: Going by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havoc
Author: Chris Schilling
Headline: Going by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havoc
Content: One for sorrow … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothView image in fullscreenOne for sorrow … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothSummer games previewsGames‘An anthem for the co-dependent’: Bad Magpie’s corvid carnage with a side of existential angstGoing by the mantra, if you want to make someone laugh, make them cry first, the game’s developers have created a lonely magpie who fills the void by wreaking havocChris SchillingFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid the gleeful anarchy of Bad Magpie’s debut trailer, there’s a striking note of melancholy. The game’s protagonist – a wounded corvid that creates havoc wherever she goes – calls out forlornly as a flock of her kind passes above, with a conspicuous gap in their formation.Milktooth games designer and co-founder Daisy Fernandez has had this particular image in her head for years. Lying in the grass one afternoon during the 2020 lockdowns, she looked up and saw a V-shaped pattern in the sky, poignantly incomplete. “It really stuck with me,” she says. “I posted about it online and someone told me about a ‘missing man’ formation, which is an aerial salute to a fallen pilot.”View image in fullscreenDistraction tactics … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothAlready, Fernandez and her then colleagues George Batchelor and Catherine Unger at State of PlayGames(South of the Circle) had been batting around ideas for a game of their own. Unger – whose brilliant artwork can currently be seen in SFB Games’ The Mermaid Mask – pitched an idea to the group. “It was a fairytale about a duck that falls in love with a star and goes on a quest to bring it gifts,” Batchelor says. “This was 2019, and because the duck was white …”The implication is clear. Any game featuring a mischievous bird was always going to draw comparisons toUntitled Goose Game, but back then the visual resemblance to House House’s Bafta winner encouraged the team to consider a different path.The star and the central quest remained, but as time went by it was clear that a magpie was a much better fit for a story about a character seeking out shiny objects as a distraction from her abandonment issues. They may have had to reverse-engineer it, Fernandez says, but it has come to feel like the ideal choice: “You know, ‘One for sorrow, two for joy …’ – that almost sounds like an anthem for the co-dependent.”View image in fullscreen‘Some surprisingly inefficient outcomes’ … Bad Magpie.Illustration: MilktoothThe game, then, is designed to be something of a collectathon – one that could be read as a meta-commentary on the way games distract us from broader existential worries. And not just in the playing, either. “One thing George and I talk about quite a bit is that making a game is the best form of avoidance, because there are endless tasks you can throw yourself into,” Fernandez says, cheerfully adding that her death anxiety “is the quietest it’s ever been” as development continues.All of which risks making a game in which you set fields of flowers aflame, launch fireworks through car windows and chase a frowning computer monitor with a trumpet in your beak, sound awfully serious. Yet there’s a thrilling through-line of experimental chaos, that Batchelor says has been somewhat inspired by Zelda: Breath of the Wild. “It means we do get some surprising outcomes,” he says. “And some surprisinglyinefficientoutcomes,” Fernandez quips.That has led to a few happy accidents, as the studio builds a sandbox that feels truly reactive to the player’s input, bolstered by Eli Rainsberry’s deft audio design that gives each object its own sonic palette. “We’re testing the whole time, so we get to see what [players] want to do and try to accommodate that – or at least make a joke that gestures at it,” Batchelor says. For all that the scope has crept, there have been a few judicious cuts: a keenness to “degoosify” the game, as Fernandez puts it, led to a model village being removed, House House having got there first.They needn’t have worried. Bad Magpie is very much its own bird – not least thanks to its higher dynamic tonal range. “There’s this expression in screenwriting that if you want to make someone laugh, you make them cry first, and vice versa,” Fernandez says. “Pixar’s so good at that – every time there’s a devastating moment there’s a slapstick beat seconds later, and you’re so relieved to laugh.” Batchelor nods in agreement: “People really picked up on that emotional beat of seeing the magpie alone. Just that one shot helped validate how it’s going to feel in the final game.”Bad Magpie is in development for PC and Xbox Series X/S.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsShareReuse this content

title: If Deadpool wants to be a true Marvel superhero, is it time he grew up and stopped joking around? | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ryan Reynolds’ sarcastic superhero is rumoured to be in Avengers: Doomsday – but how is he going to fit in the MCU proper when he spent all of his previous film mocking it?
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Ryan Reynolds’ sarcastic superhero is rumoured to be in Avengers: Doomsday – but how is he going to fit in the MCU proper when he spent all of his previous film mocking it?
Content: Ryan Reynolds in Deadpool & Wolverine, the most popular Marvel film in years.Photograph: Jay MaidmentView image in fullscreenRyan Reynolds in Deadpool & Wolverine, the most popular Marvel film in years.Photograph: Jay MaidmentWeek in geekMoviesIf Deadpool wants to be a true Marvel superhero, is it time he grew up and stopped joking around?Ben ChildRyan Reynolds’ sarcastic superhero is rumoured to be in Avengers: Doomsday – but how is he going to fit in the MCU proper when he spent all of his previous film mocking it?Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.46 EDTShareHow do you solve a problem like Deadpool in the Marvel Cinematic Universe?Deadpool & Wolverinefound a way: rather than integrate the bloodthirsty, fourth-wall-breaking merc with a mouth into the rather more sanitised world of Thor, Iron Man and Spider-Man, Shawn Levy’s 2024 film chose to lampoon it from the outside instead. Why bother to make everyone’s favourite chimichanga-munching mutant fit when you can make the fact that he doesn’t the entire joke? Why become another cog in the Marvel machine when you can stand beside it, point out the loose screws and watch the box-office greenbacks roll in like it’s Christmas 2019?Deadpool & Wolverine made $1.3bn worldwide, becoming the second highest grossing film of 2024 and the highest grossing R-rated film ever. But it did absolutely nothing to introduce Ryan Reynolds’ potty-mouthed antihero into the MCU, unless one counts the several thousand jokes about Kevin Feige. By the end of the movie,Deadpoolseems no closer to becoming the saviour of Marvel than Happy Hogan is to wielding Mjolnir. He remains a sarcastic observer from the sidelines, less a vital MCU character than its resident heckler.Which makesthis week’s newsthat Reynolds is to embark on a sequel intriguing, to say the least. Because really, about what exactly? How do you make another Marvel movie when you have systematically pulled the whole enterprise apart? How could Deadpool emerge as the hero of Avengers: Secret Wars, and perhaps sacrifice himself to stop Doctor Doom from folding the multiverse into one vast Latverian theme park, when he has already treated Marvel continuity as something to be rummaged through for disposable cameos?Is Deadpool waiting in the wings? Watch the new Avengers: Doomsday trailerNobody has much inkling of how another Marvel-era Deadpool film might pan out. Butsome reports suggestthe character will play a role in the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday, albeit most probably not as part of the titular superhero combo.A new trailer for Doomsday, released earlier this week, does little to clarify matters. Reynolds is nowhere to be seen, but Channing Tatum’s Gambit, introduced in memorably bizarre fashion in Deadpool & Wolverine, features prominently. Patrick Stewart’s Professor X and Ian McKellen’s Magneto appear to be caught up in the film’s multiversal collision course, while Rebecca Romijn’s Mystique is once again prowling around in blue body paint. All of them belong to the same sprawling, hopelessly tangled 20th Century Fox-era mutant continuity that Deadpool calls home. It’s not hard to imagine Reynolds is hovering somewhere nearby, waiting to burst through the scenery and complain about Robert Downey Jr’s salary.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBest in an ensemble? … Reynolds with Hugh Jackman as Wolverine.Photograph: Jay Maidment/APAnd yet if Wade Wilson is capable of becoming more than just the man shouting jokes from the cheap seats, if he is eventually to be seriously integrated into the MCU, he will at some point need to stop mocking the Fox-era mutants who appear to be caught up in no less than saving the known multiverse.Reynolds has recently suggestedthat Deadpool works best as part of an ensemble, but that is only interesting if the other characters are allowed to matter. A reunion with Gambit and other assorted denizens of Charles Xavier’s mansion cannot simply become another procession of cameos to be mocked, dismembered and discarded. At some stage Deadpool must stop treating the Fox universe as a box of comedy props, and confront the possibility that its destruction might genuinely mean something to him.That need not mean sanding off the obscenity or forcing Wade to deliver a solemn speech about responsibility beneath a swelling Alan Silvestri score. The first two Deadpool films occasionally managed to create genuine feeling without requiring their hero to stop being a complete clown. But if he is to play any meaningful role in the end of the multiverse, the joke cannot always be that superhero stories are stupid and the whole enterprise is one enormous corporate fever dream. The most popular Marvel movie in the last four years may have done its best to persuade us we should not be watching Marvel films in the first place, but there are only so many times Reynolds can trot out a glorified SNL sketch about how silly superhero flicks are and persuade us all that he has actually made a movie.Sooner or later Deadpool has to stop sneering at the apocalypse and try to do something about it.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekDeadpoolAvengers: DoomsdayScience fiction and fantasy filmsComics and graphic novelscommentShareReuse this content

title: Bedlam dreamscapes, digital-age aliens and a summer pastoral – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The terrifying visions of Richard Dadd, UFOs, aliens and Van Gogh’s troubled peasant woman
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The terrifying visions of Richard Dadd, UFOs, aliens and Van Gogh’s troubled peasant woman
Content: Creepy baby … detail from Puck by Richard Dadd, 1841.Photograph: Simon Critchley/© Harris Museum and Art GalleryView image in fullscreenCreepy baby … detail from Puck by Richard Dadd, 1841.Photograph: Simon Critchley/© Harris Museum and Art GalleryArt Weekly newsletterArt and designBedlam dreamscapes, digital-age aliens and a summer pastoral – the week in artThe terrifying visions of Richard Dadd, UFOs, aliens and Van Gogh’s troubled peasant woman –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 24 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekRichard Dadd: Beyond BedlamTerrifying creatures of the night and surreal dreamscapes galore – and those are just the “sane” canvases this Victorian artist painted before he was confined to Bedlam, where his visions became truly unsettling.Royal Academy, London, 25 July to 25 OctoberAlso showingFelicity PowellDreamlike images across many media by this artist who died in 2015 after documenting her own cancer.Richard Saltoun Gallery, London, until 3 OctoberAutopsyUFOs, the Roswell “alien” and the inaccessibility of truth in the digital age provide suitably strange fodder for Paul McCarthy, Chino Moya and many more.Seventeen Gallery, London, until 15 AugustElizabeth Blackadder: A Life in ColourTapestries by this colour-loving Scottish artist are accompanied by her paintings and drawings.Dovecot Studios, Edinburgh, until 14 NovemberClare Woods: Garden Without SeasonsPastoral and horticultural new paintings that delve into nature in a show that suits the season.Pitzhanger Manor and Gallery, London, from 29 July until 8 NovemberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Jem SouthamRay Exworth spent his life filling Cornish sheds with breathtaking sculptures – but wouldn’t let anyone in to view them. Now, after his death, his secret body of work has been revealed.Read the full articleWhat we learnedAt 100, painter, sculptor and performance artist Ken Turner is still smashing the system … and the occasional TeslaSheffield’s Designers Republic lit up the north with their work for Aphex Twin, Pulp … and PringlesTrent Park House museum reveals the story of its wartime ‘secret listeners’The Manifesta biennale brings radical community spirit to struggling German townsThe artful work of hundreds went into dazzling textiles show Entangled and WovenJessica Morgan has taken ‘a big pay cut’ to become Tate’s new directorMasterpiece of the weekHead of a Peasant Woman by Vincent van Gogh, about 1884View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Imagedoc/AlamyWhen Vincent van Gogh gave up his early attempts at art dealing, teaching and missionary work to learn to paint, he saw art as a social vocation. Instead of saving the poor by preaching he would help them by depicting their harsh lives. This peasant woman is one of the folk he painted from life in Nuenen in the south Netherlands in his first really ambitious art project: a passionate attempt to document rural poverty that culminated in his famous 1885 painting The Potato Eaters. He sees sadness and distraction in her eyes as she patiently sits for him, her individual presence heightened by the vague background that leaves nothing to look at but the figure. Van Gogh suggests a tension between her workaday appearance and a richer, more elusive inner life. He would later embrace expressionism and wild colour in search of ways to open that subjective realm of the soul.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the great pandemic drama you might have missed | Television | The Guardian
description: Station Eleven comes to Sky Atlantic, starring Himesh Patel and Mackenzie Davis. Plus: Boris Johnson’s Ukraine documentary. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Station Eleven comes to Sky Atlantic, starring Himesh Patel and Mackenzie Davis. Plus: Boris Johnson’s Ukraine documentary. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Survival mode … Himesh Patel in Station Eleven.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenSurvival mode … Himesh Patel in Station Eleven.Photograph: APTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the great pandemic drama you might have missedStation Eleven comes to Sky Atlantic, starring Himesh Patel and Mackenzie Davis. Plus: Boris Johnson’s Ukraine documentary. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Alexi Duggins,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellFri 24 Jul 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStation Eleven9pm, Sky AtlanticA great – and somehow hopeful – apocalyptic drama, which deserved more love when it first streamed in 2022. (Perhaps the story of a pandemic wiping out 99% of the world was too close to home.) It’s set across two timelines, with young actor Kirsten (Matilda Lawler) being looked after by writer Jeevan (Himesh Patel) when the killer flu strikes; 20 years later (now played by Mackenzie Davis) she tours with the Travelling Symphony.Hollie RichardsonProg Rock at the Proms7pm, BBC FourIt was probably only a matter of time before this once scorned but now largely rehabilitated rock subgenre got its Albert Hall moment. Stuart Maconie presents a selection of musically complex epics, with music by Genesis, Jethro Tull, Mike Oldfield and Emerson, Lake and Palmer.Phil HarrisonAbbey Clancy: Celebrity Homes7.30pm, ITV1One of those things we all take for granted in life is the ease of furnishing a modern subterranean home. So thank goodness for this profile of influencer Lorna Luxe’s abode, where she’s able to reveal its challenges. Clancy also visits an off-grid farmhouse owned by Jo Wood.Alexi DugginsGranite Harbour8pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenFashion-forward … DC Davis Lindo (Romario Simpson) in Granite Harbour.Photograph: LA Productions/BBC ScotlandThe Aberdeen-set cop drama returns for a third outing. Fashion-forward duo DC Lindo and DS Bartlett investigate the death of a young woman on a country estate that hosts a Traveller community. Monarch of the Glen star Alastair Mackenzie is well cast as the local laird terribly concerned by it all.Graeme VirtueBoris Johnson: Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone9pm, Channel 5Our erstwhile prime minister travels beyond Kyiv to witness the realities of modern war at close range and explore the human cost of Ukraine’s desperate battle. Embedded with Ukrainian soldiers, he visits shattered villages, a frontline chapel, drone bases and a makeshift bomb factory.PHAnn Droid9.30pm, BBC OneDiane Morgan has found her perfect role as hilariously vacant, deeply unhelpful support robot Linda in this sitcom. Sue (Sue Johnson) offers to work in the charity shop for a day but thanks to the interventions of her automaton pal, nothing is simple.PHFilm choiceThe Dink(Josh Greenbaum,2026),Apple TVView image in fullscreenAmiable … Mary Steenburgen and Jake Johnson.Photograph: Andrew Cooper/Apple TVThere is plenty of comic potential to be found in has-been sports pros still living off former glories. In Josh Greenbaum’s amiable comedy, that figure is Dusty “the Hammer” Boyd (New Girl’s Jake Johnson), a tennis prodigy who failed to make the grade and is now reduced to coaching nine-year-olds at his father’s country club. Dad Chuck (a wonderfully dismissive Ed Harris) is fighting a rearguard action against tennis’s increasingly popular offshoot pickleball – “the coronavirus of sport” – and his son is desperate to please him. But when Dusty checks out the new game, he meets sparky older woman Candace (Mary Steenburgen, delightful) and his priorities change.Simon WardellPreschool (Josh Duhamel,2026),Paramount+Michael Socha is becoming a very accomplished comic actor, and his trademark deadpan desperation is well used in Josh Duhamel’s amusing caper about stupidly competitive dads. Brian (Socha) and Alan (Duhamel) just want the best for their children – but when there is only one place up for grabs at an exclusive private preschool, they will do anything to beat the other man. Antonia Thomas and Charity Wakefield play their more sensible other halves, reduced to spectators in a game of class-tinged male one-upmanship involving indoor skydiving, judo, padel violence and more.SWJanet Planet (Annie Baker,2023),11.05pm, BBC TwoFriendless 11-year-old Lacy (Zoe Ziegler) has just demanded to come back from summer camp early. So for the rest of the holidays her world revolves round her acupuncturist single mother Janet (Julianne Nicholson). Pulitzer-winning playwright Annie Baker’s languid drama offers a child’s-eye view of adult relationships, with Lacy party to situations involving her mum she only partly comprehends or cares about – from Janet’s troubles with boyfriend Wayne (Will Patton) to the visit of Sophie Okonedo’s sort-of-cult escaper Regina.SWLive sportCommonwealth Games,8.30am, TNT Sports 2Day one from Glasgow, featuring swimming and para swimming, boxing, para powerlifting and artistic gymnastics. Scotland’s Duncan Scott will be aiming for another medal in the 200m individual medley.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Unsayable by Michael Cunningham review – The Hours author on the insecurities that powered his creative life | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The American novelist and screenwriter’s memoir covers sex work, Virginia Woolf and Hollywood success
Author: Alex Clark
Headline: The American novelist and screenwriter’s memoir covers sex work, Virginia Woolf and Hollywood success
Content: Michael Cunningham.Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMichael Cunningham.Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty ImagesBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewUnsayable by Michael Cunningham review – The Hours author on the insecurities that powered his creative lifeThe American novelist and screenwriter’s memoir covers sex work, Virginia Woolf and Hollywood successAlex ClarkFri 24 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an eight-year-old in comfortable, solid, suburban California,Michael Cunninghamfelt compelled to make art before he quite understood what it was, or could do: a painting of souls ascending to heaven, for example, in which paradise resembled the Griffith Park Observatory and the dead were all depicted in profile because their creator felt unequal to the challenge of full faces. There was also a cigar box covered in gold-sprayed macaroni and a clay representation of the animals on Noah’s Ark – anything, in fact, that would challenge the painting of a placid white chicken that hung in a gilt frame on his parents’ wall.If Cunningham moved on fairly rapidly from the visual arts, either sparing or denying us the fruits of a more fully formed talent, it wasn’t because the impulse to create had withered. Rather, it was that the experience of making material art had functioned as a temporary outlet, being less painful, less embarrassing – both emotions he ascribes to his young, sensitive self – than attempting to capture the world in words.Unsayable, an intriguing combination of memoir and writing guide, asks us to consider what causes those feelings of embarrassment and pain, and what powers them. Do they proceed, almost inevitably, from the gap between language and the vast, mysterious terrain it tries to describe? Cunningham’s writerly insecurity, from childhood to maturity, seems to live in that gap, and to feel it as an ever-present judgment on his endeavours, impossible to expunge. Success is no antidote and, he points out, might even contribute to a feeling of isolation from other writers, or a quickening fear of a return to obscurity.View image in fullscreenNicole Kidman as Virginia Woolf in The Hours.Photograph: Paramount/AllstarCunningham did become successful, and extremely so, when in 1998 he publishedThe Hours, a triple-stranded, time-shifting riff on Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway; his celebrity increased four years later, when Stephen Daldry and David Hare released a film adaptation starring Nicole Kidman, Meryl Streep and Julianne Moore. Several novels and 25 years later, he was to return to a similar structure – compressed time and multiple interior monologues – in Day. “I don’t work on an epic scale”, he tells us in this book, “though my ambitions run to more epic proportions than I like to admit.” This, one might say, is the tension at the heart of modernism, perhaps Cunningham’s greatest stylistic influence: the attempt to render the grandeur of consciousness that also shows us its fragility, how easily it evaporates on examination.Fragility and contingency recur throughout Unsayable. Cunningham might never have discovered Woolf unless he’d found himself secretly smoking at high school alongside a cool girl called Natalie, whom he desperately wanted to impress, despite his increasing suspicion that heterosexuality was not available to him. He’d overheard her mention Allen Ginsberg and asked what she was reading now. “It’s funny you should ask,” she replied. “I’m being just so completely transformed by Virginia Woolf.” Pretty soon, he was too.There are plenty of observations that feel like familiar territory when it comes to writers on writing, most of them of the “fail again, fail better” variety. But where Cunningham is most engaging, and in a much more offbeat way, is in his repeated depictions of himself – mostly younger, but not always – as a man anxious to fit in, to lay claim to experiences that are far more recherché, more daring, than he really is. His flair for pace is no hindrance, and the chapter that begins, with no prior ground-laying, “During my senior year at Stanford, I started going to San Francisco on weekends to work as a rent boy” is a brilliant evocation of bravado, precarity and pathos.So, too, are the episodes and people about whom he won’t write: his beloved sister, for instance, or – beyond a series of respectful vignettes – an elderly and gracious gay couple who befriended him when he briefly lived in Provincetown, who fed him delicious dinners and gasped delightedly in mock horror at his mildly exaggerated tales of sexual abandon. After their deaths, he wonders about the extent to which they had chosen their lives, or whether they had adapted to what, at the time, society would allow them to have. It’s a few pages, but so touching, so unsentimental, so enlarging a view of these two incidental men that you feel sure that Cunningham made the right choice, all those years ago, when he shelved the gold pasta cigar box.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
