title: Add to playlist: the ramshackle, soulful twang of Twisted Teens and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: The New Orleans country-punk duo are on a hot streak, about to release their third album in a year, and the crunchy, literate hooks keep coming
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: The New Orleans country-punk duo are on a hot streak, about to release their third album in a year, and the crunchy, literate hooks keep coming
Content: Twisted Teens, a ragtag, deeply charismatic band from Louisiana.Photograph: Bobbi RichView image in fullscreenTwisted Teens, a ragtag, deeply charismatic band from Louisiana.Photograph: Bobbi RichAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the ramshackle, soulful twang of Twisted Teens and the week’s best new tracksThe New Orleans  country-punk duo are on a hot streak, about to release their third album in a year, and the crunchy, literate hooks keep comingShaad D'Souza,Ben Beaumont-Thomas,Claudia EfeminiandLaura SnapesFri 24 Jul 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromNew OrleansRecommended if you likeParquet Courts, Sheer Mag, Royal HeadacheUp nextHoly Cross Tigers out later this yearNot one but two of the year’s best albums so far are authored by a ragtag, deeply charismatic band from Louisiana named Twisted Teens, who bear Pynchonian names – Caspian Hollywell and RJ “Razor Ramone” Santos – a console steel guitar and, in Hollywell’s case, one of rock’s greatest, most soulful voices in many years. Virtuosic when it counts, ramshackle when necessary, Twisted Teens feel like they could slot nicely on to a bill with Parquet Courts and the late, greatRoyal Headache– crunchy, literary rock bands who seemed to shyly conceal their music’s anthemic nature.Twisted Teens broke through earlier this year with their second album Blame the Clown, a set of 12 country-punk tracks that’s hooky and effusive enough to give any major-label pop record released this year a run for its money. A couple of weeks ago, they released its followup, the rangier and slightly more introspective Florida Water Blues, and before the year’s out they’ll have dropped Holy Cross Tigers, a release schedule befitting a band on a hot streak.The pair’s origin story is foggy – the most one can glean from interviews is “they were neighbours, then Santos travelled cross-country to buy a steel guitar” – which feels appropriate for this kind of grimy, mythic music, which is raw and self-consciously handmade. Part of that feeling can be put down to Hollywell’s voice, a gritty and pockmarked thing which he uses to great effect, interspersing deadpan meditations on life and love with a rich, almighty howl that’s ostentatious but unpretentious. In other words, Twisted Teens are two of 2026’s true originals – a breakout band whose kooky, ultra-clarified vision outstrips the hype.Shaad D’SouzaThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenClub-ready … John Glacier.Photograph: Ayanna AllenJohn Glacier – Bond GirlThe peerless UK MC’s most club-ready cut to date: a hip-house track with a Detroit-ish bassline, topped with Glacier airily pronouncing her fashion bona fides.BBTJeffrey Silverstein–Portland WorksSilverstein was raised in New Jersey, based in the Pacific Northwest and, here, inspired by a Sheffield factory – yet this radiant cosmic Americana smear of pedal steel, acoustic and honeyed synths exudes pure wild west.LSProtomartyr – Sounds We Cannot HearWith a central riff like a siren sounding through a hurricane of hail, this is an enormous return for the Detroit post-punks, who as usual get to the heart of today’s ennui and horror.BBTNamesblissxPaul Stephan–Run ItThe two London MCs engage in a back and forth of fluid flows on brotherhood, faith and dreams, over a stuttering, saxophone-laced beat by producer T.o.CEMurex–Flock of Swans Fly inV’sFrom her thrillingly innovative debut album, the Swedish artist offers the delightful vision of sprites playing hide-and-seek around a glitching harp.LSChad Hugo–Jumpupw!nya (ftTierra Whack and Leikeli47)The non-Pharrell half of the Neptunes brings every ounce of his considerable production nous and sense of funk to these aerobic breakbeats, with both guest MCs on equally oxygenated form.BBTCole Pulice – The Limits of the FrameEven when deconstructing their trademark sax – this track was somehow made without using the mouthpiece or breath – Pulice makes reliably soothing, detail-laden sound miasmas to take a moment in.LSSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Zarabanda Variations review – free jazz project is a thrillingly original dive into colonial history | Music | The Guardian
description: US composer Keir GoGwilt’s collaborative album uses poetry and atonal music to trace the roots of Spain’s sarabande dance: a fascinating listen, though not easy
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: US composer Keir GoGwilt’s collaborative album uses poetry and atonal music to trace the roots of Spain’s sarabande dance: a fascinating listen, though not easy
Content: Singer Mariana Flores Bucio, who features on The Zarabanda Variations.Photograph: Lawrence SumulongView image in fullscreenSinger Mariana Flores Bucio, who features on The Zarabanda Variations.Photograph: Lawrence SumulongGlobal album of the monthMusicReviewThe Zarabanda Variations review – free jazz project is a thrillingly original dive into colonial history(Carrier)US composer Keir GoGwilt’s collaborative album uses poetry and atonal music to trace the roots of Spain’s sarabande dance: a fascinating listen, though not easyAmmar KaliaFri 24 Jul 2026 03.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 20.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClassical music aficionados will be familiar with the stately form of the sarabande – a Spanish dance adopted into a languorous and tender musical style favoured by baroque composers such as Bach and Handel. For American composer Keir GoGwilt, however, the sarabande contains something far more radical. On his collaborative project The Zarabanda Variations, he enlists a 10-piece ensemble that combines free jazz with baroque strings and spoken-word poetry to delve into the colonial Latin American roots of the dance before it was popularised in 17th and 18th-century Spain.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for The Zarabanda Variations.On first listen, it’s hard to hear how this music could relate to the classical sarabande at all. Scrapes of atonal strings, clattering percussion, guttural vocalisations and sharp whistles create a cacophony of tension throughout, as if mirroring the passionate, whirling energy supposedly contained in the original forms of the dance. In fact, rather than creating a baroque sarabande fusion, GoGwilt’s compositions embrace its lesser-known historical references to produce something entirely new.The wonky metre of Matachín alludes to the contemporaneous Spanish carnival dance of the same name and embodies its riotous energy in Alec Goldfarb’s muscular, finger-picked jazz guitar, while Otra Llorona, composed by Vicente Atria, calls to the sarabande’s Mexican influences with yearning folk vocal melodies from singer Mariana Flores Bucio. Tonada Americana (also by Atria) is a highlight, combining the swaying rhythm of the 17th-century Hispanic dancetonadawith shards of frenetic atonal violin bowing that create a jolting sense of anticipation for a resolution that never arrives.This is by no means an easy album, with the several spoken-word interludes from poet Edgar Garcia often containing confounding references, but its instrumentation is virtuosic and its scope is remarkable. Through the strange reimagining of this courtly dance, GoGwilt uncovers depths to keep composers interested in the sarabande for generations to come.Also out this monthBrazilian-German duoCurió Curiórelease their self-titled debut album (Mr Bongo), blending the warm analogue sound of 70smúsica popular brasileirawith funk breakbeats, soulful horn fanfares and jazz improvisation. A retro pastiche that nonetheless engages thanks to its slick production values. A rare unearthing of 60s and 70s Malaysian jazz,Alfonso Soliano’sTiga Trombone(Audible Beauty) contains a tantalising insight into a psych-influenced improvisatory niche that drew on Malay influences as much as big band melodics. SingerSomireleases What Does It Take to Bloom? (Salon Africana), a charmingly breezy collection of classic deep-swinging jazz vocals that reaches a peak on the fierce Nina Simone references of So You Want to Be a Woman.This article was amended on 24 July 2026 to credit another composer on the Zarabanda Variations album, Vicente Atria.Explore more on these topicsMusicGlobal album of the monthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: John McCabe: Symphonies 2 & 3 and Cello Concerto album review – writing of enormous scope and colour | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The pianist and composer, who died in 2015, deserves a wider audience for the edgy, lucid soundworld of his compositions
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The pianist and composer, who died in 2015, deserves a wider audience for the edgy, lucid soundworld of his compositions
Content: Overdue recordings … conductor Kenneth Woods.Photograph: GlennRossView image in fullscreenOverdue recordings … conductor Kenneth Woods.Photograph: GlennRossClassical musicReviewJohn McCabe: Symphonies 2 & 3 and Cello Concerto album review – writing of enormous scope and colourBBCSSO/Woods/WallfischSignumThe late pianist and composer deserves a wider audience for the edgy, lucid soundworld of his compositionsErica JealFri 24 Jul 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn McCabe, who died in 2015, made some important recordings of other people’s music – he championed Carl Nielsen, and his survey of the complete Haydn piano sonatas has held its place in the Decca catalogue for half a century – but when it comes to his own works there are still gaps to be filled. Alongside the Symphony No 2, completed in 1971, the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra and the conductor Kenneth Woods here supply the overdue premiere recordings of McCabe’s 2007 cello concerto Songline and his 1978 Symphony No 3.View image in fullscreenJohn McCabe: Symphonies 2 & 3 and Cello Concerto.The Symphony No 2 is tense and edgy, musing on the cyclical nature of violence; the cello concerto, its title inspired by ancient Aboriginal pathways, is restless in a different, searching way, which the soloist Raphael Wallfisch captures eloquently. What is striking and gratifying about both is the lucidity of McCabe’s music, its textures remaining clearly defined through writing of enormous colour and scope. The Symphony No 3, Hommages, inhabits a lusher soundworld, densely weaving in nods to Haydn and Nielsen while also looking in other directions – one passage with muted strings and celeste could almost be Shostakovich reimagined by the Strauss of Der Rosenkavalier. Vividly energised and expressive throughout, the performances do all three works justice.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: ‘Full of zesty colour and flavour’: readers’ favourite food festivals in Europe | Food and drink | The Guardian
description: From the Tiramisù World Cup in Italy to street food ‘battles’ in Newcastle, your culinary highlights range from the sublime to the delicious
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From the Tiramisù World Cup in Italy to street food ‘battles’ in Newcastle, your culinary highlights range from the sublime to the delicious
Content: A sculpture made with lemons and oranges for the  Lemon Festival in Menton, France.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAView image in fullscreenA sculpture made with lemons and oranges for the  Lemon Festival in Menton, France.Photograph: Sébastien Nogier/EPAReaders' travel tipsFood and drink‘Full of zesty colour and flavour’: readers’ favourite food festivals in EuropeFrom the Tiramisù World Cup in Italy to street food ‘battles’ in Newcastle, your culinary highlights range from the sublime to the deliciousTell us abouta book that inspired you to travel– the best tip wins £200 towards a Coolstays breakGuardian readersFri 24 Jul 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 04.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSun and citrus in the south of FranceThe town ofMentonon the French Riviera is beautiful at any time of the year but becomes even more of a treat during the annualLemon festival(Fête du Citron, 10-28 February 2027). Its microclimate, courtesy of the Alps to the north blocking colder winds, gives Menton lemons a distinct fragrance, flavour and quality that set them apart. For me, the event transformed a damp cold UK winter into a fortnight of colour, taste and light. There were food tastings, salads made with lemons, tarts, cakes and pies all full of zesty colour and flavour at stalls and markets in the town. There are sculptures made from citrus fruit, parades and exhibitions in the Golden Garden of Light (Jardins Biovès). More than a food festival, it’s a celebration of what nature can give to the world.AprilVeneto’s Tiramisù World CupView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stefano Mazzola/Getty ImagesLast autumn, I discovered there is an annualTiramisù World Cup. I was staying in Treviso (the lovely town near Venice where the dessert originated) during the three-day event featuring tastings, demonstrations from local chefs and a judging contest involving the public. There’s also folk music in the streets, and restaurants offer promotional prices on set meals from about €20 for two courses. In fact, sitting in a mini gondola, prosecco in one hand, bowl of tiramisu in the other, gliding along a canal past ornate houses while the distant snow-capped mountains of the Dolomites sparkled in the sunshine, certainly aided my appetite for food and life.PeterProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.A cheeky celebration in TuscanyView image in fullscreenThe Gota Cotta festival takes place in the village of Colle di Val d’Elsa.Photograph: Silvan Bachmann/AlamyTheGota Cotta festivalin Tuscany (4 October) is a celebration of local meat – pork cheeks. It was a niche product, falling out of favour, but a group of local butchers created the festival to celebrate the local delicacy. It takes over the medieval hilltop town of Colle di Val d’Elsa in Siena province with stalls selling everything from pasta to gelato – all made with pork cheek. There’s also excellent wine and craft beers … all in the most beautiful setting.Rebecca NichollSwitzerland knows its onionsView image in fullscreenModels made from onions on display at the Bern onion fair.Photograph: Alistair Scott/AlamyI stumbled acrossZibelemärit, Bern’s annual onion fair, on a chilly November morning. The old town was packed with farmers selling beautifully braided onions, garlic and seasonal produce. The streets were filled with tempting aromas from stalls frying onion tarts and serving steaming bowls of onion soup and cafes selling sweet onion-shaped pastries. A mug of warmingglühwein was the perfect accompaniment. It was a wonderfully local event and chatting to growers about their harvest made me feel part of a genuine celebration of Swiss farming traditions. Zibelemärit takes place on the fourth Monday in November.SusannaThe Italian town devoted to leeksView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Lorenza photography/AlamyYou have to admire the town of Cervere in Piedmont, south of Turin, which is so devoted to its leeks that it has erected a permanent pavilion called the Palaporro (porrois Italian for leek) for its annual festival, calledFiera del Porro Cervere(7-22 November). Book ahead for the sit-down tasting menu, or buy leeky treats such as gratin and risotto to take away, as we did. During thesagra, the town centre is packed with stalls, many heaving with the distinctive bunches of extra-long local leeks. Our favourite part was taking a shuttle bus down to the sandy leek fields in the valley, where enthusiasts explained the traditional cultivation techniques.MarthaFarmers and brass bands in North YorkshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Wise/AlamyMalton is a little village in North Yorkshire that punches way above its size when it comes to food festivals. Theannual festivalis worth a visit in late spring (29-30 May 2027), but so are the monthly farmers’ markets that bring together incredible local suppliers and makers. Plus, there’s a good chance of hearing a top-class brass band while you mooch and taste. Bloomin’ marvellous!Bethskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNewcastle’s battle of the food vendorsView image in fullscreenThe Wylam BreweryPhotograph: Ben Hughes/Food BattlesWylam Brewery’s street vendor food battles in Newcastle upon Tyne showcase local independent eateries serving their bestselling dishes to win a chance at being crowned the culinary King of Newcastle at the finalBattle Royale(28 & 29 August). The competitions are wittily titled, for example Lord of the Wings for the chicken wings competition (23 & 24 October) and Argie Bhaji (27 & 28 November) for Indian street food. The concept is simple: each event offers different cuisines from pizza to pan-Asian to plant-based. The winner of each event is the vendor with the most pre-paid tokens. Set in the idyllicExhibition Park, with DJs playing into the night, locals know not to miss these summer festivals.Carly Bamborough‘A proper northern’ affair in BoltonPhotograph: Paul HeyesBolton food & drink festival(28-31 August) is brilliant because it feels properly northern: busy streets, good smells, live music and families everywhere. It is not trying to be too polished, which is why it works. You can wander from stall to stall, try something different, grab something sweet for the kids and still feel like you are part of the town. The best bit is the atmosphere. Chefs, local businesses, music and people all come together in one place. It is simple, affordable and full of energy. For a family day out, it is hard to beat.Nicholas PearceThe pride of PlymouthView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Roy Perring/AlamyPlymouth Flavour Fest, at the end of May each year, ranks among the finest food gatherings I’ve experienced anywhere. Boutique delicatessens form neat rows, with smartly dressed stallholders presenting produce with infectious pride. Pies, salamis, chillies, confectionery, preserves, hot food – all the good stuff laid out irresistibly. Take a cool bag and budget for things you never knew you needed. Plymouth’s Armada Way is perfect for the event, never claustrophobic when busy. A short stroll takes you to the Hoe, perfect for munching on a treat overlooking one of the finest harbours in the world. Good food brings out the best in people and, for a few hours at least, the world is put to rights.Grant Wyness‘Ireland’s culinary playground’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Valerie O’Sullivan/Visit IrelandEvery October, the charming fishing town of Dingle transforms into Ireland’s ultimate culinary playground. TheDingle food festival(2-4 October) brings more than 60 venues to life for the famous Taste Trail, where pubs, galleries and shopfronts serve up local seafood, artisan cheeses and much more. Add bustling market stalls, cookery masterclasses and workshops, live street music and a strong zero-waste ethos, and you’ve got a weekend that celebrates the best of Irish food, drink and hospitality, all with Irish small-town warmth.John O’KellyView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsFood and drinkReaders' travel tipsTop 10sEurope holidaysFood festivalsFestivalsUnited Kingdom holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Orange wine and mezcal mingle in this smoky, Georgian-inspired drink
Content: DakaDaka's Qvevri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenDakaDaka's Qvevri.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: DakaDaka’s qvevri – recipeOrange wine and mezcal mingle in this smoky, Georgian-inspired drinkJack PorterFri 24 Jul 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsmoky, refreshing highball inspired by Georgia’s amber wines andqvevriwinemaking tradition (large clay vessels buried underground for fermentation). The mezcal works beautifully with the wine, which traditionally has structure and tannin from extended skin contact in those qvevri, and with the hint of citrus. The result is a cocktail that feels ancient and modern at the same time.QvevriServes125ml mezcal– we useQuiquiriqui Espadín, but any will do75ml orange wine, or, if you can get hold of some, Georgian amber wine25mlCocchi Americano, or white vermouth10ml crème de cassis10ml Cointreau10ml simple 1:1 honey syrup5ml fresh lemon juiceSoda water, to top1 strip orange peel, to garnishFill a highball glass with ice, then measure in all the liquids bar the soda. Stir gently to combine, then top with a splash of soda water to taste and garnish with the orange peel (if you’re feeling really fancy, or you’re Georgian, use a strip oftklapi, or fruit leather, instead).Jack Porter,DakaDaka, London W1Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodWineEastern European food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for pineapple and mango paletas | Food | The Guardian
description: These bright, sharp Mexican iced treats are the perfect summer cooler – with a spiky kick
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: These bright, sharp Mexican iced treats are the perfect summer cooler – with a spiky kick
Content: Helen Goh's pineapple and mango paletas.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh's pineapple and mango paletas.Photograph: Rita Platts/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull.The sweet spotFoodHelen Goh’s recipe for pineapple and mango paletasThese bright, sharp Mexican iced treats are the perfect summer cooler – with a spiky kickHelen GohFri 24 Jul 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 24 Jul 2026 07.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first time I encounteredpaletasin Mexico, they felt strangely familiar. They reminded me of the iced treats of my Malaysian childhood: fruit-driven, brightly coloured and made less to indulge than to relieve the heat. What struck me most was the flavour logic shared by both countries, where sweetness is often enlivened with salt, chilli, tamarind or citrus, each sharpening the fruit in its own way and making it seem brighter, cooler and somehow more vivid. Paletas are rarely perfectly smooth; little pieces of fruit suspended in the ice give them texture and interest. These two paletas take different paths from the same base: pineapple – sharp, clean and bright with lime and ginger – and mango – sweeter, rounder and more indulgent, which I’ve spiked with chilli, lime and salt.Pineapple and mango paletasPaleta moulds are easy to find online and in many kitchenware shops, but if you don’t have them, small paper cups and wooden sticks work perfectly well, too.Prep10 minCook15 min, plus coolingFreeze6 hr+Makes10-12For the base syrup70g caster sugarFor the pineapple, lime and ginger paletas600g fresh pineapple flesh, cut into chunks, plus 70g finely diced into 5-7mm pieces1 quantity base syrup(see above)1 tbsp lime juice20g fresh ginger, finely gratedPinch of fine sea saltFor the mango and Tajín paletas500g ripe mango flesh, cut into chunks, plus 70g finely diced into 5–7mm pieces1 quantity base syrup(see above)1½ tbsp lime juiceSmall pinch of fine sea saltTajín or other chilli-lime seasoning, to serveTo make the base syrup, place the sugar and 70ml water into a small saucepan on a medium heat and stir until dissolved. Remove from the heat and cool completely.For the pineapple paletas, blend the pineapple chunks with the cooled syrup, lime juice, ginger and salt until very smooth. Taste – it should seem slightly brighter and sharper than you’d like, as freezing dulls flavour. Pour the fruit puree into the paleta moulds, leaving about 1cm space at the top. Drop a few pieces of the finely diced fruit into each mould, gently nudging them down with a skewer or teaspoon so they’re suspended throughout the mixture. Tap the moulds lightly on the bench to remove air bubbles, then insert sticks and freeze for at least six hours or overnight. To unmould, briefly run the moulds under warm water.For the mango paletas, blend the mango chunks with the cooled syrup, lime juice and salt until smooth. Taste and adjust if needed: mangoes vary enormously in sweetness and acidity, so you may wish to add extra lime. Drop a few pieces of the diced fruit into each mould, gently nudging them down with a skewer or teaspoon so they are suspended throughout the mixture. Freeze and unmould as above. Sprinkle the Tajín over the mango paletas just before serving; this keeps the flavours bright and distinct.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotFruitMexican food and drinkBakingrecipesShareReuse this content
